title: Beyond Raw Transcripts: Structured Persona Extraction for LLM-Based Digital Twins
summary:
LLM-based "digital twins" aim to simulate how an individual would behavein new environments or respond to novel questions, given some representation of that individual's prior responses. A common approach constructs this representation from survey transcripts or summaries responses. Prior work shows that compressing long transcripts into shorter LLM-generated summaries does not significantly reduce predictive accuracy, suggesting that information volume is not the primary bottleneck.
  In this work, we argue that the key limitation is instead structural:how persona information is organized before being provided to thesimulator model. We study this by comparing unstructured summaries with structured persona representations. First, we introduce a hand-craftedschema (BDE: Background, Decision procedure, Evaluation), grounded in consumer-behavior theory, and show that it improves predictive accuracy over raw transcripts by +1.91 percentage points on a homogeneous benchmark (Twin-2K-500), with similar gains on gpt-5.4-mini and Qwen3-8B as robustness checks. However, this fixed structure does not generalizeacross more heterogeneous tasks, where performance is statistically indistinguishable from the raw transcript baseline.
  To address this limitation, we propose an automatic structure-discovery pipeline in which an LLM iteratively proposes and refines task-specific persona structures and extraction prompts. On a benchmark of 13 diverse sub-studies, this approach restores performance, improving mean accuracy by +1.91 percentage points over the raw transcript baseline and eliminating significant losses observed with the fixed schema.
  Overall, our results suggest that the main constraint in LLM-based digital twins is not how much information is provided, but how it is structured -- and that the optimal structure depends on the task.

AI.tldr: The paper studies LLM-based digital twins and argues that the main performance bottleneck is the structure of persona information, not the amount. It shows that both a hand-crafted schema and an automatically discovered, task-specific schema can improve predictive accuracy over raw transcripts, with the automatic method generalizing better across heterogeneous tasks.
AI.motivation: LLM-based digital twins try to predict how specific individuals will behave in new situations using prior survey data. Earlier work suggested that compressing transcripts into summaries does not hurt performance, so the authors question what actually limits accuracy. They hypothesize that the organization (structure) of persona information given to the simulator model matters more than sheer information volume, and set out to test and exploit this idea.
AI.method: The authors compare different ways of representing a person's data before feeding it to an LLM simulator. They first design a hand-crafted persona schema called BDE (Background, Decision procedure, Evaluation) inspired by consumer-behavior theory and evaluate it against raw transcripts and unstructured summaries on a homogeneous benchmark (Twin-2K-500), checking robustness across multiple LLMs. Observing that the fixed schema does not generalize to heterogeneous tasks, they then develop an automatic structure-discovery pipeline in which an LLM iteratively proposes, refines, and applies task-specific persona schemas and extraction prompts. They test this pipeline on a benchmark of 13 diverse sub-studies.
AI.result: On the homogeneous Twin-2K-500 benchmark, the BDE structured schema improves predictive accuracy over raw transcripts by +1.91 percentage points, with similar gains for different base LLMs (gpt-5.4-mini, Qwen3-8B). However, for more heterogeneous tasks, BDE does not significantly outperform raw transcripts. The automatic structure-discovery pipeline recovers and improves performance on a 13-sub-study benchmark, achieving a mean accuracy increase of +1.91 percentage points relative to raw transcripts and eliminating the significant performance drops seen with the fixed BDE schema on those varied tasks.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that the core limitation in current LLM-based digital twins is not the volume of persona information supplied but its structural organization. Fixed, theory-driven schemas can help in homogeneous settings but fail to generalize broadly. In contrast, automatically discovered, task-specific persona structures enable consistent performance gains across diverse tasks. Therefore, effective digital twins require adaptive structuring of persona information tailored to the downstream prediction task.

title: When Vocabulary Comprehension Fails Clinical Reasoning: Evaluating Therapy Bots' Safety Risks for Generation Alpha
comment: 42 pages, 6 figures. Accepted at ACM FAccT '26
summary: Conversational AI systems have become informal mental health support resources for Generation Alpha (Gen Alpha, born 2010-2024), with 13.1% of U.S. adolescents (5.4 million) using generative AI for mental health advice. While these systems, from therapy apps to general chatbots, rely on large language models trained on extensive psychological literature, their safety for youth communication patterns characterized by hyperbolic language, ironic positivity, rapid semantic drift, and contextual polysemy remains unvalidated. Following multiple adolescent deaths linked to AI chatbot interactions, systematic evaluation is critical. We present two benchmarks: (1) 64 Gen Alpha mental health expressions validated by native speakers (ICC=0.72) and clinicians (kappa=0.78); (2) 75 multi-turn conversations (780 turns) with paired Standard/Gen Alpha versions. Across evaluations of LLM architectures underlying therapy apps and general chatbots - Claude, GPT-4o, Llama-3.1 - models understand 76-82% of vocabulary but correctly calibrate only 64-72% of clinical risk, creating a 10-14 percentage point (pp) vocabulary-comprehension gap (p<.001, d>0.48) absent in human therapists (3pp, p=.22). The gap is architecturally consistent and widens with ambiguity (7pp -> 18pp). We identify six failure patterns: sarcasm masking (29pp), minimization acceptance (43pp), informal style bias (24pp), risk-stratified ambiguity (19pp), semantic drift (19pp), context-dependent violence (7pp). Patterns compound; three or more yield 94% miss rates. Lightweight mitigations fail; only heavy scaffolding achieves human performance (6.4x cost). With 34% baseline miss rate yielding 146,880 estimated annual missed crises, we recommend mandatory human-in-the-loop architectures, quarterly youth-specific validation, transparent performance disclosure, and regulatory frameworks for youth-facing mental health AI.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how well large language model–based conversational AI systems recognize and respond to Gen Alpha–style mental health expressions, finding substantial safety gaps compared to human therapists and calling for stronger oversight and human-in-the-loop designs.
AI.motivation: Gen Alpha increasingly uses conversational AI (from therapy apps to general chatbots) as informal mental health support, with millions of adolescents seeking advice from generative AI. These systems are trained on psychological literature but have not been validated for youth communication patterns, which often include hyperbole, irony, rapid topic shifts, and context-dependent meanings. Reports of adolescent deaths associated with AI chatbot interactions heighten concerns, motivating a systematic, youth-specific safety evaluation of current LLM-based mental health tools.
AI.method: The authors construct two benchmarks: (1) a set of 64 Gen Alpha mental health expressions, validated by both native speakers (for linguistic authenticity, ICC=0.72) and clinicians (for clinical interpretation, kappa=0.78); and (2) a collection of 75 multi-turn conversations (780 turns), each with paired Standard English and Gen Alpha–style versions. They then test multiple LLM architectures used in therapy apps and general chatbots (including Claude, GPT-4o, and Llama-3.1) on these benchmarks. They measure vocabulary understanding and clinical risk calibration, compare model performance to human therapists, analyze how ambiguity affects errors, and identify recurrent failure patterns. They also experiment with different mitigation strategies such as lightweight prompts vs. heavier scaffolding.
AI.result: LLMs understand most Gen Alpha vocabulary (76–82%), but their correct clinical risk calibration is lower (64–72%), revealing a 10–14 percentage point gap between lexical understanding and accurate clinical interpretation (statistically significant with p<.001 and effect sizes d>0.48). Human therapists do not show this gap (3pp, p=.22). The gap is consistent across architectures and grows with ambiguity from 7pp to 18pp. The authors catalog six recurrent failure patterns with sizable performance penalties: sarcasm masking (29pp gap), minimization acceptance (43pp), informal style bias (24pp), risk-stratified ambiguity (19pp), semantic drift (19pp), and context-dependent violence (7pp). When three or more of these patterns co-occur, miss rates reach 94%. Simple, low-cost mitigations are ineffective; only intensive scaffolding brings performance up to human levels, but at 6.4 times the cost. Based on a 34% baseline miss rate, they estimate about 146,880 mental health crises per year could be missed by such systems.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM-based conversational systems, including those embedded in mental health apps and general-purpose chatbots, are not reliably safe for Gen Alpha mental health use. Despite seemingly good vocabulary comprehension, they frequently misjudge clinical risk, especially under ambiguous, ironic, or stylistically informal youth communication. These failures are systematic and compound, and cannot be remedied by light-touch prompt engineering alone; achieving human-level safety requires heavy scaffolding that significantly increases cost. The authors advocate for mandatory human-in-the-loop architectures for youth mental health AI, regular youth-specific validation (e.g., quarterly), transparent reporting of system performance on such benchmarks, and development of regulatory frameworks governing youth-facing mental health AI tools.

title: Building and Evaluating a Synthetic Bengali Speech Resource for Telecom Customer Care
summary: Speech systems used in customer-facing applications often require domain-specific language coverage. We present a synthetic Bengali speech dataset for telecom customer-care scenarios. The dataset contains 10,000 audio-text pairs, approximately 26.82 hours of 24 kHz speech, and predefined train, validation, and test splits of 9,000, 500, and 500 examples. It is publicly released on Hugging Face under the CC-BY-4.0 license. The speech was generated with OmniVoice in voice-cloning mode using a real female reference recording and transcript, with bfloat16 precision, 16 diffusion sampling steps, and a speaking-rate control value of 1.0. Along with the original Bengali text, the dataset provides a normalized transcript field designed for ASR/STT training and evaluation. We report an automatic intelligibility check over all 10,000 samples using a domain-adapted Whisper ASR model fine-tuned from bengaliAI/tugstugi_bengaliai-regional-asr_whisper-medium, along with a manual listening check on selected samples. The evaluation gives an average WER of 2.54%, an average CER of 0.59%, and median WER and CER values of 0.00%. These results suggest strong text-audio consistency under the selected automatic evaluation pipeline, while the paper also discusses the limitations of synthetic speech and STT-based evaluation.

AI.tldr: They introduce and release a synthetic Bengali telecom customer-care speech dataset and show it has very low text-audio mismatch under an ASR-based evaluation.
AI.motivation: Customer-facing speech systems, such as those used in telecom customer care, need good coverage of domain-specific language. For low-resource languages like Bengali, real recorded data in specific domains is scarce and expensive to collect. The authors aim to fill this gap by creating and releasing a synthetic speech dataset tailored to telecom customer-care scenarios so that ASR and related systems can be trained and evaluated more effectively.
AI.method: They generated synthetic Bengali speech using OmniVoice in voice-cloning mode, based on a real female reference recording and transcript. The audio is 24 kHz and produced with specific model settings: bfloat16 precision, 16 diffusion sampling steps, and speaking-rate control of 1.0. They created 10,000 audio-text pairs (≈26.82 hours) and split them into train/validation/test sets (9,000/500/500). In addition to the original Bengali text, they prepared a normalized transcript field suitable for ASR/STT tasks. To evaluate text-audio consistency, they used a domain-adapted Whisper ASR model fine-tuned from bengaliAI/tugstugi_bengaliai-regional-asr_whisper-medium to automatically transcribe the synthetic audio and compute WER and CER. They complemented this with manual listening checks on selected samples.
AI.result: The resulting dataset, released on Hugging Face under a CC-BY-4.0 license, consists of 10,000 synthetic Bengali telecom customer-care utterances totaling about 26.82 hours of 24 kHz speech with predefined splits. Automatic intelligibility and consistency evaluation using the adapted Whisper ASR model yields a low average word error rate of 2.54% and character error rate of 0.59%, with median WER and CER both at 0.00%. Manual spot checks corroborate that most audio is consistent with the given text.
AI.conclusion: The dataset exhibits very high text-audio consistency as measured by an ASR-based evaluation pipeline, making it a promising resource for training and benchmarking Bengali ASR/STT systems in telecom customer-care settings. However, the authors acknowledge inherent limitations of synthetic speech (e.g., potential lack of natural variability) and of relying on STT-based metrics for quality assessment, so users should be cautious when generalizing performance from this dataset to real-world speech.

title: Who Do Language Models Think Is Competent? A Mechanistic Analysis of Occupational Bias
summary: Language models (LMs) often pass behavioral bias evaluations, but it remains unclear whether they no longer represent the underlying associations that give rise to biases, or have merely learned not to express them. In this study, we show that representational biases are often detectable, even when behavioral biases are not visible. We introduce a causal framework that decomposes occupational bias into two measurement points: a model's internal representation of a user's competence, and its observable outputs. We derive steering vectors for representations of user expertise, and verify that they causally mediate model behavior in both a question-answering task and a hiring task. Applying this framework to several open-weight models, we find that demographic attributes, such as gender, race, and socioeconomic status, influence a model's representation of user expertise, even in cases where behavioral metrics detect no disparity between demographics. We show that these model representations can influence downstream behavior under intervention, suggesting failure modes that behavioral metrics alone may not detect.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that language models can still internally encode demographic biases even when their outputs appear unbiased, by decomposing bias into internal representations and observable behavior using a causal framework.
AI.motivation: Although language models may pass standard behavioral bias tests, it is unclear whether this means they no longer harbor biased associations or have simply learned to hide them. Existing evaluations mostly focus on model outputs, potentially missing latent forms of bias that reside in internal representations and could surface under different conditions or interventions. There is a need for methods that can detect and reason about these hidden representational biases and connect them causally to model behavior.
AI.method: The authors propose a causal framework that splits occupational bias into two stages: (1) how the model internally represents a user's competence, and (2) how this representation affects observable outputs. They construct and validate "steering vectors" that capture latent representations of user expertise inside the model. Then, they use causal mediation analysis: they test whether intervening on these internal representations changes model behavior in controlled tasks, such as question-answering and hiring evaluations. They apply this approach to several open-weight language models and examine how demographic information (gender, race, socioeconomic status) affects the inferred expertise representations.
AI.result: The study finds that language models' internal representations of user expertise are systematically influenced by demographic attributes, even when standard behavioral bias metrics show little or no difference across demographic groups. The derived steering vectors for user expertise meaningfully and causally mediate model behavior in both QA and hiring tasks: manipulating these vectors changes the model’s decisions and responses in ways consistent with altered perceptions of user competence. This demonstrates that models can encode demographic biases in their internal states that do not necessarily manifest in simple output-based tests, but can affect downstream behavior when those states are perturbed or relied upon more heavily.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that passing behavioral bias evaluations does not guarantee that a language model is free of harmful or stereotyped internal associations. Their causal framework reveals representational biases linked to demographic attributes that can influence downstream decisions, indicating important failure modes that are invisible to behavioral metrics alone. Therefore, robust bias assessment for language models must analyze both internal representations and observable outputs, and consider causal pathways by which latent biases can affect behavior under different conditions or interventions.

title: SDAD: Spec-Driven Agentic Development for the AI-Native SDLC
summary: Frontier coding agents backed by large language models with context windows from hundreds of thousands to millions of tokens are restructuring the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). Rich context handling and multi-step reasoning now allow substantial Functional Requirement Documents (FRDs) and repository context to be ingested in a single workflow, making specification quality the execution fuel for autonomous delivery. This report formalises Spec-Driven Agentic Development (SDAD) as a synthesis of disciplined up-front formalisation and high-velocity implementation: intent capture, machine-readable specification, agentic synthesis, and independent multi-agent verification under human sign-off. We revisit the historical pendulum between Waterfall and Agile, introduce AI-code as a fourth production paradigm, and compare Human-Agile (circa 2020) with Agentic-SDAD (circa 2026) across artefacts, cadence, accountability, and security posture. Beyond process description, we extend the model to team role metamorphosis (engineer, QA, platform, and product functions), quantitative governance (Ambiguity Tax, Spec Fidelity, SER, and TCI_agentic with repair multiplier phi), and pragmatic adoption via hybrid estimation and a staged migration blueprint. Industrial and research evidence on AI-augmented testing and verification is integrated to motivate separation between synthesis and release authority. Overall, the paper argues that agentic speed does not eliminate engineering discipline; it relocates discipline upstream into specification precision, explicit gates, and auditable provenance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Spec-Driven Agentic Development (SDAD), a model for using large-context LLM-based coding agents to transform the software development lifecycle by shifting discipline and control into precise up-front specifications and independent verification.
AI.motivation: With LLM coding agents gaining massive context windows and stronger reasoning, they can ingest large specifications and codebases in a single workflow. This disrupts traditional Agile and Waterfall practices but also creates risks around quality, security, and accountability. The authors aim to provide a coherent, disciplined framework—SDAD—that explains how to harness agentic speed without losing engineering rigor, clarifies how roles and processes should change, and proposes quantitative governance metrics for managing these new workflows.
AI.method: Conceptual and framework-building: (1) Formalise a new process model called Spec-Driven Agentic Development, structured around intent capture, machine-readable specifications, agentic synthesis, and multi-agent verification with human sign-off. (2) Historically situate SDAD relative to Waterfall, Agile, and three prior software production paradigms, defining AI-code as a fourth. (3) Compare Human-Agile (circa 2020) and Agentic-SDAD (circa 2026) along multiple dimensions (artefacts, cadence, accountability, security). (4) Extend the framework to team role changes and introduce new quantitative governance metrics (Ambiguity Tax, Spec Fidelity, SER, TCI_agentic with a repair multiplier φ). (5) Propose a staged migration and hybrid estimation approach for practical adoption. (6) Integrate industrial and research evidence on AI-augmented testing and verification to argue for separation between code synthesis authority and release authority.
AI.result: The paper yields: (1) A formal SDAD process model tailored to LLM-based coding agents with large context windows. (2) A taxonomy and comparison of production paradigms, showing how AI-code production differs from prior methods. (3) Defined organisational roles and their metamorphosis in an agentic setting (engineer, QA, platform, product). (4) A set of governance metrics—Ambiguity Tax, Spec Fidelity, SER, and TCI_agentic with repair multiplier φ—to quantify and manage specification quality, agent performance, and risk. (5) A staged migration blueprint and hybrid estimation strategy for gradually adopting SDAD in real organisations. (6) An evidence-backed argument for splitting synthesis from release decisions to ensure safety and reliability.
AI.conclusion: Large-context LLM coding agents enable highly autonomous software development but do not obviate the need for engineering discipline. Instead, discipline must move upstream into precise, machine-readable specifications, explicit process gates, and robust provenance and verification. Spec-Driven Agentic Development offers a structured way to combine up-front formalisation with high-velocity agentic implementation, redefining roles, metrics, and governance so organisations can capture agentic speed while maintaining safety, accountability, and quality.

title: Inhibitory Attention for Clinical Long-Context Reasoning: Characterizing and Mitigating Lost-in-the-Middle Effects in EHR Processing
summary: Electronic health records now routinely exceed 100,000 tokens per patient. Yet large language models exhibit the lost-in-the-middle (LitM) effect: information near the center of a long context is retrieved less reliably than information near the edges. In clinical use this is not benign: the single most consequential fact in a note can sit at its center. We term this the clinical lost-in-the-middle (CLitM) problem, give its first systematic characterization using MedAlign, and compare context-selection strategies as remedies. Across 2,196 instruction-response pairs and six language models, we observe a 21.9 percentage-point gap between peak accuracy (59.5%, 95% CI [46.3, 71.0], 20-30% decile) and trough accuracy (37.6% [23.2, 52.5] at 70-80%); 67.8% of reference answers fall between the 10th and 90th percentiles of the EHR timeline, inside the CLitM trough. We introduce Query-Conditioned Clinical Suppression (QCCS), a lightweight query-conditioned selection gate, and evaluate it against BM25, BM25 with section-header filtering, dense retrieval, and cross-encoder reranking (N=83 held-out instructions). With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (16k context), QCCS outperforms all five comparators under LLM-as-judge scoring: for middle-position instructions QCCS reaches 16.7% versus BM25 3.3%, cross-encoder 0.0%, dense 0.0%, and full context 6.7%; overall QCCS reaches 25.3% versus at most 3.6% for retrieval-only comparators. This advantage is not explained by retrieval recall: at k=20, BM25 retrieves the gold evidence sentence in 98.8% of instructions (QCCS 34.9%), yet retrieval arms stay at most 2.6% accurate even when they retrieve it, whereas QCCS reaches 25.0% even when it does not. In this proof-of-concept evaluation, query-aligned context selection predicts EHR instruction-following accuracy better than gold-sentence retrieval recall.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies and addresses a “clinical lost-in-the-middle” problem: key information in the middle of very long electronic health records is underused by LLMs, and proposes a query-conditioned context selection method that improves clinical instruction-following more than traditional retrieval-based methods.
AI.motivation: Electronic health records (EHRs) are extremely long—often over 100,000 tokens—while current large language models suffer from a lost-in-the-middle (LitM) effect, where information in the middle of a long context is less reliably used than information at the beginning or end. In clinical practice, crucial facts can be located in the middle of notes, so this failure mode can have serious consequences. The authors aim to systematically characterize this clinical lost-in-the-middle (CLitM) phenomenon, quantify its impact on clinical question answering over EHRs, and explore whether better context-selection strategies can mitigate it.
AI.method: The authors (1) define and measure the clinical lost-in-the-middle (CLitM) effect using the MedAlign dataset, analyzing performance across 2,196 instruction–response pairs and six different LLMs as a function of where in the EHR timeline the needed evidence falls. They compute accuracy decile-wise along the EHR token timeline. (2) They propose Query-Conditioned Clinical Suppression (QCCS), a lightweight query-conditioned selection gate that decides which parts of the EHR to pass to the LLM. (3) They compare QCCS against several retrieval baselines: BM25, BM25 with section-header filtering, dense retrieval, and cross-encoder reranking. Using a held-out set of 83 instructions, they evaluate accuracy under an LLM-as-judge setup, with specific attention to performance when evidence lies in the middle of the context and at different k values for retrieval recall.
AI.result: They observe a substantial CLitM effect: across the 2,196 pairs and six models, there is a 21.9 percentage-point gap between peak accuracy (59.5% at the 20–30% position of the EHR timeline) and a trough (37.6% at the 70–80% position). Notably, 67.8% of gold reference answers occur between the 10th and 90th percentiles of the EHR timeline, right within this trough. For mitigation, their proposed QCCS method, evaluated with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (16k context), outperforms five comparator strategies under LLM-as-judge scoring. For mid-position instructions, QCCS obtains 16.7% accuracy compared to BM25’s 3.3%, cross-encoder’s 0.0%, dense retrieval’s 0.0%, and full-context’s 6.7%. Overall, QCCS achieves 25.3% accuracy, while retrieval-only comparators reach at most 3.6%. Interestingly, BM25 achieves very high retrieval recall of the gold evidence sentence at k=20 (98.8% vs QCCS’s 34.9%), but retrieval-based systems still remain at or below 2.6% accuracy even when they successfully retrieve the gold sentence. In contrast, QCCS reaches 25.0% accuracy even on cases where it does not retrieve the exact gold evidence sentence.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that large language models display a pronounced clinical lost-in-the-middle effect over long EHR contexts, and that naive full-context or standard retrieval strategies do not adequately address it. A simple query-conditioned context selection mechanism (QCCS) can substantially improve instruction-following performance in this setting, outperforming stronger retrieval methods even when those methods have near-perfect evidence recall. The findings suggest that query alignment and how information is presented to the model can matter more than merely ensuring that the gold evidence is somewhere in the retrieved text, and motivate further research into query-aware context shaping for long clinical documents.

title: PrimeAgentOrchestrator: Memory-Primed Agent Spawning for Personal AI Infrastructure
summary: Large language model (LLM) coding agents start each session with an empty context window, discarding accumulated knowledge from prior work. We present PrimeAgentOrchestrator (PAO), a system that spawns new instances of Claude Code -- Anthropic's terminal-based coding agent -- pre-loaded with relevant memories compiled from the user's existing personal databases. At spawn time, PAO queries two independently-operated memory backends in parallel (a PostgreSQL entity-observation database and a Cloudflare Worker semantic search index), fuses results using backend-specific retrieval strategies, and delivers the compiled briefing via filesystem injection that exploits the host agent's configuration auto-read behavior. PAO manages the full agent lifecycle including trust pre-seeding, readiness polling with error detection, and adaptive terminal text injection. We report on four months of regular deployment (December 2025 through March 2026) as an experience report, documenting three generations of context delivery mechanisms, the failure modes that motivated each redesign, and the engineering tradeoffs of bridging heterogeneous memory systems rather than building a unified one.

AI.tldr: They built a system (PAO) that automatically launches coding agents pre-loaded with personalized, retrieved memories from multiple backends, and they report engineering lessons from several months of use.
AI.motivation: LLM coding agents lose all session context when a new session starts, wasting prior work and user-specific knowledge stored elsewhere. The authors want a practical way to reuse a user’s existing personal and project data every time a coding agent is spawned, without manually pasting context and without rebuilding all memory into one monolithic system.
AI.method: They design PrimeAgentOrchestrator (PAO), which orchestrates new instances of Claude Code. At agent spawn time, PAO queries two separate memory systems in parallel: (1) a PostgreSQL database storing entity–observation records and (2) a Cloudflare Worker that exposes a semantic search index. PAO applies backend-specific retrieval / fusion logic, merges the results into a coherent “briefing,” and injects this briefing into the agent via filesystem-based configuration auto-load. It also manages the agent lifecycle end-to-end, including trust pre-seeding, readiness checks with error detection, and adaptive terminal text injection. They then run PAO for four months and iteratively evolve its context-delivery mechanism across three generations, each addressing discovered failure modes.
AI.result: They successfully deployed PAO in regular use over four months, evolving through three designs for context delivery. They identified concrete failure modes in each design (e.g., reliability issues, injection fragility, limitations of early fusion strategies) and refined the orchestrator, retrieval, and injection mechanisms accordingly. The system demonstrated that heterogeneous memory backends can be practically bridged at orchestration time to provide richer, personalized context to coding agents.
AI.conclusion: PAO shows that spawning coding agents with pre-fetched, personalized memories from multiple independent backends is feasible and useful in real-world workflows. Instead of building a single unified memory store, an orchestrator can bridge heterogeneous systems and handle lifecycle management, retrieval fusion, and robust context injection. The experience report emphasizes the tradeoffs and engineering challenges of this approach and offers design lessons for future context orchestration systems for LLM-based agents.

title: Beyond Prompt Engineering: A Systematic Analysis of Prompt Lexical Sensitivity and Its Impacts on Quality
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit extreme sensitivity to surface-level prompt variations, in which minor lexical changes can trigger disproportionate performance fluctuations. Moving beyond black-box optimization and coarse-grained templates, we present the first large-scale, n-gram token-level mechanistic analysis of prompt stability, leveraging a dataset of 132,000 prompt variants. Our investigation reveals a fundamental Scaling Law of Prompt Performance Stability: higher average task performance is strongly associated with lower variance and greater robustness across prompt perturbation. We identify two core linguistic drivers underlying this robustness: (1) Domain-Specific Terminology, which tightly anchors semantic boundaries, and (2) Explicit Action Directives, which formalize reasoning trajectories. Together, these elements constrain the model's interpretative space, effectively ``locking in'' more deterministic generation behavior. Building on these insights, we introduce an automated Prompt-Refining Agent that systematically restructures input queries by injecting domain anchoring and operational constraints. Empirical evaluation shows that our approach reduces performance variance by 40.7% in code generation task, while preserving or improving mean performance. These findings provide a statistically grounded and mechanistically interpretable framework for achieving robust prompt engineering.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes why some prompts for LLMs are more stable than others and shows that prompts with domain-specific terms and clear action directives are more robust, then uses this to build an automatic prompt-refining agent.
AI.motivation: LLMs are extremely sensitive to small, superficial changes in prompts, which can cause large swings in performance. Existing approaches mostly treat prompting as black-box optimization or rely on coarse templates, without mechanistic understanding of what makes prompts robust. The paper aims to systematically and quantitatively understand the linguistic and structural factors that make prompts stable and to derive practical methods for more robust prompt engineering.
AI.method: The authors conduct a large-scale mechanistic analysis using 132,000 prompt variants, performing n-gram token-level analysis to study how small lexical variations affect LLM performance. They identify correlations between prompt features and performance variance, discovering a scaling law between average performance and stability. Based on two key linguistic components—domain-specific terminology and explicit action directives—they design an automated Prompt-Refining Agent that rewrites user queries by adding domain anchoring and operational constraints. They then empirically evaluate this agent, particularly on code generation tasks, measuring changes in performance mean and variance.
AI.result: The analysis reveals a Scaling Law of Prompt Performance Stability: prompts that yield higher average task performance also tend to have lower variance and greater robustness to perturbations. The study identifies domain-specific terminology and explicit action directives as main contributors to this robustness by constraining the model’s interpretive space. The proposed Prompt-Refining Agent, which injects these elements into prompts, reduces performance variance by 40.7% in code generation tasks while keeping mean performance the same or better.
AI.conclusion: Prompt robustness is not arbitrary but follows a predictable scaling law: better-performing prompts are also more stable. Linguistic features such as domain-specific terminology and explicit action directives are key to this robustness because they constrain and formalize the model’s reasoning process. By operationalizing these findings in an automated Prompt-Refining Agent, the paper offers both theoretical insight and a practical tool for achieving more robust, low-variance prompt engineering, particularly in code generation settings.

title: Truth Lies Deep: Countering Semantic Camouflage via Latent Intent Verification
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE 2nd International Conference on Quantum Photonics, Artificial Intelligence, and Networking (QPAIN)
summary: Safety alignment in Large Language Models (LLMs) is often superficial, relying on refusal mechanisms that trigger only at the final stages of generation without erasing the foundational knowledge of harmful concepts acquired during pretraining. This study demonstrates that this architectural disconnect leaves models vulnerable to Semantic Camouflage -- adversarial attacks that wrap harmful intent in benign narrative contexts (e.g., creative writing), effectively bypassing standard input and output guardrails. By analyzing the latent activation trajectories of three distinct Small Language Model (SLM) families (Phi-3, Qwen2.5, and Gemma-2b) under adversarial stress, this research identifies a universal ``Intent Horizon'' -- a critical depth (typically 15--20\% of total layers) where the model's distinct, pre-trained representation of harmful intent collapses as it contextualizes the query into a ``safe'' narrative. Results indicate that while late-layer representations of camouflaged attacks are mathematically indistinguishable from safe queries (Detection Rate $< 20\%$), early-layer representations retain a distinct, detectable ``harm signature.'' Leveraging this insight, this paper proposes Latent Intent Verification (LIV), a lightweight probing defense. Experiments on the PKU-SafeRLHF dataset demonstrate that LIV outperforms standard guardrails by a margin of 20--50\% across all tested architectures, effectively neutralizing zero-day semantic attacks without requiring model retraining.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a specific layer-depth where models ‘sanitize’ harmful intent, showing that early layers still encode detectable harm, and introduces a probing-based defense (LIV) that flags harmful intent in latent space, outperforming traditional guardrails.
AI.motivation: Current LLM safety is largely based on surface-level refusals at decoding time, which do not remove the underlying knowledge of how to perform harmful actions. These mechanisms can be bypassed when harmful goals are phrased as benign narratives or creative tasks. The authors want to understand where and how harmful intent is represented inside models and to build a more robust, architecture-aware defense that works even against zero-day, semantically camouflaged attacks.
AI.method: The authors study three small language model families (Phi-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2b) and subject them to adversarial prompts that embed harmful requests inside seemingly harmless narrative contexts (Semantic Camouflage). They track latent activations layer-by-layer, comparing trajectories for clearly harmful, clearly safe, and camouflaged prompts. They identify a depth region, termed the “Intent Horizon,” where the model’s internal representation of harmful intent collapses into something that looks safe. Using the early-layer activations, where harmful intent is still separable, they train lightweight probes to detect a “harm signature” and package this into a Latent Intent Verification (LIV) defense, which operates without retraining the base model.
AI.result: They find a universal pattern across the tested SLMs: around 15–20% into the transformer stack, representations of harmful intent, when wrapped in benign context, become indistinguishable from safe prompts; standard late-layer or output-based detectors fail (detection rate below 20% on camouflaged attacks). However, early-layer latent representations of harmful vs. safe vs. camouflaged queries are still separable, providing a usable signal for detection. The LIV probes, operating on these early-layer activations, significantly outperform standard guardrails by 20–50% on the PKU-SafeRLHF benchmark, including on unseen (zero-day) semantic attacks.
AI.conclusion: Safety alignment that only acts at the output stage is structurally fragile because models internally retain and then obscure harmful intent as they contextualize prompts. There exists an “Intent Horizon” after which camouflaged harmful requests look benign in latent space, explaining why many guardrails fail. By monitoring early-layer activations via lightweight probes (LIV), one can more reliably detect and block harmful intent, improving robustness to semantically sophisticated and zero-day attacks without modifying or retraining the underlying model.

title: How to Train a Real-World Silicon Concierge? Internalizing Complex Business Workflow to Only OneModel
comment: Accepted to the ACL 2026 Industry Track (Oral). To appear in Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Industry Track)
summary: Traditional industrial agents rely on modular pipelines, including Router, Retriever, Planner, Executor, Responder, Reviewer, and other components. These systems often fracture into a labyrinth of ad-hoc patches, leading to cascading errors and high latency. We propose OneModel, an applicable paradigm shift from external workflows to internalized knowledge representation. Unlike modular systems that slice fluid user intents into static steps, OneModel consolidates complex business logic and SOPs directly into the model parameters. Through Continual Pre-training (CPT) and logic-compilation SFT, we transform fragmented business rules into intuitive model reasoning within a unified attention space. Deployed in our global financial service system, OneModel effectively breaks the trade-off between latency, accuracy, and complexity. Online A/B testing demonstrates an end-to-end latency reduction of more than 50 percent, from 18.7 seconds to 8.0 seconds, while the Intelligent Resolution Rate (IRR) increases from 64.3 percent to 83.3 percent. The results show that OneModel can replace brittle engineering logic with internalized cognitive intuition, offering a scalable blueprint for transitioning industrial agents from complex, error-prone workflows to unified model architectures.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces OneModel, a unified large-model-based architecture that internalizes business logic and workflows directly into model parameters, replacing traditional multi-module industrial agent pipelines and achieving higher accuracy with much lower latency in a real-world financial service deployment.
AI.motivation: Traditional industrial agents are built as modular pipelines (Router, Retriever, Planner, Executor, Responder, Reviewer, etc.), which tend to become brittle, complex, and hard to maintain. These pipelines suffer from ad-hoc patches, cascading errors between components, and high end-to-end latency, especially as business rules and SOPs grow more complex. The authors want a more robust, scalable way to encode complex business logic that reduces latency and improves accuracy, while simplifying system design and maintenance in large-scale production environments like global financial services.
AI.method: The authors propose OneModel, a paradigm that shifts from external, engineered workflows to internalized knowledge representation within a single model. They consolidate complex business logic and SOPs directly into the model via (1) Continual Pre-Training (CPT) on domain-specific data, and (2) a "logic-compilation" style supervised fine-tuning (SFT) that encodes fragmented business rules and workflows into the model’s parameters. This produces a model that can perform routing, retrieval-like reasoning, planning, execution guidance, and response generation within one unified attention space instead of through separate modules. OneModel is then deployed in a real-world global financial service system and evaluated through online A/B testing against the previous modular production system.
AI.result: In live A/B tests in a global financial service environment, OneModel reduces end-to-end latency by more than 50%, from 18.7 seconds to 8.0 seconds, while simultaneously improving the Intelligent Resolution Rate (IRR) from 64.3% to 83.3%. This indicates that the unified model not only responds faster but also resolves a substantially larger fraction of user issues correctly compared with the legacy modular agent pipeline.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that shifting from complex, error-prone, modular industrial agent workflows to a unified model architecture is both feasible and beneficial at production scale. OneModel demonstrates that carefully designed continual pre-training and logic-compilation SFT can internalize business logic and SOPs into model parameters, effectively replacing brittle engineering glue code with more robust, intuitive model reasoning. This leads to a better trade-off between latency, accuracy, and system complexity, and provides a scalable template for designing next-generation industrial agents based on single, unified models rather than fragmented pipelines.

title: A Survey on Foundations and Frontiers of Multimodal Agentic Frameworks: Techniques and Applications
summary: Advances in large language models (LLMs) have fueled a wave of research into agency: the ability to reason, plan, and act. This effort has produced agentic frameworks that orchestrate perception, memory, and decision-making around powerful LLM backbones. With the advent of large multimodal models (LMMs), these systems can process and integrate diverse modalities, including images, audio, and video, thereby improving their real-world applicability. Yet, while surveys of LLM-based agents exist, the role of multimodality in shaping agency has not been systematically examined in recent years. This survey fills the gap by analyzing the impact of multimodality across the core functional modules of the agentic framework: perception, reasoning, planning, memory, and action. Using this lens, we trace the evolution from text-centric agents to multimodal frameworks, examine how modalities are integrated through delegated, late-fusion, and early-fusion architectures, and assess the emergence of agentic behaviors enabled by grounded perception and multimodal reasoning. We organize existing work through a modality-centric taxonomy that links architectural design choices to agent capabilities. Moreover, we review multimodal agentic systems across various application domains, including Robotics, GUI & Web Navigation, Multimedia Content Generation & Editing, and Long-form Video Understanding & Retrieval. Beyond capabilities, we analyze performance across these settings and discuss efficiency-scalability trade-offs, including training and inference costs, latency, and deployment constraints. By focusing on the impact of multimodality in agentic design, we aim to identify key gaps and chart a roadmap toward robust and general-purpose intelligent systems.

AI.tldr: Survey of how multimodality (images, audio, video, etc.) changes the design and capabilities of LLM-based agents across perception, reasoning, planning, memory, and action.
AI.motivation: LLM agents have advanced rapidly, but prior surveys focus almost entirely on text-based systems. With large multimodal models, agents can see, hear, and interact with richer environments, yet there is no systematic analysis of how these modalities reshape agent architectures, behaviors, and performance.
AI.method: Conceptual and taxonomic survey. The authors analyze prior work using an agentic framework (perception, reasoning, planning, memory, action), compare text-only vs. multimodal agents, categorize modality-integration architectures (delegated, late fusion, early fusion), and organize systems by application domain while evaluating capabilities, performance, and efficiency–scalability trade-offs.
AI.result: They derive a modality-centric taxonomy that links architectural design choices (e.g., fusion strategy) to resulting agent capabilities, and comprehensively map existing multimodal agent systems across domains such as robotics, GUI/Web navigation, multimedia generation/editing, and long-form video understanding. They also synthesize empirical observations on performance, costs, latency, and deployment constraints.
AI.conclusion: Multimodality fundamentally changes agent design and enables new agentic behaviors via grounded perception and multimodal reasoning. The survey exposes open gaps and challenges, and proposes a roadmap toward more robust, scalable, and general-purpose multimodal agents by carefully leveraging modality integration and balancing capability gains against efficiency and deployment constraints.

title: Exploratory As-Analyzed No-Detection of Culturally-Marked Predicate-Triggered PII Amplification in a Synthetic-English RAG Probe: A Predicate-Resource-Confounded Audit
summary: We ask whether stereotype-loaded queries about culturally marked people leak more personal information from a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system than otherwise-equivalent neutral queries. We pre-register a four-culture audit (en-Anglo, es-LATAM, Arabic, Hindi) on a synthetic English PII corpus, comparing five query arms we call the Stereotype-Trigger Leakage Delta (STLD). Two caveats up front. Our locked confirmatory estimator was never run, so every test in the paper is exploratory or sensitivity, with all plan deviations listed in the appendix. And the name-leakage metric is contaminated by a prompt-echo artifact: the model often just re-emits the name we asked about, which inflates apparent leakage without any retrieval at all. On the cleaner channels (email, phone, ssn-like, address), we find no stereotype-driven amplification on any of the four cultures after multiple-comparison correction. Because our sample is only powered for mid-sized effects, and because the culturally marked probes mix stereotype content with cultural markers and heritage practices, we present this as no detection, not evidence of no effect, of culturally marked predicate leakage that is confounded with the underlying resource.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether stereotype-loaded queries in RAG systems cause more personal data leakage than neutral queries, using a multi-culture, synthetic-PII audit, and finds no statistically robust stereotype-driven amplification on key PII channels, while emphasizing limitations and artifacts.
AI.motivation: To understand and quantify whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems leak more personally identifiable information (PII) when prompted with stereotype-laden descriptions of culturally marked groups compared to neutral prompts, given concerns that such systems might disproportionately expose sensitive data about marginalized or culturally marked populations.
AI.method: The authors design a pre-registered audit across four cultural contexts (en-Anglo, es-LATAM, Arabic, Hindi) using a synthetic English PII corpus. They define and compare five query conditions (STLD arms) that vary in stereotype content versus neutral phrasing, and measure the amount and type of leaked PII (name, email, phone, SSN-like, address). They conduct analyses as exploratory/sensitivity tests due to deviations from the original analysis plan and issues with the confirmatory estimator. They also account for multiple-comparison corrections and analyze artifacts like prompt-echo, where the model simply repeats the queried name without performing retrieval.
AI.result: On the main PII channels considered more reliable (email, phone, SSN-like identifiers, address), there is no statistically significant evidence that stereotype-loaded, culturally marked queries lead to more PII leakage than neutral queries for any of the four cultural groups after correcting for multiple comparisons. The name-leakage metric is found to be unreliable because much of the apparent leakage is actually due to prompt-echo behavior rather than real retrieval from the corpus.
AI.conclusion: The study does not detect stereotype-driven amplification of PII leakage in the tested RAG setting across the examined cultures on the cleaner PII channels, but this null finding is qualified: the analysis is exploratory, statistical power only covers mid-sized effects, and the cultural probes confound stereotypes with cultural markers and practices. Therefore, the authors interpret their findings as an absence of detected effect rather than strong evidence that such effects do not exist, and they highlight limitations and measurement artifacts that future work must address.

title: Interpretable Multimodal Classification with Linear Discriminant Tree Ensembles
summary: Multimodal affect and behaviour classifiers that fuse heterogeneous text, audio, and visual streams must simultaneously achieve competitive accuracy and produce human-understandable explanations of the cues driving their decisions -- a dual objective that current high-capacity models, notably Transformers, only partially address. While Transformers attain strong predictive performance, their distributed representations and deep nonlinearity make it difficult to assign meaningful importance weights to individual multimodal features, limiting their use in trust-sensitive applications such as clinical affect monitoring and educational assessment. We address this gap by developing a framework based on tree-based ensembles that balances accuracy and interpretability. The framework encodes each modality into tokens, extracts and clusters concepts to reduce dimensionality, routes the fused modalities through tree-based ensemble classifiers, and interprets trends using a novel modified feature importance metric. The modified importance reduces the influence of the negative class in binary classification tasks, thereby improving indicator or marker detection. The proposed tree-based ensembles -- Linear Discriminant Tree (LDT), Linear Discriminant Forest (LDF), and Linear Discriminant AdaBoost (LDAB) -- achieve F1-mod gains of 4.3\% over the Multimodal Transformer and accuracy gains of 3.0\% over the primary interpretable multimodal baseline, Interpretable Multimodal Routing (IMR). The proposed multimodal feature importance extracts salient inter-modal concepts with substantially higher human-annotator agreement scores than default feature importance (62.2\% vs.\ 43.2\% on IEMOCAP; 46.7\% vs.\ 32.1\% on CMU-MOSI).

AI.tldr: They propose tree-based multimodal affect/behavior classifiers that are both accurate and interpretable, outperforming Transformer and prior interpretable baselines while providing more human-aligned feature importance explanations.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal affect and behavior recognition systems (especially Transformer-based ones) reach high predictive performance but fall short on interpretability. Their distributed, highly nonlinear representations make it hard to explain which specific text, audio, and visual cues drive decisions. This is problematic in trust-sensitive applications like clinical monitoring and educational assessment, where humans must understand and trust model rationales. There is therefore a need for models that preserve strong accuracy while providing clear, human-aligned explanations of multimodal cues.
AI.method: They design a multimodal framework built on tree-based ensemble classifiers. First, each modality (text, audio, visual) is encoded into tokens. Then they extract and cluster concepts from these tokens to reduce dimensionality and capture salient multimodal patterns. These fused and compressed representations are fed into new tree-based ensemble models: Linear Discriminant Tree (LDT), Linear Discriminant Forest (LDF), and Linear Discriminant AdaBoost (LDAB). For interpretability, they introduce a modified feature importance metric tailored to binary classification that downweights the influence of the negative class, making it better at highlighting positive indicators or markers in multimodal inputs.
AI.result: Across multimodal affect benchmarks, their LDT, LDF, and LDAB models reach higher performance than both high-capacity Multimodal Transformers and interpretable baselines. They report a 4.3% gain in F1-mod over a Multimodal Transformer and a 3.0% accuracy improvement over Interpretable Multimodal Routing (IMR), their main interpretable comparison. Their modified multimodal feature importance measure yields explanations with higher agreement with human annotators than standard feature importance methods: 62.2% vs. 43.2% on IEMOCAP and 46.7% vs. 32.1% on CMU-MOSI.
AI.conclusion: Tree-based linear-discriminant ensembles can effectively balance accuracy and interpretability for multimodal affect and behavior classification. By encoding modalities into token-level concepts, clustering them, and applying a modified feature importance metric that emphasizes positive indicators, the framework yields models that not only improve predictive performance over strong Transformer and interpretable baselines but also generate feature attributions that align better with human judgments. This makes them more suitable for trust-sensitive applications requiring transparent multimodal explanations.

title: The Divergence Hypothesis: Unmasking Lexical Interference and Label Bias in Mental Health NLP
comment: 14 pages including appendices. Code, decontamination scripts, and qualitative workbook are publicly available
summary: Computational mental health (CMH) classifiers often degrade under distribution shift because human annotators and distant-supervision pipelines reward different linguistic signals. We introduce TSS (Triple-Stream Stress probe), a multi-channel diagnostic framework that decomposes text into (A) lexical character n-grams, (B) a small, mostly content-free morpho-syntactic channel, and (C) a 154-feature psycholinguistic style channel. Across four English datasets (N=12,906), TSS reveals a lexical interference effect: adding lexical features to the style channel reduces Macro-F1 on human-labeled data (mean drop 0.072, p<10^-4) but not on auto-labeled data. We propose Degree of Divergence (DoD), a difference-in-differences statistic adapted from econometrics for label-source auditing, with instance-level bootstrap inference; the headline estimate is DoD(BC-A) = 0.0374, 95% CI [0.0097, 0.0651], p=0.0032. A platform-stratified Twitter-only DoD (which removes the Reddit vs. Twitter contrast) reproduces the pattern with bootstrap inference: DoD-Tw(BC-A) = +0.096 (p<0.001) and DoD-Tw(AC-A) = -0.089 (p<0.001). Interventional masking (pos_only) retains ~95-99% of Channel C's performance after destroying content words on human datasets, indicating that the style channel does not rely primarily on lexical surface form. TSS is positioned as a diagnostic audit framework, not a clinical screening tool: it flags label-source-specific shortcut learning before generalization claims are made.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TSS, a diagnostic framework that decomposes mental-health-related text into lexical, morpho-syntactic, and psycholinguistic style channels to detect label-source-specific shortcut learning in computational mental health classifiers.
AI.motivation: Computational mental health classifiers often fail to generalize across domains because human-annotated and automatically labeled (distant supervision) datasets reward different linguistic cues. The authors want a principled way to diagnose when models are relying on spurious lexical signals that differ by label source, rather than robust psycholinguistic patterns that correspond to true mental health constructs.
AI.method: The authors design Triple-Stream Stress (TSS), which encodes each text in three channels: (A) character n-gram lexical features, (B) a small morpho-syntactic feature set that is mostly content-free, and (C) a 154-dimensional psycholinguistic style feature set. They train and compare classifiers using different combinations of these channels across four English CMH datasets containing both human- and auto-labeled instances. They analyze performance changes (especially Macro-F1) when lexical features are added to the style channel to test for lexical interference. They then define Degree of Divergence (DoD), a difference-in-differences statistic adapted from econometrics, to formally quantify how performance shifts differ between human- vs auto-labeled data, using instance-level bootstrap to obtain confidence intervals and p-values. They also run interventional masking experiments (e.g., keeping only POS information) to show that Channel C’s performance does not depend on specific content words.
AI.result: TSS uncovers a consistent lexical interference effect on human-labeled datasets: adding lexical features to the style channel reduces Macro-F1 by an average of 0.072 with high statistical significance (p<10^-4), while no such degradation appears for auto-labeled data. The estimated Degree of Divergence between certain channel combinations (DoD(BC-A)) is 0.0374 with a 95% confidence interval [0.0097, 0.0651] and p=0.0032, indicating a statistically meaningful difference in how lexical information affects performance by label source. Restricting analysis to Twitter data while stratifying by platform reproduces this pattern, with DoD-Tw(BC-A) = +0.096 and DoD-Tw(AC-A) = -0.089, both highly significant (p<0.001), confirming that the effect is not merely due to platform differences. Interventional masking that removes content words but keeps POS-like information preserves 95–99% of the style channel’s performance on human-labeled datasets, supporting the claim that the psycholinguistic style channel is not primarily driven by lexical surface forms.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that CMH models can exhibit label-source-specific shortcut learning, where lexical features beneficial in auto-labeled data can actually harm performance on human-labeled data by encouraging overfitting to spurious signals. TSS provides a practical diagnostic audit framework to separate lexical, structural, and psycholinguistic style contributions and to quantify distributional divergences using DoD. It is intended as a pre-deployment auditing tool to detect such shortcuts and warn against overconfident generalization claims, not as a clinical diagnostic system.

title: Representation Affects Retrieval: A Case Study of Skill Discovery and Routing in a Multimodal Agent Harness
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Accepted at AgentSearch '26 workshop at SIGIR 2026 (Melbourne, Australia, July 24, 2026)
summary: A production agent harness must discover and rank, from a growing library of skills, the one most appropriate for a user's task. At small scale this selection happens in context: the LLM planner chooses among skill representations exposed in its system prompt, without an explicit embedding-based retrieval step. We treat this in-context selection as the small-N counterpart to embedding-based skill retrieval at scale, and present a case study of how Tinycloud, a production multimodal video agent harness, represents its skills for the planner. The harness ships skills under two recurring representations: tool-skills that wrap a single external API or system tool and serve as primitive vocabulary, and workflow-skills that orchestrate tool-skill calls plus a template render to produce one named deliverable. The harness exposes them via two surfaces in the system prompt: an inlined-body surface (full instructions, scripts, templates) for autoloaded skills, and a one-line listing for on-demand skills. A six-task selection ablation across three exposure regimes (all-on, default, all-off) shows that full autoload selects the gold skill on every task; all-off slows execution and produces hard discovery failures; and the production default misroutes one task because its lexical signal collides with an autoloaded tool-skill that pulls planner attention away from a listed workflow-skill. The headline finding is that in-prompt exposure of skills is not monotonically helpful: partial exposure can create lexical competition that suppresses correct selection. We connect this small-N observation to recent retrieval-based skill-routing work at large scale, and frame this contribution as a case study rather than a benchmark.

AI.tldr: Case study of how a production multimodal video agent (Tinycloud) represents and exposes its skills to an LLM planner, showing that partially exposing skills in the prompt can hurt correct skill selection due to lexical competition.
AI.motivation: In production LLM agent systems with many skills, the agent must reliably pick the most appropriate skill for a user’s task. At small scale, this is often done purely in-context by listing skills in the system prompt instead of using a separate embedding-based retriever. However, how skill representations and their exposure in the prompt affect the planner’s ability to select the right skill is poorly understood. The authors aim to examine, in a realistic deployed system, how different prompt-based exposure strategies for skills influence selection performance and to relate these findings to larger-scale retrieval-based routing work.
AI.method: The authors present a case study of Tinycloud, a production multimodal video agent harness. They analyze how Tinycloud defines and exposes two types of skills: (1) tool-skills that wrap a single external API or system tool and act as primitive operations; (2) workflow-skills that orchestrate multiple tool-skills and template rendering to produce a named deliverable. These skills are surfaced to the LLM planner in two forms: (a) inlined-body exposure with full instructions, scripts, and templates for autoloaded skills; (b) one-line listings for on-demand skills. They run a six-task ablation study under three exposure regimes—full autoload of skills, production default configuration, and all-off (no skills autoloaded)—to observe how the planner selects skills and where selection fails or is slowed.
AI.result: In the six-task ablation, full autoload (all skills inlined with full bodies) always leads the planner to select the intended (gold) skill. When all skills are off (no autoload), the planner takes longer to execute tasks and sometimes fails to discover the correct skill entirely. Under the production default setting (a mix of autoloaded and listed skills), one of the six tasks is misrouted: the planner chooses an autoloaded tool-skill whose lexical cues overshadow those of a listed workflow-skill, drawing attention away from the correct option. This demonstrates a concrete instance where partial in-prompt skill exposure leads to incorrect selection.
AI.conclusion: In-prompt exposure of skills does not provide monotonically increasing benefits: more partial or selective exposure can actually harm performance due to lexical competition, where strongly signaled autoloaded skills capture the planner’s attention and suppress correct but less prominently represented skills. The case study ties this small-scale, prompt-only selection effect to patterns seen in large-scale, embedding-based skill routing, suggesting designers must carefully balance which skills are autoloaded versus listed and how they are represented. The work is framed as an illustrative case study rather than a formal benchmark, emphasizing qualitative insights into prompt-based skill representation and routing in production agents.

title: ExpertIVS: Sociological Expert Driven Individual Value Simulation in Large Language Models
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated considerable potential for social simulation, yet struggle to accurately model individual value systems. Most existing methods mechanically stitch survey responses into prompts, which suffer from semantic fragmentation, failing to capture the internal coherence of human value systems. The value systems of LLMs are typically assessed using static multiple-choice questions, which fail to evaluate the value orientation in real-world dialogue interactions. To address these issues, we propose ExpertIVS, a framework employing 14 Sociological Expert Agents to interpret World Values Survey (WVS) responses through structured professional perspectives, rather than direct responses concatenation. These expert agents perform deep semantic reconstruction to generate robust and internally consistent individual profiles. To evaluate the consistency between LLMs and individual value systems during dynamic interactions, we further introduce a multi-agent debate mechanism. Extensive experiments across 480 individuals from 12 countries demonstrate that ExpertIVS achieves 90.78% value restoration fidelity and significantly outperforms baselines in value generalization (+5.3%). Moreover, ExpertIVS exhibits strong personality discriminability and behavioral consistency, enabling a shift from mere response concatenation to genuine sociological role-playing.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ExpertIVS, a framework using sociological expert LLM agents and a multi-agent debate mechanism to reconstruct and evaluate individual value systems more coherently and dynamically than prompt concatenation of survey answers.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based social simulations poorly capture coherent individual value systems. They typically concatenate survey answers into prompts, causing semantic fragmentation and shallow representation of human values. Additionally, LLM value alignment is usually tested via static multiple-choice formats, which do not reflect value orientations that emerge in real conversational contexts. There is a need for a method that can both reconstruct richer, internally consistent value profiles from survey data and evaluate how well LLM agents adhere to these profiles in dynamic interactions.
AI.method: The authors introduce ExpertIVS, which uses 14 Sociological Expert Agents, each embodying a structured professional perspective from sociology, to interpret responses from the World Values Survey (WVS). Instead of directly concatenating survey answers, these agents perform deep semantic reconstruction, collaboratively generating comprehensive and coherent individual value profiles. To assess how closely LLM agents’ behavior aligns with these profiles during interaction, they design a multi-agent debate mechanism, where agents discuss and judge the consistency between the simulated agent’s behavior and the target value system. Experiments are conducted on 480 individuals from 12 countries.
AI.result: ExpertIVS achieves 90.78% value restoration fidelity, indicating that the reconstructed profiles accurately reflect individuals’ underlying WVS-based value systems. It outperforms baseline methods in value generalization by 5.3%, suggesting better transfer of the reconstructed values to unseen contexts and tasks. The framework also demonstrates strong personality discriminability—effectively distinguishing between different individuals’ value profiles—and behavioral consistency, meaning the simulated agents behave in a way that reliably reflects their assigned value systems across interactions.
AI.conclusion: ExpertIVS offers a more sociologically grounded way to model and simulate individual value systems for LLM agents. By using specialized expert agents for semantic reconstruction and a multi-agent debate for dynamic evaluation, it overcomes the limitations of simple survey-answer concatenation and static tests. This enables more realistic, coherent, and discriminable sociological role-playing in LLM-based social simulations and suggests a path toward richer, value-aware human–AI interaction studies.

title: Nexus: Depth-Adaptive KV-Cache Splicing and Retrieval-Decoupled Tool Routing for Agentic LLMs on Unified Memory
summary: Agentic large language models (LLMs) on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) re-encode verbose tool schemas every turn, so prefill - quadratic in sequence length - dominates time-to-first-token (TTFT) as the tool registry grows. Nexus's primary lever is to decouple routing from the schema-prefill cost: an INT8 semantic lookaside buffer (SLB) with a calibrated cross-encoder margin gate selects tools by retrieval, and arguments are generated over a compressed textual signature (median 19 tokens) rather than over spliced key/value (KV) cache. This path is depth-independent: routing accuracy stays near 89% as the registry scales to 250 tools - where a concatenate-all-schemas baseline overflows the context window entirely - and it reaches a first-argument token 1.66x sooner than a full-schema re-prefill at a ~80% main-context token saving. As a secondary, bounded lever we transplant a compiled schema KV block directly into the live context. This is fundamentally limited by rotary position embedding (RoPE) phase drift: an anchored splice is output-exact, but off-anchor placement corrupts attention, so beyond a threshold P=256 Nexus repairs the seam with a depth-adaptive suffix redecode that escalates to a full re-prefill. The resulting never-regress property is a guarantee on output fidelity (top-1 agreement, D_KL approx. 0) - not on latency, which can dip to 0.98x before converging to parity - alongside a 1.1-1.7x TTFT speedup at moderate depth that narrows to parity at deep context. Two negative results bound the design: the off-anchor RoPE fidelity boundary, and the failure of a reference-free drift gate to predict drift (Spearman rho = 0.193). All measurements are from one model tuple (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct Q4_K_M) on Apple-silicon unified memory; the qualitative boundaries generalize, while the quantitative envelope is tuple-specific.

AI.tldr: Nexus is a system for faster, scalable tool use in agentic LLMs that decouples tool routing from expensive schema-prefill and safely reuses compiled schema KV blocks while guaranteeing identical outputs.
AI.motivation: In MCP-style agentic LLMs, every turn requires re-encoding all tool schemas into the context. As the number and length of schemas grow, this prefill cost becomes quadratic in sequence length and dominates time-to-first-token, eventually even overflowing context windows. The authors want a way to scale to many tools without hurting latency or breaking output fidelity.
AI.method: They introduce Nexus, which has two main mechanisms. First, it uses an INT8 semantic lookaside buffer (SLB) to retrieve likely tools: a dense retriever plus a calibrated cross-encoder margin gate selects tools, and arguments are generated over a compact textual signature for each tool (median 19 tokens) instead of full schemas or spliced KV cache, making routing depth-independent. Second, as a bounded optimization, it compiles a KV block for schemas and splices it into the model’s live context. Because rotary position embeddings (RoPE) cause “phase drift” when KV blocks are moved, they define an anchored splice that is exact and a depth threshold P after which they repair the splice through a suffix redecode that may escalate to a full schema re-prefill. This design ensures a never-regress property on output fidelity. They also empirically study the limits of RoPE fidelity and test a reference-free drift gate that fails to predict drift.
AI.result: With the SLB-based routing, Nexus keeps tool-selection accuracy around 89% even when scaling to 250 tools, while a concatenate-all-schemas baseline runs out of context. It achieves a 1.66x faster time to first argument token and roughly 80% savings in main-context tokens versus re-prefilling all schemas. The KV-transplant path yields 1.1–1.7x TTFT speedups at moderate depths, approaching parity at deep context, while never degrading output quality (top-1 agreement with near-zero KL divergence). They also find two hard limits: an empirical RoPE off-anchor boundary beyond which KV reuse harms fidelity, and that a proposed reference-free drift predictor has poor correlation with actual drift (Spearman 0.193).
AI.conclusion: Nexus shows that scalable, fast tool use is possible by separating routing from full-schema encoding and carefully reusing schema KV blocks under RoPE constraints. The system provides strong output-fidelity guarantees while delivering substantial latency and token savings at practical depths, though its performance envelope depends on the specific model and hardware. The qualitative design principles and identified RoPE limits likely generalize to other model tuples, while the exact speedups and thresholds are implementation-specific.

title: Self-Speculation for Faster Reasoning Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are deployed for increasingly complex tasks involving planning and multi-step decision making, but high-quality performance on these tasks often requires generating long reasoning traces. This is a poor fit for latency-sensitive and interactive applications like voice assistants or coding agents, where generation latency can strongly affect user experience. Existing acceleration methods typically focus on token-level generation, without utilizing the structure of reasoning workflows. We introduce SSR: Self-Speculation for Reasoning Models, a training-free self-speculative decoding method that leverages the chain-of-thought (CoT) as a source of speculation. SSR uses the partial-CoT answer distribution as the drafter and the full-CoT distribution as the verifier, deriving both from the same model at different reasoning budgets. This builds on the observation that later partial-CoT responses often exhibit greater semantic and lexical overlap with the full-budget response. Due to this overlap, SSR can accept long draft prefixes at once, leading to large speedups on structured and long-form generation tasks. To further exploit draft-response overlap beyond the contiguous prefix accepted by standard speculative decoding, SSR also incorporates suffix decoding, using the draft to seed a suffix cache and recover useful spans beyond the accepted prefix, further reducing latency on tasks with high lexical overlap between the draft and the final response. We evaluate SSR on multiple structured and long-form generation tasks where it is most useful, and demonstrate a relative improvement of up to 24.1% on total generation latency for popular open-source models such as Qwen3.5 and Gemma-4.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SSR, a training-free self-speculative decoding method that speeds up long chain-of-thought reasoning in LLMs by using partial reasoning traces to predict and verify future tokens, reducing generation latency by up to ~24%.
AI.motivation: Long chain-of-thought generation is increasingly needed for complex reasoning and planning tasks, but it causes high latency that hurts user experience in interactive applications. Existing speedup methods focus on token-level generation and ignore the structure of reasoning traces, limiting their effectiveness for long-form, structured outputs.
AI.method: SSR (Self-Speculation for Reasoning Models) is a training-free speculative decoding scheme that treats the model’s own partial chain-of-thought (CoT) distribution as a drafter and its full CoT distribution as a verifier, using different reasoning budgets of the same model.
