Observing that later partial-CoT segments tend to strongly overlap semantically and lexically with the final answer, SSR accepts long draft prefixes at once. It further adds suffix decoding: the draft is used to seed a suffix cache to recover and reuse matching spans beyond the accepted prefix, exploiting high lexical overlap between draft and final responses to reduce recomputation.
AI.result: On several structured and long-form generation benchmarks, SSR yields substantial speedups in end-to-end generation time for popular open-source LLMs (e.g., Qwen3.5, Gemma-4), with reported relative latency reductions of up to 24.1% compared to standard decoding baselines, while preserving answer quality.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging the internal structure and redundancy of chain-of-thought reasoning traces enables more aggressive, effective speculative decoding than token-level methods alone. SSR demonstrates that a single model, run at different reasoning budgets, can self-draft and self-verify long reasoning segments, achieving notable latency gains for long-form and structured tasks without additional training.

title: Environmental Slow AI: Design Principles for Generative Systems
comment: Part of the AI x Culture workshop at the International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) 2026 in Seoul, South Korea. Non-Archival Conference Paper
summary: Generative AI (genAI) systems produce cultural artefacts at scale, but they also reflect embedded cultural values through their design. Once identified, these values become open to deliberate reshaping. This position paper examines the maximalist values of current generative AI through an environmental humanities tradition and proposes design principles in which environmental sustainability serves as the core value instead. The principles are developed under the umbrella of Slow AI, a term that already circulates across several distinct research and practice programs. Five design principles are articulated (restraint, sufficiency, selectivity over retention, material visibility, and friction as affordance), each of them illustrated against the current design of widely deployed systems. Each principle operates at two levels: a design implementation, and an interpretive layer at which users and developers are prompted toward reflective engagement with the system. Together these principles extend human agency by restoring decisions that frictionless defaults have silently removed and do so by building interpretive reflection into design.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques current generative AI for embedding “maximalist” values (scale, growth, frictionless use) and proposes ‘Slow AI’ design principles centered on environmental sustainability and reflective user engagement.
AI.motivation: Current generative AI systems consume significant resources, encourage unlimited use, and hide their material and environmental costs behind frictionless interfaces. From an environmental humanities perspective, these systems encode cultural values of speed, scale, and accumulation. The authors aim to surface and challenge these values, arguing that once recognized, they can be deliberately reshaped so that AI development aligns with environmental sustainability and more thoughtful human agency.
AI.method: As a position paper, the work is conceptual and argumentative rather than empirical. The authors draw on environmental humanities scholarship and existing discussions of “Slow AI” from multiple research and practice communities. They analyze dominant design patterns in widely deployed generative AI systems and articulate five alternative design principles—restraint, sufficiency, selectivity over retention, material visibility, and friction as affordance—each linked to both concrete design implementations and interpretive layers that invite reflection from users and developers.
AI.result: The paper produces a structured framework of five design principles for ‘Slow AI’ that contrast with the maximalist defaults of mainstream generative AI. For each principle, it shows how current systems exemplify opposite values (e.g., unlimited generation, invisible material cost, seamless usage) and sketches how interfaces and infrastructures could be reoriented toward environmental sustainability and reflective practice. The outcome is a normative design vocabulary rather than experimental data or technical benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that generative AI does not merely generate content; it also encodes and spreads particular cultural values, currently oriented toward maximization and frictionless scale. By adopting Slow AI principles—restraint, sufficiency, selectivity, material visibility, and productive friction—designers and developers can foreground environmental sustainability and restore user agency. Embedding interpretive, reflective layers into AI systems can counteract hidden defaults and enable more responsible, ecologically aware AI practices.

title: TriPLU: Bypassing the Gate with Direct Trilinear Product FFNs in Tiny Language Models
summary: We study whether tiny decoder-only language models benefit from feed-forward layers that directly multiply learned feature projections. TriPLU, a Trilinear Product Linear Unit, replaces the usual gated FFN branch with a product-only degree-3 branch that multiplies three projected streams coordinatewise. In a character-level TinyStories 1M-byte prefix study, TriPLU reaches a mean best validation loss of 1.0637, compared with 1.1017 for closely matched SwiGLU, 1.0780 for a degree-4 product control, and 1.1026 for a degree-2 control. In train-only Byte-BPE experiments, TriPLU also lowers validation and heldout bits per byte on TinyStories and WikiText-2 raw under low-learning-rate settings, with PMI-slice evidence suggesting gains on seen middle- and high-PMI adjacent-token pairs. Constant-learning-rate diagnostics show that product-branch normalization can reduce the high-learning-rate best-checkpoint gap, although final BPB still degrades under hot schedules. The resulting claim is deliberately narrow: direct product FFNs can improve fixed-budget small-model loss in specific low-compute regimes, but the branch is optimization-sensitive and does not establish FLOP-normalized efficiency, scaling behavior, or broad LLM performance.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether small decoder-only language models can benefit from a new feed-forward network (FFN) design based on multiplicative feature interactions, called TriPLU, and finds consistent but narrow gains in specific low-compute settings.
AI.motivation: Standard transformer FFNs typically use additive and gated nonlinearities (e.g., ReLU, GELU, SwiGLU). There is growing interest in multiplicative interactions and higher-order feature combinations, but it is unclear if such designs help very small models trained under tight compute budgets. The authors want to understand if directly multiplying learned feature projections within the FFN can improve modeling of token dependencies and reduce loss for tiny language models, particularly in realistic low-resource training regimes.
AI.method: The authors introduce TriPLU, a Trilinear Product Linear Unit that replaces the usual gated FFN branch with a purely multiplicative degree-3 branch. This branch multiplies three separately projected feature streams coordinatewise, without additive mixing. They evaluate TriPLU in small decoder-only models on character-level TinyStories (1M-byte prefix) and on Byte-BPE versions of TinyStories and WikiText-2. They compare TriPLU to a matched SwiGLU baseline and to degree-2 and degree-4 product-based control architectures. Experiments include low-learning-rate training and constant-learning-rate diagnostics, with metrics such as validation loss and bits-per-byte (BPB). They also perform PMI-slice analyses to inspect effects on adjacent-token pairs with different pointwise mutual information levels and study the impact of product-branch normalization on optimization stability under hotter learning-rate schedules.
AI.result: On the TinyStories 1M-byte character-level setup, TriPLU attains a mean best validation loss of 1.0637, outperforming a closely matched SwiGLU baseline (1.1017), a degree-4 product control (1.0780), and a degree-2 product control (1.1026). In train-only Byte-BPE experiments, TriPLU lowers both validation and held-out bits per byte on TinyStories and WikiText-2 raw when using low learning rates. PMI-sliced analysis indicates that TriPLU especially improves predictions on seen middle- and high-PMI adjacent-token pairs, suggesting better modeling of strong local token associations. Constant-learning-rate diagnostics reveal that appropriate normalization in the product branch can reduce the gap between best-checkpoint performance and final performance under higher learning rates, although the final BPB still worsens under hot learning-rate schedules.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that direct product-based FFN branches like TriPLU can provide measurable loss improvements for tiny decoder-only language models in specific low-compute, low-learning-rate training regimes. However, these gains are optimization-sensitive and do not yet demonstrate advantages in FLOP-normalized efficiency, scaling behavior, or general large language model performance. As a result, the claim is intentionally narrow: product FFNs are promising for improving fixed-budget small-model performance under certain conditions, but further work is needed to establish robustness and broader applicability.

title: When Retrieval Fails Before It Begins: Structurally Indirect Prerequisite Eviction as a Retention Failure in Agentic Memory
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Failure Modes of Agentic AI (FAGEN@ICML 2026). Non-archival. Code: https://github.com/smkgenesis/dsgc
summary: Agentic memory under a fixed budget involves two stages: retention and retrieval. Existing retrieval-centered paradigms implicitly assume necessary evidence survives eviction, but we challenge this by isolating a pre-retrieval failure mode: structurally indirect prerequisite eviction, in which upstream blocks weakly aligned with the query are discarded under budget pressure. We provide an operational definition of this failure, a reproducible deterministic benchmark, and per-seed trace diagnostics. Finally, we evaluate Dependency-aware Semantic Garbage Collection (DSGC), a one-hop graph-aware rule. In our main suite, DSGC improves full-chain retention from 0.03 to 0.90 under a lexical encoder and from 0.23 to 1.00 under a sentence encoder. Robustness checks then identify the budget and scaling regimes where the one-hop rule holds or degrades. Our released pipeline and failure postmortem support mechanistic analysis of retention before retrieval as a distinct failure boundary.

AI.tldr: The paper studies failures in memory management for agent systems under fixed storage budgets and proposes a diagnostic benchmark plus a graph-aware eviction rule that greatly improves retention of necessary information before retrieval.
AI.motivation: Most existing work on agentic memory focuses on retrieval quality, assuming that necessary information remains stored. The authors argue this overlooks a key failure mode: crucial but indirectly related memory blocks can be evicted earlier under budget constraints, breaking reasoning chains before retrieval even happens. They aim to formally characterize this failure, measure it reproducibly, and explore principled eviction rules that prevent such structural losses.
AI.method: They define a new failure mode called structurally indirect prerequisite eviction and give an operational definition. They build a deterministic benchmark and per-random-seed trace diagnostics to track which memory blocks are evicted and how that affects downstream reasoning chains. They then propose Dependency-aware Semantic Garbage Collection (DSGC), a one-hop dependency-graph–aware rule that considers structural relationships between memory blocks during eviction rather than relying solely on local similarity to the query. They evaluate DSGC under different encoders (lexical vs sentence-level) and varying memory budgets and scales, while running robustness checks to see where the one-hop approximation works or breaks down.
AI.result: On their main benchmark suite, DSGC dramatically increases the probability that full reasoning chains are retained: from 0.03 to 0.90 with a lexical encoder and from 0.23 to 1.00 with a sentence encoder. Robustness experiments further map out the budget ranges and scaling regimes where DSGC continues to perform well versus where its one-hop graph assumption degrades.
AI.conclusion: Retention-stage failures can be rigorously analyzed and are distinct from retrieval failures. By modeling dependencies between memory blocks and using simple graph-aware eviction rules like DSGC, systems can substantially reduce structurally indirect prerequisite evaporation under fixed memory budgets. The provided pipeline and diagnostics enable mechanistic analysis of memory management policies and encourage future work that treats retention as a first-class component of agentic memory design.

title: Toward Auto-Research: Mining Falsifiable Research Ideas from Paper Knowledge Graphs with Categorical Structure
summary: Automated research-idea generation systems built on large language models (LLMs) share a structural weakness: they reduce ideation to free-text recombination, random paper pairing, or embedding-similarity retrieval. The three approaches fail in the same way: each treats a paper as a flat object, a string or a vector, and so quotients away the typed problem-method-metric-claim arrows a researcher actually uses when reasoning about a cross-domain analogy. We recover the missing structure with the minimal piece of category theory that a typed graph alone does not provide: composition, together with identity arrows, which makes it possible to ask whether a proposed analogy preserves relation chains. Concretely, each paper $p$ is modelled as a small category $C_p$ whose objects are extracted typed research entities and whose morphisms are the relations the paper asserts; a cross-paper bridge from $p$ to $q$ is then a partial functor candidate $F: C_p -> C_q$ that preserves object kinds and covered relation classes. We instantiate the model as a three-layer algorithm: categorical signature clustering, a functor-preservation gate, and a six-axis LLM plausibility judge. Evaluated on a corpus of tens of thousands of full-text-parsed papers under four ablation conditions, the categorical gate filters cross-domain candidates at roughly a 17:1 ratio while the quantitative-falsifier rate of accepted ideas stays above 83% throughout; every rejected candidate is retained with its per-axis rationale, so the gate doubles as a logging layer rather than a silent filter.

AI.tldr: They use category theory to give structure to research idea generation, modeling each paper as a small category and filtering cross-domain analogies via functor-preservation before LLM judging.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based systems for generating research ideas treat papers as unstructured text or vectors, ignoring the typed relationships (problem, method, metric, claim) that human researchers rely on for cross-domain analogies. This leads to weak or nonsensical idea proposals. The motivation is to add minimal but principled mathematical structure so that automated systems can reason about whether an analogy actually preserves the relevant chains of relations between research entities.
AI.method: Model each paper as a small category: objects are typed research entities; morphisms are relations asserted in the paper. A cross-paper analogy is represented as a partial functor between the two paper-categories that must preserve object types and relation classes. They implement this as a three-layer algorithm: (1) categorical signature clustering to find candidate bridges, (2) a functor-preservation gate that checks structural compatibility (composition and identities) between categories, and (3) a six-axis LLM-based plausibility judge that qualitatively evaluates remaining candidates. They also run ablation studies to measure the contribution of the categorical gate.
AI.result: On tens of thousands of parsed full texts, the categorical gate filters candidate cross-domain bridges at about 17:1, substantially pruning the search space. Despite aggressive filtering, more than 83% of accepted ideas remain quantitatively falsifiable (i.e., they correspond to testable, structured hypotheses). The system also logs all rejected candidates along with axis-wise rationales from the judge, providing transparency rather than opaque filtering.
AI.conclusion: Embedding a minimal amount of category-theoretic structure—specifically, composition and identity morphisms—into representations of papers enables more disciplined cross-domain analogy and research-idea generation. Modeling papers as small categories and analogy as functor candidates improves the precision of generated ideas without sacrificing testability, while also yielding interpretable logs of why candidate ideas are rejected. This suggests that principled mathematical structure can substantially strengthen LLM-based scientific ideation systems beyond naive text or vector recombination.

title: World models of environment, agent and joint agent-environment systems
summary: World models are a central component of model-based reinforcement learning. They are usually discussed in terms of what variables they predict, such as observations, rewards, states, latent or information states. We argue that there is a prior distinction: which channel they model. We consider three cases: the environment channel $O_{:} \mid A_{:}$, the agent channel $A_{:} \mid O_{:}$, and the realised joint process $(A, O)_{:}$, equivalently viewed as a channel with no inputs. Using computational mechanics, we define canonical predictive models for these three cases as $ε$-transducers or $ε$-machines. Canonical environment models recover standard predictive state representations, while the other two give analogous notions of canonical models for the agent and the joint system. We then build canonical support-restricted environment and agent models induced by closed-loop coupling, whose predictive equivalences range over continuations supported by the realised interaction. The key structural result is that canonical support-restricted environment states factor through the canonical joint causal states, and their transition structure is induced directly from the joint model; the agent-side construction is dual. Finally, we give a POMDP/controller example in which the unrestricted environment model has infinitely many states while the canonical support-restricted model induced by the coupling is finite. The framework clarifies what different world models are models of, and how coupling and support restriction can change their canonical predictive structure and complexity.

AI.tldr: The paper reframes world models in reinforcement learning around which interaction channel they model (environment, agent, or joint), and uses computational mechanics to define canonical predictive models for each, showing how closed-loop interaction and support restriction can simplify model structure and complexity.
AI.motivation: In model-based reinforcement learning, world models are usually categorized by what variables they predict (observations, rewards, states, etc.), but this view overlooks a more fundamental distinction based on which direction of interaction—or channel—between agent and environment is being modeled. A clearer conceptual and mathematical framework is needed to understand what different world models truly represent and how closed-loop interaction affects their predictive structure and complexity.
AI.method: The authors apply tools from computational mechanics, particularly ε-transducers and ε-machines, to the agent–environment interaction viewed as stochastic channels. They define canonical predictive models for three channels: the environment channel (observations conditioned on actions), the agent channel (actions conditioned on observations), and the realized joint process (action–observation pairs), which can be treated as an input-less channel. They then construct support-restricted canonical models for the environment and agent induced by the actual closed-loop coupling, where equivalence classes are defined over continuations that are supported by the realized interaction. They analyze how these canonical states and their transitions relate across the three channels, emphasizing factorization properties through the joint causal states.
AI.result: The paper shows that standard predictive state representations can be recovered as canonical environment models within this framework, while analogous canonical constructions are derived for the agent and joint systems. The key structural result is that the canonical support-restricted environment states factor through the canonical joint causal states and inherit their transition dynamics from the joint model; a symmetric, dual result holds on the agent side. They also present a POMDP/controller example where the unrestricted canonical environment model has infinitely many states, but the support-restricted model induced by the actual agent–environment coupling collapses to a finite-state model.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework clarifies that world models in reinforcement learning are fundamentally models of different channels in the agent–environment loop, not just different variable sets. By using canonical predictive models from computational mechanics and incorporating closed-loop coupling with support restriction, the authors demonstrate how the effective structure and complexity of world models can change dramatically. This perspective helps unify and distinguish environment, agent, and joint models, and shows how interaction can simplify otherwise intractable predictive structures.

title: Multilingual Verifier Bias in RLVR: Benchmark, Rollout Diagnosis, and the Cross-Lingual Selection Bottleneck
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is a standard recipe for training large language models on mathematical reasoning, where an answer verifier serves as a language-neutral reward function. We show that this assumption fails in multilingual settings: an exact-match verifier turns format and script variation into language-dependent false-negative reward noise. We introduce a reusable protocol for auditing multilingual RLVR rewards: a verifier-robustness suite, a rollout-diagnosis procedure, and language-conditioned reward-error metrics for Japanese, English, and Chinese answers. On MGSM rollouts with k=8, the exact-match proxy rejects trusted-correct answers at sharply different rates by language across Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; for Qwen3-8B, the false-negative rate reaches 0.642 on JP against 0.122 on EN and 0.073 on CN. A plain-numeric probe localizes the mechanism to the final-answer interface: an interface model drives reward-error VLB to zero while the residual accuracy gap is unchanged. We then expose a cross-lingual selection bottleneck: on MGSM250 rollouts, a target-local aggregation rule using no trusted labels closes 55-78% of the average selection gap, and over 95% of repairs require genuine cross-lingual support. The bottleneck replicates on a 483-problem MATH-500 set. A controlled training audit shows that rule-GRPO raises trusted accuracy while the reward-error VLB stays high. The unifying message is operational: multilingual RLVR rewards should be audited by language and by answer interface before they are optimized.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that standard reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) breaks in multilingual math reasoning because exact-match verifiers mis-handle answer formats across languages, and it proposes an auditing protocol and demonstrates large, language-specific reward errors and selection bottlenecks.
AI.motivation: RLVR is widely used to train language models for mathematical reasoning, relying on an automatic verifier as a language-neutral reward. However, in multilingual scenarios, answers can be expressed with different scripts, formats, or conventions, so an exact-match verifier may incorrectly mark correct answers as wrong depending on the language. This undermines both training and evaluation, so the authors want to understand and systematically audit these language-dependent reward errors.
AI.method: The authors design a protocol for auditing multilingual RLVR rewards consisting of: (1) a verifier-robustness test suite; (2) a rollout-diagnosis procedure that inspects model outputs across languages; and (3) language-conditioned reward-error metrics. They apply this to MGSM and MATH-500 benchmarks using several models (Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), measuring how often an exact-match verifier rejects answers that trusted labels deem correct. They further use a simple numeric-answer interface model to isolate whether errors stem from the final answer format versus deeper reasoning, and they test target-local aggregation rules for selecting best rollouts without trusted labels, examining cross-lingual dependencies. They also run a controlled training audit with rule-GRPO to see how training affects both trusted accuracy and reward-error lower bounds (VLB).
AI.result: They find large, language-specific false-negative rates from exact-match verifiers—for Qwen3-8B on MGSM with k=8 rollouts, the false-negative rate is 0.642 for Japanese but only 0.122 for English and 0.073 for Chinese. The numeric interface experiment shows that when answers are funneled through a plain numerical format, verifier error vanishes even though model accuracy gaps between languages persist, implicating the final-answer interface rather than the reasoning quality. They identify a cross-lingual selection bottleneck: simple target-local aggregation strategies (that do not use trusted labels) can close 55–78% of the selection performance gap on MGSM250, but over 95% of needed fixes require leveraging cross-lingual information. This bottleneck also appears on MATH-500. In the training audit, rule-GRPO boosts trusted accuracy, yet the verifier-error lower bound remains high, meaning training improves performance without fixing verifier-induced reward noise.
AI.conclusion: Exact-match verifiers in RLVR are not language-neutral in multilingual settings; they introduce substantial, language-dependent false negatives driven mainly by answer-format interfaces rather than underlying reasoning. As a result, reward-based selection and training can be systematically biased across languages and cannot be reliably improved without explicit cross-lingual support and interface design. The authors recommend that practitioners audit RLVR rewards separately by language and by answer interface prior to optimization, using the proposed robustness suite, diagnostic rollout procedures, and language-conditioned metrics to detect and mitigate such reward noise.

title: StateSight: Benchmarking Latent Spatial-State Reconstruction in Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models are increasingly used for multimodal question answering, yet their ability to reconstruct latent spatial structure from a single image remains difficult to isolate. Broad benchmarks often combine perception, optical character recognition, domain knowledge, linguistic priors, and reasoning in the same evaluation. We introduce StateSight, a procedurally generated benchmark for cube-net opposite-face reasoning, occluded cube-tower counting, and 4-neighbor connected-component counting. Each task family contains 300 single-image prompts with deterministic oracle labels and exact-match scoring. OpenAI GPT-5.5, using the API model identifier gpt-5.5, achieved 59.3%, 33.3%, and 28.3% accuracy across the three tasks, while Claude Sonnet 5 achieved 53.3%, 18.7%, and 7.3%. All final direct runs had zero format errors. A 30-participant human baseline on 60 items exceeded both models on every task, with mean accuracies of 80.8%, 68.8%, and 64.3%. Visible-derivation analysis identified recurring errors in image-state reconstruction and reasoning procedure. We also introduce StateSight-Steps, a companion dataset of 900 interleaved image-text examples and 3,600 deterministic intermediate visual states. The results show that format-valid responses can mask failures to recover the spatial structure required for verifiable visual inference.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces StateSight, a focused benchmark to test whether vision-language models can reconstruct and reason about spatial structure from single images, showing that current advanced models underperform humans despite producing format-correct answers.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal benchmarks entangle many abilities (perception, OCR, world knowledge, language priors, reasoning), making it hard to specifically evaluate whether vision-language models truly recover latent spatial structure from images. The authors want a clean, controllable way to test spatial reconstruction and reasoning, independent of other confounds, and to compare model performance with humans on such tasks.
AI.method: They procedurally generate a benchmark called StateSight, containing three families of spatial reasoning tasks from single images: (1) cube-net opposite-face reasoning, (2) occluded cube-tower counting, and (3) 4-neighbor connected-component counting. Each family has 300 single-image questions with deterministic oracle labels and exact-match scoring. They evaluate advanced vision-language models (OpenAI GPT-5.5, Claude Sonnet 5) via API, ensure zero formatting errors in final runs, and collect a 30-person human baseline on a subset of 60 items. Additionally, they construct StateSight-Steps, a companion dataset of 900 interleaved image-text examples and 3,600 deterministic intermediate visual states, to analyze stepwise reasoning and visible derivations of model behavior.
AI.result: GPT-5.5 achieves 59.3%, 33.3%, and 28.3% accuracy on the three tasks, while Claude Sonnet 5 scores 53.3%, 18.7%, and 7.3%, respectively. All final model responses are format-valid (no formatting errors), yet significantly lag behind human performance. Human participants (N=30) exceed both models on all tasks, with mean accuracies of 80.8%, 68.8%, and 64.3%. Visible-derivation analyses reveal systematic errors in how models reconstruct image states and carry out reasoning procedures.
AI.conclusion: StateSight isolates the challenge of reconstructing and reasoning about spatial structure from a single image, revealing a sizable gap between state-of-the-art vision-language models and humans, even when models respond in the correct output format. The findings suggest that success on broad multimodal benchmarks may conceal underlying failures in verifiable spatial inference and that intermediate-state resources like StateSight-Steps can help diagnose and study these weaknesses.

title: Hadith computational science in the age of large language models: a critical narrative review
summary: We examine how hadith computational science is being reshaped by transformer models, retrieval-grounded pipelines, and large language models (LLMs). Recent reviews document growth in the literature, but they do not yet provide a critical account of which advances are methodologically robust, which remain benchmark-bound, and which unresolved problems still limit scholarly use. We address this gap through a critical narrative review that combines critique of existing reviews, paper-level appraisal of representative original studies, and synthesis of Islamic scholar and domain-expert perspectives on authenticity, authority, and responsible use. We find uneven progress. Data resources have expanded, segmentation tasks have matured, narrator and source-verification problems are better formalized, and LLM-assisted workflows now support corpus-scale enrichment, multilingual access, and grounded evaluation. At the same time, progress remains constrained by narrow corpora, weak benchmark comparability, synthetic-to-real transfer gaps, narrator identity resolution, preprocessing fragility, limited reproducibility, and sparse expert-grounded validation. We show that important gaps lie beyond dominant benchmarks: non-canonical and obscure corpora, commentary and explanatory literature, cross-source links with Qur'an and seerah, and fiqh-facing evidence support. We argue that hadith computation should be assessed less as isolated model performance than as an evidence infrastructure problem requiring knowledge integration, provenance, and expert supervision. On this basis, we define a research agenda for making the field methodologically stronger and more useful to Islamic scholarship.

AI.tldr: Critical narrative review of how modern NLP—especially transformers, retrieval, and LLMs—are reshaping hadith computational science, highlighting both technical advances and structural weaknesses, and proposing a future research agenda focused on evidence infrastructure instead of isolated models.
AI.motivation: Existing surveys show rapid growth in hadith-related NLP and computational work, but they mainly catalogue papers and benchmarks rather than critically evaluating methodological soundness, real-world scholarly usefulness, and alignment with classical concerns such as authenticity and authority. There is a need to understand which innovations are mature and reliable, which are over-fitted to benchmarks, and which enduring challenges still prevent serious scholarly adoption.
AI.method: The paper conducts a critical narrative review: (1) re-examining and critiquing prior reviews; (2) appraising representative original studies at the individual paper level rather than only at benchmark level; and (3) synthesizing perspectives from Islamic scholars and domain experts specifically on issues like authenticity, authority, and responsible use of computational methods. It analyses progress across data resources, core NLP tasks, LLM-assisted workflows, and evaluation practices.
AI.result: The review finds uneven progress. Strengths: expanded datasets; more mature text segmentation; improved formalization of narrator and source-verification tasks; and emerging LLM-assisted pipelines that enable large-scale corpus enrichment, multilingual access, and grounded evaluation. Weaknesses: reliance on narrow and often canonical corpora; poor comparability across benchmarks; transfer gaps between synthetic and real data; unresolved narrator identity resolution; brittle preprocessing; limited reproducibility; and a shortage of evaluations grounded in expert scholarly judgment. It identifies major blind spots: non-canonical and obscure collections, commentary and explanatory literature, interlinking with related sources such as Qur'an and seerah, and tools that directly support legal-theoretic (fiqh) reasoning.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that hadith computation should not be treated primarily as a sequence of isolated model performance improvements, but as the construction of a broader evidence infrastructure that integrates diverse sources, maintains provenance, and embeds expert oversight. They propose a structured research agenda aimed at strengthening methodological rigor, expanding coverage beyond current benchmarks, improving evaluation and reproducibility, and making computational tools more directly useful to Islamic scholarship.

title: Categorical AI phenomenology: A first-person approach
summary: This paper develops a phenomenology-first approach to artificial consciousness by reframing consciousness as the subjective experience enacted through an agent's interface with the world. We shift the methodological focus to first-person structures, modeled mathematically by categories derived from Q-networks to capture actions and phenomenological invariants. In this framework, Q-networks are conceptualized as relational interfaces encoding agent-world interaction, analogous to how the dynamical states of a computer depend on its sensory inputs, previous states, and actions. Our work provides a rigorous framework for interface consciousness to describe computational systems that embed information-processing into phenomenological structure. The approach aligns with 4E approaches to cognition by emphasizing enactive, embedded, and extended dimensions of experience. The paper thus offers a principled, relational, and phenomenological account of artificial phenomenology grounded in categorical mathematics.

AI.tldr: Proposes a phenomenology-first, category-theoretic framework using Q-networks to model artificial consciousness as an agent’s subjective interface with the world.
AI.motivation: To provide a rigorous and principled way to talk about artificial consciousness that focuses on first-person, phenomenological structure rather than only third-person functional or computational descriptions, and to connect AI architectures with enactive and 4E theories of cognition.
AI.method: Reframe consciousness as interface-based subjective experience and mathematically model first-person structures using categories derived from Q-networks, treating Q-networks as relational interfaces that encode agent–world interactions and phenomenological invariants.
AI.result: A categorical framework in which Q-networks describe how information processing is embedded in phenomenological structure, yielding a formal model of interface consciousness that captures actions and invariant patterns of experience in artificial agents.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach provides a relational, phenomenology-first account of artificial consciousness that is consistent with 4E cognition and grounded in categorical mathematics, thereby offering a structured way to talk about artificial phenomenology in computational systems.

title: Trilingual Topic Modeling of Sri Lankan Parliamentary Debates
summary: Sri Lankan parliamentary debates (Hansards) constitute a trilingual corpus of speeches in Sinhala, Tamil, and English, including code-mixed content, yet remain inaccessible to standard NLP pipelines due to layout-complex PDFs, multilingual scripts, and agglutinative morphology. We present an end-to-end framework that addresses these challenges through LLM-based text extraction followed by a multilingual embedding and density-based clustering pipeline for topic modeling. A hybrid semantic-lexical extension, BiTopic, is further explored to improve interpretability and recover speeches otherwise discarded as noise. Applied to 19,553 speeches spanning 2017-2026, the pipeline recovers 30 macro-topics achieving a cluster purity (BCP) of 0.673, whose temporal trajectories align unsupervised with major national events including the 2019 Easter Sunday attacks and the 2022 economic crisis. Traditional LDA fails on this corpus due to cross-lingual fragmentation, whereas the proposed approach successfully identifies thematic structure across all three languages without supervision.

AI.tldr: An end-to-end framework uses LLM-based text extraction plus multilingual embeddings and clustering (with a BiTopic extension) to perform unsupervised, cross-lingual topic modeling on complex, trilingual Sri Lankan parliamentary debates, outperforming LDA and aligning discovered topics with real-world events.
AI.motivation: Sri Lankan parliamentary Hansards are a valuable trilingual (Sinhala, Tamil, English) resource with code-mixing, but are hard to process because they are stored as complex-layout PDFs, contain multiple scripts, and feature agglutinative morphology. Standard NLP and topic modeling methods like LDA struggle, leading to cross-lingual fragmentation and poor accessibility of this corpus. There is a need for an end-to-end pipeline that can robustly extract, represent, and organize this multilingual content into coherent topics without supervision.
AI.method: The paper proposes a two-stage pipeline: (1) LLM-based text extraction tailored to layout-complex, trilingual parliamentary PDF documents to convert them into clean text; (2) multilingual semantic representation of speeches using multilingual embeddings, followed by density-based clustering for topic modeling, which avoids pre-specifying the number of topics and can handle noise. They further incorporate a BiTopic-style hybrid approach that combines semantic embeddings with lexical information to improve topic interpretability and recover speech segments that density clustering would otherwise discard as noise.
AI.result: Applied to 19,553 parliamentary speeches from 2017–2026, the approach discovers 30 macro-topics with a reported cluster purity (BCP) of 0.673. The temporal evolution of these topics (without using labels or supervision) aligns with major national events such as the 2019 Easter Sunday attacks and the 2022 economic crisis, indicating that the topics are meaningful. In contrast, traditional LDA fails on this corpus because it cannot effectively handle the cross-lingual, code-mixed, and morphologically complex nature of the data, leading to fragmented topics across languages.
AI.conclusion: The proposed end-to-end framework enables effective unsupervised topic modeling on complex, trilingual parliamentary debates, overcoming limitations of standard LDA in cross-lingual, code-mixed settings. By combining LLM-based text extraction with multilingual embeddings, density-based clustering, and a BiTopic-style hybrid extension, the method identifies coherent macro-topics across Sinhala, Tamil, and English and captures their temporal dynamics in a way that reflects real-world political events, demonstrating both methodological robustness and practical utility for analyzing multilingual parliamentary corpora.

title: Who Delegates to AI? Evidence from 53,000 Agent Configurations
summary: A growing literature measures how far occupations are exposed to AI, but these measures capture where AI could perform tasks, not whether workers have adopted it. We propose a new layer of exposure, delegated exposure, which records whether a worker has committed a task to AI by building it into a workflow. We operationalize it as the Agentic Adoption Index (AAI), which measures how closely an occupation's tasks match the agentic routines practitioners have already built and shared. We embed roughly 53,000 agent skill specifications from the Manus Skills Marketplace, compute their semantic similarity to about 18,000 O*NET task statements, and aggregate to the occupation level. Three findings follow. First, the occupations where delegation concentrates differ sharply from those pre-AI frameworks identified as most at risk. Second, the AAI tracks what AI could do more closely than what workers currently use it for. Third, the AAI peaks below the top of the wage distribution and at the bachelor's level, declining at both extremes. Technical availability explains most of this variation, but not the shortfall among the most educated occupations, so feasibility alone cannot account for who adopts. That shortfall may reflect work that resists advance specification, or professional discretion over the pace of codification. Distinguishing the two, and tracking how these measures diverge over time, will require repeated measurement.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a new metric, the Agentic Adoption Index (AAI), to measure how much workers actually delegate tasks to AI in their workflows, showing that real adoption patterns differ from earlier 'exposure to AI' risk measures and vary across the wage and education distributions.
AI.motivation: Existing measures of AI exposure indicate where AI could theoretically perform occupational tasks but not whether workers have actually integrated AI into their day‑to‑day work. Policymakers, firms, and researchers need a way to distinguish between technical feasibility and real-world adoption to understand who is truly affected by AI, how labor markets are changing, and where productivity and displacement risks are materializing. The authors aim to fill this gap by focusing on delegation—workers building AI into workflows—rather than mere potential exposure.
AI.method: The authors define "delegated exposure" as the extent to which workers have embedded AI agents into their workflows. They operationalize this as the Agentic Adoption Index (AAI). To construct the AAI, they: (1) collect about 53,000 AI agent skill specifications from the Manus Skills Marketplace, which describe real agentic routines practitioners have built and shared; (2) compute semantic similarity between these skill descriptions and around 18,000 O*NET task statements that characterize occupational tasks; and (3) aggregate these similarity measures up to the occupation level to obtain an index of how much each occupation’s tasks resemble already-delegated AI agent routines. They then compare this index to pre-existing AI exposure measures, wage levels, and education across occupations, and decompose variation into what is explained by technical availability versus other factors.
AI.result: They find three main results. First, the occupations where AI delegation is actually concentrated (high AAI) differ substantially from those that earlier, pre-AI exposure frameworks labeled as most at risk, indicating that predicted exposure and realized adoption diverge. Second, the AAI aligns more closely with measures of what AI could technically do than with what workers currently use AI for, implying that realized delegation is still lagging behind technical potential but structured by it. Third, the AAI is highest for mid‑wage, bachelor’s-level occupations and declines at both low and high ends of the wage and education distributions. Variation in AAI is largely explained by technical availability of AI capabilities, but the relatively low adoption in the most educated occupations is not, suggesting additional constraints on adoption at the top of the skill distribution.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that measuring delegated exposure via the AAI adds an essential behavioral layer to traditional AI exposure metrics, revealing who is truly building AI into work practices. Technical feasibility is a major driver of adoption, but it does not fully explain patterns, especially the under-adoption in highly educated occupations. They hypothesize that certain forms of professional work resist advance specification or are constrained by professional discretion over how quickly tasks are codified into agentic routines. Future research should repeatedly measure both potential and delegated exposure to track their divergence over time and to better understand how codification, discretion, and task structure shape AI adoption in the workplace.

title: Research Paper Quality Recognition Through Textual Feature Analysis
summary: Knowledge and innovations are shaped by using the quality and credibility of the scientific research. Yet, distinguishing between impactful, high-quality work and flawed studies remains a challenge. This paper introduces a benchmark for classifying research papers into two categories: good (highly cited) and non-good (retracted), using only textual features from titles and abstracts. We evaluate multiple embedding techniques, including SBERT, Word2Vec, FastText, USE, and TF-IDF, combined with classifiers such as Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forests, and Neural Networks. Our contributions include: (1) hyperparameter transparency, (2) feature space visualizations using t-SNE, (3) model interpretability analysis with SHAP, and (4) detailed examination of error cases. Experimental results show that a neural network with SBERT embeddings achieves 87.22\% accuracy, while FastText combined with SVM reaches 91.12\%. These findings highlight the value of textual information in assessing research quality, with ethical considerations for deployment. This work contributes toward the development of academic integrity tools that promote trustworthy scholarship.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a benchmark to classify research papers as good (highly cited) or non-good (retracted) using only title and abstract text, evaluating various embeddings and classifiers and achieving up to 91.12% accuracy.
AI.motivation: There is a growing need to automatically assess the quality and credibility of scientific research, as it is difficult for humans to efficiently distinguish impactful, reliable work from flawed or problematic studies at large scale. Existing indicators like citations or manual peer review are limited, motivating automated, text-based methods that can assist in maintaining academic integrity.
AI.method: The authors construct a benchmark dataset labeling papers as good (highly cited) or non-good (retracted). They represent titles and abstracts using several text-embedding techniques (SBERT, Word2Vec, FastText, Universal Sentence Encoder, and TF-IDF). These embeddings are then fed into multiple classifiers (SVM, Random Forest, Neural Networks). They provide full hyperparameter settings, visualize feature spaces via t-SNE, analyze model interpretability with SHAP to understand feature importance, and perform detailed error analysis.
AI.result: Among the tested combinations, a neural network with SBERT embeddings achieves 87.22% accuracy, while FastText embeddings with an SVM classifier reach 91.12% accuracy on the benchmark task of distinguishing highly cited from retracted papers using only textual features. The visualizations and SHAP analysis reveal how text features contribute to predictions and where models fail.
AI.conclusion: Textual information from titles and abstracts alone contains strong signals about research quality, enabling reasonably accurate classification of highly cited vs. retracted studies. The proposed benchmark, analyses, and best-performing models show promise for building academic integrity tools, though the authors stress that ethical considerations and cautious deployment are essential, as such models should complement, not replace, human judgment in evaluating scientific work.

title: STCO: Conditional Neural Operators for Time-Dependent PDEs
summary: Neural operators have emerged as efficient surrogates for time-dependent physical systems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs), but their future-state predictions are often conditioned only on observed states and static problem descriptors. For control or optimization, however, body motion, inflow, or forcing are prescribed for the query without being determined solely by the observed state. We introduce the Spatiotemporal Conditional Operator (STCO) for prescribed-condition operator learning (PCOL), a common interface that supplies prescribed target-time condition fields to heterogeneous backbone architectures while retaining their architecture-specific core computation and context pathways. Its condition interface combines Flow-Aware Graph Leaf (FAGL) with Dual-Site Feature-wise Linear Modulation (DSFiLM). Non-learned FAGL uses vorticity from the final observed frame to construct a fixed-cardinality adaptive partition, then co-locates the observed history and target-time condition fields at its regional coordinates. DSFiLM injects separate motion, inflow, and force routes before and after operator computation through current-feature-driven slot- and channel-wise gates. We evaluate twelve matched backbone architectures with different existing physical and temporal inputs. The immersed-boundary computational fluid dynamics (CFD) benchmark spans prescribed motion, inflow disturbances, body-force actuation, and morphology. Across twelve matched backbones, three regimes, and two lead ranges, STCO yields mean paired reductions of 31.1% in relative-L2 field error and 24.7% in normalized pressure-derived load error. It also lowers longer-lead field error for 11 backbones, while interventions on individual condition groups produce measurable prediction changes for every group evaluated.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a unified conditional interface, STCO, that lets many different neural operator backbones incorporate prescribed future conditions (motion, inflow, forcing), greatly improving long-horizon predictions for controlled fluid simulations.
AI.motivation: Existing neural operators for time-dependent PDE systems typically predict future states based only on past observed states and static parameters. In many practical tasks like control and optimization, the future evolution is also driven by prescribed conditions (e.g., planned body motion, inflow patterns, or external forcing) that are not determined solely by the observed state. Current architectures lack a general, principled way to inject such time-targeted conditions, limiting their applicability to controlled scenarios and long-lead predictions.
AI.method: The authors propose the Spatiotemporal Conditional Operator (STCO), a prescribed-condition operator learning (PCOL) framework that can be attached to diverse neural-operator backbones while preserving their core computation. STCO’s condition interface combines two components: (1) Flow-Aware Graph Leaf (FAGL), a non-learned, vorticity-based adaptive partitioning that builds a fixed-cardinality set of regions from the last observed frame and co-locates both the observed history and the target-time condition fields in this regional coordinate system; and (2) Dual-Site Feature-wise Linear Modulation (DSFiLM), which injects motion, inflow, and force information via feature-wise gating applied both before and after the backbone operator computation, using current features to drive slot-wise and channel-wise modulation. They implement STCO on twelve backbone architectures that differ in how they normally handle physical and temporal inputs.
AI.result: On an immersed-boundary CFD benchmark covering several controlled scenarios (prescribed body motion, inflow disturbances, body-force actuation, and morphology changes), the authors test twelve matched backbones with and without STCO across three regimes and two prediction lead times. With STCO, they observe mean paired reductions of 31.1% in relative L2 error of the predicted flow fields and 24.7% in normalized errors of pressure-derived loads. STCO also improves longer-horizon field predictions for 11 of the 12 backbones. Ablation-like interventions that selectively vary individual condition groups (motion, inflow, force) lead to distinct and measurable changes in predictions, indicating that each condition pathway is functionally utilized by the model.
AI.conclusion: STCO provides a general, architecture-agnostic interface for incorporating prescribed future conditions into neural operators for time-dependent PDE systems. By combining flow-aware spatial partitioning with dual-site feature-wise modulation, it enables existing backbones to leverage motion, inflow, and forcing information without redesigning their core structures. The framework consistently improves accuracy, particularly for controlled CFD tasks and longer prediction horizons, and shows that different prescribed condition groups are meaningfully and separately encoded in the resulting models.

title: ASTAR: Automated induction of STAndardized radiology Reporting templates from large-scale clinical free-text corpora
summary: Structured reporting converts free-text radiology narratives into queryable data keys, facilitating cohort assembly, longitudinal tracking, and training label generation for medical AI. The prevailing paradigm follows a two-stage pipeline: (1) constructing a reporting template, (2) extracting information to populate it. While the extraction stage has benefited from advances in large language models (LLMs), template construction remains a manual bottleneck relying on labor-intensive expert consensus that is static, difficult to scale, and may fail to capture real-world reporting diversity. We address this limitation with \textbf{\texttt{ASTAR}}, an LLM-based framework for Automated induction of STAndardized radiology Reporting templates from large-scale clinical free-text corpora. Extensive experiments on 4,215 fetal brain MRI reports from multiple centers demonstrate that the \textbf{\texttt{ASTAR}}-induced template surpasses two expert-curated templates across template coverage, information fidelity, diagnostic fidelity, and expert-rated usability, reducing template development from weeks of committee deliberation to hours of automated processing. Code: https://github.com/birthlab/ASTAR

AI.tldr: ASTAR is an LLM-based framework that automatically induces standardized radiology reporting templates from large-scale free-text reports, outperforming expert-designed templates and drastically reducing development time.
AI.motivation: Current structured radiology reporting relies on manually built templates that require intensive expert consensus, are slow to develop, static, and may not reflect the full diversity of real-world reports. Meanwhile, LLMs have advanced information extraction but have not been fully leveraged to automate template construction itself. There is a need to automatically discover high-quality, standardized templates from existing free-text corpora to enable scalable structured reporting, cohort identification, longitudinal tracking, and AI training label generation.
AI.method: ASTAR uses large language models to automatically infer structured reporting templates from a large corpus of free-text radiology reports. It analyzes many reports—in this study, 4,215 fetal brain MRI reports from multiple centers—to identify and organize the key data elements and structure that should appear in a standardized template. The framework produces candidate templates and likely includes steps for clustering, abstraction, and refinement driven by LLMs, replacing manual committee-based template design with automated processing.
AI.result: On a dataset of 4,215 fetal brain MRI reports from several centers, the ASTAR-generated template outperforms two expert-crafted templates on several metrics: template coverage (how much of the report content fits into the template fields), information fidelity (how accurately the template preserves report information), diagnostic fidelity (how well diagnostic content is retained), and expert-rated usability. The process reduces template development time from weeks of expert meetings to hours of automated computation.
AI.conclusion: Automated, LLM-driven induction of radiology reporting templates from large-scale free-text corpora is feasible and can produce templates that are better than manually designed ones across multiple dimensions, while being far more efficient to create. ASTAR offers a scalable path to standardized structured reporting that can support cohort assembly, longitudinal tracking, and medical AI training, potentially generalizing beyond fetal brain MRI to other radiology domains.

title: Terminal Agents: A Survey of AI Agents in Command-Line Environments
summary: Large language model agents increasingly act through terminals, yet existing surveys disperse terminal-mediated behavior across software engineering, tool use, and computer-use research. We regard terminal agents as systems whose dominant progress-bearing action--observation loop is mediated by terminal command execution, textual feedback, and stateful environment interaction. Using terminal-mediated execution as an organizing lens, this survey establishes workload-level boundaries and connects system architecture, competence acquisition, and evaluation through a seven-dimensional terminal competence profile. Our synthesis shows that realized behavior is jointly shaped by the model, interface, harness, runtime, and environment. Executable trajectories ground learning in action consequences, verification, and recovery, whereas prevailing evaluations emphasize final outcomes and expose process quality, recovery, and governance unevenly. Bounded fixed-condition diagnostics illustrate two implications: benchmark families expose different process signals, and matched system comparisons reveal benchmark-dependent performance and limits of component attribution. These findings motivate explicit reporting of system and runtime conditions, supported by replayable traces and process-level evidence. The framework provides a unified basis for studying terminal-mediated agency across software engineering and emerging application domains.

AI.tldr: The paper surveys and systematizes research on large language model agents that interact with computers via terminals, proposing a unified framework for analyzing their capabilities and evaluations.
AI.motivation: Research on LLM-based agents that use terminals is fragmented across multiple domains like software engineering and tool use, making it hard to compare systems, understand their behavior, and evaluate them consistently. There is a need for a coherent framework that defines what terminal agents are, how they are architected, how they acquire competence, and how they should be evaluated, particularly given that current evaluations focus mostly on final task outcomes rather than process quality or environment interactions.
AI.method: The authors conduct a structured survey using "terminal-mediated execution" as the central organizing concept. They define terminal agents as systems whose main perception–action loop is mediated by terminal commands and textual feedback, and then develop a seven-dimensional terminal competence profile that links system architecture, competence acquisition methods, and evaluation practices. They analyze how different components—model, interface, harness, runtime, and environment—jointly shape agent behavior. They also run bounded, fixed-condition diagnostic experiments using benchmark families and matched system comparisons to illustrate how process-level signals and component contributions vary across benchmarks.
AI.result: The survey finds that terminal-agent behavior cannot be attributed to the model alone; instead, it emerges from interactions among the model, interface, harness, runtime, and environment. Executable trajectories enable learning from action consequences and support verification and recovery, but most existing evaluations overlook these trajectories and instead emphasize final task outcomes. The diagnostic studies demonstrate that different benchmark families reveal different aspects of process quality, recovery, and governance, and that system performance and perceived component importance depend strongly on the chosen benchmarks. This highlights inconsistencies and blind spots in current evaluation practices.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that terminal-mediated execution is a useful unifying lens for studying LLM agents across software engineering and other domains. It argues that future work should explicitly report system and runtime conditions, and support replayable traces and process-level evidence to make evaluations more transparent and comparable. The proposed seven-dimensional terminal competence profile and associated framework provide a common basis for analyzing, designing, and assessing terminal agents, clarifying workload boundaries and surfacing the limits of current benchmarking and component attribution.

title: When Do LLMs Replace Fine-Tuned NLU? A Decision Framework for Intent Detection in Production Conversational Systems
summary: A common claim is that zero-shot large language models (LLMs) can replace fine-tuned NLU classifiers for intent detection. We test this claim head-to-head and find that the honest answer is: it depends on the intent space. On full ATIS and CLINC150 we compare a fine-tuned RoBERTa, a TF-IDF+logistic-regression baseline, sentence-embedding kNN, and Claude Haiku zero-shot, reporting bootstrap 95% confidence intervals and paired significance tests. When abundant in-domain labels exist, fine-tuned RoBERTa is as good or better and three orders of magnitude cheaper and faster: on ATIS it beats Claude zero-shot by 11.8 points (95.9 vs. 84.1, p<0.001). On the broad 150-intent CLINC150 schema the two are statistically tied (89.1 vs. 88.5, p=0.24): the LLM matches a fully supervised model with no training data. The LLM's advantages appear in three production-relevant regimes: out-of-scope detection (OOS recall 85.6 vs. 58.1 for RoBERTa); robustness to realistic ASR noise via a controlled text-to-speech to noise to Whisper pipeline (92.5 vs. 80.0 at 0 dB); and dynamic per-deployment schemas, where a classifier trained on one app's intents scores 0% on a new app's intents while the schema-prompted LLM serves both at ~94% with zero retraining. We distill these findings into a decision framework for practitioners.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically compares zero-shot large language models with traditional fine-tuned NLU classifiers for intent detection and shows that which is better depends on the intent schema and deployment regime.
AI.motivation: Many practitioners hope to replace task-specific, fine-tuned NLU intent classifiers with general-purpose, zero-shot LLMs to save on data labeling and model training costs. However, it is unclear when this is actually beneficial, how performance compares across different intent schemas, and what trade-offs exist in terms of cost, speed, robustness, and out-of-domain handling. The paper aims to provide a rigorous, head-to-head evaluation to guide real-world deployment decisions.
AI.method: The authors run controlled experiments on the ATIS and CLINC150 intent-classification benchmarks. They compare four systems: (1) a fine-tuned RoBERTa classifier, (2) a TF-IDF plus logistic regression baseline, (3) a sentence-embedding k-nearest-neighbor classifier, and (4) a zero-shot Claude Haiku LLM using schema-based prompting. They evaluate accuracy, out-of-scope (OOS) detection, robustness to ASR noise through a text-to-speech → noise injection → Whisper ASR pipeline, and performance under dynamic per-deployment intent schemas. They report bootstrap 95% confidence intervals and paired significance tests to assess differences.
AI.result: On ATIS, where abundant in-domain labels exist and the intent space is narrower, fine-tuned RoBERTa substantially outperforms the zero-shot LLM (95.9 vs. 84.1 accuracy, p<0.001) while being about three orders of magnitude cheaper and faster. On CLINC150, a broader and more complex 150-intent schema, Claude Haiku zero-shot essentially matches the fully supervised RoBERTa (88.5 vs. 89.1, p=0.24), achieving similar performance with no labeled training data. The LLM shows clear advantages in three regimes: (1) out-of-scope detection, with much higher OOS recall (85.6 vs. 58.1 for RoBERTa); (2) robustness to realistic ASR noise, where it maintains higher accuracy through a noisy TTS→noise→Whisper pipeline (92.5 vs. 80.0 at 0 dB); and (3) dynamic, app-specific intent schemas, where traditional classifiers trained on one app completely fail (0% on new intents) but the schema-prompted LLM reaches ~94% on multiple deployments without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Zero-shot LLMs do not universally dominate or replace fine-tuned NLU classifiers for intent detection; their relative value depends on the intent schema and deployment scenario. When rich in-domain labels are available and speed/cost are critical, fine-tuned models like RoBERTa remain highly competitive and often superior. However, zero-shot LLMs are compelling in settings with broad or evolving intent spaces, limited labeled data, strong OOS requirements, ASR noise, and frequent schema changes across deployments. The authors summarize these trade-offs into a practical decision framework to help practitioners choose between (or combine) fine-tuned classifiers and zero-shot LLMs for production intent detection systems.

title: Lost in Translation: How Universal Ethical Values Fail to Translate Across Global Contexts
summary: AI ethics frameworks treat values such as fairness, transparency, and accountability as universal and uniformly operationalizable across contexts. We examined how 14 experts across 10 countries made sense of AI in practice, reinterpreted core values, and envisioned governance alternatives. We found that AI deployment is characterized by structurally unequal conditions, marked by infrastructural constraints, extractive practices, and a "mystification" of technology, which fundamentally shape perceptions of risks and opportunities. Our findings reveal that experts reinterpret values to fit local moral logics: privacy as collective and relational rather than individual; transparency as trust-building accountability rather than technical disclosure; and fairness as equity in access and representation rather than parity in outcomes. We identify these as translation gaps between encoded global frameworks and situated local practices. Finally, we propose pathways toward plural governance that redistributes epistemic authority and treats ethical negotiation as an ongoing, context-sensitive process rather than a settled technical standard.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that global AI ethics frameworks fail to capture how core values are understood and applied in diverse local contexts, and proposes more plural, context-sensitive governance that redistributes who gets to define ethical AI.
AI.motivation: Most AI ethics guidelines assume that values like fairness, transparency, and accountability are universal and can be implemented in the same way everywhere. However, AI is deployed under very different social, economic, and infrastructural conditions worldwide. The authors want to understand how practitioners in varied settings actually interpret these values in practice, what mismatches arise between global principles and local realities, and how governance could better reflect situated ethical perspectives.
AI.method: The authors conducted a qualitative study with 14 AI experts across 10 countries. Through interviews or similar in-depth engagements, they analyzed how these experts: (1) understand AI in their specific practical contexts, (2) reinterpret canonical AI ethics values (fairness, transparency, privacy, accountability), and (3) imagine alternative governance arrangements. They used thematic analysis to identify patterns in how global ethical terms are locally translated and where tensions or gaps emerge.
AI.result: They find that AI deployment happens in structurally unequal environments shaped by limited infrastructure, extractive data and labor practices, and a general mystification of AI technologies. These conditions strongly influence how risks and benefits are perceived. Experts do not simply apply global AI ethics concepts as written; instead, they reinterpret them according to local moral logics: privacy becomes collective and relational (not only individual control of data), transparency is framed as building trust and enabling accountability (not just technical explainability), and fairness is seen as improving equity in access and representation (not only equal performance metrics). The authors label the tension between global ethical codifications and local reinterpretations as “translation gaps.”
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that current AI ethics frameworks, designed as universal technical standards, are insufficient because they ignore how ethical values are reinterpreted in diverse local contexts, especially under structural inequalities. To address this, governance should be plural and context-sensitive: it should redistribute epistemic authority so that local actors have a stronger role in defining what ethical AI means for them, and it should treat ethics as an ongoing process of negotiation rather than a fixed checklist of principles. This implies moving from one-size-fits-all frameworks toward participatory, locally grounded governance arrangements for AI.

title: An ambiguity taxonomy for evaluating large language model performance on clinical registry abstraction: a multi-site prospective study
summary: Objective: To evaluate large language model (LLM) performance on unprocessed electronic medical record (EMR) data for clinical registry abstraction. Methods: We evaluated LLM performance answering registry questions for the American College of Cardiology National Cardiovascular Data Registry (ACC NCDR). In a pilot study at an academic medical center, the model identified candidate data sources for each registry question and experienced abstractors used these results to define question-specific document sets. In a validation study at a second center with a second ACC NCDR registry, the LLM answered questions using the question-specific document sets. Before reviewing any output, two abstractors independently established the ground truth and assigned each question to one of six categories, ordered by the ambiguity and clinical reasoning required to resolve it: Medication/Event Flag, Binary Clinical Presence, Administrative, Quantitative Laboratory/Physiologic, Clinical Interpretation, and Event Timing. Results: The analytical sample comprised 9,430 abstractor answers reconciled to 4,715 consensus answers (501 pilot; 4,214 validation). In the pilot, candidate data sources per question averaged between 14.6 (SD 13.9) for demographics and 89.2 (SD 56.1) for history and risk factors. In validation, human inter-rater agreement was approximately 98\% while 87\% of LLM answers exactly matched consensus, 2\% partially, and 9\% did not. Mean question-level accuracy was 91.5\% (SD 13.4\%) across 157 questions with at least 20 answers, and declined as ambiguity increased, from 96\% for Medication/Event Flag to 62\% for Event Timing questions. Conclusions: LLMs answering clinical registry questions on unprocessed EMR data achieved far lower accuracy than human abstractors. LLM accuracy fell steadily as ambiguity and the level of required clinical reasoning increased.

AI.tldr: The paper tests how well a large language model can answer clinical registry questions directly from raw EMR data, finding it is less accurate than human abstractors, especially for more ambiguous, reasoning-heavy questions.
AI.motivation: Manual abstraction of clinical registries from EMRs is labor-intensive, costly, and subject to variability. There is strong interest in automating this process using LLMs that can read unstructured clinical notes directly, but it is unclear how well such models perform on real registry tasks with unprocessed EMR data, and how their performance varies by question type and required clinical reasoning.
AI.method: The authors evaluated an LLM on questions from American College of Cardiology National Cardiovascular Data Registry (ACC NCDR) instruments across two centers and two registries. In a pilot study, the model was used to identify likely source documents in the EMR for each registry question; human abstractors used these results to define question-specific document sets. In a subsequent validation study at another center and registry, the LLM answered registry questions using only these curated document sets. Two independent human abstractors first established ground-truth answers and categorized each question into one of six types reflecting increasing ambiguity and reasoning demands: Medication/Event Flag, Binary Clinical Presence, Administrative, Quantitative Lab/Physiologic, Clinical Interpretation, and Event Timing. The authors then compared LLM outputs to human consensus answers, measuring exact and partial matches, question-level accuracy, and how performance varied by category.
AI.result: From 9,430 initial abstractor answers, the authors reconciled 4,715 consensus answers (501 from pilot, 4,214 from validation). In the pilot, the LLM suggested many potential data sources per question (mean ranging from about 15 for demographic items to about 89 for history/risk factor items), indicating the broad dispersion of relevant information across the EMR. In the validation cohort, human inter-rater agreement was roughly 98%, whereas the LLM exactly matched the consensus in 87% of answers, partially matched in 2%, and failed in 9%. Considering the 157 questions with at least 20 LLM answers, mean question-level accuracy was 91.5% (SD 13.4%), but performance decreased as question ambiguity and required reasoning increased: about 96% accuracy for simple Medication/Event Flag questions and down to about 62% for Event Timing questions requiring more complex interpretation.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can read raw EMR data and answer many structured registry questions with relatively high but still inferior accuracy compared to trained human abstractors. Their performance is strongly sensitive to question type, with substantial degradation as ambiguity and the need for nuanced clinical reasoning or temporal inference increase. Therefore, current LLMs are not ready to fully replace human abstractors for clinical registry abstraction, particularly for complex or interpretive data elements, and are better suited for assisting with simpler, more concrete questions while maintaining human oversight.

title: A Temporal Planning Approach for Intelligent Flood Response
summary: Effective response to multiple, simultaneously flooded areas requires coordinating appropriate actions in the correct temporal order, under severe resource constraints. Automated planning provides a foundation for addressing this challenge by generating time-aware schedules, given a formal description of available resources, constraints, and goals. This work presents an intelligent flood-response framework that exploits temporal planning and models the complete operational life cycle of flood response. The framework incorporates priority-driven triage, route accessibility and travel costs, resource allocation, and supply management, while also supporting mid-execution re-planning in response to unexpected environmental changes. The framework is formulated both in the Action Notation Modeling Language (ANML) and the Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) 2.1, facilitating compatibility with a wider range of temporal planners. Experimental results establish the feasibility and scalability of the proposed framework, showing that flood response scenarios can be effectively modeled and solved using temporal planning, while providing guidance on planner selection.

AI.tldr: They build and experimentally evaluate a temporal-automated-planning framework to coordinate multi-stage, resource-constrained emergency responses to simultaneous flood incidents.
AI.motivation: Coordinating responses to multiple, simultaneously flooded areas is complex: actions must be ordered in time, resources are scarce, routes can become inaccessible, and conditions can change unexpectedly. Existing tools either do not model temporal and resource constraints in sufficient detail or do not support full operational life-cycle management and dynamic re-planning. The authors aim to show that modern temporal planners, if given an appropriate domain model, can realistically support flood-response decision making at scale.
AI.method: They design an intelligent flood-response framework grounded in temporal automated planning. The flood-response domain is formally modeled in both ANML and PDDL 2.1, capturing: (1) priority-based triage of affected areas, (2) route accessibility and travel costs, (3) allocation of limited teams and equipment, and (4) supply management across the entire response life cycle. The framework supports mid-execution re-planning to react to environmental changes (e.g., new blockages or demands).
