They run experiments with different temporal planners to test feasibility, scalability, and performance on synthetic or realistic flood scenarios.
AI.result: The experiments show that temporal planners can generate feasible, time-aware response schedules for complex, multi-area flood scenarios within reasonable computational limits. The modeling in both ANML and PDDL 2.1 is expressive enough to capture key operational constraints, and the planners can scale as scenario size and complexity grow, though with performance differences that provide empirical guidance on which planners are better suited under various conditions.
AI.conclusion: Temporal automated planning is a viable and scalable approach for coordinating complex flood-response operations under resource and timing constraints. The proposed framework successfully models the entire operational life cycle, handles priorities, travel and accessibility, resource allocation, and supply logistics, and can adapt plans mid-execution as conditions change. The dual ANML/PDDL 2.1 formulation broadens compatibility with existing planners and offers practical guidance on planner selection for real-world flood-response decision support systems.

title: VA-DPO: Valence-Arousal Direct Preference Optimization for Controllable Emotion Generation in Language Models
summary: How precisely can we tell a language model how to feel? Most work on emotional generation answers with a discrete label - happy, angry, sad - which cannot express a target like "mildly downcast but calm." We instead specify the desired affect as a continuous point (v*, a*) in the Valence-Arousal plane and train the model to hit it. Our method, VA-DPO, is a small modification to Direct Preference Optimization: a frozen VA regressor scores each sampled generation by its Euclidean distance to the target, we keep only candidate pairs whose distance gap clears a margin tau, and we optimize a LoRA adapter with the ordinary DPO loss against a frozen reference. The DPO objective itself is unchanged; what is new is how the preference data is built. On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct this cuts mean VA distance to the target by 33% over system-prompting and 25% over few-shot prompting, lifting valence/arousal correlation to r_v=0.93 and r_a=0.75. The gains carry over to Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.2-3B, and they do not come at the usual price: MMLU is unchanged (Delta=+0.0) and HellaSwag and TruthfulQA are preserved. We release the code, configs, and the preference-construction pipeline.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VA-DPO, a method to steer language models toward precise, continuous emotional targets in the Valence-Arousal space, improving control without hurting general capabilities.
AI.motivation: Existing emotional text generation mostly uses coarse, discrete emotion labels (e.g., happy, sad, angry), which cannot express nuanced affective targets such as “mildly downcast but calm.” The authors want a way to control a model’s emotional tone more precisely and continuously, while preserving its general task performance.
AI.method: They represent desired affect as a continuous point (v*, a*) in the Valence-Arousal (VA) plane. For training, they adapt Direct Preference Optimization (DPO): (1) Use a frozen VA regressor to score generations by Euclidean distance to the target (v*, a*). (2) Construct preference pairs only from samples whose distance difference exceeds a margin τ, treating the closer one as preferred. (3) Optimize a LoRA adapter on top of a base model with the standard DPO loss, using a frozen reference model; the DPO objective remains unchanged, only the data construction is new. This pipeline is called VA-DPO.
AI.result: On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, VA-DPO reduces mean VA distance to the target by 33% compared with system-prompt-based control and by 25% compared with few-shot prompting. It also increases correlation with target valence and arousal to r_v = 0.93 and r_a = 0.75. The improvements generalize to other models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.2-3B). Importantly, standard benchmarks like MMLU, HellaSwag, and TruthfulQA show no degradation (MMLU Δ = +0.0, others preserved).
AI.conclusion: VA-DPO enables fine-grained, continuous control over the emotional tone of language model outputs in the Valence-Arousal space by repurposing DPO with a VA-based preference construction process. It significantly improves alignment with target affect while maintaining general performance, and the authors provide code, configurations, and the data construction pipeline for reproducibility and adoption.

title: FL-MAESTRO: Multi-Agent LLM Orchestration for Resource-Constrained Federated Learning
summary: In Federated Learning (FL), the communication topology is a runtime variable rather than a fixed design choice, since links and edge devices drop in and out during training. Each round, the server must commit three coupled decisions, namely the communication topology, per-client resource allocation, and the aggregation rule for combining local updates. Recent agentic systems have begun bringing large language models (LLM) into FL, but the existing line of work either operates at setup time or handles a single runtime dimension such as client selection. We propose FL-MAESTRO, a multi-agent orchestrator that makes the joint runtime FL decision directly through three specialist LLM agents, one per decision dimension. A coordinator combines their analyses into a single decision, and a non-LLM feasibility check confirms it before the round executes. Because the orchestrator consumes the server's predicted-failure list, it withholds clients whose updates would never be aggregated, which removes the dominant source of wasted round energy in classical FL on volatile edge networks. Because client state is read as natural-text profiles, the same orchestrator extends to heterogeneous device classes without per-class energy models. On a non-IID CIFAR-10 benchmark, FL-MAESTRO matches the accuracy of the strongest energy-aware baseline while cutting wasted round energy from over a third to near zero. Code is available at https://github.com/denoslab/FL-MAESTRO.

AI.tldr: Proposes FL-MAESTRO, a multi-agent LLM-based orchestrator that jointly decides FL communication topology, per-client resource allocation, and aggregation rules at runtime, significantly reducing wasted energy while maintaining accuracy.
AI.motivation: In real-world federated learning, edge devices and links frequently drop in and out, making the communication topology a dynamic runtime variable rather than a fixed design parameter. Existing LLM-based or heuristic approaches either only configure FL at setup time or focus on a single runtime aspect like client selection, failing to holistically manage topology, resource allocation, and aggregation under volatility. This leads to substantial wasted energy, especially on clients whose updates are never aggregated due to failures, and complicates handling heterogeneous device classes that require different energy models.
AI.method: Introduce FL-MAESTRO, a multi-agent LLM-based orchestration framework for FL. It uses three specialist LLM agents, each responsible for one of the joint runtime decisions: (1) communication topology, (2) per-client resource allocation, and (3) aggregation rule for combining updates. A coordinator agent fuses the three agents’ analyses into a unified decision. Before execution, a non-LLM feasibility check validates the joint decision. The orchestrator ingests the server’s predicted-failure list and natural-language client profiles, enabling it to proactively exclude clients whose updates are unlikely to be aggregated and to generalize across heterogeneous device classes without explicit per-class energy models.
AI.result: On a non-IID CIFAR-10 benchmark, FL-MAESTRO attains accuracy comparable to the strongest existing energy-aware baseline while drastically reducing wasted round energy from more than one-third of total energy to nearly zero. The method thus preserves model performance while achieving substantially improved energy efficiency in volatile federated settings.
AI.conclusion: Joint, runtime decision-making for topology, resource allocation, and aggregation in FL can be effectively managed by a multi-agent LLM-based orchestrator. By leveraging predicted-failure information and natural-language client profiles, FL-MAESTRO generalizes across heterogeneous devices and nearly eliminates wasted round energy without sacrificing accuracy, offering a practical path to more efficient, robust federated learning on volatile edge networks.

title: GRAFT: Adaptive DLM-Based Draft Tree Construction with Target-Distilled Edge Scoring
summary: Tree-based speculative decoding raises the mean accepted tokens of standard speculative decoding by verifying multiple draft paths, and existing tree builders typically construct these paths through parent-conditioned expansion, where each child token is generated conditioned on its parent path. This construction is incompatible with diffusion language model (DLM) drafters such as DFlash, which produces all future-position distributions in a single forward pass. DDTree bridges this gap by treating high-probability tokens from each future-position distribution as candidate nodes and selecting edges between consecutive positions under a fixed node budget. However, its edge selection relies on token probability alone without modeling parent--child compatibility, so target-compatible tokens can be attached to wrong parents; moreover, its fixed budget ignores that the throughput-optimal tree size varies with the decoding state. We propose GRAFT, a draft-tree construction framework for DLM-based speculative decoding. GRAFT introduces Target-Distilled Edge Scoring (TDES), which distills parent--child preferences from target-model traces to select target-compatible edges, and State-Aware Budget Allocation (SABA), which sets the per-round tree budget by balancing expected draft gain against verification cost. Across multiple models and tasks, GRAFT achieves $2.13\times$--$6.36\times$ end-to-end speedup over autoregressive decoding while adding less than $0.5$\,ms of overhead per round, approximately $1.4\%$ of the target-model verification latency.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GRAFT, a new framework to construct speculative decoding trees for diffusion language models, improving speed while keeping overhead very low.
AI.motivation: Existing tree-based speculative decoding methods assume parent-conditioned expansion and thus are incompatible or suboptimal for diffusion language model drafters that output all future token distributions at once. Prior DLM tree methods like DDTree ignore parent–child compatibility and use a fixed tree-size budget, which can attach tokens to wrong parents and fail to adapt tree size to the current decoding state, limiting throughput and speedup.
AI.method: The authors introduce GRAFT, a draft-tree construction framework for DLM-based speculative decoding. It has two main components: (1) Target-Distilled Edge Scoring (TDES), which learns or distills edge scores (parent–child preferences) from target model traces so that candidate edges in the tree better reflect which child tokens are compatible with which parent tokens; and (2) State-Aware Budget Allocation (SABA), which dynamically allocates a tree size (node/edge budget) per decoding round by trading off expected draft gain against the cost of verifying the draft with the target model. The framework operates under a fixed node budget but selects edges using these refined scores, constructing more target-compatible and throughput-optimal trees for DLM drafts.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple models and tasks show that GRAFT yields between 2.13× and 6.36× end-to-end speedup over standard autoregressive decoding, while its own overhead per speculative round is less than 0.5 ms—about 1.4% of the target model’s verification latency. This demonstrates both substantial performance gains and negligible additional compute cost for tree construction.
AI.conclusion: Modeling parent–child compatibility in draft-tree construction and adapting the tree budget to the decoding state are crucial for getting the most benefit from DLM-based speculative decoding. GRAFT, via TDES and SABA, significantly improves throughput and speed over both autoregressive decoding and prior DLM tree builders like DDTree, with minimal overhead, making it a practical solution for accelerating diffusion language model decoding.

title: Volumetric Radiology AI in the Era of Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are extending radiological artificial intelligence (AI) beyond task-specific image analysis toward multimodal understanding and reasoning. Volumetric radiology, however, presents a fundamental representational mismatch: clinical interpretation often requires full-volume spatial context and acquisition-dependent quantitative information, whereas current MLLMs are commonly conditioned on selected two-dimensional (2D) images, compressed visual representations, or report-derived text. Reliable volumetric radiology AI therefore requires representations that preserve task-relevant three-dimensional (3D) information and systems that can access, verify, and integrate this information across clinical workflows. In this Review, we examine more than 200 publications through July 2026. We organize the literature around volumetric representation and multimodal understanding at the model level, agentic orchestration at the system level, and their links to clinical applications and evaluation. We review volumetric foundation models, language alignment and compression strategies, and agentic systems that extend MLLMs through planning, tools, memory, and workflow interaction. We distinguish settings in which selected 2D views or report-mediated reasoning may suffice from those that warrant native volumetric modeling. We also introduce a Claim-Design-Validation framework to assess whether technical, workflow, and clinical claims are matched by appropriate design and validation. Across the literature, native volumetric modeling and agentic capabilities depend on the spatial, quantitative, contextual, and workflow requirements of the intended task. Clinical credibility requires faithful volumetric representation, traceable system behavior, claim-aligned validation, and clearly defined human oversight in realistic workflows.

AI.tldr: The paper reviews how multimodal large language models can be extended for volumetric (3D) radiology, emphasizing the need for representations and systems that preserve full 3D information and integrate into clinical workflows.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal large language models mostly use 2D images or text, which mismatches the inherently 3D, quantitative nature of volumetric radiology. There is a need to understand how to build AI systems that can handle full volumetric data and operate reliably within clinical settings.
AI.method: The authors conduct a narrative review of over 200 publications up to July 2026. They organize prior work into categories: volumetric representation and multimodal understanding at the model level; agentic orchestration at the system level; links to clinical applications and evaluation. They analyze different representation strategies, model architectures, and system designs, and propose an assessment framework (Claim-Design-Validation).
AI.result: The review identifies key approaches for volumetric foundation models, language alignment and compression, and agentic systems (planning, tools, memory, workflow interaction). It clarifies when 2D or report-based reasoning is sufficient versus when native volumetric modeling is necessary. It shows that successful systems must match their technical choices and evaluation methods to the task’s spatial, quantitative, and workflow demands.
AI.conclusion: Effective AI for volumetric radiology requires native 3D representations where clinically needed, along with agentic systems that can access and reason over volumetric data within real workflows. Clinical credibility hinges on faithful volumetric modeling, transparent and traceable behavior, validation aligned with stated claims, and explicit human oversight in realistic clinical settings.

title: TH-GNN: Heterogeneous Temporal Graph Neural Networks for LLM-Agent Shilling Attack Detection
summary: LLM agents can now generate realistic shilling profiles, fluent reviews, and coherent ratings at scale, systematically defeating recommender-system defenses. Text-only detectors that flag semantic drift in review embeddings are blind to graph structure and temporal coordination, while graph-only detectors that exploit neighborhood anomalies cannot reason over review semantics or the cross-modal inconsistencies produced by LLM-generated content. We propose TH-GNN, a heterogeneous temporal graph neural network with a two-layer Heterogeneous Graph Transformer backbone that applies per-type and per-relation attention augmented with learnable sinusoidal temporal encodings on every edge. Cross-modal attention fuses structural user embeddings with frozen RoBERTa representations of reviews and item descriptions, while a GRU operating over log inter-arrival times captures temporal burstiness. Evaluated across five attack families and four benchmark datasets, TH-GNN achieves a grand-mean F1 score of 0.870, outperforming the strongest text-only baseline on Agent4SR attacks by 10.9 percentage points and 11.5 percentage points at the lowest injection rate. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of jointly modeling temporal, structural, and semantic signals for detecting sophisticated LLM-driven shilling attacks.

AI.tldr: They propose TH-GNN, a temporal heterogeneous graph neural network that jointly models graph structure, time, and text to detect sophisticated LLM-driven shilling attacks in recommender systems, substantially outperforming text-only and graph-only defenses.
AI.motivation: Current recommender-system defenses are increasingly vulnerable to shilling attacks generated by large language model (LLM) agents, which can create realistic profiles, reviews, and ratings at scale. Existing detectors are limited: text-only methods rely on semantic signals and ignore the relational and temporal coordination patterns of attacks, while graph-only methods cannot interpret review semantics or inconsistencies between text and user/item graphs. There is a need for a unified approach that leverages structural, temporal, and semantic cues to robustly detect coordinated, LLM-based shilling campaigns.
AI.method: They introduce TH-GNN, a heterogeneous temporal graph neural network tailored to user–item–review data. The backbone is a two-layer Heterogeneous Graph Transformer that applies attention specific to node/edge types and relations, enhanced by learnable sinusoidal temporal encodings on every edge to capture time information. The model uses cross-modal attention to fuse structural user embeddings with frozen RoBERTa text embeddings of reviews and item descriptions, enabling reasoning over both graph structure and semantics. Additionally, a GRU processes log inter-arrival times of events to model temporal burstiness indicative of coordinated attacks.
AI.result: Across four benchmark datasets and five types of shilling attack families, including sophisticated Agent4SR LLM-based attacks, TH-GNN attains a grand-mean F1 score of 0.870. It outperforms the best text-only baseline by 10.9 F1 points on Agent4SR attacks and by 11.5 points under the lowest attack injection rate, indicating superior robustness in challenging and low-signal settings.
AI.conclusion: Jointly modeling temporal dynamics, graph structure, and textual semantics via a heterogeneous temporal GNN with cross-modal fusion significantly improves detection of advanced, LLM-driven shilling attacks in recommender systems. The TH-GNN framework addresses the blind spots of text-only and graph-only defenses and offers a more resilient approach against coordinated, realistic adversarial behavior at scale.

title: Consilience: Conformally Calibrated Communication Control for Hidden-Profile Multi-Agent Reasoning
comment: 39 pages, 2 figures, 9 tables. Includes appendix with full proof of Proposition 1, expanded results, ablations, and complete prompt templates
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems can improve reasoning by pooling diverse perspectives, but their effectiveness depends on coordinating communication, particularly in hidden-profile settings where each agent holds only part of the evidence required for a correct decision. Existing protocols, including fixed schedules, round-robin exchange, and unstructured debate, provide no guarantee that a conversational action is appropriate. We propose Consilience, an inference-time orchestration framework that both steers and certifies multi-agent communication under distributed private information. At each turn, Consilience summarizes the discussion using a compact state capturing uncertainty, disagreement, evidence gain, redundancy, and premature consensus, then selects both a communication intervention (challenge, clarify, seek evidence, or route) and an appropriate speaker. Its central contribution is a round-wise conformal calibration procedure that provides a distribution-free, finite-sample guarantee: at each discussion round, conditional on reaching that round, the one-step regret of a controller's proposed action is bounded by a calibrated threshold with marginal probability at least 1 - alpha; an acceptance mechanism enforces the same guarantee for the executed action by replacing inadmissible proposals. On HiddenBench-style hidden-profile tasks spanning 12 open and closed weight language models, Consilience improves decision accuracy and communication efficiency over fixed and unstructured discussion protocols, sometimes surpassing a full-information baseline where every agent observes all evidence. These results demonstrate that certified adaptive communication control can be more valuable than increasing information availability, providing a practical mechanism for reliable multi-agent LLM coordination.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Consilience, a framework that orchestrates and certifies multi-agent LLM discussions under distributed, private evidence, improving accuracy and efficiency in hidden-profile tasks with formal regret guarantees.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM setups can reason better by combining diverse agents, but current communication protocols (fixed schedules, round-robin, free-form debate) lack any guarantee that each conversational move is useful, especially when evidence is privately distributed across agents. In hidden-profile settings, this can lead to missed critical evidence, premature consensus, and inefficient or redundant communication. The authors aim to design a controller that not only coordinates which agent speaks and how, but also offers statistical guarantees that each step is near-optimal, making multi-agent communication reliable rather than ad hoc.
AI.method: They propose Consilience, an inference-time orchestration framework for multi-agent LLMs. At each discussion turn, Consilience builds a compact state summarizing the conversation so far, encoding uncertainty, disagreement among agents, evidence gained, redundancy, and indicators of premature consensus. Based on this state, a controller chooses both (1) a communication intervention type (e.g., challenge a claim, clarify something, seek new evidence, or route information) and (2) which agent should speak. The key technical ingredient is a round-wise conformal calibration procedure: for each round, conditional on having reached that round, they estimate a calibrated threshold on one-step regret (the performance gap between the chosen action and the best possible action). They then enforce a guarantee that the proposed action’s regret stays below this threshold with probability at least 1 − alpha. An acceptance mechanism can reject inadmissible proposed actions and replace them to maintain this guarantee. They evaluate Consilience on HiddenBench-style hidden-profile benchmarks across 12 language models of varying sizes and architectures.
AI.result: On hidden-profile decision-making tasks, Consilience yields higher final decision accuracy and better communication efficiency (fewer, more targeted exchanges) than standard baselines like fixed turn-taking or unstructured debate. In some cases, its performance even surpasses a strong baseline where every agent has full access to all evidence, despite Consilience operating under partial information. The conformal calibration ensures that, at each round, the expected one-step regret of the controller’s action is bounded with high probability, and this extends to the actually executed actions through the acceptance mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Consilience shows that adaptively controlled, statistically certified communication among LLM agents can outperform naive multi-agent protocols and even some full-information setups. Rather than simply giving all agents more data, the framework demonstrates that carefully orchestrated, evidence-aware, and regret-bounded interaction can be more valuable. This provides a practical and theoretically grounded method for reliable coordination in multi-agent LLM systems dealing with distributed private information.

title: EditPPT: Faithful Long-Deck Slide Editing via Structured Tool-Using Multi-Agent with Dual-Modal Validators
comment: 30 pages, 7 figures, 17 tables, EMNLP 2026 submitted, under review
summary: Automating slide editing requires simultaneously satisfying modification accuracy, preservation fidelity, and robustness to deck length. Existing LLM-based systems often fail on real-world presentation files because they rely on idealized intermediate representations or open-ended code generation, which are prone to cascading errors in long decks. We introduce EditPPT, a multi-agent framework that reformulates slide editing as a constrained tool-selection problem. By executing localized shape-level operations through the native PowerPoint COM interface, EditPPT narrows the LLM action space while preserving the application-resolved structure of user-authored decks. By separating validation across modalities, our dual-modal validation provides more robust assessment of both instruction fidelity and visual quality. We also present DeckEdit-Bench, a benchmark with 28 human-authored decks, 582 slides, and 183 editing prompts across short, medium, and long deck tiers. Experiments show that EditPPT achieves a 99.5% execution rate, 88.7% slide-targeting F1, 82.5% instruction following, and 91.5% object preservation overall, while maintaining strong performance on long decks. Our code and benchmark are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EditPPT-0E27/

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EditPPT, a multi-agent, tool-based system that reliably edits real-world PowerPoint decks by issuing constrained, shape-level operations via the native COM interface, along with a new benchmark (DeckEdit-Bench) for systematic evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based slide editing systems often fail on realistic, large presentation decks because they depend on idealized intermediate formats or unconstrained code generation, which leads to cascading errors, poor instruction fidelity, and difficulty scaling to long decks. There is a need for a robust, accurate, and scalable method that can operate directly on user-authored PowerPoint files while preserving their structure and visual integrity.
AI.method: The authors propose EditPPT, a multi-agent framework that treats slide editing as a constrained tool-selection problem rather than open-ended code generation. The system interacts directly with PowerPoint through the COM interface to perform localized shape-level edits, reducing the action space and preserving the application-resolved deck structure. It incorporates dual-modal validation that separately evaluates textual/instructional correctness and visual quality. Additionally, the authors create DeckEdit-Bench, a benchmark composed of 28 human-authored decks (582 slides) and 183 editing prompts spanning short, medium, and long decks to test robustness and performance.
AI.result: On DeckEdit-Bench, EditPPT reaches a 99.5% execution success rate, an 88.7% F1 score for correctly identifying and targeting the intended slides, 82.5% instruction-following accuracy, and 91.5% object preservation, while maintaining strong performance even on long decks. These metrics indicate that the system substantially improves reliability and fidelity over prior LLM-based slide editing approaches.
AI.conclusion: EditPPT demonstrates that framing slide editing as constrained tool selection with localized COM-based operations and dual-modal validation leads to robust, high-fidelity editing of real-world PowerPoint decks, including long ones. The accompanying DeckEdit-Bench provides a standardized evaluation suite, and the released code and benchmark aim to facilitate further research on practical, trustworthy slide-editing agents.

title: Open-Weight Masked Introspection: Measuring What Language Models Can Report About Their Own Computation
comment: We release OWMI as a library so that this emerging ability can be measured as it develops. Hugging Face OWMI library: https://huggingface.co/emilioferrara/owmi
summary:
Are frontier models able to introspect about their internal states? Recent work suggests that under certain conditions a complex enough model can audit its own internals, call out what changed, and report back confidently about it. We tested that claim on eight open-weight models from seven families and found no such ability: asked whether their own computation had been altered, none answered better than chance. To test it we built Open-Weight Masked Introspection (OWMI), a framework that intervenes on residual-stream sites, attention heads and sparse-autoencoder features, then interrogates the model about the change against the null conditions an answer has to beat: sham runs where nothing was altered, impact-matched random perturbations, and a text-only observer that sees only the visible output.
  Over 78,000 measurements, no model's report discriminates a real intervention from a sham beyond chance (AUROC ~0.5007), and an equivalence test bounds the effect below 0.15 percentage points of AUROC. Surprisingly, all the information needed is in the models. A model fine-tuned to report this class of intervention reaches near-perfect recovery on held-out directions, and a linear probe recovers intervention presence from the same activations at 75% to 95.8% accuracy, sharpening to no held-out error at the last layer before the model speaks. In one model the signal surfaces in the confidence rather than the words: its yes-or-no report never varies, while the confidence attached to it separates intervention from sham at AUROC 0.647. The failure sits in the path from internal state to verbal report, so oversight that reads a model's own testimony needs validating against an internal reference.
  While our results show the inability of current open-weight models to introspect, the debate is not settled for future models.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether large open-weight language models can accurately introspect about interventions to their internal activations, and finds they cannot, despite the relevant information being linearly recoverable from their states.
AI.motivation: There is growing interest in using models' own verbal reports as a tool for oversight, safety, and interpretability—for example, having a model explain if it has been manipulated or if certain internal circuits are active. Some prior work suggested that sufficiently advanced models might reliably describe changes to their own internals. This paper aims to rigorously test that claim under controlled conditions and quantify how well current open-weight models can detect and report interventions in their own computations.
AI.method: The authors build a framework called Open-Weight Masked Introspection (OWMI). They intervene in specific internal components of models—residual stream positions, attention heads, and sparse autoencoder features—while the model processes text. They then ask the model to verbally report whether an intervention occurred. They compare these reports against several null conditions: sham runs with no intervention, random perturbations matched in impact, and a text-only observer that only sees the outputs. Performance is measured via AUROC over roughly 78,000 measurements across eight open-weight models from seven architectures. They also train a fine-tuned version of a model specifically to report these interventions and fit linear probes to check how easily the intervention signal can be read from activations.
AI.result: Across all tested base models, introspective reports perform no better than chance at distinguishing true interventions from sham conditions, with AUROC around 0.5007, and an equivalence test bounding any effect to within 0.15 percentage points of AUROC. In contrast, the underlying activations contain a strong signal: a simple linear probe can detect interventions with 75–95.8% accuracy, and a fine-tuned model can almost perfectly identify held-out intervention directions. In at least one model, the intervention signal appears in the confidence scores rather than the verbal answer: the model's yes/no text output is constant, but the confidence associated with it separates intervention from sham with AUROC 0.647.
AI.conclusion: Current open-weight frontier models do not possess robust verbal introspective access to whether their internal computations have been perturbed, even though the necessary information is linearly present in their activations and can be exploited by fine-tuning or probes. The limitation lies in the mapping from internal state to natural-language report, meaning that naive reliance on a model's own testimony for oversight is unreliable unless calibrated against internal-readout methods. However, the authors leave open the possibility that future, more advanced or differently trained models could develop reliable introspective capabilities.

title: Decoupled Vision-Language System for Multimodal Understanding and Generation
summary: We introduce a new architecture design for multimodal large language models (MLLMs), Libra, capable of both multimodal understanding and generation. Libra architecture contains one vision system and one language system, connected by cross-modal bridges. This design decouples self-modal modeling and cross-modal interaction, enabling each modality to learn its unique representations while maintaining effective cross-modal comprehension. The decoupling is mainly achieved in a switch attention module and a switch FFN module, which dynamically routes the computation flow for self-modal modeling and cross-modal interaction scenarios. We evaluate the effectiveness in two important settings: \textbf{Libra-1} for the understanding-only image-to-text setting, and \textbf{Libra-2} for unified image-to-text understanding and text-to-image generation. In addition to the architecture design, we discuss various improvements on tokenization, positional encoding, and supervision. Experiments demonstrate that the dedicated Libra design enables mutual improvements on multimodal understanding and generation, achieving strong performance on both understanding and generation benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Libra is a new multimodal large language model architecture that separates within-modality processing from cross-modal interaction via switch attention and switch FFN modules, improving both vision-language understanding and text–image generation.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal LLMs often entangle vision and language processing, which can limit how well each modality learns its own rich representations and how efficiently cross-modal reasoning is performed. There is a need for an architecture that allows strong, specialized modeling for each modality while still supporting effective and flexible multimodal interaction, and that can handle both understanding (image-to-text) and generation (text-to-image) tasks within one framework.
AI.method: The authors design Libra, an MLLM with a separate vision system and language system connected by cross-modal bridges. They introduce switch attention and switch FFN modules that dynamically route computation either to self-modal modeling or to cross-modal interaction paths. They instantiate two variants: Libra-1 for image-to-text understanding only, and Libra-2 for both image-to-text understanding and text-to-image generation. They also refine tokenization, positional encoding, and supervision strategies. They then evaluate Libra on multimodal understanding and generation benchmarks.
AI.result: Libra achieves strong empirical performance on standard benchmarks for both multimodal understanding and text-to-image generation. The architecture’s decoupled design leads to mutual improvements across tasks: enhancing the quality of multimodal understanding also benefits generation, and vice versa. The experiments validate that the switch-based bridging between dedicated vision and language systems is effective.
AI.conclusion: A decoupled yet bridged architecture for MLLMs, realized via switch attention and switch FFN modules between separate vision and language systems, can effectively support both multimodal understanding and generation. Libra’s design and accompanying implementation details (tokenization, positional encoding, supervision) yield strong and mutually reinforcing performance across these tasks, showing that carefully structured cross-modal interaction is a promising direction for future multimodal LLMs.

title: FlavourBench: Ranking Frontier Language Models with Executable Culinary Ground Truth
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures. Evaluation of 27 frontier language-model endpoints on 534 identical tasks per model, comprising 14,418 scored model-task cells. Code: https://github.com/josefchen/flavourbench Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/josefchen/flavourbench Interactive leaderboard: https://huggingface.co/spaces/josefchen/flavourbench
summary: Open-ended language-model benchmarks usually inherit a judge: a human preference panel, another model, or a brittle exact-match key. We introduce FlavourBench, an automated benchmark in which a versioned culinary system supplies dense, executable ground truth. Each task presents eight ingredients and asks for a three-ingredient portfolio; before model execution, Epicure scores all 56 possible portfolios. We evaluate 27 frontier endpoints on an identical 534-task core spanning substitution, pairing, and constrained composition. Every ranked model has exactly 89 valid responses per panel and family (14,418 model-task cells total), eliminating differential missingness from the leaderboard. The FlavourBench Score is the equal-family mean of the frozen task scores. We use 50,000 anchor-cluster bootstrap replicates for simultaneous 95% score bands and 100,000 sign-flip draws for all 351 paired model contrasts, with Holm control. The two independently compiled panels correlate at r = 0.89 (rank rho = 0.80). Grok 4.6 has the largest point estimate at 65.1 (simultaneous 95% CI 61.0-69.2); 101 of 351 model pairs are resolved. The release includes the prompts, all portfolio score maps, raw responses, exact routes, content hashes, and an offline verifier that reconstructs every result.

AI.tldr: FlavourBench is an automated, fully reproducible benchmark for evaluating open-ended language models on culinary reasoning tasks using dense, executable ground truth instead of subjective judges.
AI.motivation: Existing open-ended language-model benchmarks often rely on subjective or fragile evaluation: human preference panels, other models as judges, or exact-match criteria that do not capture nuanced correctness. These approaches introduce noise, bias, and incomplete coverage, and can make leaderboards sensitive to missing or invalid responses. The authors want a benchmark where ground truth is dense, operational, and reproducible, and where scoring is statistically rigorous and not confounded by differential missingness across models.
AI.method: They build an automated culinary evaluation system, Epicure, that assigns scores to all possible 3-ingredient portfolios chosen from 8-ingredient sets in each task (56 portfolios per task). FlavourBench consists of 534 tasks covering substitution, pairing, and constrained composition. For each of 27 language-model endpoints, they collect exactly 89 valid responses per panel and model family, ensuring 14,418 model-task evaluations with no missingness. The FlavourBench Score is defined as the mean task score, averaged equally across model families. For uncertainty and comparison, they run 50,000 anchor-cluster bootstrap replicates to obtain simultaneous 95% confidence bands on scores and 100,000 sign-flip permutations to test all 351 model pairwise contrasts with Holm correction for multiple testing. They compile two independent evaluation panels to test robustness.
AI.result: The two independent panels show strong agreement (correlation r = 0.89, rank correlation rho = 0.80), indicating that the evaluation is stable across panel constructions. Among the 27 evaluated endpoints, Grok 4.6 achieves the highest FlavourBench Score with an estimated 65.1 and a simultaneous 95% confidence interval of 61.0–69.2. Out of 351 possible pairwise model comparisons, 101 are statistically resolved under the sign-flip tests with Holm correction, meaning clear performance differences are established for those pairs.
AI.conclusion: FlavourBench provides a dense, automated, and reproducible benchmark for open-ended language models on culinary reasoning, avoiding the subjectivity and brittleness of traditional judges. Its design enforces equal coverage across models, eliminating differential missingness from leaderboards, and uses rigorous resampling-based statistics for uncertainty quantification and model comparison. The strong agreement between independent panels and the resolution of many pairwise model differences demonstrate that FlavourBench can reliably discriminate between frontier models. The public release of prompts, score maps, responses, verification code, and hashes supports transparency and full offline reproducibility.

title: Using Human-LLM Disagreement to Improve Checklist-Based Quality Appraisal
summary:
Systematic reviews rely on quality appraisal of included studies, a process that is time-consuming and sensitive to ambiguity in checklist criteria. Although large language models (LLMs) offer opportunities to support these tasks, appraisal checklists are typically treated as fixed inputs, and it remains unclear how their design affects agreement with expert judgments. Therefore, we investigate (1) whether LLMs can approximate human judgments in checklist-based appraisal and (2) whether patterns of human-LLM disagreement can be used to identify and improve ambiguous checklist items. Using the Guidelines for Reporting on Latent Trajectory Studies (GRoLTS) checklist, we compare LLM-generated assessments with expert annotations across three research topics and two checklist versions. Agreement is assessed using item-level accuracy, chance-corrected agreement, and preservation of study-level rank ordering.
  We find that performance varies substantially across checklist items, with ambiguous and conditional criteria producing the greatest disagreement. Revising these items improves both raw and chance-corrected agreement. Although item-level misclassifications persist, LLM-generated scores often preserve the relative ranking of studies when high-agreement items are retained. These results indicate that reliable LLM-assisted appraisal depends not only on model choice but also on checklist design. The findings suggest that analyzing human-LLM disagreement can help identify problematic checklist items and support the iterative improvement of research synthesis workflows.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how well large language models can perform checklist-based quality appraisal in systematic reviews, and shows that adjusting ambiguous checklist items improves agreement with human experts and preserves study rankings.
AI.motivation: Systematic reviews need rigorous, checklist-based quality appraisal of studies, but this process is slow and prone to disagreement because checklist criteria can be ambiguous. While LLMs could potentially automate or assist this task, existing work treats appraisal checklists as fixed and does not examine how checklist design itself affects LLM–human agreement. The authors aim to understand both whether LLMs can approximate human judgments and how disagreement patterns can guide refinement of the checklists.
AI.method: The authors use the GRoLTS (Guidelines for Reporting on Latent Trajectory Studies) checklist as a testbed. They obtain expert annotations for studies across three research topics and apply two versions of the GRoLTS checklist (original and revised). They then prompt an LLM to generate checklist-based appraisals for the same studies and compare these to the expert ratings. Agreement is quantified using item-level accuracy, chance-corrected agreement metrics, and the ability of LLM-derived scores to preserve the rank ordering of studies at the overall appraisal level. They further analyze which specific checklist items show most disagreement and revise ambiguous/conditional items to see how performance changes.
AI.result: Performance of the LLM varies markedly by checklist item. Items that are ambiguous or depend on conditional interpretations show the highest human–LLM disagreement. After revising such items, both raw item-level accuracy and chance-corrected agreement between the LLM and experts improve. Even when some item-level errors remain, the aggregate LLM-based scores often maintain the relative ranking of studies, especially when low-agreement items are removed from the scoring. This indicates that LLMs can capture much of the comparative appraisal signal used by experts.
AI.conclusion: LLM-assisted quality appraisal in systematic reviews is feasible but strongly influenced by how appraisal checklists are written. Ambiguous and conditional criteria reduce agreement with expert judgments, whereas refining these items increases reliability. Analyzing where LLMs disagree with humans is a useful diagnostic for identifying problematic checklist items and iteratively improving them. Consequently, future workflows for research synthesis should consider co-designing checklists and LLM prompts, using disagreement analyses to optimize both human and automated appraisal performance.

title: Difficulty-Aware Semantic-ID Optimization for Generative Recommendation
summary: Semantic-ID-based generative recommendation casts retrieval and ranking as autoregressive generation over hierarchical item identifiers. A common recipe is SFT followed by GRPO, yet vanilla GRPO is poorly matched to this tree-structured task. Under the frozen SFT checkpoint, the exact target is absent from the first 16 candidates of the 50-beam constrained ranking for many prompts, and in harder cases none of these candidates enters the target SID branch. This prompt-level diagnostic motivates a training concern: when on-policy GRPO groups are similarly target-missing, item-level rewards may produce weak or degenerate reward variation even if some candidates follow part of the target path. We propose Difficulty-Aware Semantic-ID Optimization (DASO), a tree-aware post-training method that addresses this failure mode as an online rollout-allocation problem. Instead of using fixed difficulty buckets or uniformly injecting ground-truth completions, DASO profiles each current rollout group by prefix-match depth, locates the bottleneck SID levels where candidates leave the target path, and reallocates a bounded portion of the group to prefix-guided completions while retaining raw rollouts for contrast. A SID-prefix reward provides graded credit, while an auxiliary SFT anchor mitigates regression on examples already solved by the SFT checkpoint. On the public benchmarks, DASO improves over MiniOneRec-style GRPO on 11 of 12 metrics and achieves the best result on 9 of 12 metrics; it also improves most level-wise recall metrics on the internal recommendation task.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DASO, a tree-aware post-training method that improves generative recommendation with Semantic-IDs by dynamically reallocating rollouts based on difficulty and prefix matches to the target item path.
AI.motivation: Semantic-ID-based generative recommenders treat item retrieval and ranking as sequence generation over hierarchical item identifiers. Standard post-training uses SFT followed by GRPO. However, GRPO is not well-suited to the tree-structured SID space: for many prompts, even a strong SFT checkpoint fails to generate candidates that reach the correct target branch within a large beam. This implies that, during GRPO, many on-policy rollout groups contain no exact target and may even miss the target branch altogether, causing weak or degenerate reward signals based on item-level rewards. The authors aim to address this mismatch and the resulting inefficiency and instability in training.
AI.method: They propose Difficulty-Aware Semantic-ID Optimization (DASO), a tree-aware post-training framework. DASO treats training as an online rollout allocation problem over the SID tree. For each prompt and its associated rollout group, DASO measures difficulty via prefix-match depth between generated SIDs and the ground-truth SID. It then detects bottleneck SID levels where candidates diverge from the target path. Based on this, DASO reallocates a bounded fraction of rollouts away from purely on-policy sampling to prefix-guided completions that continue along the correct SID prefix, while retaining some raw rollouts for contrastive learning. A SID-prefix reward assigns graded credit according to how far a candidate matches the target path in the tree, rather than only rewarding exact hits. An auxiliary SFT-style anchor loss is used to prevent regression on examples that the original SFT model already solves, stabilizing performance.
AI.result: On public benchmarks, DASO surpasses MiniOneRec-style GRPO baselines on 11 out of 12 overall metrics and sets new best scores on 9 out of 12 metrics. On an internal recommendation task, it improves most level-wise recall metrics across the SID hierarchy, indicating better performance not only at exact item prediction but also at intermediate levels of the tree.
AI.conclusion: DASO effectively adapts GRPO-style post-training to the hierarchical nature of Semantic-ID-based generative recommendation. By being difficulty-aware, using prefix-match diagnostics, reallocating rollouts toward informative prefix-guided completions, and employing graded SID-prefix rewards plus an SFT anchor, it alleviates degenerate reward issues and yields consistent improvements over standard GRPO across public and internal benchmarks.

title: Poly-InstructTTS: Learning In-the-Wild Expressive Speech Synthesis from Open-Ended Instructions
summary: While recent text-to-speech (TTS) models achieve high naturalness, controlling fine-grained expression via natural-language instructions remains challenging. We introduce Poly- InstructTTS, which learns expressive speech from open-ended instructions using in-the-wild audiovisual data. We build a scalable multi-modal pipeline to construct a 1,000-hour instruction-annotated corpus covering 1,000+ fine-grained emotions and styles. The framework uses a prompt-free GPT with attribute-based thinking tokens, followed by a flow-matching module that injects timbre from a reference audio. We also present a speaker fine-tuning procedure to transfer instruction control to specific speakers while preserving persona. We further extend InstructTTSEval with broader tasks. Experiments show that Poly-InstructTTS delivers strong performance in instruction adherence and expressiveness. Audio demos and the expanded testset are available on our project page.

AI.tldr: Poly-InstructTTS is a text-to-speech system that uses large-scale audiovisual data and natural-language instructions to generate highly expressive, controllable speech across many emotions and speaking styles.
AI.motivation: Although modern TTS systems sound natural, they are hard to control at a fine-grained emotional and stylistic level using open-ended natural-language prompts. Existing methods often rely on limited, curated labels, simple style tokens, or reference audio, which restricts expressiveness and scalability. The paper aims to bridge this gap by enabling robust, instruction-driven control of detailed emotions and speaking styles, using large-scale, in-the-wild data.
AI.method: The authors construct a 1,000-hour multimodal corpus where each speech segment is annotated with open-ended natural-language instructions that describe 1,000+ fine-grained emotions and styles. They create a scalable data pipeline from in-the-wild audiovisual sources and use a prompt-free GPT variant augmented with attribute-based thinking tokens to interpret and encode the instructions. A flow-matching module is then used to inject the timbre information from reference audio, separating speaker identity from expressive style. They also design a speaker fine-tuning strategy so that the instruction-based control can be transferred to new speakers while keeping their vocal persona intact. Finally, they extend an existing benchmark, InstructTTSEval, with broader evaluation tasks to better measure instruction adherence and expressiveness.
AI.result: Poly-InstructTTS achieves strong quantitative and qualitative results on instruction following and expressive speech generation compared with baselines. It demonstrates that the model can reliably render a wide spectrum of nuanced emotions and speaking styles directly from textual instructions, while maintaining the intended speaker timbre via the flow-matching module. The extended InstructTTSEval benchmark confirms these gains across more diverse tasks.
AI.conclusion: Learning from large-scale, instruction-annotated, in-the-wild audiovisual data and using a prompt-free GPT with attribute-based thinking tokens enables fine-grained, natural-language control of TTS expressiveness. By decoupling style from speaker timbre and providing a practical speaker fine-tuning method, Poly-InstructTTS offers a scalable approach to controllable expressive TTS, validated by strong performance on an expanded instruction-based evaluation suite.

title: Evaluating Skills, Not Just Agents: Agentic Continuous Evaluation of Skills
comment: 15 pages. Extended preprint incorporating versions accepted at Agent Skills '26 (ACM CAIS 2026) and the KDD 2026 Workshop on Enterprise AI Agents: From Prototypes to Production (oral presentation). Open-source implementation: https://github.com/NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator
summary:
Enterprise agent programs are moving from prototypes into production, where reusable skills, tools, and workflow packages must be reviewed with evidence rather than prose. Current gates often scan these artifacts for structure, style, and security, but they do not answer the deployment question: does the capability package help a live agent complete enterprise tasks under the same model, sandbox, and grading policy?
  We present ACES (Agentic Continuous Evaluation of Skills), a repository-native framework for evaluating skills and product capability packages as executable agent artifacts. ACES runs paired live trials with and without a target skill, normalizes trajectories into the Agent Trajectory Interchange Format (ATIF), grades six default runtime metrics, and reports Skill Lift: the target skill's added value for a fixed task, harness, workspace, and scorer. The same protocol supports product-owned task suites that compare baseline, skill, bundle, team-skill, and plugin targets.
  On 145 real skills from internal enterprise repositories and public catalogs, scan-only gates surface useful authoring issues but measure complementary facets (structural versus LLM-judge Spearman $ρ= 0.14$). Across 947 scored paired cases from 58 of 64 production skills and four primary harnesses, mean composite Skill Lift is 0.2134 (95\% paired-case CI [0.1967, 0.2301]); mean outcome-only lift, the average of accuracy and goal accuracy, is 0.1799. Composite lift is positive in 72.8\% of paired cases. The largest process-metric gains appear in skill execution, behavior check, and skill efficiency---signals about discovery, routing, workflow following, and tool use that document scans cannot observe. An open-source implementation of the methodology is available in NVIDIA SkillEvaluator.

AI.tldr: ACES is a framework to quantitatively evaluate whether enterprise agent skills and capability packages actually help agents perform real tasks, by running paired live trials and computing a Skill Lift metric.
AI.motivation: As enterprise agent systems move from prototypes to production, organizations need objective, repeatable evidence that reusable skills, tools, and workflows genuinely improve task performance under real deployment conditions, beyond existing static checks for style, structure, or security that do not answer whether a skill actually helps an agent complete tasks.
AI.method: ACES defines a repository-native evaluation framework that (1) runs paired live trials of agents with and without a target skill under the same model, sandbox, and grading policy; (2) logs and normalizes agent trajectories into the Agent Trajectory Interchange Format (ATIF); (3) computes six default runtime metrics; and (4) aggregates them into a Skill Lift score that quantifies the added value of the skill. The framework supports evaluating single skills, bundles, team-skills, and plugins across product-owned task suites and multiple harnesses.
AI.result: On 145 real skills from internal and public catalogs, the authors find that existing scan-only gates capture mainly structural aspects and are weakly correlated with LLM-judge evaluations (Spearman ρ = 0.14). Across 947 scored paired cases involving 58 production skills and four main harnesses, the average composite Skill Lift is 0.2134 (95% CI [0.1967, 0.2301]) and outcome-only lift is 0.1799, with 72.8% of paired cases showing positive composite lift. The most substantial improvements are seen in process metrics related to skill execution, behavior checking, and efficiency.
AI.conclusion: ACES provides an executable, quantitative way to validate the real-world impact of enterprise agent skills and capability packages, complementing static document scans by capturing dynamic process signals like discovery, routing, workflow adherence, and tool use. The open-source NVIDIA SkillEvaluator implementation demonstrates that many production skills yield measurable performance gains, and the framework can serve as a standard protocol for continuous skill evaluation in enterprise settings.

title: Intent Engine: Natural-Language Intent Translation for Intent-Driven Orchestration in the Compute Continuum
summary: Microservice placement in the compute continuum is driven by low-level Service-level Objectives (SLOs), but requiring users to specify metric-level constraints creates an adoption barrier and increases misconfiguration risk. Although large language models (LLMs) can interpret natural-language intents, direct generation of orchestration-consumable SLO artifacts remains unreliable due to unsupported constraints, incorrect grounded values, and schema violations. These errors can propagate to downstream placement logic and produce infeasible or incorrect placements. This paper presents Intent Engine, a natural-language intent translation architecture that constructs validated SLO artifacts for compute-continuum service placement. Intent Engine acts as an intent acquisition and SLO construction layer for existing intent-driven orchestration and placement frameworks; it does not perform placement or runtime QoS optimization. The architecture combines schema-constrained extraction, retrieval-grounded value construction from monitored infrastructure state, and validation against supported constraints before emitting the final SLO artifact. We evaluate Intent Engine using a 716-record intent-to-SLO dataset derived from an edge-cloud testbed, including valid and invalid intents. Across GPT-4.1 mini, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and DeepSeek V4-Flash, Intent Engine outperforms prompting baselines and a non-LLM rule-based parser. With GPT-4.1 mini, it achieves 0.941 total F1 Score and reduces aggregate hallucination by 85.1%, while lowering downstream placement failure from 30.8% to 2.1%.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Intent Engine, a system that translates natural-language user intents into validated SLO artifacts for microservice placement across edge–cloud environments, significantly reducing misconfigurations and hallucinations compared to direct LLM prompting and rule-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Current microservice placement in edge–cloud (compute continuum) environments requires users to express their needs as low-level, metric-specific SLOs. This is hard for non-experts, creates an adoption barrier, and often leads to misconfigurations. While LLMs can understand natural language, using them to directly generate SLO artifacts is unreliable because they may invent unsupported constraints, use incorrect values, or violate required schemas, which then break or misguide downstream placement logic. There is a need for a robust, validated translation layer between user intents in natural language and the strict SLO specifications required by orchestration systems.
AI.method: The authors design Intent Engine, an architecture that sits in front of existing intent-driven orchestration and placement systems. It does not perform placement itself; instead, it acquires user intent in natural language and constructs valid SLO artifacts. The system combines: (1) schema-constrained extraction to ensure the generated SLOs conform to an expected structure, (2) retrieval-grounded value construction that pulls concrete values from current monitored infrastructure state instead of letting the LLM hallucinate them, and (3) validation of the produced SLOs against the set of supported constraints before emitting the final artifact. They build a 716-record dataset of natural-language intents and corresponding SLOs from an edge–cloud testbed, including both valid and intentionally invalid intents, and evaluate Intent Engine with three LLMs (GPT-4.1 mini, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and DeepSeek V4-Flash), comparing against prompting-only baselines and a non-LLM rule-based parser.
AI.result: On the 716-record dataset, Intent Engine improves both correctness and robustness relative to baselines. Using GPT-4.1 mini, it achieves a total F1 score of 0.941 for intent-to-SLO translation. It reduces hallucinations (unsupported or fabricated constraints/values) by 85.1% compared to baselines, and substantially decreases downstream placement failures caused by bad SLOs—from 30.8% down to 2.1%. Similar improvements are seen across Claude Sonnet 4.5 and DeepSeek V4-Flash, where Intent Engine consistently outperforms both naive LLM prompting and a rule-based parser.
AI.conclusion: Intent Engine demonstrates that a structured, validated LLM-based pipeline can reliably translate natural-language intents into orchestration-ready SLO artifacts for compute-continuum microservice placement. By combining schema constraints, retrieval-grounded value construction, and constraint validation, the system mitigates common LLM failure modes such as hallucinations and schema violations, and dramatically reduces downstream placement errors. This makes intent-driven orchestration more usable and dependable for practitioners who prefer to express requirements in natural language rather than low-level SLO metrics.

title: Dual-Cache Latent Space Communication between Heterogeneous Language Models
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems split work across models, so answering often requires knowledge that sits in another agent's context: a Sharer has encoded information that a Receiver needs to complete its task. They usually communicate by exchanging text, which puts autoregressive decoding on the critical path and reduces the exchange to a discrete message written without sight of the receiver's state. Recent latent protocols instead translate the sharer's key-value (KV) cache into the receiver's: C2C supports heterogeneous models but requires both to read the same input, while LCF-X removes this shared-context requirement through position-free sharer-cache pooling. Three restrictions remain: LCF-X compresses the sharer alone, supplies the same layer-local summary to every receiver position with no joint cross-layer memory to retrieve from, and assumes matched layer count and KV geometry. We introduce XKV, which lifts all three: learned-query attention pools both caches; self-attention over receiver-aligned layer tokens, with a learned layer map reconciling different depths, mixes the pooled summaries into a compact joint memory; and a shared position decoder lets every raw receiver cache position retrieve its own per-head-gated residual in the receiver's native KV geometry. Both models stay frozen and may differ in family, depth, KV-head count, head dimension, and tokenizer; only the translator is trained. Across 45 dataset-model-pair settings (six heterogeneous and three same-model ordered pairings, five datasets), XKV attains the highest macro score and best average rank, improving on LCF-X on every dataset (by 4.6 exact-match and 4.2 F1 points on ROPES) and surpassing text communication on four of the five, while training 76% fewer parameters and translating a cache pair 10.3x faster (5.8 vs. 59.9 ms); end to end, XKV is 26% faster than LCF-X and 6.8x faster than text communication.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes XKV, a learned latent cache-to-cache communication mechanism between heterogeneous LLM agents that is faster and more accurate than prior latent and text-based protocols.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems often need to share internal knowledge, but existing communication via text is slow and constrained, while current latent cache-to-cache methods either require shared input context or impose structural constraints on the models and the cache mapping. The authors aim to design a more general, efficient, and expressive latent communication protocol that works across heterogeneous models without modifying them.
AI.method: The authors introduce XKV, a trainable translator network that operates only on key-value (KV) caches of a Sharer and a Receiver model. XKV first uses learned-query attention to pool information from both the Sharer and Receiver caches. It then applies self-attention over receiver-aligned layer tokens, using a learned layer-mapping mechanism to reconcile differing depths between models, to build a compact joint memory. Finally, a shared position decoder maps this joint memory back to the Receiver’s native KV geometry, allowing each receiver position and head to retrieve a gated residual update to its cache. Both LLMs remain frozen and may differ in architecture, depth, head configuration, and tokenizer; only the translator is trained.
AI.result: Across 45 combinations of datasets and model pairings (including six heterogeneous and three same-model pairings over five datasets), XKV achieves the best macro performance and average rank. It consistently improves over LCF-X on all datasets (e.g., +4.6 exact match and +4.2 F1 on ROPES) and outperforms standard text-based communication on four of five datasets. XKV also reduces translator parameters by 76% compared to LCF-X and translates a KV cache pair 10.3x faster (5.8 ms vs 59.9 ms), leading to an overall end-to-end speedup of 26% over LCF-X and 6.8x over text communication.
AI.conclusion: XKV is an effective and general latent communication protocol for multi-agent LLM systems, enabling efficient cache-to-cache knowledge transfer across heterogeneous models without shared inputs or architectural alignment. It addresses key limitations of prior work by jointly compressing sharer and receiver caches, creating a cross-layer joint memory, and handling differing layer structures and KV geometries. Empirically, it delivers better accuracy and significantly lower latency and parameter cost than both LCF-X and text-based communication, suggesting that such latent communication mechanisms can be a practical replacement for textual messaging in multi-agent LLM setups.

title: Ansari: A Retrieval-Grounded Islamic AI Assistant -- Architecture, Deployment, and Lessons from 140,000 Conversations
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Live system: https://askansari.ai . Code: https://github.com/ansari-project
summary: General-purpose large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to answer religious questions, but for Islamic content they carry two serious risks: factual fabrication (inventing Qur'anic verses or hadith) and subtle value misalignment. We present Ansari, a deployed, retrieval-grounded Islamic AI assistant that has handled more than 140,000 conversations across 25+ languages since June 2023. Ansari is built around an agentic retrieval loop: a tool-using language model issues searches against authenticated Islamic corpora -- the Qur'an, hadith collections, a multi-volume jurisprudence (fiqh) encyclopedia, and exegetical (tafsir) sources -- and answers only on the basis of what it retrieves, with citations attached for verification. We describe the system's architecture (the agent loop, the retrieval tools, the corpora, and the system prompt that encodes editorial and theological policy), its multi-platform deployment (web, mobile, WhatsApp, and as a Model Context Protocol server and an Agent Skill), and what 140,000 real conversations reveal about how Muslims actually use such a tool. We report results on several complementary evaluations -- zero-shot performance on accredited institutional exams, a human-rated validation during Ramadan, and two independent, externally run benchmarks on which Ansari currently tops the public IslamicMMLU leaderboard ahead of frontier models and is competitive on Islamic legal reasoning (IslamicLegalBench) while strongly resisting false premises -- and draw out lessons that generalize beyond Islam to any faith- or values-sensitive deployment of LLMs: grounding is necessary but not sufficient, the system prompt is a theological as much as a technical artifact, and the absence of community in how models are formed remains a hard gap.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Ansari, a retrieval-grounded Islamic AI assistant designed to reduce hallucinations and value misalignment in Islamic Q&A, details its architecture and deployment, evaluates it against exams and benchmarks where it performs strongly, and distills lessons for value-sensitive LLM applications.
AI.motivation: General-purpose LLMs are increasingly used for religious questions, but in the Islamic context they risk inventing scriptural content and reflecting misaligned values. There is a need for a system that can answer Islamic queries faithfully, verifiably, and in line with specific theological and editorial guidelines, while serving real users at scale.
AI.method: The authors build Ansari, an agentic retrieval-based assistant. A tool-using LLM runs a retrieval loop over vetted Islamic sources (Qur’an, hadith, fiqh encyclopedia, tafsir). The model is constrained to answer only from retrieved texts and must provide citations. The system includes a carefully designed system prompt encoding editorial/theological policy, and is deployed across multiple platforms. They then evaluate Ansari using institutional exams, a human-rated study during Ramadan, and two external benchmarks (IslamicMMLU, IslamicLegalBench), and analyze 140k real conversations.
AI.result: Ansari has been used in over 140,000 conversations in 25+ languages. On evaluations, it achieves top performance on the public IslamicMMLU leaderboard, is competitive on IslamicLegalBench for legal reasoning, shows strong resistance to accepting false premises, and performs credibly on zero-shot accredited exams and in human evaluations during Ramadan. Usage logs reveal how Muslims actually interact with such a tool in practice.
AI.conclusion: Grounding answers in authenticated sources greatly helps but is not by itself sufficient to ensure safe, value-aligned religious AI. The system prompt acts as both a technical and theological artifact, shaping how doctrine and values are encoded. Moreover, there is a structural gap because communities currently have little role in model formation. These lessons generalize to other faith- or value-sensitive LLM deployments.

title: Applying Anthropic Primitives at Large Enterprises: Harness Paradigm for Knowledge Work
summary:
Frontier models have collapsed the cost of writing custom code: a niche problem a specialist sees in their own domain now costs an afternoon. The cost of reviewing and maintaining that code hasn't collapsed. Each solution drifts from the next; understanding one means reading its codebase from scratch. Large enterprises build something centrally governed instead: at worst an off-the-shelf product, at best a graph-orchestration framework wired bespoke per use case, or a low-code platform used as the orchestrator. These are custom every time and limited in scope. Enterprises don't weigh a third option that escapes both constraints: the harness paradigm.
  Recent work treats the coding-agent harness as enterprise infrastructure rather than a coding tool, converging on three findings: harnesses suffice at the task level and outperform more elaborate architectures on enterprise work (arXiv:2604.00073, arXiv:2604.13107); harness choice accounts for most of the variance in agent benchmark results, more than model choice does (arXiv:2605.23950); and the gap between that finding and enterprise adoption is governance (arXiv:2605.10223, arXiv:2605.18747).
  We propose an architecture that closes that gap. One harness runs unmodified as the backbone; the code stays identical across every deployment, so reviewing what gets built collapses to reading its instructions file. Section 4 gives four mechanisms: credential-scoped tooling, where each backend gets one generic request tool and a scoped credential instead of a hand-built method; authorization logic outside the harness, so one artifact runs as a cron backbone, a chat-surface engine, and a terminal tool; registration is a side effect of pushing code, collapsing an audit a review of a text file.
  Built on microcc (<https://pypi.org/project/micro-cc/>), our reference harness.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a standardized, centrally governed “harness” architecture for coding agents so enterprises can reuse the same backbone across use cases, cutting review and governance costs while maintaining flexibility.
AI.motivation: While advanced language models make it cheap and fast to write custom code for niche problems, it remains expensive for enterprises to review, govern, and maintain many diverging codebases. Existing enterprise solutions—central frameworks, graph orchestrators, or low-code platforms—are bespoke, limited in scope, and must be rebuilt for each use case. Recent work shows that simple coding-agent harnesses are often sufficient and that harness design explains more performance variance than model choice, but governance challenges prevent widespread enterprise adoption. The paper aims to bridge this gap between technical capability and enterprise governance needs.
AI.method: The authors conceptualize the coding-agent harness as reusable enterprise infrastructure rather than a per-task coding tool. They design an architecture with a single, unmodified harness acting as the backbone across all deployments. Governance and configuration are externalized into an “instructions file” and supporting mechanisms. They specify four key mechanisms: (1) credential-scoped tooling, providing each backend a generic request tool plus a scoped credential instead of bespoke methods; (2) authorization logic moved outside the harness so the same artifact can serve multiple roles (cron backbone, chat engine, terminal tool) with different policies; and (3) automatic registration as a side effect of pushing code, enabling audits by reviewing a text file. The architecture is instantiated using microcc as a reference harness implementation.
AI.result: From the abstract alone, the results are architectural and conceptual rather than empirical. The authors claim, based on prior work they cite, that harness-based approaches already match or beat more complex agent architectures on enterprise tasks and that harness choice is the dominant factor in benchmark variance. Their contribution is a concrete design that keeps the harness code identical across deployments, so review focuses on a compact instructions file and associated configurations. This promises lower review and governance overhead, easier auditing, and improved reusability of the same harness across cron jobs, chat interfaces, and terminal tools.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that enterprises should treat coding-agent harnesses as standardized infrastructure rather than bespoke tools, and that a single, unmodified harness backbone combined with externalized governance and credential-scoped tooling can resolve the main barrier to enterprise adoption: governance and review cost. By collapsing variability into an instructions file and using microcc as a reference harness, they provide a practical path for organizations to adopt coding agents at scale while maintaining strong control, auditability, and reuse across many use cases.

title: ImmigrationReason: A Structured Dataset of U.S. Immigration Appeals for Legal Reasoning Research
summary: Most legal NLP resources draw from federal case law and focus on coarse classification, leaving administrative adjudication, where the vast majority of government decisions occur, essentially unaddressed. We introduce ImmigrationReason, a large-scale structured dataset derived from 12,375 non-precedent decisions of the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) Administrative Appeals Office (AAO) spanning 2005 to 2026. Each record captures the applicable legal framework, per-criterion evidence-sufficiency findings under a five-category label, verbatim adjudicator-criticism quotes, all citations, and final dispositions, alongside high-quality Claude-transcribed source text. Extraction quality is validated through a three-pass pipeline combining two independent modalities with comparison-prompt adjudication by Opus 4.7, and verified by domain experts on a 500-record sample. The dataset documents nearly 9,000 verbatim instances of AAO-identified legal errors, spans a natural legal-regime transition (the 2016 Dhanasar rule change), and covers 21 years of adjudication. We analyze the dataset in detail and outline research directions it enables, from outcome prediction and adjudicator-error analysis to agent design for high-stakes regulatory domains.

AI.tldr: Introduces ImmigrationReason, a large-scale structured dataset of 12,375 USCIS AAO immigration decisions with fine-grained legal reasoning annotations, enabling research on administrative adjudication, legal errors, and outcome prediction.
