AI.motivation: Most existing legal NLP datasets focus on federal courts and coarse labels, neglecting administrative adjudication where most government decisions actually occur. There is a need for a large, structured, fine-grained dataset capturing how adjudicators reason, apply legal standards, and commit errors in administrative immigration decisions over time, especially across major doctrinal changes.
AI.method: Construct a dataset from 12,375 non-precedent AAO decisions (2005–2026). For each decision, extract structured fields: legal framework applied, per-criterion evidence-sufficiency judgments with five-category labels, verbatim quotes where adjudicators criticize evidence or reasoning, all legal citations, final disposition, and high-quality transcribed full text. Use a three-pass extraction-validation pipeline combining two independent extraction modalities and an adjudication/comparison step by an LLM (Opus 4.7), then have domain experts validate a 500-record sample for quality assurance. Analyze the dataset’s characteristics, including documented legal errors and coverage of a key rule change (Dhanasar).
AI.result: The authors create ImmigrationReason, a 21-year dataset of 12,375 AAO decisions with rich structured annotations, including roughly 9,000 verbatim instances of adjudicator-identified legal errors and detailed per-criterion evidence sufficiency labels. The data spans a major doctrinal transition (the 2016 Dhanasar rule change) and is validated through a multi-pass LLM pipeline plus expert review, yielding high-quality, research-ready annotations. They present descriptive analyses of the dataset’s structure and content.
AI.conclusion: ImmigrationReason fills a significant gap in legal NLP by providing a fine-grained, high-quality dataset of administrative immigration adjudications rather than just federal court cases. Its detailed annotations on legal frameworks, evidence sufficiency, and adjudicator-identified errors, together with long temporal coverage across a doctrinal shift, enable new research on outcome prediction, error analysis, doctrinal change, and the design of AI agents for high-stakes regulatory and administrative domains.

title: SAGE: A Unified Algebra and Self-Adaptive Execution for AI Functions in SQL
summary: SQL systems increasingly expose AI functions for tasks such as classification, extraction, filtering, ranking, retrieval, joining, and summarization. Despite their diverse APIs, these functions play only three relational roles: transforming individual rows, aggregating groups, or generating relationships between row pairs. We present SAGE (Self-Adaptive Generative Execution), a unified logical and physical framework that captures these roles with three typed primitives, AI_SCALAR, AI_AGG, and AI_JOIN, and composes them naturally with standard relational operators. All primitives share a confidence-gated execution interface while supporting physical strategies tailored to their relational shape. The main challenge is AI_JOIN, where SAGE analyzes the predicate, decomposes compound conditions when possible, and uses a recipe card together with a small label-free probe to select among complete execution strategies. Across a broad audit of public AI operators and evaluations spanning scalar, aggregate, and join workloads, this formulation covers common AI functionality while consistently improving execution quality and efficiency. SAGE achieves the strongest overall SemBench performance and, on a representative factorable join, reduces pairwise model calls by more than two orders of magnitude, yielding a 358-fold measured cost reduction.

AI.tldr: SAGE is a unified framework that models AI functions in SQL systems using three relational primitives—AI_SCALAR, AI_AGG, and AI_JOIN—to improve execution quality and efficiency.
AI.motivation: AI functions are increasingly integrated into SQL databases for tasks like classification, extraction, and ranking, but they come with diverse APIs and ad hoc designs. There is a need for a unified, relationally principled way to represent and execute these AI operations efficiently and reliably within database systems.
AI.method: The paper introduces SAGE (Self-Adaptive Generative Execution), which defines three typed AI primitives corresponding to relational roles: AI_SCALAR for per-row transformations, AI_AGG for group-level aggregation, and AI_JOIN for creating relationships between row pairs. These primitives share a confidence-gated execution interface and integrate with standard relational operators. For AI_JOIN in particular, SAGE analyzes join predicates, decomposes compound conditions when possible, and employs a recipe card along with a small, label-free probe workload to adaptively choose among different physical execution strategies that minimize model calls and cost.
AI.result: The authors audit a broad set of public AI operators and show that the three SAGE primitives can express common AI functionality used in SQL systems. Experimental evaluations across scalar, aggregate, and join workloads demonstrate that SAGE improves both execution quality and efficiency compared to existing approaches. On the SemBench benchmark, SAGE delivers the strongest overall performance, and for a representative factorable join workload, it reduces the number of pairwise model calls by more than two orders of magnitude, achieving a 358× cost reduction in practice.
AI.conclusion: SAGE provides a unified logical and physical foundation for integrating AI into relational database systems via three core primitives. This formulation is expressive enough to cover typical AI-enhanced SQL functionality while substantially improving efficiency, especially for AI-driven joins, and strengthening end-to-end query performance and cost-effectiveness.

title: Evaluation-as-Search: Adaptive Discovery of Grounding Failures in Meeting Assistants
summary: LLM-powered meeting assistants are deployed at scale, yet systematic evaluation of their grounding fidelity remains limited to static benchmarks that miss failure modes tied to specific discourse structures or reasoning demands. We propose Evaluation-as-Search (EaS), a feedback-driven methodology that frames quality evaluation as an adaptive search over the space of natural questions a meeting participant might ask. Rather than sampling uniformly, EaS learns from evaluator feedback across iterations to concentrate probing effort on cognitive demands where failures are most likely, guided by a UCB-scored coverage map and blind multi-dimensional quality evaluation. Using EaS, we construct MeetingProbe, a benchmark of over $3{,}000$ annotated question--answer pairs spanning 20 transcripts from three meeting genres and three LLM assistants. In ablations, adaptive search surfaces $2.5\times$ more failures than random probing ($7.1\%$ vs. $2.9\%$ finding rate), with the strategic planner contributing the largest individual effect. Across three models, we observe a clear capability gradient and identify eight recurring failure categories dominated by discourse-pragmatic challenges rather than factual recall errors. We further validate MeetingProbe across multiple model families and providers, finding a clean capability gradient and a curated subset of universal failures that no model handles. MeetingProbe is released publicly to support reproducible evaluation of meeting assistant grounding fidelity.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Evaluation-as-Search (EaS), an adaptive, feedback-driven method to systematically probe and evaluate the grounding fidelity of LLM-powered meeting assistants, resulting in the MeetingProbe benchmark that reveals richer and more realistic failure patterns than static random benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM meeting assistants are widely deployed, but their grounding fidelity—how accurately they base responses on meeting content—is poorly understood. Current evaluations rely on static, uniformly sampled benchmarks that fail to expose errors tied to particular discourse structures, pragmatic cues, or reasoning loads that arise in real meetings. The authors are motivated to develop a more targeted, systematic, and realistic way to stress-test these systems along dimensions where they are most likely to fail, and to create a reusable benchmark that captures such nuanced failures.
AI.method: The authors propose Evaluation-as-Search (EaS), which treats evaluation as an adaptive search over the space of questions a meeting participant might naturally ask about a transcript. Instead of uniformly sampling questions, EaS iteratively generates and tests questions, using evaluator feedback to guide future probing toward regions with higher failure likelihood. A UCB-scored coverage map balances exploration and exploitation over different cognitive demands, while quality assessment is done via blind, multi-dimensional human evaluation focused on grounding fidelity. Using this pipeline, they construct MeetingProbe: over 3,000 annotated question–answer pairs across 20 real meeting transcripts from three genres, evaluated against three different LLM assistants. They also conduct ablation studies to quantify the benefit of the adaptive search components, including the strategic planner.
AI.result: EaS-based adaptive probing discovers significantly more failures than random question sampling: a 2.5× higher failure finding rate (7.1% vs. 2.9%). Ablations show that the strategic planning component is the single largest contributor to this improvement. Applying EaS across three LLM assistants reveals a consistent capability gradient—stronger models fail less—but also identifies eight recurring failure categories. These errors are dominated by discourse-pragmatic and reasoning issues (e.g., tracking who said what, interpreting intentions, or following long-range context), rather than simple factual recall mistakes. When validated across multiple model families and providers, MeetingProbe continues to show a clear capability ranking and exposes a curated subset of particularly challenging cases—universal failures that no tested model can handle correctly.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation-as-Search is an effective, scalable methodology for stress-testing LLM meeting assistants, uncovering more and richer failure modes than static, randomly sampled benchmarks. The resulting MeetingProbe benchmark captures nuanced, discourse-heavy grounding challenges and yields a robust capability gradient across models, along with a set of universal hard cases. By releasing MeetingProbe, the authors aim to standardize and improve the reproducible evaluation of grounding fidelity in meeting assistants and, more broadly, highlight the importance of adaptive, feedback-driven evaluation frameworks for complex language tasks.

title: Weighted Memory Tree: Remembering What Matters for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated the ability to solve multi-step tasks requiring planning, tool use, and external information access, yet growing execution histories increase inference cost and expose reasoning to outdated, irrelevant, or misleading information, potentially degrading reasoning quality. Existing memory approaches organize or compress execution histories but provide limited mechanisms for deciding which memories remain active. We introduce the, a hierarchical memory system that organizes execution into tasks, subtasks, and actions while assigning each memory a dynamic retention score. Event-based updates and selection-based decay revise these scores, allowing WMT to preserve useful information, fold completed trajectories, suppress low-utility content, and retain access to folded context. We evaluate WMT on GAIA-Text using Qwen3-8B, Gemma 4 E4B, and Llama-3.1-8B, with ablations and memory-poisoning experiments. Relative to linear memory, WMT improves accuracy by an average of 9.97 percentage points while reducing prompt-token usage by 32.8%. Memory-poisoning experiments show that WMT limits the persistence and propagation of unreliable information. Our results suggest that effective long-horizon agent memory depends less on storing more information than on deciding which information should remain active.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hierarchical memory system for LLM agents that dynamically decides which past information stays active, improving both accuracy and token efficiency over naive linear histories and reducing the impact of poisoned memories.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents tackle long, multi-step tasks, their execution histories grow large, increasing inference cost and exposing the model to outdated or misleading information, which can degrade reasoning. Existing memory strategies mostly focus on organizing or compressing histories, but they lack effective mechanisms for deciding what information should remain active and influential over time. The authors aim to design a memory system that can selectively retain useful content while suppressing noise and harmful or obsolete context, thus enabling more robust, long-horizon reasoning.
AI.method: The authors introduce a hierarchical memory framework that structures an agent’s experience into tasks, subtasks, and actions, and assigns each memory item a dynamic retention score. These scores are updated through event-based mechanisms and decreased via selection-based decay, controlling which memories stay active. The system can: (1) preserve high-utility information; (2) fold completed trajectories into compressed forms; (3) suppress low-utility or misleading content; and (4) maintain access to folded context when needed. They implement this framework for LLM agents and evaluate it on GAIA-Text with several base models (Qwen3-8B, Gemma 4 E4B, Llama-3.1-8B), including ablation studies and dedicated memory-poisoning setups to test robustness against unreliable information.
AI.result: Compared to a linear memory baseline that simply appends all past interactions, the proposed system increases task accuracy on GAIA-Text by an average of 9.97 percentage points while cutting prompt token usage by 32.8%. In memory-poisoning experiments, the system significantly limits how long unreliable information persists and how much it affects subsequent reasoning. Ablation results indicate that both the hierarchical organization and the dynamic retention scoring contribute to performance gains and robustness.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that the key to effective long-horizon memory in LLM agents is not maximizing the amount of stored information but intelligently deciding which information remains active and influential. Hierarchical organization combined with dynamic retention and decay enables agents to maintain concise, relevant working memory, improving both performance and efficiency while mitigating the risks of outdated or poisoned context. This suggests future research should focus on more principled, adaptive memory selection mechanisms rather than only compression or storage capacity increases.

title: Knowledge-Graph-Gated Defactualization for Style-Controllable and Fact-Preserving Generation in Agentic Conversational AI
summary: Agentic large language models (LLMs) deployed in fact-sensitive applications such as customer support must simultaneously preserve factual correctness and generate responses in a controllable stylistic register. Activation steering enables fine-tuning-free style control by perturbing hidden representations, but it lacks an explicit mechanism for distinguishing verifiable facts from stylistic content, leading to semantic leakage. We address this challenge through \emph{Defactualize-Steer-Rehydrate} (DSR), a knowledge-engineering framework that integrates a typed, salience-weighted knowledge graph (KG) with activation steering. DSR extracts salient entities using a layered regex or NER or lexical-classifier pipeline, replaces them with typed placeholders prior to steering, and deterministically restores verified values through salience-guided rehydration after generation. DSR is evaluated across six LLaMA-family models (1B--13B parameters) on 600 A2A-generated customer-support cases (1,200 generations), with a dedicated KG ablation study. DSR significantly increases verified-entity recovery relative to a steering-only baseline (Cohen's $d=0.225$, $p_{\text{Bonf}}=1.0\times10^{-4}$), though the absolute recovery rate remains modest, while preserving effective style control across diverse model families. Layer-wise separability and steering-strength diagnostics further show previously unexplored interactions between representation-level steering and factual grounding. hese results demonstrate that explicit knowledge engineering can systematically enhance trustworthy, controllable, and reproducible generative AI without requiring model fine-tuning. Code, cached steering vectors, and evaluation scripts are publicly released to support reproducibility.\footnote{https://github.com/Tanmay-IITDSAI/KG-Gated-Defactualization}

AI.tldr: The paper proposes DSR, a framework combining knowledge graphs with activation steering to control style in LLM responses while protecting factual content, improving entity-level factual recovery without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Activation steering can control the style of LLM outputs but often entangles style with factual content, causing semantic leakage where facts are inadvertently altered. For fact-sensitive applications like customer support, systems need a way to separate and protect verifiable factual information while still adjusting stylistic aspects. The authors aim to provide a principled, engineering-focused approach to disentangle and safeguard factual entities during style control.
AI.method: The authors introduce Defactualize-Steer-Rehydrate (DSR), which integrates a typed, salience-weighted knowledge graph with activation steering. First, salient entities in the input are detected using a layered pipeline based on regex, NER, or lexical classifiers. These entities are replaced by typed placeholders (defactualization) before applying activation steering, so steering operates only on non-factual parts of the representation. After the model generates a response, DSR uses the knowledge graph and salience scores to deterministically restore (rehydrate) verified factual values into the placeholders. The framework is evaluated on six LLaMA-family models (1B–13B parameters) on 600 customer-support cases, with additional ablations removing or altering the KG to isolate its contribution. Diagnostics on layer-wise separability and steering strength are used to analyze how steering interacts with factual grounding in the representations.
AI.result: Across 1,200 generations, DSR notably improves the recovery of correct, verified entities compared with a steering-only baseline, with an effect size of Cohen’s d = 0.225 and Bonferroni-corrected p = 1.0×10⁻⁴. This indicates that explicit defactualization plus KG-guided rehydration helps protect factual content during style control, although the absolute level of recovered entities is still modest. At the same time, DSR maintains effective stylistic control across various LLaMA model sizes, showing that protecting factual content does not substantially degrade style steering. The layer-wise and strength diagnostics reveal nontrivial interactions between where and how strongly steering is applied and the model’s factual grounding mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that coupling activation steering with explicit knowledge engineering—via typed, salience-weighted knowledge graphs and a defactualize-steer-rehydrate pipeline—can systematically enhance the trustworthiness, controllability, and reproducibility of LLM outputs without needing model fine-tuning. While there is still room to improve the absolute rate of factual recovery, DSR demonstrates that separating factual entities from stylistic content during steering meaningfully reduces semantic leakage and preserves verifiable information in fact-sensitive applications. The released code and artifacts support further research on robust, knowledge-aware style control in generative AI.

title: Beyond Effectiveness: A Multi-Criteria Framework for Comparing Practical Socio-Technical Interventions
summary: Designers and policymakers in sociotechnical domains like content moderation, privacy interfaces, recommender systems and beyond, must choose among a growing menu of proposed interventions, but typically lack a principled basis for comparing them. Prior work tends to evaluate interventions individually and mostly along the effectiveness criteria, while implementation constraints such as cost, effort and feasibility are often considered separately. We present a multi-criteria framework for evaluating sociotechnical interventions. This framework is instantiated through the case of misinformation, a domain of intense focus for proposed countermeasures. We survey $N=39$ researchers on 40 operationalized interventions across five evaluative criteria: political feasibility, effectiveness, user acceptance, cost, and implementation effort. We find that the interventions that experts judge to be the most effective are not always the most acceptable to the public or the most feasible to implement. We also discuss how this tension has implications for the design of sociotechnical interventions beyond misinformation, and offer a decision framework for practitioners navigating the trade-offs of sociotechnical interventions.

AI.tldr: A multi-criteria framework to evaluate sociotechnical interventions (e.g., against misinformation), revealing trade-offs between effectiveness, feasibility, cost, and public acceptance, and providing a decision aid for practitioners.
AI.motivation: Current work on sociotechnical interventions—such as in content moderation, privacy, and recommender systems—usually evaluates single interventions primarily on effectiveness, without systematically accounting for other crucial constraints like political feasibility, user acceptance, cost, and implementation effort. Designers and policymakers therefore lack a principled way to compare and prioritize among many competing intervention ideas.
AI.method: The authors propose a multi-criteria evaluation framework and instantiate it in the domain of misinformation. They operationalize 40 distinct interventions and survey 39 researchers with relevant expertise. Each intervention is rated along five explicit criteria: political feasibility, effectiveness, user acceptance, monetary cost, and implementation effort, enabling comparative analysis and identification of trade-offs across interventions and criteria.
AI.result: Survey results show that interventions judged by experts to be highly effective are often not those that are most politically feasible, acceptable to users, or easy/cheap to implement. This reveals systematic tensions and trade-offs across evaluation criteria rather than a single “best” intervention. The study maps how different interventions rank along these five criteria and highlights clusters and conflicts between them.
AI.conclusion: A single-focus evaluation on effectiveness is insufficient for guiding real-world deployment of sociotechnical interventions. Instead, practitioners should use a multi-criteria decision framework that explicitly incorporates feasibility, cost, effort, and user acceptance alongside effectiveness. The proposed framework and empirical findings from the misinformation case study illustrate how to navigate these trade-offs and can generalize to other sociotechnical domains such as content moderation, privacy interfaces, and recommender systems.

title: Self-Supervised Speech Representations Track Spoken Language Convergence to Adult Models in Infants and Children Who Are Deaf/Hard-of-Hearing
summary: Language development is characterized by a gradual convergence of children's speech toward adult patterns. Measuring this process has traditionally required detailed transcription and language-specific expertise, limiting scalability across languages and populations. Here, we use speech embeddings to capture this convergence directly from the acoustic signal in longform, child-centered recordings, taken as children go about their daily lives. Using HuBERT-BASE, we extracted embeddings from speech vocalizations of children who are deaf/hard-of-hearing and their female adult caregivers ($>$925 hrs. observation). Embedding distance between children and caregivers decreased with hearing age, controlling for pitch and vocalization length, indicating, as expected, that children's speech patterns converge to caregivers over development. This single distance metric likewise related to multiple standardized measures of speech and language from infancy through preschoolhood. These results suggest a path toward scalable, language-neutral assessment of spoken language development from children's everyday lives.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a scalable, language-neutral way to quantify how children’s speech converges toward adult speech, using speech embeddings from long, naturalistic recordings instead of manual transcription.
AI.motivation: Traditional measures of children’s language development rely on detailed, language-specific transcription and expert annotation, which are time-consuming, expensive, and hard to scale across languages and large populations. There is a need for an automatic, language-agnostic, and scalable method to quantify how children’s speech becomes more adult-like over time, especially in natural daily-life settings and in populations such as deaf or hard-of-hearing children.
AI.method: The authors use HuBERT-BASE, a self-supervised speech model, to extract acoustic embeddings from long-form, child-centered audio recordings of deaf/hard-of-hearing children and their female adult caregivers (over 925 hours). They compute an embedding distance between child and caregiver vocalizations, while statistically controlling for basic acoustic confounds like pitch and vocalization length, and track how this distance changes with children’s hearing age. They also correlate this single distance metric with standardized clinical and developmental measures of speech and language from infancy through preschool.
AI.result: The embedding distance between children’s and caregivers’ speech decreases as children’s hearing age increases, even after controlling for pitch and vocalization length. This indicates that children’s acoustic speech patterns become more similar to those of their caregivers over development. The single embedding-distance measure is significantly related to multiple standardized speech and language assessments across early developmental stages.
AI.conclusion: A simple embedding-based distance between child and caregiver speech can serve as a robust, scalable, and language-neutral indicator of spoken language development in naturalistic settings. This approach could reduce dependence on manual, language-specific transcription and enable broader, more efficient monitoring and assessment of children’s speech and language growth, including in clinical populations such as deaf or hard-of-hearing children.

title: Auditable by Construction: An Ontology-Driven Framework for Trustworthy LLM Analytics in Enterprise Finance
comment: 20 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables, 1 algorithm. Artifact deposit with configurations, ontology schema, prompts, audit reports and reconstruction scripts: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22022068
summary:
Enterprise adoption of large language models in finance is constrained less by fluency than by trust: in Financial Planning and Analysis (FP&A) and other regulated workflows, an answer is usable only if it is traceable to authoritative sources and auditable after the fact. This paper argues that retrieval-augmented generation for enterprise finance should be evaluated on auditability alongside accuracy, and presents the Knowledge-Driven Analytics Framework (KDAF), which builds ontology-driven knowledge systems through six iterative stages and retrieves evidence via Context-Aware Relevance Propagation (CARP), so that every retrieved fact carries its relationship type, confidence, and source lineage.
  An evaluation on FinanceBench (145 questions) compares KDAF against zero-context inference, BM25, concept-weighted lexical retrieval, and ungrounded graph traversal. First, retrieval is necessary: zero-context inference reaches 4.1% correctness against 10-12% for retrieval-augmented conditions. Second, on answer correctness the retrieval conditions are statistically indistinguishable (KDAF vs BM25: -0.007, 95% CI [-0.021, 0.000]), so accuracy alone does not justify structured retrieval here -- a negative result we report explicitly. Third, on auditability the ordering reverses: KDAF attains the highest citation traceability F1 (0.515), exceeding ungrounded traversal by +0.027 (CI [0.006, 0.050]) and BM25 by +0.052 (CI [0.024, 0.083]), intervals excluding zero. Graph-structured retrieval also admits no evidence from outside the question subject entity (0 of 426 items, against 16.8% and 20.2% for lexical baselines), and every selected item resolves to a complete provenance chain. We argue that auditability, not accuracy, is the axis on which ontology-grounded retrieval earns its cost.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces KDAF, an ontology-driven retrieval framework for finance LLMs, and shows it mainly improves auditability, not accuracy.
AI.motivation: In enterprise finance, especially FP&A and other regulated workflows, LLM answers are only useful if they are fully traceable to authoritative data and auditable afterward. Existing RAG systems focus on accuracy and fluency but often lack structured provenance, relationship types, and confidence, which undermines trust and regulatory compliance. The authors aim to design and evaluate a retrieval framework that directly targets auditability as a primary objective, not just answer correctness.
AI.method: The authors propose the Knowledge-Driven Analytics Framework (KDAF), which constructs ontology-driven knowledge systems in six iterative stages. Retrieval is performed via Context-Aware Relevance Propagation (CARP), which retrieves facts along graph structures while preserving relationship types, confidence scores, and full source lineage for each item. They evaluate KDAF on the FinanceBench dataset of 145 questions, comparing it against zero-context LLM inference, BM25 lexical retrieval, concept-weighted lexical retrieval, and ungrounded graph traversal. Metrics include answer correctness and multiple measures of auditability, especially citation traceability and provenance completeness.
AI.result: Zero-context inference achieves only 4.1% correctness, showing retrieval is essential, while all retrieval-augmented methods (including KDAF and lexical baselines) achieve around 10–12% correctness. Differences in answer correctness between KDAF and BM25 are statistically indistinguishable (e.g., KDAF vs BM25: -0.007, 95% CI [-0.021, 0.000]). However, KDAF significantly outperforms others on auditability: it achieves the highest citation traceability F1 (0.515), improving over ungrounded traversal by +0.027 (CI [0.006, 0.050]) and over BM25 by +0.052 (CI [0.024, 0.083]). KDAF’s graph-structured retrieval admits no evidence from outside the question’s subject entity (0/426 items, vs 16.8% and 20.2% for lexical baselines), and every retrieved item has a complete provenance chain.
AI.conclusion: Ontology-grounded, graph-structured retrieval (as in KDAF) does not significantly increase answer accuracy over strong lexical retrieval in this setting, so accuracy alone cannot justify its complexity and cost. Its value lies in substantially improving auditability: traceable citations, constrained and relevant evidence, and complete provenance. The authors argue that for regulated financial applications, evaluation and system design should prioritize auditability as the key dimension on which such structured retrieval frameworks provide a meaningful advantage.

title: LingShu: A Large-Scale Symptom-Centric Contextualized Knowledge Graph Bridging Traditional Chinese Medicine and Modern Biomedicine
summary: Biomedical knowledge graphs (KGs) are pivotal for knowledge organization, yet traditional binary relations often struggle to represent the conditional nature of biomedical knowledge. Symptoms provide a shared phenotypic layer for linking Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), which relies on symptom patterns for syndrome differentiation and treatment selection, with modern biomedicine, which connects clinical manifestations to diseases and molecular mechanisms. We present LingShu, a large-scale symptom-centric contextualized knowledge graph designed to bridge TCM and modern biomedicine. The exported version of LingShu analyzed in this study comprises 17.33 million atom-level entity records and 39.47 million relation records, including 17.19 million semantic triples and 22.29 million contextualized quadruples. LingShu integrates multi-source data, including clinical electronic medical records, authoritative TCM texts, biomedical ontologies, and curated knowledge bases, through a pipeline combining natural language processing, terminology normalization, and human-in-the-loop verification. A key innovation of LingShu is its hybrid data model: it maintains 64 typed triple relation patterns to ensure broad connectivity, while incorporating 35 contextual quadruple relation patterns to capture conditional medical associations. This dual-structure approach explicitly encodes conditional knowledge, providing a granular representation of the contexts associated with medical relations. These contextualized relations cover syndrome-dependent herb efficacy, disease-contextualized drug effects, population-specific clinical associations, and mechanism-related therapeutic responses. Furthermore, we developed a web platform (http://www.tcmkg.com/) that integrates graph visualization, graph-based reasoning, and an evidence-grounded knowledge question-answering agent.

AI.tldr: LingShu is a large, symptom-centric contextual biomedical knowledge graph that bridges Traditional Chinese Medicine and modern biomedicine using both triples and contextualized quadruples.
AI.motivation: Existing biomedical knowledge graphs mainly use simple binary relations, which are inadequate for representing conditional and context-dependent biomedical knowledge such as symptom patterns, population-specific effects, or syndrome-dependent herb efficacy. There is also a lack of structured, large-scale resources that systematically connect Traditional Chinese Medicine, which is organized around symptom patterns and syndromes, with modern biomedicine, which links clinical manifestations to diseases and molecular mechanisms. This paper aims to fill this gap by building a contextualized KG centered on symptoms as a shared phenotypic layer, thereby enabling integrated reasoning across TCM and contemporary biomedical knowledge.
AI.method: The authors construct LingShu, a symptom-centric contextualized knowledge graph, by integrating multiple heterogeneous data sources: clinical electronic medical records, authoritative TCM texts, biomedical ontologies, and curated knowledge bases. They employ a pipeline that combines natural language processing for information extraction, terminology normalization to harmonize different vocabularies across TCM and biomedicine, and human-in-the-loop verification for quality control. LingShu uses a hybrid data model with two types of relations: (1) 64 typed triple relation patterns that provide broad connectivity using standard subject–predicate–object semantic triples; and (2) 35 contextual quadruple relation patterns that extend triples with an additional contextual dimension to explicitly encode conditions such as syndromes, diseases, populations, and mechanisms. They also implement a web platform that offers graph visualization, graph-based reasoning, and an evidence-grounded knowledge question-answering agent on top of LingShu.
AI.result: The exported version of LingShu analyzed in the study contains 17.33 million atom-level entity records and 39.47 million relation records, composed of 17.19 million semantic triples and 22.29 million contextualized quadruples. The hybrid triple–quadruple schema successfully captures both broad relational connectivity and fine-grained conditional associations. The contextualized relations explicitly represent knowledge such as syndrome-dependent herb efficacy, disease-contextualized drug effects, population-specific clinical associations, and mechanism-related therapeutic responses. The authors also deliver a functional web platform (http://www.tcmkg.com/) that allows users to explore the graph, perform reasoning, and interact with an evidence-grounded question-answering system.
AI.conclusion: LingShu demonstrates that a symptom-centric, hybrid triple–quadruple data model can effectively encode the conditional and contextual nature of biomedical and TCM knowledge at scale. By using symptoms as a shared phenotypic layer and explicitly representing contexts in quadruple relations, LingShu provides a rich, integrative resource that bridges Traditional Chinese Medicine with modern biomedicine. The accompanying web platform further shows the practical utility of this KG for graph exploration, reasoning, and knowledge-based question answering, suggesting potential to support research, clinical decision-making, and translational applications across TCM and contemporary biomedical domains.

title: DreamBench-SWE: A Multi-Session Memory-Hygiene Benchmark for Software Agents
comment: 67 pages. Public benchmark and evidence release: https://github.com/iroiro147/dreambench-swe/releases/tag/v2.1.0
summary: DreamBench-SWE is a multi-session benchmark for software-agent memory hygiene in which later software tasks depend on non-inferable evidence from earlier sessions and are scored by executable hidden oracles. We report the original scaled v2 fold and a separately preregistered v2.1 successor audit designed after that study but frozen before successor outcome inspection. The successor run completed 360/360 work units and 720/720 S3 cells across four conditions. In the original fold, the primary DF-hybrid--B5 contrast was null (95/180 versus 89/180; clustered p=.518, Holm p=1), not evidence of equivalence, and C9/C10 retained B0-headroom limitations. In the successor, no external memory achieved 21/180 passes (rate 0.1167), deterministic verbatim event memory 82/180 (rate 0.4556), the typed-plus-raw reference probe 83/180 (rate 0.4611), and one pinned hosted Mem0 literal-storage configuration 97/180 (rate 0.5389). The registered six-slot Family A retained unavailable slots at p=1; all three available comparisons against no memory rejected after Holm correction. Both preregistered mechanism contrasts were unavailable after pre-evaluation conformance rejection. The secondary literal-storage-versus-verbatim comparison was nonconfirmatory and sensitivity-dependent, while the comparison with the reference probe did not reject. The audit therefore supports DreamBench-SWE as a discriminating executable profile benchmark and characterizes one exact hosted-memory configuration, but it does not establish an external-system mechanism, superiority among memory-bearing conditions, equivalence, or broad product generality. The original v2.0.5 findings and artifacts remain unchanged.

AI.tldr: DreamBench-SWE is a benchmark for testing how well software agents use and retain information across multiple sessions, showing it can distinguish between memory setups but not yet proving any memory system is generally superior.
AI.motivation: To rigorously evaluate “memory hygiene” in software agents—whether they can correctly use information from past sessions that cannot be inferred from current context—using an executable, objective benchmark and preregistered analyses.
AI.method: They use DreamBench-SWE, a multi-session benchmark where later software tasks require specific, non-inferable information from earlier sessions. Performance is scored automatically via executable hidden oracles. The authors compare multiple memory configurations (no external memory, deterministic verbatim event memory, literal storage via hosted memory, and a typed-plus-raw reference probe) across preregistered experimental conditions, with statistical tests (clustered tests, Holm correction) and a successor audit (v2.1) that was preregistered after the original v2 fold but frozen before inspecting outcomes.
AI.result: In the original fold, the main planned comparison between a hybrid memory condition and a baseline was statistically null and did not show equivalence, with some headroom limitations. In the preregistered successor audit, conditions with external memory showed substantially higher pass rates (up to 97/180) than no-memory baselines, and all available comparisons of memory vs. no memory were statistically significant after Holm correction. However, some preregistered mechanism contrasts became unavailable due to conformance issues, and key comparisons among memory-bearing mechanisms (e.g., literal storage vs verbatim memory or reference probe) were either nonconfirmatory, sensitivity-dependent, or not statistically significant.
AI.conclusion: DreamBench-SWE works as an executable, discriminating benchmark for profiling software-agent memory behavior and identifying at least one strong hosted-memory configuration. However, the current evidence does not yet establish which external memory mechanism is generally best, nor demonstrate equivalence or broad generality across products; earlier v2.0.5 results and artifacts remain valid but unchanged.

title: ARGUS: Theory-of-Mind Guided Argument Generation with Strategy-Aware Planning and Knowledge Grounding
summary: Persuasive argument generation requires modeling audience beliefs, rhetorical strategies, and factual grounding. Despite recent advancements, existing methods remain largely audience-agnostic and fail to integrate strategy selection to improve persuasiveness. To bridge this gap, we propose Argus, an agent-based framework that operationalizes classical rhetoric for persuasive writing. At its core, a Theory-of-Mind (ToM) Reasoner constructs an explicit dual mental model of the audience's beliefs and values to guide downstream decisions. This representation conditions a component-aware planner that decomposes the argument into subtopics, assigns fine-grained rhetorical functions (logos, pathos, ethos, kairos), and triggers strategy-guided evidence retrieval at planning time. Finally, a refinement module iteratively targets and resolves multi-dimensional weaknesses without quality regression. We evaluate Argus across three diverse benchmarks using both automated pairwise Elo and LLM-as-judge metrics. Results show that Argus consistently outperforms strong baselines across multiple backbone models, achieving top rankings and the highest overall scores. Targeted simulation experiments further validate its effectiveness in shifting resistant audience stances.

AI.tldr: Argus is an agent-based framework that uses Theory-of-Mind reasoning and classical rhetorical strategies to generate more persuasive, audience-aware arguments.
AI.motivation: Existing persuasive text generation systems are mostly audience-agnostic and do not explicitly plan or select rhetorical strategies, which limits their effectiveness at changing the minds of specific audiences. The paper aims to create a system that can model audience beliefs and values and operationalize classical rhetoric (logos, pathos, ethos, kairos) to generate more tailored and effective arguments.
AI.method: The authors introduce Argus, an agent-based framework with three main components: (1) a Theory-of-Mind Reasoner that builds an explicit dual mental model of the audience’s beliefs and values; (2) a component-aware planner that decomposes an argument into subtopics, assigns rhetorical functions (logos, pathos, ethos, kairos) to each part, and performs strategy-guided evidence retrieval during planning; and (3) a refinement module that iteratively edits the draft argument to fix multi-dimensional weaknesses (e.g., logical gaps, weak evidence, poor emotional appeal) while avoiding quality loss.
AI.result: Across three diverse benchmarks and using both automated pairwise Elo ratings and LLM-as-judge evaluations, Argus consistently outperforms strong baselines over multiple backbone language models, obtaining top rankings and the highest overall scores. Additional targeted simulation experiments demonstrate that Argus is particularly effective at shifting the stances of resistant audiences, supporting the claim that its audience modeling and strategy planning improve persuasiveness.
AI.conclusion: Argus successfully operationalizes classical rhetoric in an agent-based, audience-aware framework for persuasive argument generation. By explicitly modeling audience beliefs and values, planning with fine-grained rhetorical functions, and iteratively refining arguments, it produces more persuasive texts than existing approaches. The results suggest that integrating Theory-of-Mind modeling and strategy-guided planning is a promising direction for future persuasive NLG research.

title: Why2Speak: Faithful Reasoning for Abstaining Action Policies
summary: Many agentic systems must repeatedly choose between acting and abstaining, making faithful reasoning important for oversight: an explanation is useful only if it reflects the computation that produced the action. We study this problem through intervention timing in multi-party conversation, where an assistant must decide whether to speak or remain silent. This setting exposes class imbalance, asymmetric action costs, and the possibility that exposing reasoning changes the policy being audited. Using Qwen3-8B, decoded with or without chain-of-thought reasoning, we compare direct decision policies, reasoning policies, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. We find a capability-auditability tradeoff: the strongest direct policy achieves higher quality but exposes no reasoning to inspect, while the reasoning policy provides a trace at the cost of lower performance, particularly recall of true intervention opportunities. Supervised fine-tuning either suppresses reasoning or preserves it without improving decision quality, while reinforcement learning also fails to improve the reasoning policy. We identify one mechanism underlying this failure: group relative objectives provide no learning signal on confidently wrong prompts when sampled rollouts all select the same action. Controlled activation probes and behavioral ablations show that standard faithfulness methods can overstate evidence that exposed reasoning reflects the underlying decision process. Probability-based metrics saturate under confident decisions, probes are vulnerable to class imbalance and textual leakage, and reasoning ablations can confound reasoning content with changes in inference mode. Together, these results show that exposing reasoning can change an agent's action policy rather than simply make it observable. We provide controls for evaluating reasoning-based oversight of agents that can act or abstain.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how requiring chain-of-thought reasoning in an agent that can act or abstain creates a tradeoff between oversight and performance, and shows that common faithfulness tests can be misleading.
AI.motivation: In agentic systems that repeatedly decide whether to act or stay silent, oversight depends on explanations faithfully reflecting the actual decision process. However, requiring explicit reasoning (like chain-of-thought) may alter the policy being audited, and standard tools to test faithfulness may be unreliable—especially with imbalanced classes and asymmetric action costs. The authors want to understand this oversight–capability tradeoff and how to more reliably evaluate reasoning-based oversight.
AI.method: They consider a multi-party conversation setting where an assistant decides when to intervene. Using Qwen3-8B with and without explicit chain-of-thought decoding, they compare several strategies: a direct decision policy (no reasoning shown), a reasoning policy (with chain-of-thought), supervised fine-tuning of these policies, and reinforcement learning to improve the reasoning policy. They analyze learning dynamics under group-relative objectives and conduct controlled activation probes and behavioral ablations to test whether exposed reasoning is causally tied to decisions. They also examine probability-based faithfulness metrics, probing under class imbalance, and the effects of ablating or modifying reasoning text.
AI.result: They find a clear capability–auditability tradeoff: the direct policy (no exposed reasoning) has better decision quality, especially higher recall for true intervention opportunities, while the reasoning policy is more auditable but performs worse. Supervised fine-tuning either suppresses the reasoning traces or keeps them without boosting decision quality, and reinforcement learning similarly fails to improve the reasoning policy. They show that group-relative RL objectives provide no gradient on confidently wrong prompts when all rollouts take the same action. Their analyses reveal that standard faithfulness diagnostics are unreliable: probability-based metrics saturate when the model is confident, probes can misinterpret signals due to class imbalance and leakage from text, and reasoning ablations can confound the effect of reasoning with shifts in inference mode.
AI.conclusion: Requiring exposed reasoning can change an agent’s policy rather than simply reveal its internal computation, producing a tradeoff between performance and auditability. Common methods for assessing faithfulness of reasoning traces can substantially overstate how well explanations track the true decision process, especially under confident and imbalanced conditions. The authors propose and demonstrate controls—via activation-level and behavioral analyses—for more robust evaluation of reasoning-based oversight in agents that can either act or abstain.

title: LiLiCorr: Lightweight Likelihood Correlation of Parallel Drafts for Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model inference by drafting future tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. A diffusion-style block head such as DFlash is an attractive drafter, predicting an entire block of future tokens in one forward pass. However, it is trained on per-position marginals rather than the joint block distribution, so the tokens it emits are individually plausible yet jointly incoherent. We introduce LiLiCorr, a Lightweight Likelihood-based model that Correlates the per-position marginal distributions a drafter already produces. It keeps the top-k tokens at each position as candidates and processes them jointly, producing for each an in and an out vector. A pair of adjacent candidates matches when the earlier one's out vector has high cosine similarity with the later one's in vector. These matches capture the block's joint structure without ever materializing the full joint distribution. One lightweight network pass produces all the vectors, and the pairwise scores are then computed in parallel as batched matrix operations, leaving only a cheap greedy walk sequential. We further co-train the drafter with LiLiCorr, so it learns to propose candidates that correlate into longer accepted sequences. Over the vanilla DFlash drafter, LiLiCorr raises acceptance length on every benchmark by 9 to 19%, while its scoring head accounts for about 2.8% of the per-block latency. Against DFlash and two concurrent methods that also restore coherence at draft time, LiLiCorr delivers the highest throughput in 70 of 72 settings: nine benchmarks at two target sizes under greedy and temperature-one decoding, and a throughput sweep over six concurrencies, two input lengths and three entropy tiers, with all systems equally optimized on a common serving stack. Extending LiLiCorr to inputs an order of magnitude longer than it was trained on preserves that lead.

AI.tldr: LiLiCorr is a lightweight add-on that makes blockwise speculative decoding more coherent by correlating per-position token distributions without modeling the full joint distribution, significantly boosting acceptance length and throughput at very low latency cost.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-style block drafters like DFlash can propose many future tokens in one pass, enabling fast speculative decoding, but they are trained on per-position marginals instead of the true joint distribution. As a result, the drafted tokens, while individually likely, can be jointly incoherent, reducing how many tokens the target model accepts and limiting actual speedups. There is a need for a lightweight method that recovers joint structure and coherence across a block of drafted tokens without incurring the heavy cost of modeling the full joint distribution.
AI.method: LiLiCorr takes the top-k candidate tokens at each future position from an existing drafter and processes all of them jointly with a small network. For each candidate, the network outputs an 'in' and an 'out' vector. A pair of adjacent candidates is scored by the cosine similarity between the earlier candidate’s out vector and the later candidate’s in vector; high similarity indicates that this local transition is coherent. These pairwise scores approximate the block’s joint structure while avoiding construction of the full joint distribution. All vectors are computed in one forward pass, and pairwise similarities are computed in parallel via batched matrix operations; only a final greedy walk over positions to pick a coherent path is sequential. The authors also co-train the drafter and LiLiCorr so the drafter learns to propose candidates that LiLiCorr can stitch into longer coherent accepted sequences.
AI.result: Compared with a baseline DFlash drafter, adding LiLiCorr increases the average number of consecutively accepted tokens (‘acceptance length’) across benchmarks by 9–19% while adding only about 2.8% latency per drafted block for the LiLiCorr scoring head. When compared against DFlash and two other concurrent coherence-restoring draft-time methods, LiLiCorr achieves the highest throughput in 70 out of 72 tested configurations, which span nine benchmarks, two target model sizes, both greedy and temperature-1 decoding, and a broad throughput sweep over concurrencies, input lengths, and entropy tiers, all run on a common optimized serving stack. The method’s advantage persists when applied to inputs an order of magnitude longer than those seen during training.
AI.conclusion: LiLiCorr provides an efficient way to impose joint coherence on blockwise speculative decoding by correlating per-position token candidates via learned in/out embeddings and cosine similarity, without ever modeling the full joint distribution. This yields longer accepted blocks and higher end-to-end throughput at minimal latency overhead. Co-training the drafter with LiLiCorr further improves performance, and the approach generalizes well to much longer inputs than those used in training, making it a practical and scalable enhancement for modern speculative decoding pipelines.

title: CDRL: Certification-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Neutrino Flavor Model Discovery
summary: Many scientific discovery problems require searching combinatorial hypothesis spaces under complex domain constraints. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising approach, but existing methods rely on scalar rewards that provide limited information about why candidate solutions fail, leading agents to repeatedly explore invalid regions. We introduce Certification-Driven Reinforcement Learning (CDRL), a framework that leverages structured feedback from symbolic reasoning tools. When a candidate violates domain constraints, these tools produce certificates identifying the actions responsible for failure. CDRL converts these certificates into reusable constraints that eliminate classes of invalid solutions and guide exploration toward valid regions. We evaluate CDRL on neutrino flavor model discovery in theoretical particle physics, where the hypothesis space exceeds $10^{26}$ possible models, and compare it with the state-of-the-art RL approach previously used for this task. Across three theory spaces, CDRL achieves up to 1.95$\times$ higher valid model rates and up to 6.33$\times$ higher neutrino model rates while evaluating up to 4$\times$ fewer candidates. We further extract 40 interpretable rules from search trajectories using a post-hoc decision-tree framework and show that reusing them as soft constraints yields gains of up to 2$\times$ in valid model rates and 3$\times$ in neutrino model discovery across all three theory spaces. These results suggest that CDRL uncovers reusable structure in combinatorial search spaces and provides a general framework for scientific model discovery.

AI.tldr: They propose Certification-Driven Reinforcement Learning (CDRL), which uses symbolic certificates of failure to prune invalid regions in combinatorial scientific model search, achieving much higher valid and high-quality model discovery efficiency than prior RL methods, and yielding reusable, interpretable rules.
AI.motivation: Many scientific discovery tasks involve exploring enormous combinatorial hypothesis spaces (e.g., >10^26 models) under strict domain constraints. Standard RL uses scalar rewards that only say whether a solution is valid or not, without explaining *why* a candidate fails. As a result, agents waste computation revisiting similar invalid regions. The authors aim to exploit richer, structured feedback—specifically, symbolic certificates explaining constraint violations—to make search more efficient and to uncover reusable scientific structure.
AI.method: They introduce Certification-Driven Reinforcement Learning (CDRL). When the RL agent proposes a candidate that violates domain constraints, a symbolic reasoning tool generates a certificate that pinpoints the actions or choices causing the failure. CDRL converts these certificates into reusable constraints that prune entire classes of invalid candidates from future exploration, effectively shaping the action space and guiding the policy toward valid regions. They apply this framework to neutrino flavor model discovery in particle physics, where the hypothesis space is extremely large. Additionally, they conduct a post-hoc analysis of RL trajectories using a decision-tree model to extract interpretable rules and then reuse these rules as soft constraints in subsequent searches.
AI.result: On neutrino flavor model discovery across three theory spaces, CDRL outperforms a prior state-of-the-art RL baseline. It achieves up to 1.95× higher rates of generating models that are valid under the domain constraints and up to 6.33× higher rates of discovering valid neutrino models (i.e., models consistent with neutrino data), while requiring up to 4× fewer candidate evaluations. The post-hoc decision-tree analysis yields 40 human-interpretable rules; using them as soft constraints provides additional gains of up to 2× in valid model rates and 3× in neutrino model discovery, consistently across all three theory spaces.
AI.conclusion: CDRL effectively incorporates structured, symbolic feedback into RL-based scientific model search. By turning failure certificates into generalized constraints, it prunes large invalid regions of combinatorial hypothesis spaces, substantially boosting sample efficiency and discovery rates relative to traditional scalar-reward RL. The interpretable rules extracted from search trajectories further demonstrate that the framework uncovers reusable domain structure. Overall, CDRL is proposed as a general, scalable approach for accelerating scientific discovery in highly constrained combinatorial domains.

title: JuryProbe: An Empirical Consensus-Risk Diagnostic for Routing Reference-Free Factuality Judge Panels to Grounded Verification
summary: Panels of inexpensive LLM judges increasingly make accept-or-escalate decisions. In factuality settings, accepting a claim because several reference-free judges agree can create a hidden risk: agreement may reflect shared false-negative blind spots rather than independent evidence. We introduce JuryProbe, an empirical consensus-risk diagnostic for reference-free factuality judge panels, paired with a calibration-based routing policy. JuryProbe estimates consensus risk from a labeled calibration probe using false-negative-only (FN-only) judge correlation and false-consensus lift; when flagged high-risk, reference-free majority accepts are routed to the same judges with trusted references. On audited FEVER corruptions, reference-free panels show correlated false negatives (FN-only correlations 0.402 and 0.368; lifts 3.13x and 18.13x), while unanimous false consensus drops to zero under a trusted-reference best-case diagnostic on both minimal-pair and non-minimal-pair evidence. In flagged settings, the routed policy is by construction equivalent to grounding every reference-free majority accept (verified in 34/34 splits): improvement comes from accept-conditioned grounding, while the diagnostic determines whether to activate it. A fixed, pre-specified rule flags 8-10 of 10 splits across synthetic, benchmark-authored, and scientific families and 0 of 10 on a negative control, where standing down avoids 28% of reference acquisitions at a 0.004 increase in false accepts. False-accept reduction persists under weak BM25 retrieval at substantial coverage cost, while stale stand-down labels require periodic recalibration. JuryProbe provides no formal risk guarantee and does not establish reliable stand-down on natural panels; its supported contribution is an empirical diagnostic of high-risk panel error dependence.

AI.tldr: They propose JuryProbe, a method to detect when panels of LLM factuality judges have correlated blind spots, and to selectively re-evaluate high-risk ‘accepted’ answers using trusted evidence.
AI.motivation: LLM judge panels increasingly decide whether to accept or escalate model outputs without direct access to ground-truth references. When multiple judges agree to accept, it seems safe, but their errors can be correlated: they might all miss the same subtle hallucinations. This creates hidden risk specifically for false negatives (accepting incorrect claims as correct). There is a need for a practical way to detect when panel agreement is actually dangerous because of shared blind spots, so that additional grounding or evidence can be used only when necessary.
AI.method: They introduce JuryProbe, an empirical diagnostic for reference-free factuality judge panels. Using a labeled calibration probe, they estimate: (1) false-negative-only (FN-only) correlation among judges (how often they jointly miss errors) and (2) false-consensus lift (how much more likely unanimous acceptance is to be wrong than expected under independence). If JuryProbe flags a setting as high-risk, then any claims that were majority-accepted in a reference-free mode are automatically re-routed to the same judges but now with access to trusted references. They evaluate this on FEVER-based corrupted datasets, across multiple split families and retrieval conditions, and also test a fixed pre-specified rule for when to ‘stand down’ (not use the extra grounding step).
AI.result: On audited FEVER corruptions, reference-free panels show strong correlated false negatives, with FN-only correlations of 0.402 and 0.368 and false-consensus lifts of 3.13x and 18.13x, meaning that unanimous agreement is much riskier than it appears if we assume independent judges. When the same items are judged with trusted references in a best-case diagnostic, unanimous false consensus essentially disappears. In all 34/34 experimental splits where JuryProbe flags high risk, the routed policy (re-grounding majority accepts) matches the hypothetical policy of grounding every accepted claim, confirming that the benefit comes from grounding conditioned on acceptance. Their fixed rule correctly flags 8–10 of 10 high-risk splits across several dataset families and flags 0 of 10 in a negative control setting. In the negative control, skipping extra references saves 28% of reference acquisitions with only a tiny 0.004 increase in false accepts. The reduction in false accepts holds even with weaker BM25 retrieval, though at the cost of coverage, and they observe that stand-down decisions can become stale over time and need recalibration.
AI.conclusion: JuryProbe is an empirical tool for detecting when panels of reference-free LLM factuality judges suffer from dangerous correlated blind spots, particularly for falsely accepting incorrect claims. While it offers no formal guarantees and does not yet validate low-risk behavior on arbitrary ‘natural’ judge panels, it provides a practical way to identify high-risk panel error dependence and to decide when to trigger more expensive, reference-grounded evaluation. This enables more efficient and safer use of LLM judge panels by focusing grounding resources where consensus is empirically shown to be unreliable.

title: VortexChat: An agentic framework for autonomous multi-objective integrated photonic design
summary: The advancement of modern integrated photonics is frequently bottlenecked by device design workflows that rely heavily on manual simulation and expert intuition. While inverse design offers an alternative, it remains constrained by expert supervision and a lack of end-to-end automation. To address these issues, we present VortexChat, an agentic framework for the autonomous, end-to-end inverse design of integrated photonic devices directly from natural language specifications. VortexChat couples a large language model (LLM) decision agent with topology generation, gradient-based refinement, and full-wave electromagnetic simulation. This closed-loop architecture enables the system to iteratively decompose design objectives, orchestrate computational tools, and update strategies based on feedback with minimal human intervention. Constrained by the absolute metrics of the Vortex100 Benchmark, VortexChat autonomously generates devices that strictly meet all predefined performance thresholds without any human-in-the-loop. As an experimental demonstration, we fabricated a broadband terahertz perfect vortex beam multiplexer, autonomously designed by VortexChat, with measurements confirming high-efficiency operation, high mode purity and low inter-channel crosstalk in agreement with full-wave simulations. These results demonstrate that an LLM agent can assume key aspects of expert decision-making in photonic inverse design while maintaining physical fidelity and fabrication feasibility, providing a scalable route towards autonomous design of complex integrated photonic systems.

AI.tldr: VortexChat is an LLM-driven, closed-loop agentic framework that autonomously performs end-to-end inverse design of integrated photonic devices from natural language specifications, validated by fabricating a high-performance terahertz vortex beam multiplexer.
AI.motivation: Modern integrated photonics design is slow and constrained because it depends heavily on manual simulations, expert intuition, and partially automated inverse design that still requires human supervision. There is a need for a scalable, fully autonomous workflow that can translate high-level natural language design goals into physically valid, fabricable photonic devices without continuous expert guidance.
AI.method: The authors build VortexChat, an agentic system where a large language model acts as a decision-making agent coordinating several tools: topology generation for initial device layouts, gradient-based refinement for optimization, and full-wave electromagnetic simulations for physics-accurate evaluation. The framework operates in a closed-loop: the LLM decomposes natural language design objectives into tasks, calls the appropriate computational tools, analyzes simulation feedback, and iteratively updates the design strategy until predefined benchmark metrics (Vortex100) are satisfied, all with minimal human involvement.
AI.result: Under the constraints of the Vortex100 Benchmark, VortexChat autonomously generates photonic device designs that satisfy all specified performance thresholds without any human-in-the-loop tuning. As a concrete proof-of-concept, the team fabricates a broadband terahertz perfect vortex beam multiplexer designed entirely by VortexChat; experimental measurements show high efficiency, high mode purity, and low inter-channel crosstalk, matching full-wave simulation predictions.
AI.conclusion: An LLM-based agent can successfully take over key expert decision-making tasks in photonic inverse design while preserving physical correctness and practical fabricability. This demonstrates a viable and scalable path toward fully autonomous design of complex integrated photonic systems directly from natural language, potentially removing major bottlenecks in the modern photonic design workflow.

title: When Failures Propagate: Causal Failure Attribution in Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) interleaves retrieval, reasoning, and answer generation across multiple hops. A retrieval error at hop 1 can surface only as a wrong answer at hop 3, while later retrieval can also repair the trajectory. This paper introduces AgenticRAG-FP, an interventional benchmark for causal failure attribution in agentic RAG. The benchmark injects a certified fault at a specified hop, re-executes the downstream trajectory, and evaluates diagnosers against the known intervention. Its central question is whether a post-hoc trace still identifies the injected hop after the suffix changes. In the completed strict dense Claude Haiku 4.5 sweep on 80 three-hop MuSiQue questions, coverage-based diagnosis is 0.91 at hop 1 and 0.00 at hops 2 and 3 (n=43,36,21 failed trajectories). A smaller content-corruption study changes an answer-bearing or bridge fact in topically intact evidence. At depth 2, where 18 failed cases remain after filtering, coverage-based diagnosis is 0.00 and a frozen-hop counterfactual probe is 0.67 in an exploratory pooled comparison. Depth-3 content estimates are descriptive only because they contain three failed cases. These results make propagation depth an explicit evaluation axis for diagnosing agentic RAG failures while distinguishing broad evidence of post-hoc signal loss from small-sample method comparisons.

AI.tldr: Introduces AgenticRAG-FP, a benchmark for causally attributing failures to specific hops in multi-hop agentic RAG by injecting controlled faults and evaluating diagnostic methods.
AI.motivation: In multi-hop agentic RAG, retrieval, reasoning, and generation are intertwined, so an early retrieval error may only appear as a wrong answer several steps later, and later steps can sometimes repair earlier mistakes. This makes it difficult to diagnose which hop actually caused a failure. Existing evaluations do not explicitly measure how well we can attribute errors to specific steps in the agentic trajectory.
AI.method: The authors propose AgenticRAG-FP, an interventional benchmark where they introduce certified faults at selected hops in an agentic RAG pipeline, then re-run the downstream trajectory while keeping the earlier hops fixed. They then test different diagnostic strategies—such as coverage-based diagnosis and a frozen-hop counterfactual probe—on their ability to correctly identify the hop at which the fault was injected, even when later steps change the trace. Experiments are run mainly on 80 three-hop MuSiQue questions with Claude Haiku 4.5 as the agent, and also on a smaller content-corruption study where specific answer-bearing or bridging facts in evidence are corrupted while the topic remains intact.
AI.result: On the three-hop MuSiQue benchmark, coverage-based diagnosis works reasonably well for first-hop failures (0.91 accuracy/coverage at hop 1) but completely fails to correctly attribute errors to later hops (0.00 at hops 2 and 3 across 43, 36, and 21 failed trajectories at each depth). In the content-corruption study at depth 2, after filtering to 18 failed cases, coverage-based diagnosis again scores 0.00, whereas the frozen-hop counterfactual probe attains 0.67 in an exploratory pooled comparison. Depth-3 content-corruption results are only descriptive due to having just three failed cases.
AI.conclusion: Propagation depth—the number of hops between where an error occurs and where it is observed—should be treated as an explicit axis in evaluating diagnostic methods for agentic RAG. The experiments show strong post-hoc signal loss as failures propagate across hops, undermining simple coverage-based diagnostics, while also highlighting that alternative interventional and counterfactual methods may better localize faults, especially at intermediate depths. The benchmark isolates and clarifies these phenomena, enabling more precise comparisons among diagnostic approaches.

title: DirEAG: Dirichlet Evidence Aggregation for Calibrating Verbalized Confidence in Mathematical Reasoning
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures. Code is available at https://github.com/horacehsugithub/DirEAG. Accepted by PRICAI 2026
summary: Reliable confidence estimation is essential for using large language models in mathematical reasoning, but black-box verbalized confidence is difficult to calibrate. When the same problem is queried under multiple confidence-steering prompts, the resulting answer-confidence observations contain useful uncertainty information, yet their scales may shift across steering levels, models, and datasets. Existing black-box uncertainty methods often rely on answer agreement, sample consistency, or entropy, which describe output variation but do not model the numerical meaning of self-reported confidence. Conversely, direct averaging or heuristic aggregation of elicited confidence cannot learn prompt- and task-dependent bias. We propose DirEAG, a Dirichlet Evidence Aggregation method that converts each elicited answer-confidence observation into calibrated soft evidence over generated candidate answers and an additional null state, allowing the model to represent cases where none of the candidates is correct. Experiments on GSM8K, SVAMP, and GSM-Hard with Qwen, Mistral, and Gemma models show that, compared with direct confidence averaging and heuristic confidence-steering aggregation, DirEAG often achieves better calibration while maintaining competitive answer selection. Ablations further reveal that evidence aggregation and final binary calibration address distinct parts of the calibration problem.

AI.tldr: They propose DirEAG, a method to better calibrate confidence estimates from large language models on math reasoning tasks by aggregating multiple confidence-steered responses into calibrated soft evidence, improving calibration while preserving answer quality.
AI.motivation: Large language models used for mathematical reasoning need reliable confidence estimates to be trustworthy, but current black-box verbalized confidences are poorly calibrated and vary with prompts, models, and datasets. Existing uncertainty methods (agreement, entropy, sample consistency) ignore the numeric meaning of self-reported confidence, while naive averaging cannot correct systematic, prompt-dependent bias. There is a need for a principled way to aggregate multiple elicited confidences into well-calibrated probabilities.
AI.method: They introduce DirEAG (Dirichlet Evidence Aggregation), which treats each answer–confidence pair from different confidence-steering prompts as a piece of soft evidence over candidate answers plus a special null state that represents “none of these is correct.” Each observation is converted into parameters of a Dirichlet distribution over this expanded outcome space and then aggregated across prompts to obtain a combined belief. A final binary calibration step is applied on top. The method is evaluated on math word problem benchmarks (GSM8K, SVAMP, GSM-Hard) using several LLMs (Qwen, Mistral, Gemma). Ablation studies separate the effects of the aggregation mechanism and the final calibration step.
AI.result: Across GSM8K, SVAMP, and GSM-Hard with Qwen, Mistral, and Gemma, DirEAG generally yields better confidence calibration than direct averaging or heuristic aggregation of the model’s self-reported confidence, while achieving similar or competitive performance in selecting correct answers. Ablation experiments show that both the evidence aggregation and the final binary calibration contribute complementary improvements to the overall calibration quality.
AI.conclusion: DirEAG provides a principled, model-agnostic way to turn multiple black-box, confidence-steered responses from LLMs into calibrated soft probabilities over answers, including the possibility that all candidate answers are wrong. This yields more reliable confidence estimates for mathematical reasoning tasks compared with naive or heuristic aggregation, and the study highlights that both structured evidence aggregation and a final calibration step are important for tackling different aspects of the calibration problem.

title: Sparse Token Routing in Efficient Transformers
summary: Efficient-transformer research often motivates token pruning and adaptive computation with the claim that not all tokens require equal computational effort. We test this claim end to end using SEWN, a two-stream Transformer that routes tokens through either lightweight or full-capacity processing using a learned gate. Across our experiments, routing introduces negligible accuracy change relative to parameter-matched baselines, while the gate's token-importance signal depends critically on how it is learned. A static lexicon-seeded prior fails a counterfactual faithfulness test on BoolQ, whereas a fully contextual gate achieves highly significant separation ($p<10^{-10}$) on both evaluated tasks without changing task accuracy.

AI.tldr: They test whether all tokens in Transformer models need equal computation by introducing SEWN, a two-stream Transformer with gated token routing, finding they can vary computation per token without hurting accuracy, but that how the gating is learned is crucial.
AI.motivation: Efficient Transformer methods often assume some tokens are less important and can receive less computation, but this assumption is rarely tested end-to-end for faithfulness and effectiveness. The paper aims to rigorously evaluate this assumption and the behavior of token-importance signals in such systems.
AI.method: They propose SEWN, a two-stream Transformer architecture where a learned gating mechanism routes tokens either through a lightweight or a full-capacity processing path. They compare different ways of learning the gate, including a static lexicon-seeded prior and a fully contextual gate, and evaluate performance and faithfulness on tasks such as BoolQ.
AI.result: Routing tokens through different-capacity streams yields negligible accuracy differences compared to parameter-matched baselines, indicating that adaptive computation can preserve task performance.
