However, the quality and faithfulness of the gate’s token-importance signal vary strongly by training scheme: the lexicon-seeded prior fails a counterfactual faithfulness test on BoolQ, while the fully contextual gate shows highly significant separation (p<1e-10) on both tasks without altering accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive token routing can be used without sacrificing accuracy, but the interpretability and faithfulness of the inferred token-importance signals depend critically on how the gating mechanism is learned. Fully contextual gating appears much more faithful and discriminative than static lexicon-based priors.

title: Calibrating Criterion Revision in LLM Agents: Failure Modes and a Trace-Anchored Protocol
comment: 18 pages, 8 tables, 1 figure. CMB-0.1 is an instrument-calibration study; CMB-0.4 is a prospective protocol, not an empirical result
summary:
Language-model agents can improve after failure or carry text across episodes without revising what counts as success. We study the narrower attribution problem of criterion revision: when criterion K0 accepts an outcome violating a broader commitment B, what observations justify saying that the system formed and persistently used K1? We require five non-compensatory conditions: criterion-failure detection, a model-emitted proposal, new-episode transfer, intervention sensitivity on the claimed carrier, and preservation.
  We evaluate CMB-0.1 on twelve cross-domain cases and four arms: stateless inference, append-only history, model-generated but harness-committed state, and evaluator-written oracle state. Seven mechanism fixtures yield 84 deterministic scorer trials; four local quantized artifacts yield 96 calls and 192 model-case-arm trials. No model trial satisfies all five conditions, but this zero does not establish general capability absence. Eleven calls remain invalid after one retry; several commitments disclose the target distinction; the harness performs commits; deletion reuses a stateless call; and conflict changes multiple factors. Qwen2.5-7B answers every transfer and preservation item without revision state, exposing zero-state reconstruction.
  These failures make CMB-0.1 an instrument-calibration result rather than a model ranking. We derive a prospective, trace-anchored CMB-0.4 protocol requiring concealed transfer, explicit WRITE/NO-WRITE/ESCALATE actions, a separately logged policy-selected commit, matched interventions, repeated hidden items, and a frozen executable oracle. It is a successor design, not a completed confirmatory result. The paper contributes a measurement chain, an empirical diagnosis of its first implementation, and a more discriminating protocol for future tests of criterion revision.

AI.tldr: The paper examines when we can justifiably claim that a language-model system has revised its own success criterion, and finds that an initial measurement protocol (CMB-0.1) fails to produce convincing instances of such revision, leading the authors to propose a more robust follow-up protocol (CMB-0.4).
AI.motivation: As language-model agents are increasingly deployed in multi-episode settings, it becomes important to know whether and when they genuinely update their internal criteria for success—especially when earlier criteria conflict with broader commitments or safety constraints. Existing evaluations tend to conflate carrying information across episodes with genuinely revising what counts as success; the authors want a principled way to attribute true criterion revision to a system.
AI.method: The authors define the "criterion revision" attribution problem and propose five non-compensatory conditions that must all be met to ascribe criterion change: (1) detection of failure under the old criterion; (2) an explicit, model-generated proposal of a new criterion; (3) successful transfer of this criterion across episodes; (4) sensitivity of behavior to interventions on the hypothesized carrier of the criterion; and (5) preservation of the new criterion over time. They instantiate these requirements in an experimental protocol CMB-0.1, testing language models across 12 cross-domain cases and 4 different state-handling arms: stateless inference, append-only histories, model-proposed but harness-committed state, and evaluator-oracle state. They run controlled trials using mechanism fixtures and quantized artifacts, logging deterministic scorer runs and multiple model-case-arm combinations.
AI.result: Across 84 deterministic scorer trials and 192 model-case-arm trials, no model instance satisfies all five conditions needed for robust attribution of criterion revision. Several artifacts in the setup undermine clean interpretation: some evaluation calls remain invalid even after retries; external commitments sometimes leak the intended distinction; the experimental harness performs state commits itself; some interventions (like deletion) inadvertently revert to stateless behavior; and conflict manipulations affect multiple variables at once. Qwen2.5-7B in particular can answer all transfer and preservation questions without needing any explicit revision state, demonstrating that behavior compatible with criterion revision can be reconstructed from zero visible state, which undercuts the attribution claim.
AI.conclusion: The CMB-0.1 protocol is better viewed as an instrument-calibration effort than as evidence for or against language models’ capability for criterion revision. On the basis of the observed failure modes, the authors propose a refined, prospective protocol (CMB-0.4) with stricter and more traceable requirements: hidden transfer conditions, explicit WRITE/NO-WRITE/ESCALATE actions, independently logged policy-chosen commits, carefully matched interventions, repeated hidden test items, and a frozen executable oracle. The core contribution is thus a clarified measurement chain and a more discriminating experimental design for future work on detecting genuine criterion revision in language-model agents.

title: AgentMercury: Your Agent Can Synthesize Verifiable Environments for Business Scenarios at scale
summary: Agents learn to act through interaction with environments, yet the environments used for training are often manually constructed or synthesized around predefined tasks and benchmarks. This task-centric paradigm makes it difficult to scale environments that reflect realistic and evolving workflows where diverse tasks can naturally emerge from the underlying world. We introduce AgentMercury, a scalable framework for synthesizing executable environments from high-level business scenarios. Rather than constructing an environment for a specific task, AgentMercury first instantiates a persistent world with entities, services, tools, state, and executable cross-service invariants, from which diverse tasks and interaction trajectories can subsequently emerge. We construct 4,783 executable environments spanning 14 industries and 50 countries, and use them as training substrates for reinforcement learning. Despite being generated without targeting the evaluation benchmarks, policies trained on these business-oriented environments improve substantially on both enterprise workflows and out-of-domain benchmarks spanning reasoning, coding, scientific computing, and tool use. In our experiments, Qwen3.5-4B improves from 12.3 to 15.7 on EnterpriseOps-GYM and from 45.9 to 56.0 on AIME26 after training on AgentMercury environments. We further show that the construction process itself can be learned: fine-tuning Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on construction traces increases executable-world authoring success from 3.3% to 83.3% on held-out business scenarios. These results show that scenario-grounded environments can provide useful and generalizable learning signals beyond benchmark-specific training, while their construction can itself become a learnable capability.

AI.tldr: The paper presents AgentMercury, a framework that automatically builds rich, executable business environments as training substrates for agents, enabling more generalizable learning beyond specific benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current RL and agent training rely on manually designed, task-centric environments tied to fixed benchmarks, which do not reflect realistic, evolving workflows and make it hard to scale task diversity. The authors want a scalable way to generate complex, persistent worlds from which many tasks naturally emerge, mimicking real business processes and improving generalization.
AI.method: They design AgentMercury, a system that takes high-level business scenarios and synthesizes persistent executable worlds populated with entities, services, tools, states, and cross-service invariants. These environments are executable, support diverse interaction trajectories, and are used as RL training substrates. They generate 4,783 such environments across many industries and countries, train policies (e.g., based on Qwen3.5-4B) in them, and also train a larger model (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B) on traces of environment construction to learn the environment-authoring process itself.
AI.result: Using AgentMercury-generated business environments, a Qwen3.5-4B-based policy significantly improves performance on both enterprise workflow benchmarks (EnterpriseOps-GYM: 12.3→15.7) and out-of-domain tasks (AIME26: 45.9→56.0) covering reasoning, coding, scientific computing, and tool use. Additionally, fine-tuning Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on environment construction traces boosts the success rate of generating executable worlds from 3.3% to 83.3% on unseen business scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Scenario-grounded, executable business environments can act as powerful, generalizable training substrates for agents, yielding improvements on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks without being designed around those benchmarks. Furthermore, the process of constructing such worlds can itself be learned by large models, making scalable environment generation a learnable capability rather than a purely manual engineering task.

title: ForeTime-VLA: Causal Future-Token Distillation from a World Action Model for Conveyor-Belt Manipulation
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures. Introduces ForeTime-VLA, a causal future-token distillation method for conveyor-belt manipulation from a frozen world action model teacher
summary: Manipulating moving objects requires a policy to anticipate contact events, yet vision-language-action (VLA) policies are commonly fine-tuned from the current observation alone. World action models (WAMs) learn predictive dynamics, but running a video-scale teacher or explicitly imagining future frames at deployment is costly. We introduce ForeTime-VLA, a dense pi0.5 policy that distills a future-aware, action-equivalent representation from a frozen Fast-WAM-derived teacher while remaining causal at inference. Offline, current and future video latents are compressed into a whitened 64-D target. Online, an eight-frame history encoder predicts this target together with manipulation phase and normalized time-to-transition. Four future tokens and one phase token condition the VLM prefix, while the predicted future and transition horizon condition the action expert. Training retains the original flow-matching action target and adds cosine, relational geometry, phase, time-to-transition, and action-equivalence objectives. On a deduplicated conveyor-belt dataset, we compare 40k-step checkpoints on 768 matched windows per split. Test MAE decreases from 0.134119 to 0.130593 (2.63%; paired-bootstrap 95% CI: 0.82-4.48% improvement), and test L2 decreases by 3.02%, at a 2.46-2.93% latency cost. In quantitative real-robot evaluation, ForeTime-VLA achieves 81.1% stationary and 58.9% slow-moving grasp success, exceeding the next-best reference by 12.2 and 22.2 percentage points, respectively. Across three belt speeds, it completes 44/90 grasps versus 23/90 for pi0.5, including 11/30 versus 2/30 at fast speed. The agreement between offline orientation gains and reduced real-robot contact-pose failures supports causal future-token distillation as an effective way to improve dynamic manipulation without deploying the world-model teacher.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ForeTime-VLA, a vision-language-action policy that distills future-aware representations from a frozen world model so it can anticipate contacts for dynamic object manipulation without expensive future rollouts at inference.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA policies for manipulation are usually fine-tuned only on the current observation and thus struggle to anticipate future contact events, especially with moving objects. World action models can predict future dynamics but are too costly to run as full video-scale teachers or to explicitly imagine future frames at deployment time. The authors aim to gain the benefits of future-aware reasoning for dynamic manipulation while keeping inference causal and efficient.
AI.method: They build ForeTime-VLA, a dense pi0.5 policy trained via distillation from a frozen Fast-WAM teacher. Offline, they compress current and future video latents into a whitened 64-D target that encodes action-equivalent, future-aware information. Online, an eight-frame history encoder predicts this target along with manipulation phase and normalized time-to-transition. These predicted future tokens (four future tokens plus one phase token) condition the vision-language model prefix, and the predicted future/time-to-transition condition the action expert. Training keeps the original flow-matching action target and adds multiple auxiliary losses: cosine and relational geometry losses on the distilled future representation, plus phase, time-to-transition, and action-equivalence objectives.
AI.result: On a deduplicated conveyor-belt dataset, ForeTime-VLA improves test mean absolute error from 0.134119 to 0.130593, a 2.63% reduction, with test L2 error decreasing by 3.02%, at a modest 2.46–2.93% latency overhead. In real-robot experiments, it achieves 81.1% grasp success on stationary objects and 58.9% on slow-moving objects, outperforming the next-best baseline by 12.2 and 22.2 percentage points, respectively. Across three conveyor speeds, it executes 44/90 successful grasps compared to 23/90 for pi0.5, including 11/30 vs. 2/30 at fast speed.
AI.conclusion: Causal distillation of future-aware tokens from a frozen world action model into a compact representation can significantly improve dynamic manipulation performance without deploying the heavy world-model teacher at inference. The gains in orientation accuracy, reduced contact-pose failures, and improved grasp success on moving objects show that ForeTime-VLA’s future-token distillation is an effective and efficient strategy for contact-anticipating control in dynamic settings.

title: MIL-BERT: Classification of Arbitrarily Large Text with Performance and Explanatory Guarantees
summary: Many text classification decisions are viable based on constituent excerpts alone. Taking inspiration from the field of multiple instance learning, we present an algorithm for training a neural network to classify text by selecting such excerpts. We show that our approach is also scalable with demonstrated learning against samples with nearly 1M tokens. We evaluate our methods on 7 datasets with emphasis on long-textual collections that far exceed the encoding limit of our base model. We present state-of-the-art results with this algorithm on 3 datasets: identification of political bias in news outlets, trigger warnings in long stories, and demographic characteristics of authors in tweet collections. Furthermore, the model trained on weakly-labeled collections of text (bags) generalizes to accurately classify constituent, smaller instances. Besides a new state-of-the-art for these problems, this approach is one of the few neural methods to excel in these datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a neural multiple-instance-learning-style method that selects informative excerpts from long texts to perform classification, achieving state-of-the-art results on several long-document tasks and generalizing from bag-level to instance-level labels.
AI.motivation: Many text classification tasks can be decided from only short parts of a document, but existing neural models struggle with very long inputs that exceed encoder length limits. There is a need for scalable methods that can learn from weakly labeled, long text collections while still identifying the key excerpts that drive classification decisions.
AI.method: The authors adapt ideas from multiple instance learning to text: they treat each long document (or collection of texts) as a bag of smaller textual instances (excerpts) and train a neural network to classify the bag by learning to select or weight informative excerpts. The base model has limited input length, so the algorithm focuses on learning which excerpts within very long documents are most predictive, enabling training on samples with up to nearly 1M tokens. The model is trained with weak supervision at the bag level but is designed so that the learned scoring over instances can be used for finer-grained predictions.
AI.result: Across 7 datasets, particularly those involving very long texts that exceed the base model's encoding limit, the proposed method is shown to be scalable and effective. It achieves new state-of-the-art performance on 3 specific tasks: detecting political bias in news outlets, predicting trigger warnings in long stories, and inferring demographic attributes of authors from collections of tweets. Moreover, the model trained only with weak labels at the bag level successfully generalizes to accurate classification of individual excerpts or smaller instances.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that treating long-text classification as a multiple-instance learning problem and training neural networks to select key excerpts is an effective and scalable strategy. This approach not only reaches or surpasses state-of-the-art performance on challenging long-text datasets but also enables models trained on weakly labeled bags to perform accurate instance-level classification, making it a promising neural method for handling extremely long textual inputs.

title: Continuous-Time Quantum Walks based Graph Neural Network
summary:
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are widely used on graph-structured data, but most suffer from two key weaknesses. First, message passing behaves as a low-pass filter under the homophily assumption, leading to poor performance on heterophilic graphs. Second, stacking layers drives node features toward constants, causing over-smoothing. Existing methods usually address these issues separately, while the few joint solutions rely largely on empirical heuristics, and many over-smoothing remedies sacrifice model expressiveness.
  We propose \textbf{CTQW-GNN}, a GNN based on Continuous-Time Quantum Walks (CTQW), to address both issues with theoretical justification. Its design exploits two properties of the CTQW propagator $e^{-\mathrm{i}Ht}$. First, it is unitary and has eigenvalues on the unit circle, so no frequency component is damped, counteracting the low-pass bias. Second, unitarity preserves feature norms and prevents the Dirichlet energy from decaying exponentially with depth, thereby mitigating over-smoothing.
  CTQW-GNN combines three complementary aggregation modules. \textit{CTQW-based Aggregation} evolves node features through the unitary propagator, preserving mid- and high-frequency signals for heterophilic graphs while preventing Dirichlet-energy collapse. \textit{CTQW-Attention Aggregation} constructs a multi-hop neighbor graph from CTQW amplitudes and applies attention over it, enabling access to distant homophilic nodes missed by single-hop aggregation. \textit{LF Aggregation} uses a standard low-pass GAT branch to retain strong performance on homophilic graphs, where pure CTQW aggregation can be suboptimal. We further provide a spectral-gap analysis explaining energy preservation and a Lieb--Robinson-type bound that gives a principled rule for selecting the walk time $t$.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CTQW-GNN, a graph neural network that uses continuous-time quantum walks to avoid low-pass bias and over-smoothing, achieving better performance on both heterophilic and homophilic graphs.
AI.motivation: Standard GNNs act like low-pass filters under homophily, which hurts performance on heterophilic graphs, and deeper models suffer from over-smoothing where node features converge to similar values. Existing approaches typically tackle only one of these issues or rely on heuristics, sometimes reducing expressiveness. The paper is motivated by the need for a principled, theoretically grounded architecture that simultaneously alleviates low-pass bias and over-smoothing without sacrificing expressive power.
AI.method: The authors design CTQW-GNN, built around the unitary propagator of a continuous-time quantum walk, e^{-iHt}. They leverage its spectral properties—eigenvalues on the unit circle and norm preservation—to construct three aggregation modules: (1) CTQW-based Aggregation that evolves node features via the unitary propagator to preserve all frequency components and avoid Dirichlet energy collapse; (2) CTQW-Attention Aggregation that uses CTQW amplitudes to define a multi-hop neighbor graph and then applies attention to aggregate from distant yet relevant nodes; and (3) LF Aggregation, a standard low-pass GAT branch, to maintain strong performance on homophilic graphs. They also provide a spectral-gap analysis for energy preservation and a Lieb–Robinson-type bound to guide the choice of walk time t.
AI.result: CTQW-GNN yields an architecture whose message passing does not damp high- and mid-frequency components and maintains feature norms across layers, theoretically mitigating low-pass bias and over-smoothing. The combination of CTQW-based propagation, CTQW-induced attention over multi-hop neighborhoods, and a low-frequency GAT branch enables the model to adapt to both heterophilic and homophilic settings. Theoretical analyses justify why energy is preserved and how to select the walk time via a Lieb–Robinson-type bound.
AI.conclusion: By leveraging continuous-time quantum walks, CTQW-GNN provides a principled solution to both low-pass bias on heterophilic graphs and over-smoothing in deep GNNs. Its unitary propagation preserves frequency content and Dirichlet energy, while complementary attention-based and low-pass branches broaden its applicability to diverse graph types. The theoretical analyses support its design choices, indicating that CTQW-style dynamics can serve as a powerful foundation for more expressive and stable GNN architectures.

title: Directional Contextual Representations for Dependency Relations: Why Cross-Direction Pairing Fails
summary: Splitting a bidirectional LSTM's contextual representation into a forward-only $F_i$ (strictly a function of tokens $1..i$) and a backward-only $B_i$ (strictly a function of tokens $i..n$) beats either alone and beats a fused self-attention representation for dependency relation-type classification. But a specific, natural extension of this idea -- pairing a token's forward state against a \emph{candidate}'s backward state (``cross-direction'' pairing, $F_i$ vs.\ $B_j$) -- consistently \emph{underperforms} same-direction pairing, and the penalty \emph{grows}, not shrinks, with token distance, both paired-bootstrap significant. We diagnose why using a frozen-trunk methodology: architectural information leakage between directions is impossible by construction (a single-layer BiLSTM, verified by code inspection); 93\% of the same-vs-cross gap survives freezing the trunk and training only fresh heads, ruling out training-co-adaptation as the primary cause; linear regression shows partial representational redundancy between $F_i$ and $B_i$ ($R^2{=}0.324$ vs.\ $0.028$ for a shuffled control) and a linear probe shows partial anticipatory encoding of upcoming tokens in $F_i$ (36.5\% vs.\ 17.2\% majority baseline) -- real effects, but neither alone, nor combined, cleanly explains the full gap. Extended frozen-trunk diagnostics (a positional probe and a distance-decay probe) show directional information is genuinely stored but not exactly positioned, and propagates only a few tokens before decaying to baseline -- consistent with, and mechanistically underneath, the distance-growth finding.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how splitting BiLSTM representations into purely forward and purely backward components affects dependency relation classification, and why pairing mismatched directions (forward of one token with backward of another) hurts performance, especially at longer distances.
AI.motivation: To understand what information is actually encoded in each directional component of a BiLSTM (forward vs backward), how redundant or complementary they are, and how this impacts downstream tasks like dependency relation-type classification, especially across distances between tokens.
AI.method: They compare different pairing schemes of BiLSTM hidden states (forward-only, backward-only, fused self-attention, same-direction pairing, and cross-direction pairing) on dependency relation-type classification. They then apply a frozen-trunk diagnostic methodology: using a single-layer BiLSTM with no architectural cross-direction leakage, freezing it and training only new classifier heads, and probing the representations with linear regression and linear probes to measure redundancy, anticipatory encoding, positional information, and distance-decay of directional signals.
AI.result: Splitting BiLSTM into separate forward (Fi) and backward (Bi) representations and using same-direction pairings outperforms using either direction alone and even beats a fused self-attention representation on dependency relation-type classification. However, cross-direction pairings (Fi vs Bj) significantly underperform same-direction pairings, with the performance penalty increasing with token distance. 93% of this performance gap remains even when the BiLSTM trunk is frozen, indicating it is not primarily due to training co-adaptation. Probes reveal partial redundancy between Fi and Bi and some anticipatory encoding of future tokens in Fi, but these do not fully account for the observed gap. Additional probes show that directional information is present but only approximately localized and decays over a few tokens.
AI.conclusion: Forward and backward states in a BiLSTM contain partially redundant and weakly anticipatory information, but their benefits for dependency relation classification rely on same-direction, short-range contextualization rather than cross-directional pairing. Directional information is real but fuzzy in position and quickly decays with distance, which mechanistically explains why cross-direction pairings degrade, and more so for long-range dependencies.

title: Is Multimodal Speculative Decoding Ready for Diffusion-Based Parallel Drafting? A Survey and Empirical Diagnosis
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by allowing a lightweight drafter to propose future tokens while a target model verifies them in parallel. Its lossless guarantee has motivated a line of work that pushes the drafter itself toward parallel generation. The most recent paradigm is block-parallel generative drafting, including diffusion-based methods such as DFlash and DSpark, achieving up to 3.6x speedup on common daily chatting tasks. While this transition is well studied in text-only LLMs, its applicability to multimodal models remains an open question. Existing multimodal speculative decoding efforts focus on input compression, adapter alignment, candidate coverage, or modality-specific verification; however, block-parallel generative drafting remains largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, this paper combines a modality-centered survey with a cross-architecture empirical study to ask: Is multimodal speculative decoding ready for diffusion-based parallel drafting? In this survey, we systematically analyze a wide spectrum of multimodal models, spanning Vision-Language, Video-Language, Audio, and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures, from the dual perspectives of drafting parallelism and cross-modal information interaction. We introduce a unified taxonomy that isolates drafter-side parallelism from orthogonal design choices such as tree construction and verification strategies. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive empirical comparison of existing methods under varying degrees of parallelism across standardized multimodal benchmarks, including OCR, VQA, visual reasoning, and image captioning. Finally, we summarize the limitations of current approaches, discuss open challenges, and outline promising future directions for this rapidly evolving field.

AI.tldr: The paper surveys and empirically studies speculative decoding for multimodal models, focusing on whether diffusion-based block-parallel drafting concepts from text-only LLMs can transfer to vision, video, audio, and action-conditioned architectures.
AI.motivation: Speculative decoding with parallel drafting has significantly sped up text-only LLM generation, especially with diffusion-based block-parallel methods like DFlash and DSpark. However, multimodal speculative decoding research has not yet explored these block-parallel generative drafting ideas, leaving a gap in understanding how or whether such techniques apply to models that handle images, video, audio, or actions.
AI.method: The authors conduct a modality-centered survey and cross-architecture empirical study. They analyze a broad set of multimodal architectures (Vision-Language, Video-Language, Audio, and Vision-Language-Action) from two angles: how well they support drafter-side parallelism and how cross-modal information flows during drafting. They propose a unified taxonomy that explicitly separates drafter parallelism from other components like tree construction and verification. They then benchmark existing multimodal speculative decoding methods under varying levels of parallelism on standardized tasks such as OCR, VQA, visual reasoning, and image captioning.
AI.result: The study produces a taxonomy of multimodal speculative decoding designs, characterizing how different architectures support or hinder diffusion-based block-parallel drafting. It delivers empirical performance and speed comparisons across multiple multimodal tasks at different parallelism degrees, revealing where current methods succeed or break down when pushed toward diffusion-like parallel drafting regimes.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal speculative decoding is not yet fully ready for diffusion-based block-parallel drafting across all architectures, but the paper clarifies the main bottlenecks and design trade-offs. It identifies limitations in current multimodal models and decoding schemes, highlights open research challenges around enabling efficient drafter parallelism and robust cross-modal interaction, and points to promising research directions for future multimodal speculative decoding methods.

title: AsmEvo: Agentic Assembly-Level Optimization of AMD GPU Kernels with Functional Equivalence Verification
summary:
High-performance ML systems increasingly rely on GPU kernels whose editable source is unavailable, generated, or too distant from final machine code to expose remaining optimizations. Existing LLM kernel optimizers and autotuners mainly operate on CUDA, Triton, HIP, or tensor-program source and validate against reference implementations. We study a stricter setting: optimizing an already compiled AMDGPU code object, where the deployed binary is the only behavioral oracle.
  We present AsmEvo, an agentic assembly-level optimizer for AMD GPU kernels. Given an AMDGPU code object K0, AsmEvo reconstructs a reassemblable representation, proposes low-level edits with a long-horizon agent, rebuilds an ABI-preserving optimized object, and accepts candidates only after differential verification against K0 under identical launches. AsmEvo combines code-object recovery, metadata-aware rebuilding, profiling-guided hot-window editing, correctness-gated timing, and conservative in-place patch fallback.
  We conduct extensive experiments with AsmEvo on various AMD GPU kernels. On MI308X, AsmEvo improves 29 of 30 selected KernelBench kernels, reaching 1.35x geometric-mean and 3.88x maximum speedup. On MI300X production workloads, it improves all evaluated AITer binaries and vLLM/SGLang Triton assembly kernels, reaching 1.09x/1.31x and 1.18x/1.34x geometric-mean/maximum speedups, respectively, while preserving functional equivalence.

AI.tldr: AsmEvo is an agent-based system that directly optimizes compiled AMD GPU kernels at the assembly level, achieving significant speedups while guaranteeing functional equivalence to the original binaries.
AI.motivation: Many high-performance ML workloads depend on GPU kernels whose source code is unavailable or too far from the final machine code to enable low-level optimization. Existing LLM-based kernel optimizers and autotuners work at higher-level representations (CUDA, Triton, etc.) and rely on separate reference implementations for correctness, which is not always possible for deployed binaries. There is a need for a method that can further optimize already-compiled AMD GPU code objects, using only the deployed binary as the behavioral specification, while ensuring correctness.
AI.method: AsmEvo operates directly on AMDGPU code objects. Starting from an original kernel K0, it: (1) reconstructs a representation that can be reassembled; (2) uses a long-horizon agent to propose low-level assembly edits; (3) rebuilds an ABI-preserving optimized code object; and (4) validates candidate kernels via differential testing against K0 under identical launch conditions. The system integrates several key techniques: recovery of code and metadata from code objects, metadata-aware rebuilding to keep ABI and environment compatibility, profiling-guided selection of hot instruction windows for focused editing, correctness-gated performance measurement, and a conservative in-place patch fallback strategy if more aggressive edits fail.
AI.result: On AMD MI308X hardware, AsmEvo improves 29 out of 30 kernels from KernelBench, achieving a 1.35x geometric-mean speedup and up to 3.88x maximum speedup. On MI300X production workloads, it improves all evaluated AITer binaries and vLLM/SGLang Triton-generated assembly kernels, with geometric-mean/maximum speedups of 1.09x/1.31x and 1.18x/1.34x, respectively, all while maintaining functional equivalence to the original kernels.
AI.conclusion: AsmEvo demonstrates that agentic, assembly-level optimization of already-compiled AMD GPU binaries is feasible and effective. By operating directly on code objects and using the original binary as the sole behavioral oracle, it can safely deliver substantial performance gains across benchmark and production ML workloads without requiring access to high-level source or separate reference implementations.

title: Natural-Language-Guided Generator-Agnostic Shortlisting for Protein Binder Design
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026 Workshop on Generative and Agentic AI for Biology
summary: Modern de novo design workflows generate many candidate protein binders, but wet-lab validation capacity remains limited, making shortlisting a major bottleneck. We study whether LLMs can generate multi-metric ranking policies from precomputed structural-confidence and interface-quality proxy scores. Rather than proposing a new protein binder design pipeline, we focus on post-generation binder shortlisting: selecting the final top-K candidates from already generated binder pools using a shared panel of precomputed proxy scores. On the 10-target held-out split, averaging performance over five sampled global iterative gpt-4o policies reaches 0.589 Recall@10, modestly improving over the strongest single-feature fixed baseline, Protenix binder ipTM, which reaches 0.571 Recall@10. On the 3-target held-out subset comprising Nipah, RBX1, and TREM2, target-conditioned iterative gpt-5.4 policies reach the strongest LLM performance, with 0.519 Recall@10 and 0.583 NDCG@10. These results suggest that LLM-generated ranking policies can act as an interpretable post-generation decision layer for combining heterogeneous proxy metrics to prioritize binders from large candidate pools.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether large language models can learn ranking policies to shortlist protein binder candidates using existing proxy scores, modestly improving binder selection over the best single-score baseline.
AI.motivation: De novo protein binder design generates huge numbers of candidates, but experimental validation is expensive and slow, making it crucial to shortlist the most promising binders using computational signals. Existing approaches rely on individual structural or interface-quality proxy scores, which may capture different aspects of binding quality and are hard to combine optimally. There is a need for interpretable, data-driven ranking strategies that can integrate heterogeneous metrics to better prioritize candidates without changing upstream design workflows.
AI.method: The authors treat binder shortlisting as a learning-to-rank problem over pools of already generated candidates, each annotated with multiple precomputed proxy metrics (e.g., structural confidence, interface quality). They prompt large language models—gpt-4o and a more advanced gpt-5.4—in both global and target-conditioned, iterative ranking modes to propose multi-metric ranking policies that combine these scores into a final ordering. They then evaluate these LLM-generated policies on held-out protein targets by measuring how well the top-K ranked candidates recover the truly strong binders, using ranking metrics like Recall@10 and NDCG@10, and compare against fixed, single-feature score baselines such as Protenix binder ipTM.
AI.result: On a 10-target held-out split, the average performance across five sampled global iterative gpt-4o-derived policies yields 0.589 Recall@10, slightly outperforming the best fixed baseline, Protenix binder ipTM, which achieves 0.571 Recall@10. On a more challenging 3-target held-out subset (Nipah, RBX1, TREM2), target-conditioned iterative policies generated by gpt-5.4 perform best among LLM configurations, with 0.519 Recall@10 and 0.583 NDCG@10. These results show consistent, though modest, gains over individual proxy metrics for top-K binder recovery.
AI.conclusion: LLM-generated ranking policies can serve as an interpretable, post-generation decision layer that combines diverse structural-confidence and interface-quality proxy scores to improve shortlisting of protein binder candidates. While the performance gains over strong single-metric baselines are modest, the approach demonstrates that language models can learn useful multi-metric ranking strategies without altering the upstream design process, suggesting a practical path to more effective and flexible computational triaging of large de novo binder libraries.

title: PSK at WMT 2026 MIST: Task-Specialized QLoRA Adapters for Multilingual Summarization and Question Answering
summary: We describe the PSK submission to the WMT 2026 Multilingual Instruction Shared Task. Our system uses the 3.35B-parameter Tiny Aya Global model with three QLoRA adapters, one for each task. The adapters are trained on multilingual document-summary pairs, passage-based question answering, and filtered standalone question answering. The summarization data also includes scientific papers with their author-written abstracts. On our held-out split, the context and summarization adapters perform better than our multitask adapter, which was trained only on data supplied by the organizers. Results for open QA are mixed and vary with answer length and evaluation method. We therefore submit three systems with the same context and summarization adapters but different open-QA adapters.

AI.tldr: They present a multilingual instruction-following system built from Tiny Aya Global with task-specific QLoRA adapters for WMT 2026.
AI.motivation: To build an effective multilingual instruction-following system for the WMT 2026 shared task, leveraging a relatively small base model enhanced with specialized adapters for different instruction types (summarization, context-based QA, and open QA).
AI.method: Use the 3.35B-parameter Tiny Aya Global model as a frozen base and train three separate QLoRA adapters, one per task: (1) summarization using multilingual document–summary pairs including scientific papers and their abstracts; (2) context (passage-based) QA; and (3) standalone open QA trained on filtered QA data. They also train a multitask adapter using only organizer-supplied data and evaluate variants on a held-out split, especially contrasting task-specific vs multitask adapters and different open-QA adapters.
AI.result: Task-specific context and summarization adapters outperform the multitask adapter on a held-out split. Open QA performance is inconsistent, depending on answer length and the evaluation protocol, so no single open-QA configuration is clearly best.
AI.conclusion: Specialized QLoRA adapters on a small multilingual base model can outperform a multitask adapter for summarization and context QA. Because open QA results are sensitive to evaluation details, the authors submit three systems sharing the same context and summarization adapters but differing in the open-QA adapter used.

title: Beyond Endpoint Gains: A Weight-Delta Audit of Medical Specialization
summary: Specialist language models are usually understood through endpoint gains: the generalist scores lower, the specialist scores higher, and the difference is treated as evidence of specialization. This leaves the released update itself largely unexamined. We propose a paired weight-delta path audit and apply it to two public, aligned generalist-to-medical-specialist checkpoint pairs: Gemma-3-4B-IT to MedGemma-4B-IT and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to HuatuoGPT-o1-7B. In both pairs, the full decoder-side update strongly reconstructs measured medical benchmark movement (0.974 and 1.183 endpoint-normalized retention), making each decoder delta an appropriate substrate for the audit. Yet the movement is not cleanly localized. MLP is the strongest broad component family in both pairs, but mixed off-domain movements, 10-seed matched controls, and endpoint-anchored rollbacks prevent a unique coarse-family explanation. The audit therefore separates update-level reconstruction from component-level explanation. Its claims concern text-only multiple-choice benchmark movement, not clinical validation, repair, or circuit-level mechanism.

AI.tldr: Audit of weight updates in specialist medical language models.
AI.motivation: To move beyond simple endpoint performance gains as evidence of specialization and instead directly examine how the model’s weights change when adapting a generalist language model to a medical specialist.
AI.method: Introduce a paired weight-delta path audit that analyzes the decoder-side weight updates between aligned generalist and medical-specialist model checkpoints. Apply this to two public pairs (Gemma-3-4B-IT → MedGemma-4B-IT and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct → HuatuoGPT-o1-7B). Examine reconstruction of benchmark performance changes, component-family contributions (e.g., MLP), controls with random seeds, and rollbacks anchored on endpoints.
AI.result: The decoder-side weight deltas alone almost perfectly reconstruct the movement in medical benchmark scores (endpoint-normalized retention of 0.974 and 1.183), showing that the updates encode the specialist performance shift. However, the changes are not cleanly attributable to a single model component family; although MLP layers contribute most broadly, there are mixed off-domain movements and control experiments and rollbacks rule out a simple localization of the effect.
AI.conclusion: The proposed audit can distinguish between a model update’s ability to reconstruct downstream benchmark changes and our ability to assign those changes to specific architectural components. For these medical-specialist models, specialization is distributed and cannot be uniquely explained at a coarse component-family level. The findings apply only to text-only multiple-choice benchmarks and do not constitute clinical validation or mechanistic insight at the circuit level.

title: Tree-of-Concerns: Hierarchical Multi-Agent Debate for Unstated-Limitation Extraction in Scientific Critique
comment: Accepted in the Findings of EMNLP 2026
summary: As scientific literature grows and papers increasingly under-report limitations, multi-agent LLMs offer a promising approach to systematically uncover these hidden failure modes. Here, we introduce Tree-of-Concerns, a multi-agent framework that deploys specialized skeptic personas, each operating through a category-specific analytical lens, as parallel debate trees to extract unstated limitations from scientific papers. Each persona conducts structured, evidence-grounded argumentation, while a Panel Review mechanism re-evaluates each surviving claim from all five perspectives to correct category drift and severity miscalibration. Through experiments on ToC-Bench, our benchmark of 414 research papers with 1,905 unstated limitations, sourced from reviewer-reported weaknesses and follow-up citation critiques, we demonstrate that ToC improves precision by 79% and coverage by 11% relative to strongest baselines, surfacing specific, evidence-grounded concerns that support reviewers in systematic evaluation.

AI.tldr: Introduces Tree-of-Concerns, a multi-agent LLM framework that uses specialized skeptic personas and a panel review step to systematically uncover unstated limitations in scientific papers, outperforming prior methods on a new benchmark.
AI.motivation: Scientific literature is rapidly expanding, and authors often under-report or omit limitations and failure modes in their papers. Existing automated methods struggle to reliably surface these hidden weaknesses, limiting their usefulness for peer review and critical appraisal. The authors aim to build a system that can more systematically and accurately detect unstated limitations to support reviewers and readers.
AI.method: They propose Tree-of-Concerns (ToC), a multi-agent framework where multiple specialized “skeptic personas” each analyze a paper through a distinct category-specific lens (e.g., methodological, data-related, generalizability). Each persona runs its own structured debate tree to generate and refine evidence-grounded critiques. A subsequent Panel Review mechanism then re-assesses all remaining limitation claims from all five personas’ perspectives, correcting for category drift (misclassification of concern types) and severity miscalibration (over/understated importance). Performance is evaluated on ToC-Bench, a constructed benchmark of 414 research papers paired with 1,905 unstated limitations, collected from reviewer comments and critical follow-up citations.
AI.result: On ToC-Bench, Tree-of-Concerns substantially improves over the strongest baselines, achieving a 79% increase in precision and an 11% increase in coverage when identifying unstated limitations. The system surfaces specific, evidence-backed concerns rather than vague critiques, showing that the multi-persona debate and panel review structure yields more accurate and useful limitation extraction.
AI.conclusion: Tree-of-Concerns is an effective multi-agent LLM-based framework for uncovering unstated limitations in scientific papers. By combining specialized skeptic personas with a panel review stage, it produces more precise and comprehensive lists of hidden weaknesses than existing methods. This can support peer reviewers and other stakeholders in more systematic and evidence-grounded evaluation of research, and the authors provide ToC-Bench as a benchmark to facilitate further work in this area.

title: CAS: Conformalized Agentic Search via Adaptive Retrieval and Policy Weighting
comment: 21 pages, including figures, tables, and appendix
summary:
Search Agents face a severe reliability crisis during reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning. Heuristic Top-K retrieval often causes critical evidence loss or noise inclusion, while over-confidence induced by progressive RL leads to hallucinated answers and redundant searches.
  To build highly reliable agents, we introduce Conformal Prediction (CP) and propose Conformalized Agentic Search (CAS). This framework establishes reliability guarantees on both the retrieval and training sides: on the retrieval side, an Adaptive Prediction Set (APS), a specific CP realization, translates statistical coverage into dynamic document truncation to construct prediction sets that are adaptive in size; on the training side, Adaptive Conformal Inference (ACI), a dynamic CP algorithm, dynamically constructs prediction sets with controllable coverage to quantify answer confidence, which is then used to penalize low-confidence trajectories within the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) objective, ensuring the model learns only from reliable ones.
  Experiments across single-hop and multi-hop QA datasets demonstrate that our framework significantly improves reasoning accuracy while drastically reducing redundant tool invocations, establishing a highly reliable and efficient agent paradigm. Our code is available at https://github.com/S1llyBird/CAS.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Conformalized Agentic Search (CAS), a framework that uses conformal prediction to enhance the reliability of RL-finetuned search agents in both retrieval and training, improving QA accuracy while reducing redundant tool calls.
AI.motivation: RL-finetuned search agents often suffer from unreliable retrieval (missing key evidence or adding noisy documents) and over-confident reasoning that leads to hallucinations and unnecessary searches. The authors aim to provide formal reliability guarantees and better control over both what is retrieved and which trajectories the model learns from.
AI.method: CAS integrates conformal prediction in two places. For retrieval, it uses Adaptive Prediction Sets (APS) to translate statistical coverage guarantees into dynamic Top-K style truncation, yielding prediction sets of documents whose size adapts to uncertainty. For training, it uses Adaptive Conformal Inference (ACI) to construct prediction sets over answers with controllable coverage, turning these into confidence scores that penalize low-confidence trajectories inside a GRPO reinforcement learning objective, so the agent learns predominantly from reliable rollouts.
AI.result: Across single-hop and multi-hop QA benchmarks, CAS improves reasoning accuracy and significantly reduces redundant tool or search invocations compared to standard RL-finetuned search agents and heuristic Top-K retrieval baselines.
AI.conclusion: By combining conformal prediction with RL-based agent training, CAS offers a principled way to obtain reliability guarantees for both retrieval and answer generation. This leads to more accurate, efficient, and trustworthy search agents, suggesting a promising paradigm for robust tool-using LLM agents.

title: Denoising the Future: Context-Aware Spectral Diffusion for Temporal Knowledge Graph Extrapolation
summary: Temporal Knowledge Graph (TKG) extrapolation seeks to infer future facts from time-varying relational histories. Recent diffusion-based approaches improve uncertainty modeling through generative denoising, but their aggregated conditioning on subject histories may insufficiently distinguish query-specific evidence from non-salient historical facts, thereby diluting target-discriminative signals. To bridge this gap, we propose FreqDiff, a Frequency-aware Diffusion framework for TKG extrapolation. Specifically, FreqDiff formulates future object prediction as query-slot denoising and develops a dual-stream denoiser that integrates temporal dependency modeling with context-aware spectral calibration. The spectral branch synthesizes history-conditioned filters from learnable bases to adaptively re-calibrate denoising representations, while a frequency-domain regularizer is proposed to align the denoised target with the gold object in spectral space. Experiments on four public TKG benchmarks demonstrate that FreqDiff achieves state-of-the-art performance.

AI.tldr: FreqDiff is a diffusion-based, frequency-aware framework that improves temporal knowledge graph extrapolation by better separating query-relevant signals from noisy historical facts.
AI.motivation: Existing temporal knowledge graph extrapolation methods, including recent diffusion-based ones, condition on aggregated subject histories but struggle to distinguish query-specific evidence from irrelevant past facts. This weakens target-discriminative signals and limits predictive accuracy, especially under uncertainty. The work is motivated by the need for a generative model that can more precisely focus on salient temporal patterns for each query while modeling uncertainty effectively.
AI.method: The authors introduce FreqDiff, a frequency-aware diffusion framework. Future object prediction is cast as a query-slot denoising problem in a diffusion model. They design a dual-stream denoiser: one branch focuses on temporal dependency modeling in the time domain, and another spectral branch performs context-aware spectral calibration. The spectral branch builds history-conditioned filters from learnable frequency bases and uses them to recalibrate intermediate denoising representations. Additionally, they introduce a frequency-domain regularizer that encourages the denoised prediction to align with the ground-truth object in spectral space, reinforcing frequency-consistent target reconstruction.
AI.result: On four public temporal knowledge graph benchmarks, FreqDiff outperforms existing baselines, including prior diffusion-based approaches, and sets new state-of-the-art results according to the reported metrics for future fact prediction.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating frequency-aware modeling into diffusion-based TKG extrapolation allows more effective separation of salient, query-specific temporal evidence from noisy historical context. The proposed FreqDiff framework, with its dual-stream denoiser and spectral regularization, yields superior performance on standard benchmarks, suggesting that spectral calibration is a promising direction for improving generative temporal reasoning over knowledge graphs.

title: Structure for Reading, Prose for Writing: Asymmetric Structural Conditioning in Multi-Agent Document Authoring
summary: Multi-agent pipelines that author formal documents must both read a requester's forms and write against them. We report a deployed tender-response system, running an open-weights model under sovereignty constraints, and evaluate it against human-written bids the same organisation actually submitted. On a blind comparison where the system had no worked example available, an LLM judge rated its answers at least as good as the human-submitted answer on $40$ of $55$ ground-truth sections, better on $4$, missing on none, and flagged one unsupported claim in total. Classifying every gap the judge identified shows that $68\%$ were content absent from the system's own sources -- knowledge the human author held and the pipeline was never given -- so only $6$ of the $15$ adverse verdicts involve a deficiency the system could have avoided. A divergence from ground truth is more often an information-availability result than a writing-quality one, and evaluations that do not separate the two understate such systems. Against this backdrop we report a conditioning asymmetry. It is well established that rendering documents as structural markup rather than flat prose improves extraction, and we reproduce that on three reading tasks. The benefit does not transfer to conditioning: converting a bid's \emph{instruction} material from prose to nested XML dropped answer quality from $74\%$ to $48\%$ under a paired comparison. We further find that naming a forbidden construction concentrates rather than removes it -- $96\%$ of surviving defects fall in the two forms the prompt explicitly names -- and that coupling a stochastic annotation to a deterministic windowing function moves the extracted requirement count from $68$ to $51$ on a byte-identical file. Structure belongs where the model reads; prose and self-applied tests belong where it writes.

AI.tldr: Deployed multi-agent tender-response system matches or exceeds human bids when information is available; main limitations stem from missing source content, not writing quality.
AI.motivation: To assess how well a sovereign, open-weights multi-agent system can read complex tender instructions and generate competitive bid responses, and to disentangle failures due to lack of information from failures in writing, while also probing how document structure and prompt design affect performance.
AI.method: Deploy a tender-response pipeline using an open-weights LLM that reads requester forms and writes responses; compare its outputs blindly against 55 sections from real human-submitted bids using an LLM judge; classify discrepancies by whether missing information was available in system inputs; run controlled experiments on three reading tasks to compare structural markup vs prose inputs, on conditioning by converting instructions to XML, and on prompt designs naming forbidden constructions and varying annotation/windowing strategies.
AI.result: The LLM judge rated system answers at least as good as human ones on 40/55 sections, better on 4, with no missing answers and only one unsupported claim. Of the 15 adverse judgments, 68% stemmed from information absent in the system’s sources, leaving only 6 sections where the system could plausibly have done better. Evaluations that ignore this confound underrate such systems. Structural markup aids reading: it improves extraction on three tasks. However, converting instruction text from prose to nested XML harmed writing performance, dropping bid answer quality from 74% to 48%. Prompts that explicitly name forbidden constructions concentrate residual errors into those very forms, and coupling stochastic annotation with deterministic windowing reduced the counted extracted requirements from 68 to 51 on the same file.
AI.conclusion: In this deployed setting, performance gaps largely reflect information availability rather than the system’s writing quality. Evaluation should therefore separate reading/input limitations from generation quality. Structural markup is beneficial on the reading side but detrimental when used to condition generation: instructions should remain in prose, and quality should be controlled by self-applied tests rather than rigid structural constraints. Prompt designs that enumerate forbidden patterns can inadvertently focus remaining errors into those patterns, and stochastic preprocessing can destabilize requirement extraction counts. Overall, structure is best used where the model reads, while prose and self-checking are better where it writes.

title: STAR-OPD: Structured Aspect-Cascade-Aware On-Policy Reward Distillation for ABSA Quadruple Extraction
summary: Aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) quadruple extraction requires jointly predicting target, aspect, opinion, and sentiment over reviews that often contain multiple fine-grained sentiment tuples. While large chain-of-thought (CoT) models perform well on this task, distilling them into smaller deployable models remains difficult. We identify a task-specific failure mode in distilled ABSA extraction: student errors at the target-aspect interface create structurally invalid states, such as broken target-aspect bindings and hallucinated targets, which then corrupt downstream predictions. Conventional off-policy distillation is poorly suited to this setting because it trains only on teacher-generated trajectories and provides little supervision on the student-induced structural states that dominate inference. To address this mismatch, we propose STAR-OPD (STructured Aspect-cascade-aware On-Policy Reward Distillation), which builds on generic on-policy distillation and instantiates it for ABSA quadruple extraction with cascade-aware, set-structured rewards. STAR-OPD trains on student rollouts and applies set-structured rewards that directly target binding consistency, target grounding, and fine-grained aspect disambiguation. Experiments on E-ABSA20K and SemEval-2014 show that STAR-OPD consistently outperforms off-policy and general on-policy baselines, reduces target hallucination, and substantially improves performance on structurally hard cases. With Qwen3-4B, STAR-OPD substantially narrows the student-teacher gap while improving inference efficiency, highlighting the importance of on-policy structural correction for distilled ABSA extraction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes STAR-OPD, an on-policy, structure-aware distillation method that improves aspect-based sentiment analysis quadruple extraction by correcting student-specific structural errors, significantly closing the gap between small distilled models and strong CoT teachers while improving efficiency.
AI.motivation: Aspect-based sentiment analysis requires extracting multiple fine-grained quadruples (target, aspect, opinion, sentiment) from a single review. Large chain-of-thought models handle this well but are too expensive to deploy, and distilling them into smaller models leads to specific structural errors: broken bindings between targets and aspects, hallucinated targets, and invalid quadruple structures. Standard off-policy distillation ignores these student-induced errors because it only trains on teacher trajectories, giving little feedback on the structurally invalid states that dominate student inference. The motivation is to design a distillation approach that directly addresses these structured failure modes so that small models can better mimic strong teachers while remaining efficient.
AI.method: The authors introduce STAR-OPD (STructured Aspect-cascade-aware On-Policy Reward Distillation), an on-policy distillation framework tailored to ABSA quadruple extraction. Instead of training only on teacher-generated outputs, the method trains on student rollouts and evaluates them with cascade-aware, set-structured reward functions. These rewards explicitly measure and encourage: (1) binding consistency between targets and aspects, (2) grounding of targets in the input text to avoid hallucinations, and (3) precise disambiguation of fine-grained aspects. The approach builds on generic on-policy distillation but customizes the reward design and training dynamics to the structured nature of ABSA quadruples and the cascade dependencies among target, aspect, opinion, and sentiment.
AI.result: On two benchmarks, E-ABSA20K and SemEval-2014, STAR-OPD consistently outperforms both standard off-policy knowledge distillation and more generic on-policy distillation methods. It specifically reduces the rate of target hallucination and yields larger gains on structurally difficult examples where prior approaches struggle. Using Qwen3-4B as the student, STAR-OPD significantly narrows the performance gap to its chain-of-thought teacher while also improving inference efficiency, demonstrating that small models can approach teacher-level ABSA performance when trained with structure-aware on-policy rewards.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that conventional off-policy distillation is ill-suited for structured extraction tasks like ABSA quadruple prediction because it fails to supervise the student on the structurally invalid states it actually visits. STAR-OPD addresses this by combining on-policy training with task-specific, set-structured rewards that enforce correct target–aspect bindings, textual grounding, and aspect disambiguation. This leads to higher accuracy, fewer hallucinations, and better handling of structurally challenging instances while maintaining efficiency advantages of small models. The findings underscore the broader importance of on-policy structural correction in distilling complex reasoning and extraction abilities from large CoT teachers into compact deployable models.

title: Knowing but Not Saying: Preventing Factual Access Failures in LLM SFT via Recall-Anchored Distillation
summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can degrade factual behavior outside the target domain. This degradation is often described as catastrophic forgetting, yet open-ended factual failures do not necessarily imply that the underlying facts have been erased. In this work, we identify a more specific phenomenon, factual access failure: after domain SFT, models can still recognize or rank the correct answer under constrained evaluation, while failing to produce it in closed-book generation. Through benchmark-level comparisons, same-fact multiple-choice and generation probes, and failure-mode analysis, we show that SFT-induced factual degradation reflects both genuine wrong-answer generations and expression-level failures such as verbosity, formatting mismatch, and exact-match artifacts. To address this problem, we introduce Recall-Anchored Distillation (RAD), a base-anchored self-distillation objective that preserves out-of-distribution generation behavior by aligning the adapted model with the original base model's soft continuation distribution on unlabeled OOD text. RAD requires no gold OOD answers, external judges, or labeled factual data. Across three backbones fine-tuned on MedMCQA, RAD recovers a consistent portion of the lost OOD recall while preserving target-domain adaptation. Compared with replay on the same OOD text, RAD shows that the key preservation signal is the base model's soft distribution rather than additional text exposure alone.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how supervised fine-tuning degrades factual generation and proposes a new distillation method to preserve out-of-domain factual recall.
AI.motivation: Supervised fine-tuning on a specific domain (e.g., medical QA) often hurts a model’s factual performance on out-of-domain tasks. This is often labeled as catastrophic forgetting, but observed failures in open-ended generation may not mean the model has truly forgotten the facts. The authors aim to disentangle genuine forgetting from failures in accessing or expressing retained knowledge, and to design a method that mitigates this degradation without needing labeled out-of-domain data.
AI.method: 1) Empirically characterize post-SFT factual degradation using benchmark comparisons, paired multiple-choice vs. generation probes for the same facts, and fine-grained failure-mode analysis to distinguish wrong knowledge from expression/access issues. 2) Define and study “factual access failure” where the model can still recognize the correct answer in constrained formats but fails in open-ended generation. 3) Propose Recall-Anchored Distillation (RAD), a base-anchored self-distillation objective that, during domain SFT, aligns the adapted model’s continuation distribution with that of the original base model on unlabeled out-of-distribution text, without using gold answers, judges, or labeled OOD data. 4) Experiment on three backbone models fine-tuned on MedMCQA, comparing RAD against standard SFT and replay baselines on the same OOD text.
AI.result: After domain-specific SFT, models exhibit factual access failures: they often still rank or recognize correct answers in multiple-choice settings yet fail to generate them in closed-book generation. The observed factual degradation is partly due to genuine wrong answers and partly due to expression-level issues (verbosity, formatting mismatches, exact-match quirks). Applying RAD during fine-tuning consistently recovers a substantial fraction of the lost out-of-distribution factual recall, while retaining strong adaptation to the target domain. Compared to replay on the same OOD text, RAD achieves better preservation, demonstrating that the beneficial signal comes from matching the base model’s soft continuation distribution rather than merely re-exposing the model to OOD text.
AI.conclusion: Catastrophic forgetting from domain SFT is better understood as a combination of genuine knowledge change and factual access failure, where the model retains but cannot effectively express certain facts in open-ended generation. By distilling from the base model’s soft continuation distribution on unlabeled OOD text, Recall-Anchored Distillation mitigates these issues, preserving out-of-domain factual recall without needing labeled OOD supervision and without sacrificing in-domain performance. The key to retention is leveraging the base model’s probabilistic knowledge, not just replaying additional OOD text.

title: SAC-Copula: Quality-Preserving Watermarking for Diffusion Language Models via Smooth Correlated Gumbel Fields
comment: Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026. 24 pages, 13 figures
summary: Watermarking diffusion language models (DLMs) requires mechanisms compatible with iterative parallel unmasking rather than autoregressive decoding. Existing sampling-based watermarking methods typically inject position-wise i.i.d. perturbations, which can be poorly aligned with DLM decoding dynamics and degrade generation quality. We propose SAC-Copula, a quality-preserving watermarking method for DLMs based on smooth, locally correlated Gumbel perturbation fields constructed via a Gaussian copula. We further develop a SAC-aware detector using covariance-aware filtering and native-sample calibration. Mechanism-level analysis shows that local correlation reduces latent perturbation roughness and better matches iterative refinement dynamics. Experiments on LLaDA show that SAC-Copula achieves a favorable quality-detectability trade-off compared with existing baselines. In particular, further evaluations on Dream-7B and additional datasets show that SAC-Copula substantially improves PPL tail stability over the i.i.d. Gumbel baseline, while maintaining strong low-FPR detectability and competitive overall generation quality. Additional token-edit stress tests further assess watermark robustness under controlled synchronization drift.

AI.tldr: Proposes SAC-Copula, a watermarking method for diffusion language models using smooth, locally correlated Gumbel perturbations for better quality-detectability trade-off.
AI.motivation: Existing watermarking methods for diffusion language models assume i.i.d. position-wise perturbations, which misalign with the iterative parallel unmasking dynamics of DLMs and can degrade generation quality. There is a need for a watermarking scheme that is compatible with diffusion-style decoding while preserving text quality and maintaining strong detectability.
AI.method: Introduce SAC-Copula, which constructs smooth, locally correlated Gumbel perturbation fields via a Gaussian copula, aligning noise structure with diffusion decoding dynamics. Design a SAC-aware detector that uses covariance-aware filtering and calibration on native (unwatermarked) samples. Perform mechanism-level analysis of how local correlation reduces latent perturbation roughness and fits iterative refinement. Empirically evaluate on LLaDA, Dream-7B, and multiple datasets, including token-edit stress tests for robustness under synchronization drift.
AI.result: SAC-Copula yields a better trade-off between watermark detectability and generation quality compared with prior sampling-based, i.i.d. Gumbel watermarking baselines. It notably improves perplexity (PPL) tail stability, indicating fewer low-quality outlier generations, while sustaining low false positive rate (FPR) in watermark detection and competitive overall text quality across models and datasets. Stress tests show robust watermark detection even when token-level edits introduce synchronization drift.
AI.conclusion: Smooth, locally correlated watermark perturbations constructed via a Gaussian copula are better suited to the decoding dynamics of diffusion language models than i.i.d. perturbations. SAC-Copula can watermark DLM outputs with minimal quality loss while maintaining strong, low-FPR detectability and robustness to moderate editing, making it a practical approach for watermarking diffusion-based text generators.

title: Automated Trajectory Evaluation for Mobile Agents via Step-Level Consequence Reasoning and Aggregation
summary: Evaluating language-guided mobile agents has recently shifted from rule-based to model-based approaches to achieve scalable and automated assessments. However, existing holistic evaluation paradigms process entire trajectories at once, leading to substantial context overload. Moreover, they primarily focus on task completion while overlooking operational safety. To address these limitations, we introduce CRATE, a novel two-stage VLM-as-judge framework for automated mobile agent evaluation that is compatible with both open- and closed-source models. Leveraging a step-level consequence reasoning mechanism, CRATE independently extracts task-relevant visual clues and infers action-conditioned state changes at each step. The resulting step-level textual evidence is then synthesized through trajectory-level aggregation to deliver an evidence-grounded evaluation of task completion. Building upon this evaluation scheme, we further extend CRATE to CRATE-S for operational safety assessment. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness and robustness of both CRATE and CRATE-S. Powered by Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct, CRATE achieves an F1-score of 0.833 on AndroidWorld (outperforming SPA-Bench by 20%), while CRATE-S reaches an F1-score of 0.697 on MobileRisk, demonstrating strong alignment with benchmark ground truths. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CRATE-D580.

AI.tldr: CRATE is a two-stage VLM-as-judge framework that evaluates language-guided mobile agents with step-level reasoning to reduce context overload and adds a safety-focused variant, CRATE-S, achieving strong empirical performance on mobile benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing model-based evaluations of language-guided mobile agents analyze full trajectories in one shot, which causes context overload and emphasizes task success while neglecting operational safety. There is a need for a scalable, automated evaluator that is both context-efficient and capable of judging task completion and safety risks.
AI.method: The authors propose CRATE, a two-stage framework that uses a vision-language model as a judge. First, for each step in an agent’s trajectory, the system performs consequence reasoning: it extracts task-relevant visual cues and infers how each action changes the state, generating step-level textual evidence. Second, it aggregates this evidence across the trajectory to provide an evidence-grounded judgment of task completion. They extend this design to CRATE-S, which applies a similar step-level and trajectory-level reasoning scheme, but oriented to identifying and evaluating safety-related issues in the agent’s behavior. The framework is compatible with both open- and closed-source VLMs, and they instantiate it with Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct for experiments.
AI.result: CRATE achieves an F1-score of 0.833 on the AndroidWorld benchmark, surpassing SPA-Bench by 20% in F1. The safety-focused CRATE-S obtains an F1-score of 0.697 on the MobileRisk benchmark. These results indicate that both frameworks align well with ground-truth annotations for task success and safety assessment, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Step-level consequence reasoning plus trajectory-level aggregation offers a more context-efficient and accurate way to automatically evaluate language-guided mobile agents than holistic trajectory judging. CRATE provides strong, evidence-grounded judgments of task completion, and CRATE-S extends this capability to operational safety, both demonstrating robust performance and compatibility with various VLM backbones.

title: Ontology-Driven Structural Regularization for Document-Level Relation Extraction
summary:
Document-Level Relation Extraction (DocRE) relies heavily on costly manually annotated datasets, while large distant supervision resources such as DocRED distant remain underexploited due to noise. We show that a critical yet overlooked source of noise lies in structural inconsistencies within relational triples, including violations of ontology constraints and logical contradictions.
  We introduce an ontology-driven framework to quantify and enforce structural consistency in DocRE datasets. Our analysis reveals substantial structural noise in DocRED distant and demonstrates that such inconsistencies propagate to model predictions. Enforcing structural well-formedness during training significantly reduces logical contradictions and consistently improves generalization performance. These findings establish structural consistency as a missing axis of supervision in DocRE and highlight structural regularization as an effective strategy for leveraging distant data at scale.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies and mitigates structural noise (ontology violations and logical contradictions) in distant-supervised document-level relation extraction, proposing an ontology-driven framework that improves data quality and model performance.
AI.motivation: Document-level relation extraction needs large labeled datasets, which are expensive to create. Although large distant-supervision datasets like DocRED distant exist, they are noisy. Prior work has largely focused on surface-level or instance-level noise, overlooking deeper structural inconsistencies in relational triples (e.g., violating ontology constraints or containing logical contradictions). The authors aim to understand and systematically address this structural noise so that distant data can be better exploited at scale.
AI.method: The authors propose an ontology-driven framework that formalizes structural consistency for DocRE datasets. They define structural well-formedness based on ontology constraints (e.g., type compatibility of subject/object, relation hierarchies) and logical coherence (e.g., absence of contradictory triples). They then quantify the amount of structural noise in the DocRED distant dataset and analyze how these inconsistencies propagate into model predictions. Finally, they integrate structural constraints into training as a form of regularization, enforcing or encouraging well-formed relational structures.
AI.result: Using their ontology-based consistency checks, the authors find substantial structural noise in the DocRED distant dataset. They show that models trained on this data tend to reproduce these inconsistencies in their predictions. When structural well-formedness constraints are enforced during training, logical contradictions in predictions are significantly reduced, and models show consistently better generalization on evaluation benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Structural consistency constitutes an important but previously underused supervision signal for document-level relation extraction. By detecting and regularizing against ontology violations and logical contradictions, the proposed framework effectively cleans and leverages noisy distant-supervision data. Structural regularization thus emerges as a powerful strategy for scaling DocRE using large but imperfect datasets like DocRED distant.

title: Dynamic Context Scheduling: Learning Beyond the Static Universe
summary: We study dynamic context scheduling as a training instrument for contextual re- inforcement learning.
