Rather than treating intra-episode context variation as a deployment reality, we treat it as a controlled shaping mechanism. Thereby, context evolves within each training episode according to a predetermined schedule, expos- ing the policy to a richer and more temporally structured region of the environment parameter space. We introduce DYNAMICCARLENV, a framework that wraps contextual environments with pluggable schedule families, such as sinusoidal off- sets or cosine annealing. Across CartPole, BipedalWalker and VehicleRacing with CARL contextualization, we show that dynamic schedules match or outperform static context baselines in the out-of-distribution (OOD) regimes. Interestingly, for the more complex BipedalWalker and VehicleRacing environments we also achieve higher in-distribution (ID) evaluation performance. Preliminary findings indicate that automatic search for multi-stage curricula can successfully discover schedules that improve generalization, performing comparably to extensive grid search over single-stage schedulers.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes dynamic context scheduling as a way to improve generalization in contextual reinforcement learning by varying environment parameters within each training episode according to predefined schedules, showing gains especially in out-of-distribution settings.
AI.motivation: Contextual reinforcement learning agents often overfit to static or narrowly sampled environment contexts, limiting their ability to generalize, especially to out-of-distribution settings. Existing work typically treats context variation as something that happens between episodes or only at deployment time, not as a deliberate training signal that can be shaped. The authors aim to exploit intra-episode context changes as a controlled curriculum mechanism to expose policies to a richer, temporally structured variety of environment conditions and thereby improve robustness and generalization.
AI.method: The authors introduce DYNAMICCARLENV, a framework that wraps existing contextual RL environments (e.g., from CARL) with pluggable context schedules that determine how environment parameters change over time within an episode. Example schedule families include sinusoidal offsets and cosine annealing of context variables. During training, the context within a single episode evolves according to a chosen schedule rather than remaining fixed. They compare various dynamic schedules against static-context baselines on several benchmark environments—CartPole, BipedalWalker, and VehicleRacing—each with CARL-style contextualization. They also explore automatic search for multi-stage curricula, in which schedules are composed in stages and tuned automatically instead of manually via grid search.
AI.result: Empirically, dynamic context schedules match or outperform static-context baselines in out-of-distribution evaluation regimes across all tested tasks. For the more complex BipedalWalker and VehicleRacing environments, dynamic scheduling not only improves OOD generalization but also yields higher in-distribution performance compared to static baselines. In addition, preliminary experiments show that automatic search over multi-stage curricula can find dynamic schedules that deliver generalization performance comparable to what is obtained by extensive grid search over single-stage schedules, suggesting that good curricula can be discovered with less manual tuning.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic context scheduling within training episodes is an effective tool for shaping learning in contextual reinforcement learning. By systematically varying environment parameters over the course of each episode, agents can achieve better out-of-distribution robustness and, in some complex environments, improved in-distribution performance as well. The DYNAMICCARLENV framework demonstrates that schedule-based context shaping is practical and flexible, and preliminary results indicate that automatic curriculum search is a promising direction for discovering strong schedules without exhaustive manual tuning.

title: KREL: Automatic Medical Coding via Knowledge-Guided Reasoning over Clinical Evidence with LLMs
summary: Automatic Medical Coding (AMC), which assigns standardized International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes to clinical notes, is essential for medical reimbursement, quality reporting, and clinical research. Existing pre-trained language model (PLM)-based methods typically formulate AMC as an extreme multi-label classification problem over a predefined code set, while recent large language model (LLM)-based approaches instead frame it as generation or multi-step reasoning. However, key challenges remain, including the extreme length of clinical notes that hinders effective interpretation, the vast ICD label space, and complex coding rules that are not explicitly captured by LLMs. In this work, we propose Knowledge-Guided Reasoning over Clinical Evidence with LLMs (KREL), a framework that leverages LLMs for clinical text understanding and reasoning while integrating external ICD coding guidelines as structured knowledge. This design enables tight coupling between domain knowledge and LLM reasoning, reducing hallucinations and improving compliance with coding standards. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that KREL consistently outperforms strong PLM-based and state-of-the-art LLM-based baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes KREL, a framework that integrates ICD coding guidelines as structured knowledge into LLM-based automatic medical coding, improving accuracy and adherence to coding standards over prior PLM and LLM methods.
AI.motivation: Automatic assignment of ICD codes to clinical notes is crucial for reimbursement, reporting, and research, but current methods face challenges: very long clinical notes are hard for models to interpret, the ICD label space is huge, and coding involves complex rules that typical PLM and LLM approaches do not explicitly capture. There is a need for methods that both handle long, complex clinical text and explicitly incorporate formal coding knowledge to reduce hallucinations and ensure standard-compliant coding.
AI.method: The authors introduce KREL (Knowledge-Guided Reasoning over Clinical Evidence with LLMs), a framework that uses large language models for understanding and reasoning over clinical notes while explicitly integrating external ICD coding guidelines as structured knowledge. KREL tightly couples the LLM’s reasoning process with domain knowledge, guiding how evidence from the clinical text is mapped to ICD codes and constraining outputs according to official coding standards to reduce hallucinations and rule violations.
AI.result: On benchmark automatic medical coding datasets, KREL achieves consistently better performance than strong pre-trained language model baselines that treat AMC as extreme multi-label classification, as well as state-of-the-art LLM-based approaches that rely on generation or multi-step reasoning without structured guideline integration.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating structured ICD coding guidelines into the reasoning process of LLMs leads to more accurate and guideline-compliant automatic medical coding. KREL demonstrates that tightly coupling domain knowledge with LLM reasoning can effectively address challenges related to long clinical notes, large label spaces, and complex coding rules, outperforming existing PLM and LLM methods.

title: SPARC: Single-Pass Scaling for Motion Forecasting with Conformal Bayesian Last Layers
summary: Human motion forecasters are increasingly accurate and fast, but reliable deployment requires uncertainty estimates that are structured, calibrated, and efficient. Bayesian and ensemble-based uncertainty estimates often require repeated stochastic inference [15, 26], while conformal calibration alone does not provide an epistemic signal or preserve trajectory covariance structure [14, 50]. We introduce SPARC (Single-Pass Adaptive Risk Calibration), a Bayesian-conformal uncertainty layer for motion forecasting. A deterministic MLP backbone predicts the future mean, and a conjugate Bayesian last layer converts time-domain feature leverage into an analytic horizon-wise epistemic scale $κ_t(x)$. This scale inflates a graph-temporal Gaussian covariance without changing its correlation structure, and split conformal calibration produces 95% marginal prediction tubes with finite-sample validity under exchangeability. The key interface is the structured factorization $κ_t(x)Σ_{\mathrm{str},t}(x)$, which injects feature-space epistemic uncertainty into trajectory densities without Monte Carlo sampling. Across nine dataset-protocol blocks and deterministic, multimodal, and calibration baselines, SPARC ranks first on NLL and on the combined MPJPE+NLL criterion while retaining competitive point accuracy and efficient calibrated tubes. Ranking windows by $κ$ separates high-error cases, making the scale usable as a lightweight risk monitor.

AI.tldr: Proposes SPARC, a single-pass Bayesian-conformal uncertainty layer for human motion forecasting that yields calibrated, structured uncertainty without Monte Carlo sampling.
AI.motivation: Existing human motion forecasters are accurate and fast but lack reliable, well-structured, and efficiently computed uncertainty estimates. Bayesian and ensemble methods typically require costly repeated stochastic inference, and pure conformal calibration does not provide epistemic uncertainty or preserve the covariance structure of predicted trajectories. There is a need for a method that delivers calibrated, structured trajectory uncertainty, including epistemic components, while remaining computationally efficient and deployable in real-time systems.
AI.method: SPARC uses a deterministic MLP backbone to predict the mean future motion. On top of this, it adds a conjugate Bayesian last layer that maps time-domain features into an analytic, horizon-wise epistemic scale κ_t(x). This κ_t(x) multiplicatively scales a pre-specified graph-temporal Gaussian covariance Σ_str,t(x) without altering its correlation structure, producing full trajectory covariances in a single forward pass. Split conformal calibration is then applied to the resulting predictive distributions to obtain 95% marginal prediction tubes with finite-sample validity under exchangeability. The central modeling interface is the factorization κ_t(x) Σ_str,t(x), which injects feature-dependent epistemic uncertainty into trajectory densities without any Monte Carlo sampling.
AI.result: Across nine dataset–protocol combinations and against deterministic, multimodal, and calibration-focused baselines, SPARC achieves the best performance on negative log-likelihood (NLL) and on a combined MPJPE+NLL metric. It maintains competitive point prediction accuracy while producing calibrated, efficiently computable uncertainty tubes. Furthermore, when motion prediction windows are ranked by the κ scale, high-error cases are effectively separated from low-error ones, indicating that κ serves as a practical, lightweight risk indicator.
AI.conclusion: SPARC provides a practical, single-pass framework for structured, calibrated uncertainty in human motion forecasting by combining a deterministic predictor with a Bayesian last layer and conformal calibration. It avoids the computational overhead of Monte Carlo-based Bayesian or ensemble methods while still offering epistemic uncertainty and preserving trajectory covariance structure. Its superior NLL metrics, competitive accuracy, and effective error-risk ranking demonstrate that SPARC is a strong candidate for reliable, uncertainty-aware deployment of motion forecasting systems.

title: ForeDreamer: A Self-Evolving Dual-Agent Memory Architecture for Future Event Prediction
summary: Open-web future event prediction requires agents to distill reliable signals from noisy, redundant, and incomplete evidence. Existing retrieval/memory mechanisms directly feed retrieved information to agents or rely on simple memory functions such as storing and reusing prior information for prediction, leaving them insufficient for open-web forecasting. We propose to transform raw web evidence into structured memory before prediction, enabling agents to reason over distilled, question-specific evidence rather than noisy retrieval results. This paper presents ForeDreamer, a self-evolving dual-agent framework for managing memory over open-web evidence. ForeDreamer separates factual memory, a question-specific evidence state for the current forecast, from experiential memory, persistent agent experience accumulated across forecasting episodes. It uses a main agent for search and prediction, and a memory-processing subagent to convert search results into factual memory with dedicated tools. ForeDreamer further evolves experiential memory through two tracks, improving both forecasting decisions and factual-memory construction. Experiments on Prophet Arena and FutureX demonstrate the effectiveness of ForeDreamer. Project page: https://zhongzero.github.io/ForeDreamer

AI.tldr: ForeDreamer is a dual-agent system that converts noisy open-web evidence into structured, question-specific and experience-based memories to improve future event prediction.
AI.motivation: Open-web forecasting requires sifting through noisy, redundant, and incomplete online information. Existing approaches either pass raw retrieved content directly to the agent or use simple memory mechanisms (e.g., storing/reusing past info) that are not robust enough for complex, evolving web evidence. The authors aim to build a more principled memory system that can distill and structure evidence to support accurate future event prediction.
AI.method: The paper introduces ForeDreamer, a self-evolving dual-agent framework. It employs a main agent that handles web search and forecasting, and a memory-processing subagent that transforms raw search results into structured factual memory tailored to the current question. ForeDreamer distinguishes between (1) factual memory, which is a question-specific evidence state for the current prediction, and (2) experiential memory, which is a persistent store of knowledge and patterns accumulated across many forecasting episodes. Dedicated tools support the subagent in constructing and updating factual memory, while experiential memory is evolved along two improvement tracks: one that enhances forecasting decisions and another that improves how factual memory is constructed from future searches.
AI.result: On the Prophet Arena and FutureX benchmarks for future event prediction, ForeDreamer outperforms baselines that either rely on raw retrieval or simple memory mechanisms. The empirical results validate that structuring web evidence into factual and experiential memories leads to more accurate and robust forecasts.
AI.conclusion: Transforming noisy open-web evidence into structured, dual-layer memory—separating current-question evidence (factual memory) from accumulated forecasting experience (experiential memory)—enables agents to reason more effectively about future events. The ForeDreamer framework demonstrates that a self-evolving dual-agent design with specialized memory-processing tools can significantly improve open-web forecasting performance.

title: Neuro-Geospatial Modelling of EEG Affective States Using Literature-Informed Environmental Context
summary: Environmental exposures such as air pollution and greenness have been associated with affective and cognitive outcomes, but EEG and environmental datasets are rarely jointly georeferenced. We investigate whether literature-informed environmental priors can serve as an auxiliary geospatial modality for EEG-based affective-state classification when individual-level exposure data are unavailable. We combine 30-channel EEG from the EAV benchmark (42 participants, aged 20-30 years) with environmental representations derived from OpenAQ, Sentinel-2, Sentinel-5P, and OpenStreetMap data for Astana. A dual-tower architecture combines EEG-Conformer representations with a graph-based environmental encoder. Because the datasets are not co-registered, environmental context is treated as a literature-informed prior rather than measured exposure. Subject-level repeated splits, permutation and label-shuffling controls, dose-response reversal, and domain-shift experiments distinguish architecture-level gains from prior-dependent gains. The multimodal model achieves 76.2% accuracy versus 67.4% for EEG alone. Controls disrupting environmental-label structure retain part of this gain, indicating that the improvement is not attributable solely to environmental information. Replacing the Astana environmental distribution with an independently modeled Singapore distribution reduces accuracy to 72.8%. These findings demonstrate technical feasibility but do not establish an observed or causal exposure-affect association. The study provides a framework for future jointly collected mobile EEG-environment studies. Implementation: https://github.com/r11up/geo-cog

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether environmental data, used as literature-based priors rather than true exposures, can improve EEG-based affective-state classification via a multimodal deep learning architecture.
AI.motivation: EEG-based affective and cognitive state classification is typically done without rich environmental context, even though environmental factors like air pollution and urban greenness are known to correlate with mood and cognition. Because EEG and environmental datasets are rarely collected together and georeferenced at the individual level, there is a gap in using environmental information to enhance affective-state decoding. The authors want to know if environmental information, even when only available as city-level priors rather than precise personal exposures, can still help EEG classifiers and how to separate true environmental benefits from generic architectural gains.
AI.method: The authors use the EAV benchmark dataset with 30-channel EEG recordings from 42 young adults. They construct environmental representations for the city of Astana using multiple open geospatial sources (OpenAQ for air quality, Sentinel-2 and Sentinel-5P satellite data, and OpenStreetMap for built/green environment). They design a dual-tower neural architecture: one tower is an EEG-Conformer that encodes the EEG signals; the other is a graph-based encoder that embeds environmental data. Since EEG and environmental data are not co-registered at the individual-event level, environmental features are incorporated as literature-informed priors linked to locations, not as measured exposures for each subject. They run several control experiments—subject-level repeated data splits, permutation and label-shuffling, reversing dose-response patterns, and domain-shift by swapping Astana’s environmental distribution for one modeled on Singapore—to disentangle real environmental-label structure from mere architectural or regularization benefits.
AI.result: The multimodal model combining EEG and environmental priors achieves 76.2% accuracy for affective-state classification, improving on the EEG-only model’s 67.4% accuracy. When the environmental-label relationship is disrupted via permutation and label shuffling, part of the performance gain remains, suggesting that some improvement comes from the architecture or regularization rather than meaningful environmental priors. When the Astana environmental distribution is replaced with an independent synthetic distribution based on Singapore, accuracy drops to 72.8%, indicating that realistic environmental structure still contributes to performance. Overall, the experiments show both architecture-driven gains and additional benefit attributable to coherent environmental priors.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that integrating literature-informed environmental priors with EEG in a dual-tower deep learning architecture is technically feasible and can improve affective-state classification performance even when true individual-level exposure data are absent. However, because the datasets are not co-registered and environmental context is used only as a prior, the work does not provide evidence of an observed or causal relationship between environmental exposures and affective states. Instead, it introduces and validates a methodological framework and open implementation that can be used in future studies where mobile EEG and environmental data are collected jointly and precisely, enabling more rigorous investigation of exposure-affect links.

title: Source-Free MT Evaluation Is Not MT Evaluation
summary: Reference-based metrics remain the standard choice in machine translation evaluation, partly because quality estimation methods often correlate less well with human judgments. As a result, source-free, reference-based evaluation has become the practical norm, even though it is unfaithful to the definition of translation adequacy and unfair to systems whose outputs preserve the source meaning while differing from the reference. This paper argues that adequacy must be judged with respect to the source. A reference is only one possible rendering of the source and may introduce bias, under-specification, or errors. We further argue that source-reference-hypothesis evaluation is fair only when the judge treats the reference as auxiliary evidence rather than as the primary standard. Otherwise, even source-aware evaluation can reduce adequacy to preference towards reference. We show the existing hybrid metrics are highly reliant on reference compared to source. Our argument is not that all automatic MT metrics fail to use the source. Rather, we argue that any evaluation protocol that removes the source, or allows the reference to dominate the source, is structurally incomplete for adequacy evaluation. However, existing MT papers generally prefer reference-based metrics and use QE metrics only when reference is unavailable. We therefore call for QE to be reframed as a primary approach to source-grounded adequacy evaluation, rather than as a fallback motivated by missing references. We further call for hybrid metrics whose designs explicitly prioritize source--hypothesis faithfulness while using references only as complementary evidence.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that machine translation adequacy must be evaluated with respect to the source sentence, not just a reference translation, and calls for quality estimation and hybrid metrics that prioritize source–hypothesis faithfulness while using references only as auxiliary evidence.
AI.motivation: Current MT evaluation mostly uses reference-based metrics, often even without access to the source. This is problematic because references are only one of many valid translations, may contain biases or errors, and can unfairly penalize systems that are faithful to the source but differ from the reference. Also, existing hybrid metrics and evaluation protocols tend to let the reference dominate, which is structurally incomplete for assessing adequacy, defined as preservation of source meaning.
AI.method: The authors conceptually analyze the role of source, reference, and hypothesis in MT evaluation, and examine existing hybrid metrics to show that they rely more on the reference than the source. They contrast source-free, reference-based evaluation with source-aware protocols and discuss how different metric designs implicitly prioritize the reference or the source.
AI.result: They find that hybrid metrics widely used in MT evaluation are highly reference-dependent and underuse information from the source sentence. This supports their claim that current protocols effectively reduce adequacy evaluation to similarity-to-reference, even when the source is nominally available.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that any evaluation setup that removes the source or allows the reference to dominate is fundamentally incomplete for evaluating translation adequacy. The authors advocate reframing quality estimation as the primary, source-grounded adequacy evaluation paradigm and call for the development of hybrid metrics that explicitly put source–hypothesis faithfulness first, with the reference used only as complementary evidence.

title: Certified Multi-Turn Robustness for LLM Safety via Compositional Bounds and Safety Persistence
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are vulnerable to multi-turn jailbreak attacks that progressively manipulate conversation context. Existing certified robustness methods are limited to single-turn inputs; naive multi-turn composition yields bounds that degrade exponentially in the number of turns. We introduce Multi-Turn Certified Robustness (MTCR), a framework that models conversational safety via State-Adversarial MDPs and defines $k$-turn certified robustness as the worst-case safety probability across $k$ adversarial turns. MTCR comprises: (i) compositional certification via embedding-space mode decomposition, yielding tighter certified lower bounds than naive multiplication; (ii) $(α,β)$-safety persistence, improving the degradation rate from $\underline{p}^{k}$ to $β^k$ (with $β> \underline{p}$) and yielding interpretable horizon estimates; (iii) matching information-theoretic upper bounds establishing tightness; and (iv) a unified algorithm combining these results. Experiments on six LLMs under $ε$-bounded and Crescendo-style attacks confirm that empirical safety consistently exceeds the certified bounds.

AI.tldr: They propose a framework (MTCR) to give non-vacuous, multi-turn robustness guarantees for LLM safety against adaptive jailbreak attacks, with tighter bounds than naive composition and matching upper bounds.
AI.motivation: Current certified robustness techniques for LLM safety only work at the single-turn level. When extended naively to multi-turn conversations, the certification bounds degrade exponentially with the number of turns, quickly becoming useless, even though real jailbreak attacks are often multi-turn and adaptive. There is a need for a principled, compositional way to reason about and certify safety of LLMs over multiple adversarial turns.
AI.method: They formalize conversations as State-Adversarial Markov Decision Processes and define k-turn certified robustness as the worst-case safety probability over k adversarial query-response steps. The MTCR framework has several components: (i) a compositional certification method using decomposition in the embedding space to derive tighter lower bounds on multi-turn safety than simple multiplication of per-turn guarantees; (ii) the concept of (α,β)-safety persistence, which controls how safety guarantees degrade over turns and improves the naive p^k degradation to β^k with β>p; (iii) information-theoretic upper bounds on achievable robustness showing that the proposed lower bounds are essentially tight; and (iv) a unified algorithm to compute these bounds in practice for given models and attack classes.
AI.result: On six different LLMs and under both ε-bounded attacks and stronger Crescendo-style multi-turn attacks, the framework is able to produce certified lower bounds on safety that are significantly tighter than naive composition. Across all settings, the observed empirical safety under attack is consistently higher than the certified lower bounds, indicating that the certificates are sound (not violated) but conservative, as desired.
AI.conclusion: MTCR provides the first principled way to certify conversational safety of LLMs over multiple adversarial turns with non-trivial guarantees, bridging the gap between single-turn robustness theory and the multi-turn nature of real-world jailbreaks. By introducing compositional certification, safety persistence, and tight upper bounds, it yields interpretable, theoretically grounded, and empirically validated robustness guarantees that degrade more slowly with conversation length than previous methods.

title: MentorPulse: Refreshing Cross-Model Latent Guidance for Long-Form Generation
summary: Cross-model latent guidance lets a frozen large mentor encode an input once and a frozen small student generate from the resulting signal. Existing methods keep this signal fixed, assuming it stays useful as the output grows; we show this fails in long-form generation. On multi-turn instruction following, static guidance pushes a 4B student's constraint satisfaction 2.5 points below its no-guidance baseline; a training-free refresh every 16 tokens changes only the memory content and restores a 2.0-point gain over that baseline. We propose MentorPulse to keep guidance fresh at practical cost: it compresses mentor states into a capped slot memory, incrementally processes newly generated tokens, and updates the memory that the student reads through gated cross-attention without resetting the student's KV cache. Windowed Refresh Training exposes the bridge to prefix-conditioned memory. Across thirteen datasets, MentorPulse closes 52.2% of the mentor-student gap on macro average, outperforming C2C, T2T, and equal-budget LoRA, with the largest gains on long outputs. It performs best on all eleven mentor-student pairs from three model families, with margins that narrow as the capability gap grows, and a lightweight read-pattern check predicts the gain before deployment. Measured costs identify refresh intervals that dominate text guidance on long outputs.

AI.tldr: MentorPulse is a method for dynamic cross-model latent guidance where a large frozen mentor incrementally guides a small frozen student during long-form generation, refreshing the guidance signal efficiently to maintain and improve performance.
AI.motivation: Existing cross-model latent guidance methods assume that an initial guidance signal from a large mentor model remains useful throughout generation. This assumption breaks down for long-form and multi-turn instruction following, where static guidance can degrade performance below a no-guidance baseline. The paper aims to address the need for effective, low-cost, dynamically updated guidance to close the performance gap between large mentors and small students, especially on long outputs.
AI.method: The authors introduce MentorPulse, which compresses the mentor’s hidden states into a capped slot memory. As the student generates new tokens, the mentor incrementally processes only those new tokens and updates this memory. The student reads from the memory via gated cross-attention, without resetting its own KV cache, enabling efficient, continual guidance. They also propose Windowed Refresh Training to align this mechanism with prefix-conditioned memory usage. The approach is evaluated against baselines such as C2C, T2T, and LoRA under the same compute budget.
AI.result: Static latent guidance degrades performance on long, multi-turn instruction following: a 4B student’s constraint satisfaction drops 2.5 points below its no-guidance baseline. Introducing a simple training-free refresh every 16 tokens—updating only the mentor’s memory—restores and improves performance to a 2.0-point gain over baseline. MentorPulse, with structured memory compression and incremental refresh, closes 52.2% of the mentor–student performance gap on macro average across thirteen datasets, outperforming C2C, T2T, and equal-budget LoRA, particularly on long outputs and across all tested mentor–student pairs from three model families. A lightweight read-pattern check predicts the benefit prior to deployment, and cost analyses identify refresh intervals that are more efficient than text-based guidance on long outputs.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, memory-based latent guidance is necessary for effective long-form cross-model mentoring. MentorPulse shows that periodically refreshed, compressed mentor states can provide strong performance gains for smaller students at practical compute cost, closing a substantial fraction of the mentor–student gap and outperforming popular alternatives. The method generalizes across datasets and model families, works best when outputs are long, and offers tools (read-pattern checks and cost analyses) to choose refresh intervals and anticipate benefits before real-world deployment.

title: Prediction certification cannot replace explanation certification: a competence envelope for trustworthy AI under compound stress
summary: Artificial intelligence systems increasingly make consequential judgments - which patient is deteriorating, which building is safe to enter, whether an image is authentic and are trusted on the strength of how accurately and confidently they predict. The safeguards that certify them are correspondingly prediction-based: accuracy, calibration and conformal coverage all measure how well a model performs. Whether such checks are sufficient to establish model trustworthiness has remained unclear. Here we prove that they cannot. We establish a separation theorem showing that a reliable model and a compromised one can be identical under every prediction-side certificate, including accuracy, calibration and coverage, yet differ arbitrarily in explanation fidelity and deployment behaviour. Detecting this failure requires access to the model's decision mechanism in addition to its predictions. We introduce the competence envelope as an operational framework that combines prediction and explanation certification into a single deployable criterion. Across diverse datasets and model classes, the proposed framework reveals failure modes that prediction-side certification alone does not capture. Certification against failures that are invisible in prediction behaviour therefore requires evidence about the model's decision mechanism as well as its outputs.

AI.tldr: Prediction-side metrics like accuracy and calibration are insufficient to guarantee AI model trustworthiness; inspecting the decision mechanism and explanations is also necessary.
AI.motivation: Current AI certification practices mainly rely on prediction-based metrics (accuracy, calibration, coverage) to assess trustworthiness. It is unclear whether such metrics alone can distinguish between genuinely reliable models and compromised or untrustworthy ones, especially when both exhibit similar predictive performance.
AI.method: The authors prove a separation theorem demonstrating that two models can be indistinguishable under all prediction-side certificates yet behave very differently in terms of explanation fidelity and deployment behavior. They then propose an operational framework called the competence envelope, which jointly certifies predictions and explanations by requiring access to, and analysis of, the model’s decision mechanism in addition to its outputs. They empirically test this framework across multiple datasets and model classes to show its practical utility.
AI.result: Theoretical results show that prediction-side certification alone cannot rule out severely compromised models, because such models can perfectly mimic the predictions of a reliable model while having arbitrarily bad explanations or deployment behaviors. Empirical studies with the competence envelope framework uncover failure modes that remain invisible when only accuracy, calibration, or conformal coverage are checked.
AI.conclusion: Trustworthy deployment of AI systems cannot rely solely on prediction-based metrics. Certification schemes must incorporate evidence about the model’s internal decision mechanism and explanation fidelity. The competence envelope provides a practical way to combine prediction and explanation checks into a single deployable criterion, revealing hidden risks that standard prediction-side evaluation misses.

title: Quantization-Aware Healing: A Practical Recipe for Recovering Compressed, 4-Bit LLMs
summary: Serving large language models cheaply increasingly means shipping models that are both structurally compressed to a fraction of their parameters and quantized to 4 bits. Together these steps degrade reasoning, mathematics, coding, and long-context behavior enough to require a recovery, or healing, stage before deployment. The default recipe, quantization-aware training (QAT), re-fits the compressed, quantized model to hard labels; in our pipeline it converged slowly and collapsed past its peak. We adopted Quantization-Aware Healing (QAH) instead. Because a structurally compressed model is never independently trained at full precision, its bfloat16 checkpoint is a distillation-recovered approximation of the original; QAH distills the 4-bit student directly from the original, uncompressed model. On a GPT-OSS 120B to 60B to MXFP4 pipeline, the QAH student matches or beats its bfloat16 source on 7 of 9 benchmarks at roughly 4 times less weight memory and half the teacher's parameter count, and is released open-weight as Hypernova-60B. Against a matched QAT baseline it reaches a comparable peak about 7 times faster and stays stable under continued training, without hand-tuned early stopping. We also report deployment lessons, including a large, reproducible quality gap between distributed-training backends. Our aim is a recipe deployable without a multi-week hyper-parameter search.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Quantization-Aware Healing (QAH), a distillation-based method to recover performance in heavily compressed and 4-bit quantized LLMs, achieving equal or better quality than higher-precision models with far lower memory and faster, stabler training than traditional QAT.
AI.motivation: Aggressively compressing and 4-bit quantizing large language models is necessary to reduce serving cost, but this severely harms reasoning, math, coding, and long-context performance. The standard recovery method, quantization-aware training (QAT), proved slow, unstable, and required careful early stopping in their pipeline. The authors seek a practical, stable, and efficient recipe that restores or improves model quality after structural compression and 4-bit quantization, without extensive hyperparameter search, so that cheap deployment of large models becomes more feasible.
AI.method: They introduce Quantization-Aware Healing (QAH), a variant of knowledge distillation tailored to structurally compressed and 4-bit quantized students. Instead of re-fitting the compressed, quantized model to ground-truth labels as in QAT, QAH directly distills the 4-bit student from the original, uncompressed full-size teacher model, bypassing the intermediate structurally compressed bfloat16 checkpoint (which is itself only an approximation). They apply QAH to a pipeline that compresses a 120B GPT-OSS model down to 60B parameters and quantizes it to MXFP4, then train the student using teacher outputs to recover performance. They compare QAH to a matched QAT baseline and also evaluate across multiple distributed-training backends to identify deployment issues and quality gaps.
AI.result: In their GPT-OSS 120B → 60B → MXFP4 pipeline, the 4-bit QAH-trained student Hypernova-60B matches or surpasses its bfloat16 source model on 7 out of 9 benchmarks, while using about 4× less weight memory and half the teacher’s parameters. Compared to a carefully matched QAT baseline, QAH reaches a similar performance peak about 7× faster, and unlike QAT, its quality remains stable with continued training, removing the need for hand-tuned early stopping. They also find a substantial and reproducible quality gap between different distributed-training backends, highlighting important deployment considerations.
AI.conclusion: QAH is an effective and practical alternative to standard QAT for heavily compressed, 4-bit quantized LLMs. By distilling directly from the original, uncompressed teacher rather than relying on a compressed bfloat16 intermediate, QAH recovers or even improves performance with significantly reduced memory, faster convergence, and improved training stability. The method reduces the need for extensive hyperparameter tuning and manual early stopping, making it a more deployable recipe for cost-efficient large-model serving. The authors release Hypernova-60B as an open-weight demonstration and emphasize that backend implementation details can meaningfully affect final model quality.

title: Foundation Models for Partial Causal Identification
summary: This paper investigates the development of causal foundation models for bounding the effect of interventions and counterfactuals from observational data. We show that a canonical prior can be defined with full support over the space of structural causal models with discrete observables. With this canonical prior, we translate the problem of bounding counterfactuals into that of learning distributions over functions that map data (and possibly structural assumptions) to a causal query of interest. This extends the promising causal foundational modelling paradigm to the estimation of partially-identifiable causal effects, i.e., under unobserved confounding, where multiple values are equally compatible with the observed data and prior structural assumptions.

AI.tldr: They introduce a canonical Bayesian prior over structural causal models with discrete variables and show how to turn questions about partially-identified causal effects under unobserved confounding into a problem of learning function-valued distributions that output bounds on causal queries from data and assumptions.
AI.motivation: Causal questions about interventions and counterfactuals often cannot be point-identified from observational data due to unobserved confounding. Still, it is important to characterize what can be said—i.e., derive bounds on causal effects—given both the data and any structural assumptions. Existing "causal foundation models" focus mainly on fully identifiable settings; there is a need to extend them to partially-identifiable cases and provide a principled prior over structural causal models so that Bayesian learning and uncertainty quantification over causal queries is possible.
AI.method: 1) Define a canonical prior with full support over the space of structural causal models (SCMs) with discrete observables, ensuring that any SCM consistent with the assumptions has positive prior probability. 2) Show how, under this prior, bounding counterfactuals and intervention effects can be formulated as learning a distribution over functions that map observed data and structural assumptions to the causal quantity of interest. 3) Use this formulation to treat partially identifiable causal effects—where multiple values are compatible with the same data and assumptions—as outputs of a learned functional distribution instead of fixed numbers.
AI.result: They prove the existence and construction of a canonical full-support prior over discrete SCMs and establish an equivalence between counterfactual bounding problems and learning distributions over causal-query–valuing functions. This result formally extends the causal foundation model framework to cases with unobserved confounding and partial identifiability, where the answer is a set or a distribution over possible causal effects rather than a single identified value.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that by introducing a canonical prior over discrete structural causal models, one can systematically use causal foundation models to handle partially identifiable causal problems. Counterfactual and interventional bounds under unobserved confounding can be expressed as outputs of learned function distributions conditioned on observational data and assumptions, providing a unified and flexible framework for uncertainty-aware causal inference beyond point-identifiable settings.

title: Extractive Summarization for Arabic Documents Using SAraBERT with a Semantic Siamese Similarity Evaluation Metric
summary: In this research, we introduce SAraBERT, an enhanced version of AraBERT which proposes inter-sentence transformer layers for extractive summarization tasks. To ensure that the summaries generated by SAraBERT achieve a high coverage of the document's main ideas, we propose Semantic Siamese Similarity, a novel evaluation metric that measures the level of similarity between two text inputs. We validated using BLEU, ROUGE, and Semantic Siamese similarity on Sarabert and published related models. Simulation results showed the effectiveness of our proposed model and motivate follow on research.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SAraBERT, an enhanced AraBERT model with inter-sentence transformers for Arabic extractive summarization, and introduces a new similarity-based evaluation metric.
AI.motivation: Improve extractive summarization for Arabic by better modeling inter-sentence relations and provide a more semantically grounded evaluation metric than traditional lexical overlap scores.
AI.method: Extend AraBERT with inter-sentence transformer layers (SAraBERT) tailored for extractive summarization and propose Semantic Siamese Similarity, which uses a Siamese architecture to compute semantic similarity between text pairs. Evaluate SAraBERT and related models using BLEU, ROUGE, and the new metric.
AI.result: Experiments show that SAraBERT outperforms published related models on extractive summarization benchmarks, and the Semantic Siamese Similarity metric effectively reflects semantic coverage between summaries and source documents.
AI.conclusion: SAraBERT with inter-sentence transformers is effective for Arabic extractive summarization, and the proposed Semantic Siamese Similarity metric is a useful complementary measure to standard metrics, warranting further research and development.

title: TRACE: Agentic Catalog Enrichment with Multi-source Evidence Grounding
summary: Product catalogs underpin search, discovery, and recommendation in e-commerce, yet they are often attribute-sparse: the attributes shoppers and downstream systems rely on are either buried in unstructured content such as titles and images or missing from the catalog altogether. Manually enriching e-commerce catalogs is impractical given their scale and rapid growth. This paper introduces TRACE, a novel framework for automated catalog attribute enrichment using agentic Large Language Models (LLMs). A ScoutAgent triangulates multimodal evidence across merchant catalogs, syndicated feeds, and identity-matched web search to propose candidate attribute values with supporting evidence, while a JudgeAgent verifies the proposed value for each attribute value against its supporting evidence and decides whether to publish it or route it to human review. On an offline human evaluation dataset, TRACE's proposed attribute values were 98.2% accurate at 74.7% attribute coverage. Deployed in production on an industry-scale catalog, TRACE increased impression-weighted enrichment coverage across four business verticals by 90.4%. An online experiment subsequently showed that surfacing the enriched attributes on the product detail page increased checkout conversion by 0.48%.

AI.tldr: TRACE is a two-agent LLM framework that automatically enriches sparse e-commerce product catalogs with accurate attribute values using multimodal evidence, significantly improving attribute coverage and conversion in production.
AI.motivation: E-commerce product catalogs often lack explicit, structured attribute information (e.g., material, size, color) even though such details are vital for search, recommendation, and shopper decision-making. These attributes are either hidden in unstructured data like titles, descriptions, and images or completely missing. Manual enrichment is infeasible at scale given the size and growth rate of catalogs. There is a need for an automated, accurate, and scalable method to extract and validate product attributes from multiple heterogeneous data sources and make them safely usable in production systems.
AI.method: The paper proposes TRACE, an agentic LLM-based framework with two coordinated agents: (1) ScoutAgent, which gathers and triangulates evidence from multiple sources—merchant catalogs, syndicated data feeds, and web pages found via identity-matched web search, potentially including multimodal inputs—to propose candidate attribute values along with their supporting evidence; and (2) JudgeAgent, which inspects each proposed attribute value and its evidence, then decides whether to accept and publish it directly or send it for human review. The system is evaluated both on an offline human-labeled benchmark and through online production deployment over industry-scale catalogs spanning several business verticals.
AI.result: On an offline human-evaluated dataset, TRACE achieves 98.2% accuracy for proposed attribute values at 74.7% attribute coverage, indicating high precision with substantial recall. When deployed in a real, large-scale e-commerce setting across four business verticals, TRACE increases impression-weighted enrichment coverage by 90.4%, meaning many more viewed products now have enriched attributes. An online A/B test shows that exposing these enriched attributes on product detail pages increases checkout conversion rate by 0.48%, demonstrating measurable business impact.
AI.conclusion: TRACE demonstrates that an agentic LLM-based architecture can reliably and scalably enrich sparse e-commerce catalogs with structured product attributes by leveraging multimodal and multi-source evidence plus an internal verification step. The framework delivers high offline accuracy, significantly expands attribute coverage in production, and yields a measurable lift in checkout conversion, suggesting that automated attribute enrichment via LLM agents is both technically viable and economically valuable in real-world e-commerce environments.

title: Target-Aware Calibration Data Selection for Preserving Uncertainty in Quantized Language Models
comment: 20 pages, 5 figures. Accepted to EMNLP Findings 2026
summary: Quantization is widely used to deploy large language models, but its effect on uncertainty behavior, such as confidence, margins, and abstention, is rarely treated as a primary objective. We frame calibration-data selection for quantization as a target-dependent uncertainty-preservation problem. Different deployments emphasize different regions of the input distribution, yet prior work mainly optimizes accuracy-oriented compression metrics or adjusts scores after quantization. We formalize this goal with distributional and boundary preservation risks, and provide a simple mixture-mismatch argument explaining why no single calibration recipe should be expected to fit all targets. We introduce Doubt-Preserving Quantization (DPQ), a lightweight pre-quantization recipe family that uses full-precision predictions to construct target-aligned calibration mixtures of high-doubt examples and generic anchors. Across 8 language models, 9 NLP benchmarks, and 22 comparison methods, the leading fixed recipe changes with the preservation target: DPQ-r75 leads on SQuAD2 answerability-boundary preservation, while milder or single-signal variants, including DPQ-r50, confidence-only, and entropy-only, better preserve broad multiple-choice QA behavior. These results show that calibration data should be selected for the specific full-precision score behavior a deployment needs to preserve, rather than treated as a fixed quantization detail.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how quantization affects uncertainty estimates of large language models and proposes a method (DPQ) to preserve desired uncertainty behavior by selecting calibration data tailored to specific deployment goals.
AI.motivation: While quantization is standard for efficient deployment of large language models, most work focuses on preserving accuracy or adjusting scores post-hoc, not on directly preserving how models express uncertainty (confidence, margins, abstention). Different applications care about different parts of the input/score distribution (e.g., answerability thresholds vs. general confidence), so a one-size-fits-all calibration set is inadequate. The authors aim to systematically address this gap.
AI.method: They formalize uncertainty preservation via distributional and boundary preservation risks, capturing how quantization distorts score distributions and decision boundaries. They argue, via a mixture-mismatch perspective, that no single calibration recipe can optimally serve all deployment targets. They then propose Doubt-Preserving Quantization (DPQ), a family of lightweight pre-quantization calibration-data selection recipes that use the full-precision model’s predictions to build mixtures of high-doubt examples plus generic anchors, tuned to specific targets (e.g., r75, r50, confidence-only, entropy-only).
AI.result: On 8 language models and 9 NLP benchmarks, compared with 22 existing methods, different DPQ variants perform best depending on the preservation target. DPQ-r75 is best for preserving answerability-boundary behavior on SQuAD2, while milder or single-signal variants like DPQ-r50, confidence-only, and entropy-only are better for preserving broad multiple-choice QA uncertainty behavior.
AI.conclusion: Quantization should be calibrated with deployment-specific uncertainty behavior in mind: calibration data must be chosen according to the full-precision score characteristics a given application needs to preserve. The proposed DPQ recipes demonstrate that target-aligned, uncertainty-aware calibration improves preservation of relevant model behaviors over fixed, accuracy-centric approaches.

title: RAG Deserves an Index: Why Ingest-Time Compilation Beats Query-Time Interpretation
summary:
Nearly every retrieval-augmented question-answering system in production ships with a hidden interpreter: on each query a language model re-derives the meaning of raw corpus text and then throws that work away. Cheaper models do not close the gap: per-token prices have fallen by orders of magnitude while inference spend has risen, because context volume grows faster than prices fall. This is the modern equivalent of the full-table scan, and the remedy is the one databases found fifty years ago: do the expensive work once, at write time, into a maintained structure that makes reads cheap. A corpus whose read pattern is known before it ever meets a user can and should be indexed too.
  We call the paradigm ingest-time semantic compilation (ISC): compile a corpus's meaning into a queryable substrate with two coupled layers - incrementally maintained embeddings, and atomic claims whose provenance is validated at compile time - and treat that substrate as a first-class database object with its own DDL, maintenance contract, migration contract, and cost model.
  Two existence proofs support it. Substrate upkeep scales with change rather than corpus size: incremental updates run 33.7x cheaper than reconstruction while tracking it to floating-point precision. And on a held-out sample of 500 broadcast-interview transcripts, compiled claims as the retrieval payload win all 32 budget-by-model cells: 85.2% correct from roughly 2.2k reader tokens against 72.5% from 16.3k for the best chunk configuration anywhere. The only baseline that keeps pace is a contextualized-chunk pipeline with hybrid retrieval and reranking, statistically indistinguishable from compiled claims at roughly twenty-one times the query-path tokens - and it reaches that parity, we argue, precisely because it has itself begun to compile. We close with the systems agenda this opens, from compilation planners to read planning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ingest-time semantic compilation (ISC), a paradigm where the semantic meaning of a corpus is precompiled into a structured, queryable substrate to make retrieval-augmented QA cheaper and more accurate than conventional chunk+embed pipelines.
AI.motivation: Modern retrieval-augmented QA systems repeatedly force LLMs to re-interpret raw text on every query, wasting compute like a full-table scan in databases. Even as per-token prices fall, overall inference cost grows because context windows keep increasing. The authors argue that, as in databases, expensive semantic processing should be done once at write/ingest time into an index-like structure, especially when the corpus and its read patterns are known in advance.
AI.method: They introduce ingest-time semantic compilation (ISC), which precompiles a corpus into a queryable substrate. This substrate has two main components: (1) incrementally maintained embeddings to support efficient semantic retrieval, and (2) atomic, provenance-validated claims extracted from the corpus, treated as first-class database objects with their own DDL, maintenance, migration, and cost models. They build systems that incrementally update this substrate and use it as the retrieval payload instead of raw text chunks, then compare it with strong chunk-based RAG baselines, including hybrid retrieval with reranking.
AI.result: Incremental maintenance of the compiled substrate scales with data change rather than total corpus size, making updates 33.7x cheaper than full reconstruction while staying numerically equivalent. In a test on 500 broadcast-interview transcripts, using compiled claims as retrieval payload achieves 85.2% answer correctness with ~2.2k reader tokens, outperforming the best chunk-based configuration, which reaches 72.5% with ~16.3k tokens. The only baseline that matches compiled claims is a sophisticated contextualized-chunk pipeline with hybrid retrieval and reranking, but it requires ~21x more query-path tokens and, the authors argue, effectively approximates compilation itself.
AI.conclusion: Ingest-time semantic compilation offers a database-like paradigm for RAG: do semantic work once at ingest, maintain an incrementally updated semantic index of claims plus embeddings, and treat it with formal database abstractions. This approach reduces maintenance cost, cuts query-time token usage, and improves QA accuracy over traditional chunk-based methods. The authors outline a broader systems research agenda around query planning, compilation planning, and read planning for such compiled semantic substrates.

title: Free-Text Evaluation of LLMs for 5G Domain Knowledge and Fault Analysis using LLM-as-Judge
comment: 6pages, 4figures. Accepted for presentation in IEEE CSCN conference
summary: Real-world fault analysis in 5G and emerging 6G networks demands domain expertise to analyze free-text diagnostics, including root-cause explanations and recommended actions. LLMs have emerged as a promising approach to automating this, yet whether lightweight, edge-deployable models are capable of performing in-depth free-text diagnostics remains an open question. While existing benchmarks rely on restrictive MCQs with fixed answer keys, this paper evaluates 5G domain understanding and fault analysis in a free-text generation format. Transitioning to this paradigm requires evaluating lightweight, edge-deployable AI models on open-ended diagnostic reasoning, alongside a dependable framework to validate these text outputs at scale. To address this we evaluate three lightweight LLMs, Claude-Haiku-4.5, GPT-5.4-Mini, and Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite, on free-text 5G domain knowledge and fault-analysis tasks across three benchmarks, TeleQNA ORAN FT, 5G-Faults FT, and TeleInter FT. Three independent frontier judges score outputs, and pairwise inter-judge agreement is measured as an empirical test of the LLM-as-Judge methodology. All three models reach at least 90% accuracy on fault diagnosis, while zero-shot recall of 3GPP and O-RAN specifications remains the critical gap, with all models scoring below 60%. Mean inter-judge agreement is at least 0.90 across all runs, indicating that multi-judge LLM scoring produces consistent, reproducible grades for open-ended telecom responses. Operationally, Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite offers the best efficiency trade-off, combining competitive accuracy with the lowest inference cost and latency, making it the most suitable candidate for production telecom deployments.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether lightweight, edge-deployable LLMs can accurately perform open-ended 5G/6G fault diagnosis and domain reasoning, using free-text benchmarks and LLM-based multi-judge grading.
AI.motivation: In operational 5G and emerging 6G networks, fault analysis relies heavily on human experts interpreting free-text diagnostic data. While large frontier LLMs can help, they are often too heavy for edge deployment and existing benchmarks mostly use multiple-choice questions, which do not reflect real diagnostic workflows. There is a need to understand if smaller, cost-efficient models can handle realistic free-text fault analysis and how to reliably assess their open-ended outputs at scale.
AI.method: The authors construct an evaluation setup using three free-text telecom benchmarks: TeleQNA ORAN FT, 5G-Faults FT, and TeleInter FT. They test three lightweight LLMs—Claude-Haiku-4.5, GPT-5.4-Mini, and Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite—on tasks that require 5G domain knowledge and fault analysis expressed in open-ended text. For evaluation, they employ three independent frontier LLMs as judges to score the models’ responses and measure pairwise inter-judge agreement, thereby empirically validating the LLM-as-Judge methodology for this domain.
AI.result: All three lightweight models achieve at least 90% accuracy in fault diagnosis tasks, indicating strong capability in practical diagnostic reasoning. However, when tested on zero-shot recall of standards (3GPP and O-RAN specifications), all models perform poorly, with scores below 60%, revealing a major gap in standards-level knowledge. Inter-judge agreement across all runs is at least 0.90, suggesting that using multiple LLM judges yields consistent and reproducible scoring of free-text telecom responses. Among the three candidate models, Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite provides the best balance of accuracy, cost, and latency.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight, edge-deployable LLMs can perform accurate, open-ended 5G fault diagnosis, making them viable for real-world telecom operations, especially when paired with robust LLM-based multi-judge evaluation frameworks. Nonetheless, they remain weak at spontaneously recalling formal telecom standards such as 3GPP and O-RAN specs. Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite currently offers the most attractive efficiency–performance trade-off for production deployment, but further work is necessary to close the standards-knowledge gap.

title: MGAL: A Multilingual Granularity-Aware Long-Context Benchmark
summary:
Evaluation of long-context Large Language Models (LLMs) has advanced rapidly. However, most existing benchmarks are limited to the document level and focus mainly on high-resource languages, leaving many fine-grained challenges insufficiently evaluated. To address this gap, we present MGAL, the first multilingual, granularity- and position-aware long-context benchmark. MGAL is constructed from United Nations (UN) reports spanning 8K to 128K tokens across the six official UN languages. It covers four coherent levels of linguistic granularity (word, sentence, paragraph, and document) and further stratifies entries by their position within the document (begin, middle, and end), indexed at both the document and paragraph levels. This design enables systematic diagnosis of multilingual long-context comprehension across different granularities.
  Through extensive experiments and analyses, we find that: (1) LLMs perform well at word-level tasks but struggle with coarser-grained ones; and (2) Closed-source models retain a clear performance advantage in lower-resource languages. We further identify two new challenges: (1) Under local semantic crowding, where neighboring sentences share topics and entities, models tend to follow surface cues (e.g., connectives like ``however'' or repeated entities) rather than the discourse role of the sentence in surrounding context (e.g., background, outcome); and (2) A gap between fluency and consistency in generated outputs, where models produce text that reads smoothly but drifts from the source facts. In addition, we observe several patterns in line with prior studies, including reliance on nearby evidence and reuse of options under uncertainty.

AI.tldr: MGAL is a multilingual benchmark to evaluate long-context understanding of LLMs across multiple granularities and positions in long documents.
AI.motivation: Existing long-context LLM benchmarks mostly focus on single documents in high-resource languages and lack fine-grained, position-aware evaluation. There is a need to systematically test multilingual long-context comprehension across different linguistic levels and document positions.
AI.method: The authors build MGAL from long United Nations reports (8K–128K tokens) in the six official UN languages. They design tasks at four linguistic granularities (word, sentence, paragraph, document), and stratify items by their position (beginning, middle, end) at both document and paragraph levels to probe where and at what granularity models succeed or fail. They then run extensive experiments with various LLMs on this benchmark.
AI.result: LLMs perform relatively well on word-level tasks but their performance drops sharply on sentence-, paragraph-, and document-level tasks. Closed-source models outperform open ones especially in lower-resource languages. The authors also find that models under “local semantic crowding” rely on shallow surface cues instead of modeling discourse roles, and that models often generate fluent but factually inconsistent outputs.
AI.conclusion: MGAL provides a systematic, multilingual, position- and granularity-aware benchmark for long-context evaluation. Current LLMs still struggle with coarse-grained and discourse-level understanding, particularly in lower-resource languages, and are vulnerable to local semantic crowding and fluency–truth mismatches. MGAL can serve as a diagnostic tool to guide future improvements in long-context modeling and multilingual robustness.

title: Scaling Unsupervised Word Alignment to Documents via Structural Constraints
summary: Word alignment has traditionally been studied between sentences, but many cross-lingual tasks increasingly require correspondences across full documents. While recent multilingual embedding models can encode long inputs, we show that applying algorithms designed for sentences directly to documents leads to performance degradation. To address this, we introduce CTFAlign, a lightweight, training-free approach for document-level word alignment. CTFAlign applies a coarse-to-fine refinement strategy that restricts the alignment search space to semantically similar regions. Additionally, we introduce MDPAlign, a simpler alternative that constrains alignments by position with a main diagonal prior. Both approaches operate directly on full documents without relying on sentence segmentation or sentence alignment. We evaluate these methods across six language pairs varying in typological distance, resourcedness, and document length. Averaged over three models, CTFAlign reduces word alignment error rate from 0.412 to 0.326. These gains transfer downstream, leading to improvements in document-level translation coverage evaluation and recognition of semantic differences. We release CTFAlign as a Python package and make the code and data to reproduce our experiments publicly available.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes new training-free methods (CTFAlign and MDPAlign) for document-level word alignment that improve over directly applying sentence-level algorithms to full documents.
AI.motivation: Many cross-lingual tasks need word correspondences across whole documents, not just sentences. Existing word alignment methods are sentence-focused, and naïvely extending them to documents hurts performance, even with modern multilingual embeddings that can encode long inputs. There is a need for accurate, efficient, and segmentation-free document-level word alignment methods.
AI.method: The authors introduce two alignment approaches that operate directly on full documents using multilingual embeddings. CTFAlign uses a coarse-to-fine refinement strategy: it first identifies semantically similar regions in the source and target documents, then restricts and refines alignment search within these regions, reducing noise and complexity. MDPAlign is a simpler baseline that constrains alignments primarily by token position, imposing a main-diagonal positional prior to favor roughly monotonic alignments. Both are training-free and avoid sentence segmentation or pre-aligned sentences.
AI.result: Across six language pairs with diverse typological characteristics, resource levels, and document lengths, the proposed methods are evaluated using multiple multilingual embedding models. CTFAlign, averaged over three models, reduces word alignment error rate from 0.412 to 0.326, showing clear gains over direct document-level application of sentence-based algorithms. These better alignments also improve downstream tasks such as document-level translation coverage evaluation and detection of semantic differences between documents.
AI.conclusion: Document-level word alignment cannot be effectively handled by simply scaling sentence-level methods, even with powerful multilingual embeddings. The proposed training-free methods, particularly CTFAlign with its coarse-to-fine search restriction, significantly improve alignment quality and downstream cross-lingual applications, while operating directly on full documents without sentence segmentation. The authors also support reproducibility by releasing a Python package, code, and data.

title: Coverage-Driven Verification for Safety-by-Design in AI-Based Collision Avoidance Systems
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers significant potential for future aviation systems; however, its integration into safety-critical applications requires compliance with the aviation sector's stringent safety standards. For AI and Machine Learning (ML)-based systems, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) emphasizes the need to demonstrate the representativeness and completeness of the Operational Design Domain (ODD) and the associated data distributions used during development and verification. Despite this requirement, a structured engineering process for defining target distributions and evaluating representativeness within ODDs remains largely unexplored. This work presents a method for representativeness assessment of AI/ML constituent ODDs in the context of aviation safety assurance. Starting from the methodical identification of suitable target distributions, a process flow is proposed that guides developers from ODD definition and parameter distribution modeling to the quantitative assessment and interpretation of coverage results with respect to EASA's learning assurance objectives. As quantitative measures, the chi-squared goodness-of-fit test is examined and found unsuitable for the large data sets arising in this setting, leading to the adoption of the Kullback--Leibler divergence and Cramér's $V$ for the representativeness assessment. The method is demonstrated using the example of AI-based airborne collision avoidance, employing experimental data from previous Horizontal Collision Avoidance System (HCAS) and Vertical Collision Avoidance System (VCAS) simulations. The results illustrate how statistical distribution comparison methods can support the assessment of representativeness for safety-critical AI applications and contribute toward a systematic Safety-by-Design AI engineering process aligned with emerging EASA guidance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and demonstrates a structured quantitative method to assess how representative AI/ML system data is of its Operational Design Domain (ODD) in aviation, supporting safety assurance in line with EASA guidance.
AI.motivation: Aviation safety standards require strong evidence that AI/ML systems have been trained and verified on data that is representative and complete with respect to the Operational Design Domain (ODD). EASA specifically stresses the need to justify that ODD definitions and underlying data distributions used for learning and verification match the real-world operational context. However, there is currently no well-defined engineering process for: (1) defining statistically grounded target distributions over the ODD, and (2) quantitatively evaluating the representativeness (coverage and similarity) of development/verification data against those targets, especially for large aviation datasets. This gap hinders systematic safety assurance and Safety-by-Design practices for AI in aviation.
AI.method: The authors propose a structured method for assessing the representativeness of AI/ML constituent ODDs in aviation safety assurance. The process begins with a systematic identification and definition of the ODD and its key parameters, followed by modeling of target parameter distributions that describe the intended operational environment. A process flow then guides developers to compare empirical data distributions used for training/verification against these targets. For the quantitative assessment, the paper analyzes candidate statistical measures and determines that the chi-squared goodness-of-fit test is unsuitable for the very large data sets typical in this context. Instead, the method adopts Kullback–Leibler divergence and Cramér’s V as the primary metrics for distribution comparison and dependence assessment. The full method is instantiated and evaluated using data from prior simulations of AI-based airborne collision avoidance systems (HCAS and VCAS).
AI.result: Applying the method to experimental data from Horizontal and Vertical Collision Avoidance System simulations shows that statistical distribution comparison techniques can effectively quantify how well the collected data represents the defined ODD target distributions. The case study demonstrates that chi-squared tests become impractical or misleading with large aviation datasets, whereas Kullback–Leibler divergence and Cramér’s V provide more suitable and informative measures of distribution similarity and variable association. The example illustrates how coverage and distribution differences can be made explicit and interpretable for safety assessment.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that a structured, quantitative approach to ODD representativeness assessment is both feasible and valuable for safety-critical AI in aviation. By defining target ODD distributions and evaluating empirical data with appropriate metrics (KL divergence and Cramér’s V), developers can generate clearer evidence in support of EASA’s learning assurance objectives. This contributes toward a systematic Safety-by-Design AI engineering process aligned with emerging regulatory guidance and offers a practical foundation for assessing and improving the representativeness of AI/ML training and verification data in aviation applications.

title: Evidence-Consistent Generative Detection under Scenario-Level Distribution Shift
comment: Accepted at CIKM 2026 (35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management), Rome, Italy, November 2026. 12 pages, 4 figures. Code and data: https://github.com/kimsan1120/ECoG
summary: Conventional in-distribution evaluation can overestimate robustness when training and test data share recurring task-specific patterns or surface cues. This risk is especially relevant in social-engineering fraud detection, where attackers can preserve malicious intent while changing the scenario, impersonated entity, or wording. We study this problem as scenario-level out-of-distribution (SL-OOD) detection for SMS and voice phishing, where entire attack scenarios are held out from training while the label space remains fixed. This setting tests whether models can generalize to unseen attack scenarios using decision-relevant evidence rather than familiar scenario-specific cues. Using this SL-OOD evaluation, we find that high in-distribution performance does not reliably predict held-out robustness across feature-, encoder-, and decoder-based baselines. We interpret this gap as scenario memorization: reliance on recurring scenario-specific lexical or entity cues rather than decision-relevant evidence. We propose ECoG, an evidence-consistent generative framework that combines evidence-span supervision with a rationale-label consistency objective during training. On the 0.5B decoder, relative to the same backbone trained without consistency regularization, ECoG raises Macro-F1 on OOD challenging instances by 3.22 points, reduces the share of predictions whose generated rationale supports the opposite label by 4.22 points, and increases token-level overlap with reference evidence spans by 8.38 points; the reduction in prediction-rationale inconsistency is consistent across four decoder backbones. These results suggest that compact generative detectors can benefit from evidence supervision and rationale-label consistency under social-engineering shift.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that standard in-distribution evaluation overestimates robustness of phishing detectors and introduces a scenario-level OOD setting plus a new training framework, ECoG, that improves evidence-based generalization and rationale consistency.
AI.motivation: Existing robustness evaluations for social-engineering fraud detection are misleading because training and test sets often share similar surface patterns and scenarios. Attackers can easily change the scenario, impersonated entity, or wording while keeping malicious intent, so models that memorize scenarios rather than reasoning over evidence will fail in the real world. The authors want an evaluation that reflects this threat model and methods that force detectors to base decisions on decision-relevant evidence rather than superficial cues.
AI.method: They define a scenario-level out-of-distribution (SL-OOD) setting for SMS and voice phishing, where entire attack scenarios are withheld from training but labels remain the same, creating a shift in scenarios without changing the task. They benchmark feature-, encoder-, and decoder-based baselines to show that strong in-distribution metrics do not guarantee robustness on held-out scenarios. To address this, they introduce ECoG, an evidence-consistent generative framework that trains generative detectors with (1) evidence-span supervision and (2) a rationale–label consistency objective that regularizes training so that generated rationales support the predicted label.
AI.result: Under the SL-OOD evaluation, baselines with high in-distribution performance exhibit sizable drops in performance, revealing scenario memorization. For a 0.5B-parameter decoder backbone, adding ECoG’s consistency regularization improves Macro-F1 on OOD challenging instances by 3.22 points, decreases the proportion of cases where the generated rationale actually supports the opposite label by 4.22 points, and boosts token-level overlap with gold evidence spans by 8.38 points. Similar reductions in prediction–rationale inconsistency are observed across four different decoder backbones.
AI.conclusion: Conventional in-distribution evaluation is insufficient for assessing robustness of social-engineering fraud detectors because models tend to memorize recurring scenarios instead of using genuine evidence. Scenario-level OOD evaluation better captures real-world shifts in attacker behavior. The proposed ECoG framework, which aligns model predictions with supervised evidence spans and enforces rationale–label consistency, makes compact generative phishing detectors more robust and more faithful under social-engineering shifts, as shown by better OOD performance and more consistent rationales.
