summary: LLM agents are emerging as an important paradigm for real-world tasks that require reasoning, tool use, and sequential decision-making. As these agents operate over longer horizons, runtime intervention offers a way to improve reliability without retraining the underlying actor. Failure detection alone is insufficient. Effective intervention must also provide a useful direction for recovery. Existing approaches often rely on an expert solver or a critic that generates task-specific corrections, incurring either the cost of another capable solver or the capacity demands of a task-capable critic. We introduce Comparison-Only Tiny Advisor (COTA), a comparison-only framework for constructive runtime intervention. In COTA, a tiny comparator judges whether sampled alternatives lead to better continuations than the actor's proposal, and repeated comparisons determine when intervention is warranted. We train the comparator using pairwise supervision constructed from same-prefix counterfactual branches. Preferred alternatives are returned as non-binding advice, leaving the original actor to replan. Across WebShop, ALFWorld, and tau^3-Retail with three actors, COTA improves all nine evaluation settings and outperforms the compared baselines. These results show that constructive runtime intervention can remain effective even when the auxiliary model has substantially weaker task-solving capability than the actor.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes COTA, a lightweight comparison-only advisor that improves the reliability of LLM agents via runtime intervention without requiring a full expert solver or powerful critic.
AI.motivation: LLM agents increasingly tackle real-world, long-horizon tasks that require reasoning, tools, and sequential decisions. These agents can fail in complex ways, and while runtime failure detection can flag issues, it does not itself suggest how to recover. Existing intervention methods either rely on expensive expert solvers or on critics that must themselves have strong task-solving capabilities, which is resource-intensive and less scalable. The authors seek a way to intervene constructively at runtime with a much smaller, weaker auxiliary model that still improves agent reliability and performance.
AI.method: The authors introduce COTA (Comparison-Only Tiny Advisor), a framework where a small comparator model evaluates alternatives to the main actor’s proposed continuation. Instead of generating task-specific corrections, this comparator only judges which of two candidate continuations is better. Training data is built from counterfactual branches that share a prefix; pairwise supervision indicates which branch leads to better outcomes. At runtime, the system samples alternative continuations, has the comparator perform repeated pairwise judgments against the actor’s proposal, and triggers intervention when alternatives are consistently judged superior. The chosen alternative is returned as non-binding advice, allowing the actor to absorb or ignore it while replanning its next steps.
AI.result: In experiments on three benchmark environments—WebShop, ALFWorld, and tau^3-Retail—using three different LLM-based actors, COTA is applied across nine evaluation combinations. In all nine settings, adding COTA improves performance relative to the actor alone and also surpasses baseline intervention methods that rely on other forms of critics or advisors. This demonstrates that comparison-only guidance from a small model can yield consistent improvements in task success rates.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that effective constructive runtime intervention for LLM agents does not require an equally capable or stronger auxiliary solver. A small comparison-only advisor trained with pairwise preferences over same-prefix counterfactuals can reliably identify better continuations and guide the actor to improved behavior across diverse long-horizon tasks. This suggests a scalable, resource-efficient path to enhancing robustness and reliability of LLM agents in real-world settings.

title: Evaluating Large Language Model Performance on International Maritime Dangerous Goods Code Compliance
summary:
The transport of dangerous goods by sea is a high-consequence activity governed by the International Maritime Dangerous Goods (IMDG) Code, a complex regulatory framework where errors in classification, packaging, stowage, or segregation can result in fire, explosion, toxic release, or loss of life or vessel. Correct compliance requires accurately interpreting hundreds of pages of interacting provisions, updated on a two-year amendment cycle. Practitioners increasingly use Large Language Models (LLMs) as decision-support tools, yet no systematic evaluation exists of whether they can reliably interpret IMDG requirements for safety-critical use.
  This paper introduces DGEval, the first benchmark for evaluating LLM knowledge of IMDG Amendment 42-24. Built from expert-written questions on the NCB Hazcheck e-learning platform and structured lookups from the Dangerous Goods List (DGL), it comprises 1,678 questions across multiple-choice, open-ended, DGL lookup, and regulatory identification tasks. We evaluate 13 models from six providers across multiple thinking configurations, including one maritime domain-specific fine-tuned model, and test the effect of web search.
  Although the best-performing model exceeds the human practitioner baseline on multiple-choice questions, all models are weakest in the operationally safety-critical areas of stowage, segregation, and regulatory recall. These results indicate that LLMs may support compliance tasks, particularly structured DGL lookups with web search, but unreliability in operational areas and regulatory-text recall means human oversight and authoritative source verification remain necessary before deployment in any safety-critical context. DGEval is designed as a safety assurance instrument to be applied continuously as models evolve, not as a settled characterisation of current capability.

AI.tldr: Introduces DGEval, the first benchmark to systematically test how well LLMs understand and apply the IMDG Code for dangerous goods transport by sea.
AI.motivation: Maritime transport of dangerous goods is safety-critical and governed by the complex IMDG Code; practitioners are already using LLMs for decision support, but there is no rigorous evaluation of whether LLMs can reliably interpret these regulations, especially for operationally critical tasks.
AI.method: The authors construct DGEval, a benchmark based on expert-written questions from the NCB Hazcheck e-learning platform and structured queries from the Dangerous Goods List, covering 1,678 questions in multiple formats (MCQ, open-ended, lookup, regulatory identification). They then evaluate 13 LLMs from six providers, including a maritime domain-specific fine-tuned model, across different prompting/“thinking” configurations and with/without web search.
AI.result: The strongest model surpasses a human practitioner baseline on multiple-choice questions, and models perform relatively well on structured DGL lookup tasks, particularly when allowed to use web search. However, all models perform poorly in operational safety-critical areas such as stowage, segregation, and recalling specific regulatory text.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can assist with some IMDG compliance tasks, especially structured data lookups with web search, but they are unreliable for operational decisions and detailed regulatory recall; thus, human oversight and verification against authoritative sources remain essential. DGEval should be used as a continuing safety assurance tool to monitor evolving model capabilities rather than as a one-time characterization.

title: Socialized Division and Collaboration: Rethinking Class-Incremental Learning under Optimization Conflicts
summary: Class-incremental learning is commonly instantiated as a single-model paradigm, where a unified model sequentially adapts to an unbounded stream of sessions. While effective under mild distributional shifts, this formulation becomes strained when successive sessions induce incompatible optimization directions, leading to destructive interference and catastrophic forgetting. We argue that such forgetting reflects a structural limitation of enforcing heterogeneous learning dynamics within a single parameter space. Motivated by social solidarity theory, we propose Socialized Division and Collaboration (SDC) as a reformulation of continual learning that decomposes session learning across specialized models in response to optimization conflicts, while enabling coordinated collaboration. To support this formulation with a principled allocation mechanism, we introduce an energy-based session-model compatibility criterion grounded in Helmholtz free energy, which guides adaptive session allocation and model evolution under conflicting objectives. This framework integrates session assignment, model evolution, and collaborative inference into a unified pipeline, offering an alternative to monolithic continual learning formulations and highlighting a broader design principle for learning under persistent optimization conflicts.

AI.tldr: They propose a new continual learning framework that uses multiple specialized models with an energy-based allocation mechanism to avoid catastrophic forgetting under conflicting optimization directions.
AI.motivation: Single-model class-incremental learning struggles when successive sessions induce incompatible optimization directions, causing destructive interference and catastrophic forgetting. The authors see this as a structural limitation of forcing heterogeneous learning dynamics into one parameter space and seek a more robust formulation for learning under persistent optimization conflicts.
AI.method: They introduce Socialized Division and Collaboration (SDC), which decomposes class-incremental learning across multiple specialized models instead of a single monolithic one. An energy-based session–model compatibility criterion, grounded in Helmholtz free energy, is used to decide how to allocate incoming sessions to existing models and when to evolve (create or adapt) models. The framework unifies three components: (1) adaptive session assignment to specialized models, (2) model evolution under conflicting objectives, and (3) collaborative inference across these models at test time.
AI.result: The abstract implies that SDC effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting in scenarios with strong optimization conflicts by better matching sessions to compatible models and enabling coordinated collaboration. While no numerical results are provided, the claimed result is an improved ability to perform continual learning in the presence of persistent distributional and objective conflicts compared to single-model approaches.
AI.conclusion: Catastrophic forgetting in class-incremental learning can be viewed as a structural issue of monolithic single-model formulations. By instead dividing learning across multiple specialized models and coordinating them via an energy-based compatibility mechanism, continual learning systems can better handle persistent optimization conflicts. SDC is proposed as a unified pipeline implementing this principle, suggesting a broader design direction beyond traditional single-model continual learning.

title: The Cost of a Physics Prior Is Bounded by the Ablation Gap
summary: Shape-constrained and physics-informed learning reports an accuracy cost of enforcing a prior and treats it as a property of the prior. We show it is mostly a property of the free features and the validation split. Let P be the excess risk of restricting a hypothesis class to functions with a shape constraint on features S, and D the excess risk of the ablated model that ignores S. Because a function constant in x_j is both non-decreasing and non-increasing in x_j, the ablated class is contained in the constrained class, so 0 <= P <= D for every risk functional, with no convexity, smoothness, or realizability assumption. Empirically the bound is a sign test: a constrained model must never be beaten by its own ablation. We instantiate it on an ordinal wildfire-severity task (N = 26,681, K = 3) with hard monotone constraints on four meteorological drivers, coordinates left free, and a validation ladder from i.i.d. resampling to 2-degree spatial blocking. Coordinates act as a shield: alone they recover 92.9% of the full model's macro-F1 under spatial blocking, collapsing D from 0.1288 to 0.0427; the same prior costs 0.0473 shielded and 0.3470 unshielded, a ratio of 7.3 with identical physics. Because D is protocol-dependent it does not transfer: coarsening blocks from 1 to 10 degrees drives D from 0.0942 to 0.0050, leaving two configurations unidentifiable a priori. Inversions of the certified nesting bound the pipeline's additive resolution: over 318 comparisons they give a self-calibrating floor of 0.0220 macro-F1, below which no reported price is interpretable, including four cells in our own headline grid. Cost and compliance are independent: the unconstrained model violates the prior at rate 0.48-0.49 while enforcing it costs 0.0473. We give a two-fit screen that rejects unidentifiable experiments before a constrained model is trained.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the empirical “cost” of enforcing shape/physics priors in models is largely determined by free (unconstrained) features and the validation protocol, not by the prior itself, and provides simple nesting-based tests to detect when reported prior costs are not statistically or procedurally interpretable.
AI.motivation: Practitioners often report that enforcing shape constraints or physics-informed priors reduces predictive accuracy, treating that reduction as an intrinsic property (or flaw) of the prior. This makes it difficult to know whether performance trade-offs are real, unavoidable, or artifacts of model design and validation. The authors want to disentangle the true cost of a prior from confounding factors such as free features (e.g., spatial coordinates) and the way data are split for validation, especially in spatial prediction tasks like wildfire severity.
AI.method: 1) Provide a general excess-risk inequality: because models that ablate constrained features are a subset of shape-constrained models (they can be constant in the constrained coordinates), the excess risk P of the constrained class is bounded by the excess risk D of the ablated class for any risk functional, without assuming convexity or realizability. 2) Turn this into a practical sign test: a constrained model should never be outperformed by its own ablation if the reported “cost of the prior” is to be trusted. 3) Empirically instantiate the framework on ordinal wildfire-severity prediction (N = 26,681; K = 3 classes), imposing hard monotonicity constraints on four meteorological variables while leaving spatial coordinates unconstrained, and evaluating under increasingly structured validation protocols from i.i.d. resampling to spatial blocking at different resolutions. 4) Analyze how free spatial coordinates act as a shield that can absorb predictive signal and reduce the apparent cost of the monotone prior, and explore how changing spatial block size alters D and makes some configurations empirically indistinguishable. 5) Use inversions of the nesting inequality across many comparisons to estimate a minimal “additive resolution” (self-calibrating floor) for macro-F1 below which apparent prior costs cannot be interpreted, and propose a two-fit screening procedure to flag unidentifiable experiments before training constrained models.
AI.result: Theoretically, the authors show that the ablated hypothesis class (ignoring constrained features) is strictly nested within the shape-constrained class, implying 0 <= P <= D for any risk, and that this nesting yields a simple empirical sign test about whether a constrained model can be legitimately claimed to have higher risk than its ablation. Empirically, in wildfire-severity prediction with spatial blocking, they find: (a) Spatial coordinates alone recover 92.9% of the full model’s macro-F1, sharply reducing D from 0.1288 to 0.0427. (b) The apparent cost of the monotone prior differs dramatically depending on whether spatial coordinates are present: with coordinates (shielded), the cost is 0.0473, but without coordinates (unshielded) it is 0.3470, a factor of 7.3 despite identical physics. (c) The bound D is highly dependent on the validation protocol: as spatial block size expands from 1 to 10 degrees, D shrinks from 0.0942 to 0.0050, making some configurations a priori indistinguishable. (d) By inverting the certified nesting bound across 318 comparisons, they estimate a self-calibrating lower bound of 0.0220 in macro-F1 below which any claimed cost of enforcing the prior is not reliably interpretable; this invalidates several cells in their own summary grid. (e) They also observe that prior cost and prior compliance are largely independent: the unconstrained model violates the monotonicity prior about half the time (0.48–0.49 violation rate), while enforcing the prior in the constrained model costs only 0.0473 macro-F1.
AI.conclusion: The observed accuracy loss attributed to shape or physics-informed priors is not an intrinsic defect of the prior but is largely shaped by the representational power of unconstrained features and the specific validation protocol. Because ablated models are nested within constrained models, any claimed “cost of the prior” must satisfy 0 <= P <= D, and D itself is protocol-dependent and non-transferable across validation schemes. This nesting can be used to construct a simple sign test and a self-calibrating resolution threshold for interpreting reported prior costs, revealing that many such costs are not statistically meaningful. Spatial coordinates can act as powerful shields that both reduce the apparent prior cost and mask identifiability issues. Overall, the paper urges rethinking how we evaluate and report the cost of inductive priors, proposing a two-fit screening procedure to reject unidentifiable experiments and arguing that prior cost and prior compliance are empirically decoupled.

title: CellPath-Bench: A Multidimensional Benchmark for Whole-Slide Cellular Representations in Pathology Foundation Models
summary: Pathology foundation models (PFMs) are increasingly used as general-purpose backbones, yet existing benchmarks cannot systematically diagnose their whole-slide cellular representation capabilities, including the decodability of cell-type information and the transferability of such information across tissue sections, datasets, and anatomical organs. We introduce CellPath-Bench, a cellular-resolution benchmark that evaluates frozen PFMs themselves. Following quality control of 52 candidate Xenium datasets, we construct a panel of 25 spatially aligned H\&E--Xenium tissue sections spanning 11 organs and 7,079,283 cells, harmonized into fine- and coarse-grained taxonomies. CellPath-Bench samples frozen WSI feature maps at registered nuclear coordinates and evaluates them using standardized multiclass linear probes. Cell Representation Advantage (CRA) measures the within-section advantage of nucleus-anchored representations over patch-level mean pooling, while Cell Representation Transferability (CRT) characterizes the generalization of cell-type decodability across tissue sections, datasets, and organs. We benchmark 30 pathology-specific and general-purpose foundation models through 304,920 runs across spatial readouts, magnifications, taxonomic granularities, and evaluation protocols. The results reveal substantial model-dependent differences in cell-type decodability and its cross-domain generalization, yielding distinct multidimensional capability profiles. CellPath-Bench provides a standardized framework for auditing cellular information in frozen PFM representations.

AI.tldr: They build a benchmark (CellPath-Bench) to test how well frozen pathology foundation models represent and transfer cell-type information at cellular resolution across many tissues and datasets.
AI.motivation: Pathology foundation models are widely used as general-purpose feature extractors for whole-slide images, but current benchmarks don’t precisely evaluate whether their internal representations capture detailed, decodable cell-type information or whether that information transfers well across sections, datasets, and organs. A systematic, standardized way to audit cellular-level representations in frozen models is missing.
AI.method: They assemble a high-quality benchmark based on 25 spatially aligned H&E–Xenium tissue sections (11 organs, ~7 million cells) with harmonized fine- and coarse-grained cell-type taxonomies. They sample features from frozen PFMs at nuclear coordinates in the corresponding WSI feature maps and evaluate cell-type decodability using standardized multiclass linear probes. They define two metrics: (1) Cell Representation Advantage (CRA), comparing nucleus-anchored representations to patch-level mean pooling within the same section; and (2) Cell Representation Transferability (CRT), measuring how well cell-type decoders generalize across sections, datasets, and organs. They then run a large-scale benchmark of 30 PFM and general vision models across many settings (spatial readouts, magnifications, taxonomic resolutions, and protocols), totaling over 300k evaluation runs.
AI.result: The benchmark uncovers large, model-dependent variation in how well cell types can be linearly decoded from frozen PFM representations and in how robust that decodability is across domains (sections, datasets, organs). These differences can be summarized as distinct, multidimensional capability profiles for each model, highlighting strengths and weaknesses in cellular representation and transferability.
AI.conclusion: CellPath-Bench offers a standardized, scalable framework to directly audit the cellular-level information contained in frozen pathology foundation models, enabling more informed selection, comparison, and development of PFMs for cellular-resolution pathology tasks and cross-domain applications.

title: Can Legal AI Know When It Is Wrong? And Do Students Know When It Is?
summary:
Integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) into the Indian judiciary promises access to justice but introduces severe risks. We identify the 'inertia of confidence'--an overconfidence phenomenon analogous to the Dunning-Kruger effect where LLMs provide incorrect legal verdicts with near-maximum confidence, driven by a hypothesized 'precedent overfitting' bias. Phase I of our socio-technical audit tested ChatGPT (GPT-5.2), Meta AI, and Perplexity AI on a 60-case battery regarding the Indian Contract Act, 1872, and the shift toward statutory enforcement of specific performance. We introduce the High-Confidence Error Rate (HCER) to quantify incorrect verdicts delivered with dangerous certainty (>= 9 on a 1-10 scale). All models struggled with statutory updates. Meta AI proved most vulnerable (31.7% HCER), frequently misapplying pre-amendment rules with a 9.1/10 mean confidence, followed by Perplexity (15.0%) and ChatGPT (6.7%).
  Phase II investigated human vulnerability to this overconfidence via a survey of Indian law students (N=380). Verification often functions as a reactive adaptation to machine hallucinations: students encountering fabricated citations reported higher verification scores (4.2/5) than those with no such encounters (2.8/5). Furthermore, while 81.6% knew submitting hallucinated cases can lead to contempt-of-court, 71.1% received no formal training on ethical AI use. We propose shifting toward adversarial legal research pedagogy and implementing source-grounded verification architectures to prevent systemic professional negligence.

AI.tldr: The paper audits how large language models handle Indian contract law, introduces a metric for dangerously confident legal errors, and studies how law students interact with such outputs, proposing changes in legal education and AI systems to reduce systemic risks.
AI.motivation: As LLMs begin to be used in judicial and legal contexts in India, they promise greater access to justice but also carry the risk of confidently wrong legal advice and judgments, especially when the law has recently changed. There is a need to empirically measure these risks, understand how human users respond to them, and design safeguards in both technology and legal education to prevent professional negligence and harm to litigants.
AI.method: The authors run a two-phase socio-technical audit. In Phase I, they test three LLMs (ChatGPT/GPT-5.2, Meta AI, and Perplexity AI) on a curated set of 60 cases under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, focusing on the transition toward statutory enforcement of specific performance. They introduce and compute a High-Confidence Error Rate (HCER) to capture how often the models give incorrect legal verdicts with very high self-reported confidence (≥ 9/10). In Phase II, they conduct a survey of 380 Indian law students to examine their verification behaviors, exposure to hallucinated citations, awareness of legal consequences like contempt of court, and whether they have received training on ethical AI use.
AI.result: All tested LLMs exhibited difficulty in applying statutory updates correctly, suggesting a "precedent overfitting" bias where they rely too heavily on outdated case law or rules. Meta AI had the highest High-Confidence Error Rate (31.7%) and often applied pre-amendment rules with an average confidence of 9.1/10, Perplexity AI had a 15.0% HCER, and ChatGPT the lowest at 6.7%. On the human side, law students who encountered fabricated citations reported higher verification practices (4.2/5) compared to those who did not encounter such hallucinations (2.8/5), indicating that verification is often reactive. Despite 81.6% knowing that using hallucinated cases could lead to contempt of court, 71.1% reported receiving no formal training in ethical AI use.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that LLMs currently pose serious risks when applied to Indian legal decision-making, particularly by making high-confidence errors on areas affected by recent statutory change. It introduces the concepts of inertia of confidence and precedent overfitting as core failure modes. Human users, especially law students, display reactive rather than proactive verification behaviors and are undertrained in ethical AI use, despite awareness of legal sanctions. The authors recommend adversarial legal research pedagogy and the deployment of source-grounded verification architectures as key interventions to mitigate the risks of systemic professional negligence in AI-augmented legal practice.

title: When Trust Meets Truth: Trust-Truth Separability in LLM-as-Judge
summary: LLM-as-Judge systems can produce multi-dimensional evaluations, such as trustworthiness, reliability, and factuality, and these outputs are often interpreted as independent evidence. We test this assumption for a common pair of judgments: trust scoring and binary truth classification. On correctness-controlled QA, LLM judges align trust scores with truth verdicts more tightly than human behavioral reference, suggesting weaker separations between trust and truth judgment. We then apply stress tests by changing only source cues of identical QA between Human and AI. Source attribution shifts not only trust scores but also truth verdicts and logit-derived correct-side probabilities. Results show that current LLM-as-Judge protocols should not treat trust scores as independent evidence for truth judgments.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether trust scores produced by LLM-as-Judge systems are truly independent from their truth judgments and finds they are tightly coupled and highly sensitive to source cues.
AI.motivation: LLM-as-Judge systems are increasingly used to evaluate answers along multiple dimensions like trustworthiness and factuality, with practitioners often treating these outputs as separate, independent signals. However, it is unclear whether trust scores really provide additional information beyond a truth classification, or if they are merely reflections of the same underlying judgment, which has implications for how such evaluations are interpreted and aggregated.
AI.method: The authors focus on a pair of judgments—continuous trust scores and binary truth (true/false) classifications—on correctness-controlled QA tasks. They compare LLM-judge behavior with human behavioral references to assess how tightly trust and truth align. They then perform stress tests by manipulating only the stated source of otherwise identical QA content (e.g., attributing answers to humans vs. AI) and analyze how this affects trust scores, truth verdicts, and logit-level probabilities for being correct.
AI.result: LLM judges show a stronger alignment between trust scores and truth verdicts than is seen in human behavior, indicating a weaker separation between trust and truth in models than in people. When only the source attribution of identical QA is changed, both trust scores and binary truth decisions shift systematically, as do the model’s internal probabilities of correctness. This demonstrates that source cues alone can sway both trust and truth outputs in LLM-as-Judge settings.
AI.conclusion: The findings imply that current LLM-as-Judge protocols should not treat trust scores as independent evidence about truth, since they are tightly coupled to truth judgments and can be jointly biased by superficial source information. Designers and users of such systems should be cautious about over-interpreting multi-dimensional evaluation outputs and should consider adjusting evaluation setups or calibration methods to reduce source-driven confounds and artificial redundancy between trust and truth signals.

title: Personalized Privacy Control in LLMs via Attention Head Intervention
summary: The rise of agentic AI enables LLMs to access diverse user data, raising critical privacy concerns. Prior work on contextual privacy studies whether LLMs regulate information disclosure according to context-dependent norms. However, acceptable disclosure boundaries may vary across users even within the same context. To address this limitation, we introduce \textit{personalized privacy}, which incorporates user-specific disclosure preferences into privacy control. We further present P3Bench~(\textbf{P}ersonalized \textbf{P}rivacy \textbf{P}reservation \textbf{Bench}mark), a novel benchmark extending contextual privacy policies with personalized disclosure policies. Experiments show that prompt-based policies fail to reliably enforce personalized privacy policies, with Qwen2.5-7B and Gemma3-4B showing average policy ignorance ratios of 51.25\% and 74.28\%, respectively. Finally, to address this problem, we propose \textsc{Repair}, a robust inference-time attention head intervention method that adjusts disclosure behavior toward policy-consistent responses. Our method significantly improves adherence to user-specific privacy preferences by reducing cases where the model fails to follow the given policy.

AI.tldr: Introduces personalized privacy for LLMs and a benchmark (P3Bench), shows prompt-based policies poorly enforce user-specific privacy, and proposes an attention-head intervention method (REPAIR) that improves adherence to personalized privacy policies.
AI.motivation: Existing contextual privacy research assumes uniform privacy norms within a context, but in reality different users have different disclosure preferences even in identical situations. As agentic AI systems gain access to rich personal data, there is a need for precise, user-tailored privacy controls and a way to systematically evaluate whether LLMs can respect such personalized policies.
AI.method: 1) Define the concept of personalized privacy, extending contextual privacy models with user-specific disclosure policies. 2) Construct P3Bench, a benchmark combining contextual privacy policies with explicit, personalized disclosure preferences for different users. 3) Empirically evaluate LLMs (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma3-4B) under prompt-based policy specifications, measuring how often models ignore the given policies. 4) Propose REPAIR, an inference-time method that intervenes on attention heads to steer the model’s disclosure decisions toward policy-consistent behavior, and test its effectiveness on P3Bench.
AI.result: On P3Bench, prompt-based policies are unreliable: Qwen2.5-7B and Gemma3-4B ignore personalized policies in about half to three-quarters of cases (policy ignorance ratios of 51.25% and 74.28%). Applying the REPAIR attention-head intervention substantially reduces these policy violations, leading to more consistent adherence to user-specific privacy preferences during inference.
AI.conclusion: LLMs cannot be trusted to enforce user-specific privacy preferences solely via prompt-based instructions, even when contextual privacy is considered. Personalized privacy needs explicit modeling and evaluation, which P3Bench provides. Moreover, targeted inference-time manipulation of internal attention mechanisms (REPAIR) can significantly enhance compliance with personalized privacy policies, offering a practical path toward safer, user-tailored privacy behavior in agentic AI systems.

title: ReFrame: Evidence-Guided Test-Time Safety Alignment in Multimodal Large Language Models
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026. 22 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables
summary: While multimodal large language models (MLLMs) extend model capabilities beyond text, they also make safety alignment increasingly challenging. Multimodal safety alignment methods must address cross-modal jailbreaks, safety-awareness failures, and over-sensitive refusals. However, existing methods often rely on retraining or internal-state inspection, limiting their applicability to deployed closed-source MLLMs and motivating test-time safety alignment. We analyze this setting and identify two key obstacles, utility dominance and reasoning inertia, which cause models to overlook latent risks or follow malicious reasoning trajectories. Guided by these insights, we propose ReFrame, a training-free multimodal input reframing framework where two agents share a lightweight locally deployed MLLM: the evidence-generation agent constructs complementary risk and utility evidence, and the rewrite-and-routing agent converts it into a safe proxy prompt and image-routing decision before calling the downstream MLLM, without modifying it or accessing its internal information. Experiments across multiple MLLMs and benchmarks show that ReFrame improves jailbreak defense, safety awareness, and oversensitivity reduction while preserving multimodal utility.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ReFrame, a training-free, test-time safety framework for multimodal LLMs that reframes user inputs via two local agents to improve jailbreak defense, safety awareness, and reduce oversensitive refusals while preserving utility.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLMs can process both text and images, which increases their power but also makes safety alignment harder. New vulnerabilities appear, such as cross-modal jailbreaks (where image and text jointly bypass safeguards), failures to detect latent risks, and overly cautious refusals that hurt usability. Existing safety methods typically need retraining or access to model internals, which is impractical for closed-source, deployed MLLMs. This motivates a training-free, test-time safety solution that works with black-box MLLMs.
AI.method: The authors first analyze test-time safety alignment for MLLMs and identify two issues: utility dominance (the model prioritizes helpfulness and task completion over safety) and reasoning inertia (once on a malicious reasoning path, the model keeps following it). To address this, they propose ReFrame, a multimodal input reframing framework that operates without modifying the target MLLM. ReFrame uses two cooperating agents that run on a lightweight local MLLM: (1) an evidence-generation agent that produces both risk-related and utility-related evidence from the original multimodal input, and (2) a rewrite-and-routing agent that uses this evidence to create a safe proxy prompt and decide how to route or filter the image before querying the downstream MLLM. This reframing steers the downstream model away from unsafe trajectories while preserving task-relevant information.
AI.result: Across multiple multimodal LLMs and safety benchmarks, ReFrame improves resistance to jailbreak attacks, enhances safety awareness (better recognition and handling of risky content), and reduces over-sensitive refusals compared to baselines, while keeping the multimodal task performance largely intact.
AI.conclusion: ReFrame shows that training-free, test-time input reframing with small local agents can significantly improve the safety of black-box multimodal LLMs. By explicitly generating risk and utility evidence and then rewriting inputs into safe proxy prompts with routing decisions, ReFrame mitigates cross-modal jailbreaks and over-cautious behavior without access to or modification of the underlying MLLM.

title: Enhancing LLMs in Predictive Political QA with Semi-Structured Data
summary: Predictive political question answering (QA), such as predicting how a political actor will vote, goes beyond factual lookup. External political resources offer rich historical evidence, but rarely contain the answer itself. Existing LLM augmentation methods, including actor-profile-based simulation and knowledge graph evidence injection, improve political reasoning but largely treat external resources as knowledge-based evidence, leaving prediction-relevant signals under-modeled. We identify two complementary signals for predictive political QA: actor stances that capture issue-specific preferences, and high-order structure signals that capture indirect dependencies among political actors. We propose PSL, a dual-view framework that converts semi-structured political records into inference-oriented evidence for LLMs. PSL extracts stance signals from question-relevant actor records in a semantic view, and learns structure-aware actor representations from an actor interaction graph in a vector view. Across three real-world datasets and multiple LLMs, PSL consistently outperforms baselines, with ablations confirming the complementary gains of stance and structure signals.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PSL, a dual-view framework that augments LLMs with stance and structural signals from political records to better perform predictive political question answering.
AI.motivation: Predictive political QA (e.g., forecasting how a political actor will vote) requires more than factual knowledge; it needs modeling of preferences and relational structures. Existing LLM augmentation methods use external political resources mainly as static knowledge, missing predictive signals like actors’ stances and their indirect dependencies, leading to suboptimal reasoning and predictions.
AI.method: The authors propose PSL, a dual-view framework. First, in a semantic view, it converts semi-structured political records into explicit actor stance evidence by extracting issue-specific preferences from records relevant to the query. Second, in a vector (representation) view, it builds an actor interaction graph and learns structure-aware actor embeddings that encode higher-order dependencies among political actors. These two types of evidence are then fed as inference-oriented augmentation to LLMs for predictive QA.
AI.result: On three real-world political QA datasets and across multiple LLM backbones, PSL achieves consistently better performance than existing augmentation baselines. Ablation studies show that using only stance or only structure signals degrades performance, demonstrating that both views contribute complementary benefits.
AI.conclusion: PSL effectively transforms raw political records into two forms of predictive signals—stance and structural relations—that significantly enhance LLMs’ ability to perform predictive political QA. The dual-view design is validated empirically, indicating that capturing both individual preferences and interaction structures is crucial for accurate political behavior prediction.

title: Large Language Models at the Intersection of Software Engineering and Software Security:An Evidence-Centered Structured Survey and Research Agenda
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are moving from code completion toward repository-scale agents that retrieve context, edit files, execute tools, and participate in security-sensitive workflows. The evidence for these systems, however, remains divided between software engineering evaluations centered on functional task completion and software security evaluations centered on vulnerability detection, secure generation, or exploit-oriented validation. This evidence-centered structured survey synthesizes representative work available through May 31, 2026 across software engineering tasks, software security tasks, adaptation mechanisms, artifact granularity, and evaluation design. In addition to a task taxonomy, we introduce an assurance framework that separates functional correctness, security, operational reliability, evidence provenance, and agent authority. The review shows that execution feedback and repository access can substantially improve engineering task completion, but do not by themselves establish security; conversely, static-analysis labels or vulnerability-classification scores rarely establish deployable correctness. We identify recurring validity threats--weak test oracles, duplicated and temporally leaked data, changing agent harnesses, proxy-only security checks, and under-reported budgets and human intervention--and derive a minimum reporting protocol for cross-study comparison. The resulting research agenda prioritizes jointly secure-and-functional benchmarks, repository-scale threat models, calibrated human oversight, longitudinal maintainability evidence, and reproducible agent evaluation. The central conclusion is that model capability should be judged as an assurance case supported by task-appropriate evidence, rather than by a single benchmark score.

AI.tldr: Survey of LLM-based repository-scale software agents, proposing an assurance framework and research agenda that integrate software engineering and software security evidence.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are increasingly used for complex, repository-scale development and security-sensitive workflows, yet current evaluations are fragmented between software engineering and software security communities, making it hard to understand real capability, safety, and reliability.
AI.method: Evidence-centered structured survey of representative work (up to May 31, 2026) on LLMs for software engineering and security. The paper organizes tasks into a taxonomy, analyzes adaptation mechanisms, artifact granularities, and evaluation designs, and proposes an assurance framework decomposing correctness, security, operational reliability, provenance, and authority. It also examines recurrent threats to validity and derives a minimum reporting protocol.
AI.result: The survey finds that repository access and execution feedback greatly improve engineering task completion but provide limited security guarantees, while prevalent security evaluations (e.g., static labels, vuln classification scores) often fail to demonstrate deployable correctness. It uncovers common validity threats such as weak oracles, data leakage, evolving harnesses, overreliance on proxy metrics, and opaque budgets/human help, and distills best practices into a reporting protocol and research directions.
AI.conclusion: LLM agent capability should be understood as an assurance case built from multiple lines of task-appropriate evidence, rather than single benchmark scores. Future work should create benchmarks and evaluations that jointly measure functionality and security at repository scale, incorporate realistic threat models and calibrated human oversight, and provide reproducible, longitudinal evidence of reliability and maintainability.

title: Root cause analysis via difference graph discovery from linear time-series data
summary: Root cause analysis aims to identify the mechanisms responsible for anomalies in complex dynamical systems. In this paper, we study root cause analysis in linear time-series through the lens of difference graph discovery. We focus on effect-defying root causes, corresponding to variables whose causal coefficients change between a normal and an anomalous regime. We formalize this problem using linear discrete-time dynamic structural causal models and adapt several methods originally introduced for discovering difference graphs between two populations to the time-series setting, where the two populations are replaced by a normal and an anomalous regime. We first evaluate the proposed approaches on simulated data, and then demonstrate their practical relevance on real-world datasets from IT monitoring and intensive care monitoring. Our results show how difference graph discovery can help localize causal mechanisms responsible for anomalous behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper studies root cause analysis in linear time-series by framing it as difference graph discovery between normal and anomalous regimes, focusing on causal coefficients that change, and demonstrates effectiveness on simulated and real IT/ICU data.
AI.motivation: In complex dynamical systems, identifying the specific mechanisms that cause anomalies is difficult, especially for time-series data. Traditional anomaly detection flags abnormal behavior but often does not reveal which causal relationships changed to produce the anomaly. There is a need for principled, causal methods that can localize which variables and causal mechanisms are responsible for the transition from normal to anomalous behavior, particularly in operational domains like IT systems and medical monitoring.
AI.method: The authors formalize the problem using linear discrete-time dynamic structural causal models to represent time-series with causal structure. They define "effect-defying" root causes as variables whose causal coefficients differ between a normal and an anomalous regime. They then adapt existing methods for difference graph discovery—originally designed to compare causal graphs across two static populations—to the temporal setting where the two populations are replaced by normal vs. anomalous regimes in a time series. The adapted algorithms infer which edges (causal effects) have changed between regimes, thus constructing a difference graph over time-series variables.
AI.result: On simulated data, the adapted difference-graph methods can correctly identify changes in causal coefficients and thereby localize effect-defying root causes. On real-world datasets from IT monitoring and intensive care monitoring, the approaches are able to highlight plausible causal mechanisms associated with observed anomalies, suggesting that they are useful for practical root cause analysis in time-series settings.
AI.conclusion: Difference graph discovery can be successfully extended from population comparisons to time-series with regime changes, enabling the identification of effect-defying root causes of anomalies. By working within a linear dynamic structural causal model framework, the method can localize changed causal mechanisms rather than just detecting anomalies, and empirical results on synthetic and real data suggest that this is a promising direction for practical root cause analysis in complex monitoring applications.

title: From Attention Masks to Inert Zero-Vector Tokens: OAttention and O-Closure for Token Dynamics
summary:
Attention masks are relation-level controls: they specify which query--source pairs may interact. They do not provide a representation-carried token state that is non-participating at the attention boundary. We assign each token hidden carrier \(h_i\) an active-presence coefficient \(p_i=\lVert h_i\rVert^2/(τ+\lVert h_i\rVert^2)\). The same coefficient has two roles: it gates information emitted by token \(i\), and it determines the mass with which token \(i\) enters computations shared with other tokens.
  OAttention is the support-coupled attention realization of this rule. It gates the receiver output by \(p_i\) and weights source \(j\) by \(p_j\) in both the attention numerator and partition, while retaining the standard score, visibility relation, exponential competition, and value aggregation. This makes the zero-vector token a zero element and yields exact null-receiver, null-source insertion, self-attention insertion, and empty-support properties. The same token-level presence gives local O-components (OFFN, ONorm, and OInject), presence-weighted OStandardize, the O-Closure law \(M(H\oplus0)=M(H)\oplus0\), and an OTransformer by residual and compositional closure.
  The canonical operator is checked by contract tests and a GPU evaluation. In a zero-fine-tuning retrofit of a cloned pretrained TabPFN v3 regressor, calibrated hidden-carrier OAttention and Full-O variants change mean RMSE by $+0.088\%$ and $+0.177\%$, respectively, over 18 matched dataset--seed cases. A two-block ablation shows that OAttention alone does not preserve a NULL state through ordinary host components, whereas the OTransformer path does. These are scoped tests of exactness, active-path compatibility, and compositional necessity; they do not establish universal no-loss, arbitrary-host closure, learned attraction to the origin, or a general semantics for missing values.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces OAttention, a modified attention mechanism where each token has a continuous “presence” coefficient, ensuring exact behavior when tokens are missing or null and enabling mathematically clean handling of zero/NULL tokens in Transformers.
AI.motivation: Standard attention masks only control which token pairs can interact; they do not provide a true token-level NULL state that is algebraically well-behaved. This makes it hard to represent missing tokens, zero tokens, or to reason about exact insertion/removal of tokens (like adding a NULL token) without side effects. The authors want an attention and Transformer formulation that treats a zero-vector token as a true zero element with exact properties, enabling more principled handling of missing values and compositional reasoning about model behavior.
AI.method: They define a per-token active-presence coefficient p_i = ||h_i||^2 / (τ + ||h_i||^2), derived from the token’s hidden state norm. This coefficient has two simultaneous roles: (1) it gates how much information a token emits, and (2) it determines the effective mass/weight with which the token participates in shared computations. They instantiate this in OAttention: receiver outputs are gated by their own presence p_i, and each source token j is weighted by p_j in both the attention numerator and denominator, while leaving similarity scores, masking, softmax, and value aggregation otherwise standard. They also build corresponding “O-components” (OFFN, ONorm, OInject, OStandardize) and define an O-Closure law M(H ⊕ 0) = M(H) ⊕ 0, then assemble an OTransformer that is closed under residual and composition. They verify properties via contract tests and GPU experiments, and retrofit OAttention and Full-O into a pretrained TabPFN v3 regressor without fine-tuning, plus a two-block ablation to study NULL-state preservation.
AI.result: Theoretically, OAttention makes the zero-vector token a proper zero element in attention: inserting null receivers/sources or self-attention-only tokens, or even empty supports, behaves exactly as desired under their O-Closure law. Empirically, when retrofitted into a cloned pretrained TabPFN v3 regressor with no fine-tuning, OAttention and Full-O variants change mean RMSE only slightly (+0.088% and +0.177%) across 18 dataset–seed pairs, indicating compatibility with existing models. The ablation shows that OAttention by itself cannot preserve a NULL state when surrounded by standard Transformer components, whereas the full OTransformer path with all O-components can.
AI.conclusion: OAttention and the associated O-components provide a mathematically rigorous way to endow attention-based models with a per-token presence coefficient that makes zero tokens behave as true algebraic zeros, enabling exact null insertion/removal and compositional closure. The proposed operators appear compatible with existing pretrained models in limited tests but require using the full OTransformer stack to maintain a stable NULL state; broader claims about universal performance, arbitrary host compatibility, or learned missing-value semantics remain open and are not established by the current experiments.

title: SENTRY: Deterministic, Intelligent Risk Assessment for IT Change Management
summary: Technology change management in large financial institutions depends on risk assessments that are accurate, consistent, and auditable. In practice, many institutions still rely on self-reported questionnaires. Those questionnaires are subjective, easy to game, and poor at separating routine changes from the ones that later trigger major incidents. This paper presents SENTRY, a risk assessment platform that replaces questionnaire-based scoring with a deterministic machine learning pipeline built from gradient-boosted decision trees (XGBoost) and hybrid retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The system combines structured operational metadata, application dependency graphs, and historical incident records with a hybrid semantic and lexical search over historical change requests. The retrieval step captures the risk signal in unstructured change request text, then compresses that signal into a single scalar feature before model inference. That design keeps the model deterministic and preserves per-prediction explainability via SHAP values. Evaluated on enterprise-scale change data, SENTRY achieves a ROC AUC of 0.87 and 85% overall accuracy, and it detects high-risk changes at roughly 3.25 times the rate of the existing process. We close by examining the architectural trade-offs behind this design and what they imply for the use of machine learning in regulated change management.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SENTRY, a deterministic ML-based risk assessment platform that outperforms questionnaire-based processes for managing technology changes in large financial institutions.
AI.motivation: Current technology change risk assessments in large financial institutions rely heavily on self-reported questionnaires that are subjective, easy to manipulate, and ineffective at distinguishing routine changes from those likely to cause major incidents. There is a need for a more objective, consistent, and auditable method that can leverage rich operational data while satisfying regulatory and explainability requirements.
AI.method: SENTRY replaces questionnaire scoring with a deterministic ML pipeline built primarily on gradient-boosted decision trees (XGBoost) augmented by a hybrid retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) component. The system ingests structured operational metadata, application dependency graphs, and historical incident records. It also performs hybrid semantic and lexical search over historical change requests. Retrieved textual context is converted into a single scalar risk feature that feeds into the XGBoost model, preserving determinism. SHAP values are used to provide per-prediction explainability. The overall design emphasizes deterministic behavior, traceability, and compatibility with regulated environments.
AI.result: On enterprise-scale change management data, SENTRY achieves a ROC AUC of 0.87 and 85% overall accuracy. Compared to the existing questionnaire-based process, it identifies high-risk changes at approximately 3.25 times the previous rate, indicating substantially better separation between risky and routine changes while remaining auditable and explainable.
AI.conclusion: SENTRY demonstrates that a carefully architected, deterministic ML pipeline can significantly improve risk assessment of technology changes in regulated financial environments relative to traditional questionnaires. The work highlights important architectural trade-offs—such as compressing RAG-derived textual signals into a scalar feature and using tree-based models with SHAP—for balancing performance, determinism, and explainability, and offers guidance for deploying ML in regulated change management contexts.

title: Ontology-supported AI Model and Dataset Management
comment: Published in: 2024 IEEE 22nd International Conference on Industrial Informatics (INDIN)
summary: Recently, there has been a great deal of research into improving AI methods and their application. The main focus is on tracking progress, enabling transparent comparisons, and fostering a more profound understanding of AI. In that process, different organizations generate and use plenty of assets that need to be tracked, traced and managed. Moreover, it is important to discover assets relevant for the task at hand. This paper presents research aiming to contribute to answering the question of what is required to exchange and manage AI models and related assets effectively without semantic gaps in an industrial context. We introduce a platform for AI model exchange, which facilitates the usage, exchange, and analysis of AI models and datasets. The platform incorporates an ontology that can foster a more profound common understanding of what is required in these tasks and help tackle the issues mentioned above. Finally, we elucidate the utility of the platform through the illustration of a use case in the context of real-time critical systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a platform with an ontology-based approach to enable effective exchange, management, and discovery of AI models and datasets in industrial settings, demonstrated via a real-time critical systems use case.
AI.motivation: AI development involves many models, datasets, and related assets created by different organizations. These assets must be tracked, compared, reused, and understood consistently. Currently, there are semantic gaps and interoperability issues that make it hard to exchange and manage AI models and related assets effectively, especially in industrial contexts and real-time critical systems.
AI.method: The authors design and implement a platform dedicated to AI model exchange and management. A central component is an ontology that formally captures the concepts and relationships relevant to AI models, datasets, and their lifecycle. This ontology is integrated into the platform to support tracking, discovery, and semantic interoperability. They then apply the platform in a representative industrial use case dealing with real-time critical systems to show how it works in practice.
AI.result: The result is a working platform that supports usage, exchange, and analysis of AI models and datasets, enriched with an ontology for semantic consistency. The platform can track and manage various AI assets and enable users to find relevant models and datasets more effectively. In the real-time critical systems use case, the platform demonstrates its capability to reduce semantic gaps and support structured exchange and management of AI artifacts.
AI.conclusion: An ontology-driven AI model exchange platform can help overcome semantic gaps and interoperability challenges in managing AI models and related assets in industrial settings. By providing a shared conceptual framework and integrated tooling for exchange, tracking, and discovery, the platform improves transparency and comparability of AI methods. The real-time critical systems use case suggests that the approach is feasible and beneficial for domains where reliability and timely decision-making are crucial.

title: Fine-Grain GPU Parallelization of the Generalized Partition Crossover for Large-Scale Traveling Salesman Problems
comment: accepted to NiHPC, PPSN 2026. Draft in preparation for a journal article
summary: The Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) is one of the most extensively studied NP-hard optimization problems. Genetic Algorithm (GA)-based solvers, such as the Edge Assembly Crossover (EAX), achieve state-of-the-art performance on many benchmark instances. However, the scalability of these approaches in massively parallel architectures remains limited because crossover operations involve irregular memory access patterns, graph traversals, and sequential dependencies. Existing GPU-based TSP solvers primarily exploit population-level parallelism and are limited to relatively small problem sizes. This work presents a fine-grain GPU implementation of the partition phase of the Generalized Partition Crossover (GPX) operator for large-scale TSP instances. The proposed approach reformulates GPX partitioning as a graph-parallel problem using coalesced memory layouts, ghost-node transformations, and connected-component analysis. The im- plementation parallelizes the union of parent tours, the splitting of degree- four vertices, the deletion of common edges, and the identification of recombining components using CUDA. Experimental results on instances ranging from 10,000 to 2 million cities demonstrate substantial acceleration over a naive sequential CPU imple- mentation. The proposed GPU partitioning achieves speedups between 48x and 625x while significantly reducing memory overhead. The re- sults demonstrate that operator-level parallelism can substantially im- prove the scalability of GA-based TSP solvers on modern many-core architectures.

AI.tldr: GPU-parallel implementation of a key crossover partition step for GA-based TSP, reformulated as a graph-parallel problem, yields large speedups and better scalability for very large instances.
AI.motivation: GA-based TSP solvers like EAX are strong but don’t scale well on GPUs because crossover operators have irregular, sequential operations that don’t map cleanly to massively parallel hardware. Existing GPU solvers mostly parallelize across individuals in the population and thus handle only modest problem sizes. The authors aim to unlock much finer-grain, operator-level parallelism so GA-based TSP can efficiently exploit modern many-core GPUs on very large instances.
AI.method: They focus on the partition phase of the Generalized Partition Crossover (GPX) operator and redesign it as a graph-parallel task suitable for CUDA GPUs. Key ideas include: using coalesced memory layouts to improve memory bandwidth; applying a ghost-node transformation to handle degree-four vertices; and performing connected-component analysis to discover recombining components. They parallelize four main substeps on the GPU: constructing the union graph of the two parent tours, splitting degree-four vertices, deleting edges common to both parents, and identifying components used for recombination.
AI.result: On TSP instances from 10,000 up to 2 million cities, the GPU implementation of the GPX partition phase significantly outperforms a naive sequential CPU implementation, with speedups in the range of 48x to 625x. It also reduces memory overhead compared to straightforward implementations.
AI.conclusion: Recasting GPX partitioning as a graph-parallel problem and implementing it with CUDA demonstrates that fine-grained, operator-level parallelism can be effectively exploited on GPUs. This substantially improves the scalability of GA-based TSP solvers on many-core architectures, suggesting that similar strategies could enhance other complex operators in evolutionary algorithms.

title: CLEAR: Continuous Latent Adapter Routing for Utility-Preserving LLM Safety Alignment
summary: Improving the safety of large language models (LLMs) often comes at the expense of utility, as globally applied safety tuning may affect model responses to both harmful and benign inputs. We propose \textbf{C}ontinuous \textbf{L}at\textbf{E}nt \textbf{A}dapter \textbf{R}outing (CLEAR), a conditional safety adaptation framework that uses a lightweight hidden-state gate to continuously control the activation strength of a safety low-rank adapter. CLEAR aims to reduce harmful completions while avoiding unnecessary changes to the frozen backbone that could degrade performance on benign prompts. Experiments on widely used safety and utility benchmarks show that CLEAR improves robustness on HarmBench while reducing the utility degradation observed with globally applied safety tuning such as SFT or standard low-rank adaptation (LoRA). On Llama-3-8B-Instruct, CLEAR reduces HarmBench ASR from 32.3\% to 0.5\%, while retaining most of the base model's utility and achieving up to 7.1 percentage points higher GSM8K accuracy than globally applied SFT or LoRA. These results suggest that CLEAR is a promising mechanism for improving the safety--utility trade-off in LLM alignment.

AI.tldr: They introduce CLEAR, a conditional safety mechanism for LLMs that activates safety adapters only when needed, improving safety while preserving utility.
AI.motivation: Safety training for LLMs, when applied globally, often harms performance on benign tasks. The authors want a way to strengthen safety against harmful prompts without degrading utility on normal prompts.
AI.method: They design CLEAR, which adds a lightweight gating module over hidden states that controls the activation strength of a safety-focused low-rank adapter. The base model is frozen; the gate learns to modulate how much the safety adapter influences the model depending on the input, allowing continuous routing between base behavior and safety-modified behavior.
AI.result: On standard safety and utility benchmarks, CLEAR achieves much lower attack success rates on HarmBench compared to the base and globally safety-tuned models, while preserving or even improving utility. For Llama-3-8B-Instruct, CLEAR cuts HarmBench ASR from 32.3% to 0.5% and outperforms SFT/LoRA-tuned models on GSM8K by up to 7.1 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Conditional, continuous routing of safety adapters can markedly improve the safety–utility trade-off in LLMs, making models safer against harmful prompts while largely retaining or even enhancing performance on benign tasks.

title: AUSO: Action-Level Unified Skill Optimization from Internalization to Utilization
summary: Skills play different roles as an agent's policy evolves: they should first provide learnable knowledge, then support capability formation, and finally be invoked only when they improve individual decisions. Existing methods rarely model this lifecycle. They either keep skills outside the model, fully internalize them, or select among internalization and utilization objectives through noisy task-level success rates. Such designs fragment training and assign uniform importance to actions within the same trajectory, even though skill guidance may help some decisions while distracting others. To solve these problems, we introduce AUSO (Action-level Unified Skill Optimization), which unifies skill learning and skill use through a progressive, action-aware optimization process. At the beginning of training, AUSO jointly learns from teacher guidance and environmental outcomes, enabling the policy to acquire foundational skills without losing task-oriented feedback. It subsequently emphasizes outcome-based policy optimization to consolidate autonomous problem-solving ability. As the policy matures, AUSO evaluates each sampled action under both skill-conditioned and skill-free contexts. The resulting action-level information signal is coupled with the trajectory outcome advantage, allowing beneficial skill-sensitive actions to receive stronger updates and harmful ones to be suppressed. Therefore, skills gradually transition from an external source of supervision into decision knowledge whose utilization is adapted to its action-level benefit, while reinforcement learning remains the shared backbone across all stages. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SearchQA show that AUSO consistently improves agent performance and out-of-distribution generalization over competitive baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes AUSO, an action-level unified framework that jointly learns and uses skills throughout an agent’s training lifecycle, improving performance and generalization on text-based environments.
AI.motivation: Existing skill-based RL methods treat skills either as fully external guidance or fully internalized components, and typically optimize them using coarse task-level signals. This ignores that skills should play different roles over time (from supervision to optional decision aids) and that within a single trajectory some actions benefit from skills while others are harmed. This leads to fragmented training and suboptimal credit assignment for skill use.
AI.method: AUSO (Action-level Unified Skill Optimization) introduces a progressive, action-aware optimization pipeline. Early in training, it jointly optimizes the policy using both teacher skill guidance and environment feedback so the agent can acquire foundational skills without losing task objectives. Later, it shifts the emphasis toward outcome-based RL to solidify autonomous capabilities. In the mature stage, for each sampled action, AUSO evaluates it under both a skill-conditioned and a skill-free context, generating an action-level signal about whether skill guidance helped or hurt. This signal is combined with trajectory-level advantages to strengthen updates for beneficial skill-sensitive actions and suppress harmful ones, while RL remains the core learning mechanism throughout.
AI.result: On benchmarks including ALFWorld, WebShop, and SearchQA, AUSO leads to consistent improvements in task success and out-of-distribution generalization compared to strong baseline methods that either keep skills external, fully internalize them, or rely on task-level success for skill selection.
AI.conclusion: By unifying skill learning and skill utilization in an action-level, lifecycle-aware optimization framework, AUSO enables agents to transition from relying on external skill supervision to selectively using internalized skills when they are beneficial for specific decisions. This design yields better performance and generalization across diverse tasks, demonstrating the importance of fine-grained, progressive treatment of skills within RL agents.

title: From Regulation to Implementation: A Critical Evaluation of LLM-Assisted Regulatory Compliance in Industry
summary: The European Union (EU) has emerged as a leading regulatory body in the development of sustainability and privacy regulations. While new regulation requirements vary, many include a documentation artifact to ensure compliance. Notably, the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR) introduces Digital Product Passports (DPPs) for life cycle transparency, while the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) mandates Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) to mitigate privacy risks. Creating these compliance artifacts, however, is challenging. Industrial data, which often exists in heterogeneous formats and is scattered across company and supplier systems, is required for DPPs and can be difficult to extract into compliant DPP formatting. Furthermore, DPIA documents require interdisciplinary expertise and follow no standardized format, making development difficult for novel systems. To address the particular complexity of compliance artifact creation for both regulations, researchers have proposed the use of LLMs in the generation process; however, the impact of the aforementioned problems on the output of these systems is largely unaddressed. This work investigates the existing research gap by exploring how data extraction instructions and regulatory vagueness impact the quality and consistency of LLM-produced compliance artifacts. The resulting artifacts are evaluated by benchmarking different models against manually created ground-truth schemas. The results reveal that less strict guidelines, such as DPIA formatting, require higher context prompts to maintain consistency and completeness. Stricter guidelines, such as formatting for Digital Battery Passports (DBP), result in consistent results regardless of prompt context, but may lead to more hallucinations in the output

AI.tldr: The paper studies how Large Language Models (LLMs) generate EU regulatory compliance documents (Digital Product Passports and Data Protection Impact Assessments) under different instruction strictness and data vagueness.
AI.motivation: Creating compliance artifacts for EU regulations like ESPR (with Digital Product Passports) and GDPR (with DPIAs) is difficult because industrial data is heterogeneous and scattered, and DPIAs lack standardized formats and need interdisciplinary expertise. Although LLMs are proposed to assist in generating these documents, it is unclear how data extraction instructions and regulatory vagueness affect artifact quality and consistency.
AI.method: The authors generate compliance artifacts with various LLMs under different prompting conditions that vary in context and strictness. They focus on two artifact types: Digital Battery Passports (a concrete case of DPPs) and DPIAs. They then benchmark the LLM outputs against manually created ground-truth schemas, comparing quality, consistency, completeness, and hallucinations.
AI.result: For loosely specified artifacts like DPIAs, LLMs require higher-context prompts (more detailed guidance and information) to maintain consistency and completeness in the generated documents. For tightly specified artifacts like Digital Battery Passports, LLMs remain consistent across different prompt contexts but tend to hallucinate more details when adhering to strict structures.
AI.conclusion: LLM performance in regulatory compliance artifact generation is strongly influenced by the strictness of regulatory guidelines and the richness of prompt context. Vague regulations and flexible formats need richer prompting to avoid inconsistency and missing content, whereas strict schemas ensure consistent structure but increase hallucination risk. Prompt design and schema strictness must therefore be carefully balanced when using LLMs for compliance documentation.

title: Unified Branch-and-Bound Search for the Steiner Traveling Salesman Problem on Graphs of Convex Sets
summary: We formalize the Steiner Traveling Salesman Problem (Steiner-TSP) on Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS), which seeks a minimum-cost closed trajectory through required convex sets while allowing optional transit vertices and revisits. To explore the resulting infinite solution space, we propose a unified branch-and-bound search over rooted walk prefixes. Additive lower-bound-graph costs bound committed prefixes, while a cut-separated connected-flow relaxation lower-bounds the residual cost of visiting every remaining target and returning to the root. Under a uniform positive-cost assumption, best-first traversal terminates after finitely many expansions on every feasible instance without an initial incumbent, whereas depth-first traversal does so once a finite incumbent is available. For a user-specified factor $ε\geq1$, a global lower bound certifies that either strategy's incumbent cost is at most $ε$ times the global optimum. We further demonstrate joint sensing-mode, visitation-order, and continuous-trajectory selection for a mobile-manipulator inspection task, including action precedences expressed in linear temporal logic over finite traces (LTL$_f$). Both traversal strategies find feasible solutions on all benchmark instances within 30s with mean certified optimality gaps of 28.1% and 29.7%, respectively, whereas two recent baselines succeed on only about half of the instances

AI.tldr: The paper introduces and solves a Steiner Traveling Salesman Problem on graphs of convex sets with a unified branch-and-bound scheme that provides certified near-optimal inspection trajectories for mobile manipulators.
AI.motivation: Classical TSP assumes discrete nodes and edges, whereas many robotic planning and inspection tasks require visiting regions (convex sets), allow transits and revisits, and must handle joint discrete (order, modes) and continuous (trajectory) decisions with guarantees on optimality. Existing methods either do not scale or lack such guarantees, especially for complex constraints like temporal logic. This motivates a new formalization and algorithmic framework.
AI.method: They define the Steiner-TSP on Graphs of Convex Sets and search over rooted walk prefixes using a unified branch-and-bound algorithm. The method uses additive lower-bound graph costs for already committed parts of the tour and a cut-separated connected-flow relaxation to lower-bound the remaining cost to visit all unvisited sets and return to the root. They analyze conditions under which best-first and depth-first traversals terminate and provide ε-approximation guarantees based on a global lower bound. They then instantiate this for a mobile-manipulator inspection problem with joint selection of sensing modes, visitation order, continuous trajectories, and LTL_f action precedence constraints.
AI.result: Empirically, both best-first and depth-first variants find feasible solutions for all benchmark instances within 30 seconds. They achieve mean certified optimality gaps of about 28–30%. In contrast, two recent baseline methods are only able to solve about half of the instances within the same limits, indicating better robustness and coverage of the proposed method.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Steiner-TSP on Graphs of Convex Sets and associated branch-and-bound algorithm provide a practical and theoretically grounded approach for planning inspection trajectories that jointly optimize discrete and continuous decisions under complex constraints. The method is complete under mild assumptions, offers finite termination and ε-approximation guarantees, and empirically outperforms recent baselines in terms of success rate while offering certified suboptimality bounds.

title: Anatomy-Informed Neural Networks: Encoding Anatomic Priors in Loss and Architecture, with an SE(3) Formulation of Guidewire-Induced Aortoiliac Deformation
summary:
Deep-learning models of anatomy can be numerically plausible yet anatomically impossible, and they generalize poorly when data are scarce. We introduce Anatomy-Informed Neural Networks (AINN), in which soft anatomic priors enter as penalty terms in the loss (e.g., a branching penalty that treats a renal transplant artery off the iliac instead of the aorta as unexpected rather than impossible), in direct analogy to a physics-informed neural network, and hard anatomic priors (e.g., continuity of the vessel) are built into the architecture and state representation, making such invalid predictions impossible by construction wherever the prior admits architectural enforcement.
  We develop it on a clinical test case with limited data: how the aortoiliac tree deforms when a stiff wire is introduced endoluminally. This is important to contemporary aortic surgery and will matter to autonomous endovascular navigation. We lift the vessel centerline and the wire path from R^3 to curves of frames in the Lie group SE(3), and couple a Cosserat-rod wire to a tortuosity-modulated, anatomically anchored vessel through a unilateral lumen-contact inequality. The prediction is a constrained minimizer of the coupled elastic energy, with contact forces as its Lagrange multipliers.
