Supervision is a Wasserstein-2 optimal-transport loss between the predicted projection through the C-arm geometry and the observed angiogram, so a 2D angiogram can train a 3D prediction. The kinematics, loss and projection are verified against known ground truth; the mechanics solver only against its own optimality conditions, and predicted displacement is not yet mesh-converged. Here, no network is trained. Future work will transfer this in silico model to real CT scans and test whether it improves predictive accuracy and reduces the training data required.

AI.tldr: Proposes Anatomy-Informed Neural Networks (AINN) that embed anatomical priors as both soft loss penalties and hard architectural constraints to predict vessel and wire deformations from sparse 2D angiographic data, aiming for anatomically valid, data-efficient 3D modeling.
AI.motivation: Deep-learning models for anatomical structures can produce anatomically impossible outputs and generalize poorly when only limited clinical data are available, which is common in specialized interventional settings. There is a need for models that respect known anatomy by design (e.g., correct vessel topology, continuity) while still being flexible, and that can learn reliably from sparse supervision such as 2D angiograms instead of full 3D ground truth. This is particularly important for predicting how the aortoiliac vessel tree deforms when stiff devices are introduced, which impacts surgical planning and future autonomous endovascular navigation.
AI.method: They propose the Anatomy-Informed Neural Network (AINN) concept: soft anatomical priors are encoded as penalty terms in the loss function (e.g., penalizing atypical branching patterns without forbidding them), similar to physics-informed neural networks, and hard priors such as vessel continuity are enforced directly in the network architecture and state representation, making certain anatomically invalid predictions impossible. As a concrete testbed, they model deformation of the aortoiliac tree with an endoluminal stiff wire. Both the vessel centerline and the wire are lifted from R^3 to SE(3) as curves of frames. The wire is represented as a Cosserat rod coupled to an anatomically anchored, tortuosity-modulated vessel via a unilateral lumen-contact inequality. The deformation is computed as a constrained minimum of the coupled elastic energy, with contact forces serving as Lagrange multipliers. Supervision uses a Wasserstein-2 optimal transport loss between the projected prediction (through the C-arm imaging geometry) and the observed 2D angiogram, enabling training of 3D predictions from 2D images. They verify kinematics, loss, and projection against known ground truth, while the mechanics solver is checked only against its own optimality conditions, and note that mesh convergence of displacement is not yet achieved. In this abstract, no neural network is actually trained; the work defines and validates the in silico model that will later underpin AINN training.
AI.result: They demonstrate a mechanics-based, anatomically structured modeling pipeline in which vessel and wire configurations are represented in SE(3), coupled via a contact inequality, and supervised using a Wasserstein-2 loss between simulated projections and 2D angiograms. The kinematic formulation, loss function, and imaging projection are validated against known ground truth, confirming that the forward model and supervision scheme are internally consistent. The mechanical solver satisfies its optimality conditions, but the resulting displacement fields are not yet mesh-converged, indicating that numerical aspects still need refinement. No quantitative network training results are reported; instead, the main outcome is a validated formulation ready to be combined with learning in future work.
AI.conclusion: The paper introduces the Anatomy-Informed Neural Network framework, which integrates soft and hard anatomical priors into both the loss function and architecture, analogous to physics-informed neural networks, to avoid anatomically impossible predictions and enable learning from limited data. Through an in silico example of aortoiliac deformation under an intraluminal wire, they show that 3D vessel and device configurations can be constrained by anatomical structure and supervised using only 2D angiograms via a Wasserstein-2 projection loss. While the current work focuses on model formulation and verification rather than training, it sets the stage for applying AINNs to real CT-based anatomy, with the expectation that this will improve predictive accuracy and substantially reduce labeled data requirements.

title: VIALS: A Benchmark for Visual Interpretation of Artifacts in the Life Sciences
summary: In professional life sciences workflows, scientists routinely interpret visual artifacts (gel blots, microscopy images, plasmid maps, flow cytometry plots, molecular structures, ...) to inform research decisions. We introduce VIALS, a visual question-answering benchmark with 161 such interpretation tasks, spanning the types of artifacts examined throughout experimental workflows in the biotech industry (rather than polished figures from publications and textbooks). While frontier vision-language models can now fluently describe natural images, we find that they are unable to accurately interpret these scientific images, reflecting limitations in domain knowledge and domain-specific visual reasoning capabilities. In contrast, scientists with relevant domain expertise find these visual interpretation tasks straightforward. AI that cannot similarly interpret such images will have limited utility in professional life sciences workflows, where such artifacts are central to how scientists reason, communicate, and make decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VIALS, a benchmark of 161 visual question-answering tasks based on real biotech workflow artifacts, and shows that current vision-language models fail badly at interpreting these scientific images compared to human experts.
AI.motivation: Scientists in life sciences rely heavily on interpreting domain-specific visual artifacts (e.g., gels, microscopy, flow plots) to make decisions, yet existing vision-language models are mostly evaluated on natural images and polished figures. There is a need to assess and drive progress on AI systems that can understand the messy, domain-specific visuals actually used in professional biotech workflows.
AI.method: The authors construct VIALS, a visual QA benchmark composed of 161 interpretation tasks covering diverse scientific artifacts encountered across experimental workflows in the biotech industry, deliberately using real-world artifacts rather than curated textbook or publication figures. They then evaluate frontier vision-language models on these tasks to assess their ability to perform domain-specific visual reasoning and compare their performance to that of domain experts (scientists).
AI.result: Vision-language models that perform well on natural-image description tasks perform poorly on VIALS, failing to accurately interpret scientific images and revealing gaps in domain knowledge and specialized visual reasoning. In contrast, scientists with relevant expertise solve these interpretation tasks easily, indicating a substantial performance gap between current AI and human experts in this setting.
AI.conclusion: Current frontier vision-language models lack the domain knowledge and specialized visual reasoning needed to reliably interpret core scientific artifacts used in professional life sciences workflows. Without the ability to understand such images, AI systems will have limited practical value in real-world biotech research and decision-making, underscoring the need for benchmarks like VIALS and for model development focused on scientific visual understanding.
